The three Kāśyapas, having previously attained understanding through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), clarify therein only that there is no accumulation and it is difficult to seek, while not discussing contentment.
Within the section on non-accumulation, there are three distinct points:
first, citing the inferior to illustrate the superior: "If even the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) Saṅgha has no accumulation, how much more so the unconditioned Saṅgha."
The second [section] distinguishes that the essence of the asaṃskṛta-saṃgha is precisely the Tathāgata;

the third explains the meaning of "non-accumulation" (anupacaya) by way of the Tathāgata: "How could the Tathāgata have any accumulation? This clarifies, through the Buddha’s own practice, that there is no accumulation—that he does not accumulate worldly goods for livelihood.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, as for accumulation," the text explains the absence of accumulation by way of the Buddha’s external transformation. First, it clarifies the faults of accumulation: being stingy with the Dharma and refusing to teach it is termed "concealment. From the words "For this reason" onwards, it refutes those faults to demonstrate the absence [of such accumulation].
Regarding what has been said—that there is no stinginess—how can it be called a "repository" (kośa)?
Because there is no concealment, it is termed "without accumulation.
Some claim that this statement explains the preceding "absence of repository," and thus judge it to belong to the former; however, this is categorically incorrect.
Next, as the traces of the Buddha’s manifestation are difficult to seek, the verse is presented first; its commentary consists of four points:
first, a direct exposition of the essence of the dharma that is difficult to seek, namely *nirvāṇa*;
second, from the phrase "no sun or moon" onwards, it clarifies the characteristics of being difficult to seek, for because it is free from all characteristics, it cannot be sought.

Third, it clarifies that nirvana is the abode of the Tathāgata, which exists eternally and is unchanging; because one desires to attain this abode to manifest the virtue of liberation, it is called an "abode.
Fourth, it clarifies the Buddha’s entry [into it]: since this nirvana is the abode of the Tathāgata, he has now reached it and entered parinirvāṇa.

The preceding section explained the verse to demonstrate that *nirvāṇa* is the locus of liberation; from here on, the second part examines the characteristics of that *nirvāṇa* with respect to its locus.
This section consists of three parts:

first, an explanation of the meaning of "Great *Nirvāṇa*" mentioned previously; second, a demonstration that this *nirvāṇa* is the locus of liberation; and third, a re-explanation through questions and answers regarding points in the preceding text that were difficult to understand.
Within the first section, the general meaning is first explained through three points:
first, "As for 'great,' its nature is vast," which explains greatness by means of vastness;

second, from "It is like a person" onwards, greatness is explained by means of permanence—though this lacks an explicit application (the *upanaya*), its meaning is similar to what was stated in the preceding text: "That which is great is termed permanent."
Third, greatness is explained by way of superiority.
There are two kinds of superiority:
first, it is said that "if this person abides in the True Dharma, they are called the most excellent among men"; because they abide in the True [Dharma], they are superior.
The passage beginning with "As I have taught" demonstrates superiority through the possession of complete virtues.
The reference to the "Eight Awakenings of the Great Men" cited from my teaching refers to the eight types of awakening expounded in other sūtras.

The phrase "for one person" below distinguishes [the practice] by way of the individual: "possessed by one person" refers to its accomplishment in a single person; "possessed by many persons" refers to its cultivation among many. As for the statement, "If one person possesses all eight, that is superior," this demonstrates superiority by way of accomplishment.
This one person is the Buddha; because the Buddha is endowed with the eight virtues, he is called "Victorious" (jina), and being victorious, he is called "Great.
Next, the Nirvana is explained: "That which is called Nirvana is named 'free from sores and defects,'" which explains it in terms of self-benefit.
Ulcers and warts are outflows (*āsrava*); because one is personally free from all outflows, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
From the passage beginning "For example, like a person," the text explains by means of transforming others, first providing a simile and subsequently applying it to the meaning.

There are two analogies within this section. First is the analogy of the transformation in Jambudvīpa: "Like a person" refers to the sentient beings of that Jambudvīpa; the arising of delusions that afflict them is called "being struck by a poisoned arrow"; transmigrating through birth and death is called "suffering much"; and encountering the Buddha as a holy teacher is called "meeting a skilled physician."

In Buddhism, severing delusions is called "extracting the arrow"; encouraging the practice of the Path is called "applying the wondrous medicine"; causing one to transcend birth and death is called "leaving suffering behind"; and attaining Great Nirvāṇa is called "receiving peace and bliss."

Second is the analogy of manifesting transformations in other regions: when the response [of compassion] in this region is exhausted, one manifests transformations in other regions, which is called "wandering through cities and villages. Because there are those with delusions who require rescue, it is said: "Wherever there is a wound or ailment, one goes there immediately to provide healing."
The next time they are correlated, first correlate the initial metaphor: "The Tathāgata is likewise a great king of physicians" correlates with the previous "excellent physician.

"Seeing the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa suffering from affliction" correlates with "as if there were a person struck by lust, anger, and so forth," which correlates with the previous "shot by arrows. "Undergoing great suffering" correlates with "suffering much pain."
"To preach the Mahāyāna" corresponds to applying the sublime medicine; "to extract the poisonous arrow and cause one to leave suffering" and so forth are omitted as they do not correspond.

The section beginning with "treats this" corresponds to the subsequent metaphor; "further proceeding to other regions" corresponds to wandering through the cities and so forth; "all places where there is poison" corresponds to wherever there are sores and afflictions mentioned above; "acting as a Buddha to provide treatment" corresponds to going to those places to heal the various sufferings; and "therefore it is called Great Parinirvāṇa" serves as the general conclusion.
From here below is the second section, which clarifies that this *nirvāṇa* is the locus of liberation.
“The Great Parinirvāṇa is called the locus of liberation” correctly defines its characteristic.
“Manifesting within wherever birth occurs” clarifies the arising of function from the essence; this function is precisely its merit of liberation.
Because one attains Great Nirvana and is able to manifest this function, Nirvana is named the "Abode of Liberation.
The phrase "Because this is true" and below concludes the discussion of its function to reveal its essence.
Being quiescent yet constantly active, it is called the "Profound Meaning," which differs from the "Great Nirvana" as designated by the Hinayana.
From here below is the third section, which clarifies through questions and answers those points that are difficult to understand.
This serves to clarify the preceding meaning—that [the Buddha] causes others to be free from sores—and it consists of two sets of questions and answers.
First, a question is posed based on a simile: "Does a worldly physician treat all types of sores?"
The Buddha replied:
"It is not fixed.
Subsequently, he proceeds to raise an objection based on the Dharma; first, he restates the Buddha's words, and below that, he presents the objection.
"If you say they have already been treated, how can there still be those who have not attained nirvāṇa?
If they have not all attained it, why did you previously state that after treating them, you wished to go to another land?"
The Buddha replied:
"It is not fixed.
First he raised two individuals, then listed their names, and finally, with respect to those individuals, he clarified who was to be disciplined and who was not.

The phrase "excluding the icchantikas" and below serves to exclude those who cannot be healed; it establishes the meaning of nirvana as being free from afflictions (wounds) regarding those who can be healed. From this verse until here, the section on liberation is elucidated.
From here below is the second section, which elucidates the virtue of liberation;
it contains four parts: first, elucidating the virtue of liberation with respect to *nirvāṇa*;

second, from "Kāśyapa said: 'Is liberation form, or is it non-form? onwards, clarifying the essence of liberation; third, from "I only pray that you will compassionately grant us a further extensive [explanation]" onwards, manifesting the characteristics of liberation; fourth, "Kāśyapa said:"... [text continues].
"Non-arising and non-ceasing is liberation. Below this, the explanatory descriptions are swept away.
In the first part, Kāśyapa first asks to initiate the discourse; "What is nirvāṇa? interrogates its essence and brings forth its function.
The Buddha answers him below, naming it "liberation.
In the second section, there are two questions and answers; Kāśyapa first asks whether that which is called liberation is form or non-form.
One should also ask whether this mind is the mind or not the mind; however, since the mind can be understood by examining it in relation to form (*rūpa*), this question is omitted for brevity.
In the Buddha’s response below, he contrasts the small with the great, or distinguishes between two categories: form and non-form.

Next, its characteristics are revealed: the liberation of the two vehicles is merely the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the cessation through abandonment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the fetters; it has not yet attained the eternally abiding true form of the Buddhas, nor has it attained the form of the Buddhas' transformative activity. Therefore, it is called "non-form" (*arūpa*).

The true body (*dharmakāya*) of liberation of all Buddhas is eternally abiding; because it manifests in various forms according to the conditions of transformative influence (*nirmāṇa-pratyaya*), it is called "form" (*rūpa*).
That which is manifested according to transformative influence is the Buddhas' shared body with the world, while the eternally abiding true body is the body of the Dharma-gates of all Buddhas.
What is the meaning of this?

Just as the ten characteristics of the ocean are of one essence yet distinguished by their meanings, so too is it with the Buddha: all his faculties and marks of excellence pervade the Dharma-realm, being of one essence yet distinguished by their meanings; they are not like those of a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), which are distinct and separate from one another.

Because they share the same essence, the eye is taken as the gateway; the characteristics of all the sense organs, the marks of excellence, and the Buddha-fields are all manifested within this single eye, and it is likewise for the others.

As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "All kalpas of the three periods of time, as well as all Buddha-fields, all sense faculties, minds, and mental phenomena, along with all illusory dharmas—all these are fully manifested within the body of a single Buddha."
Therefore, it is said that the discernment of bodhi is immeasurable and boundless.
The phrase "therefore" below serves as a conclusion.

From "The Tathāgata, for the sake of the śrāvakas" onwards, the previous statement is reconciled: although the liberation of all Buddhas is indeed form (*rūpa*), in the past he taught it to be non-form for the sake of the śrāvakas.
The second Kāśyapa raises a subtle inquiry: "If the liberation of the two vehicles is not form (*rūpa*), how can it abide?
Below, the Buddha answers this.
What is the intent of his answer?
It clarifies that the liberation attained by those of the two vehicles is both form and non-form; because it is form, the two vehicles are able to abide therein.
Within this, there are first the metaphors, which consist of two parts:
the first clarifies that the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" is both form and non-form, yet the Buddha taught it as non-form.

The four formless realms possess form; this is largely consistent across various sūtras. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* proclaims that the olfactory faculty of a bodhisattva perceives the fragrance of the palaces in the formless realm.
In the *Āgama Sūtras*, it is said that when Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, tears fell from the heavens of both the form and formless realms like a fine spring rain.

Furthermore, when Mahāprajāpatī entered parinirvāṇa, the devas of the form and formless realms stood to one side before the Buddha; this indicates that they possess form similar to that of the [other] realms.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, there is a formal discussion concerning persons: this is the realm of the Buddha, not something known by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Below, the text correlates and clarifies the Dharma: "Liberation is also like this: it is both form and non-form, yet it is described as non-form;
it is both perception and non-perception, yet it is described as non-perception. This correlates with the first phrase above.
Question:
How is it that the liberation of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is both form and perception,
yet is further said to be neither?
The commentary states:
When those of the Two Vehicles enter nirvana, the objective consciousness (*samsvabhāva-vijñāna*), along with its faculties and objects, all cease; therefore, it is said that they are "not form.

However, their deluded consciousness, true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), and their respective faculties and objects all remain present; therefore, it is said that they are "also form" and "also perception."
What is the meaning of this?

When those of the Two Vehicles enter nirvana, although they extinguish the *vijñāna* of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*), their deluded mind still persists; thus it is said that they "still possess ideation" (*saṃjñin*).

Because the mind remains, the root-faculties and sense-objects manifested by that deluded mind also persist without perishing; thus it is said that they "still possess form" (*rūpin*). This is like one who has not yet awakened from sleep, for whom the root-faculties and sense-objects arising from the dreaming mind do not cease.
Furthermore, when those of the Two Vehicles enter *nirvāṇa*, their true mind (*tathatā-citta*) does not perish; this is called "also having thought" (*sa-saṃjñaka*).

The reality of the Two Vehicles is the *tathāgatagarbha*; the *tathāgatagarbha* is the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*. Within this *dharmakāya*, there are inherent the natures of the Buddha’s eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth; this is called "also having form" (*sa-rūpaka*). Therefore, the Sūtra says that within the bodies of sentient beings there are the Tathāgata’s eyes, the Tathāgata’s ears, and so on, because the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* shares the same nature as that of sentient beings and possesses no separate essence.

Therefore, the text below states that the reality of the Four Noble Truths is itself the Tathāgata; this principle is present within the liberation of both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and for this reason it is described as being both form and non-form, and both perception and non-perception.
The phrase "such meaning" below joins with the latter part of the preceding sentence: it is the domain of the Buddha alone, not something known by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
On the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month in the third year of the Ōei era (1396), this manuscript was revised and supplemented to correct missing characters. The end. *Nirvāṇa-gi-ki*, Volume Two.
The Record on the Meaning of Nirvāṇa, Part Three, by the Dharma Seal Provisional Great Sōjō Kenpō;
composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingying Temple during the Sui Dynasty.
From here below is the third section, which distinguishes the characteristics of liberation. Kāśyapa first requested, "I only pray that you will explain it again.
This is called "reiteration" (*punaḥ-kathana*) because it is spoken in contrast to the previous explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

The Buddha first offers praise and subsequently provides an analytical explanation, with the meanings following one another in sequence. Within this, there are ninety-four phrases; when subdivided according to their specific distinctions, there are one hundred and nine phrases. Specifically, within the twenty-second [category], "Absence of Oppression," there are seven phrases; within the twenty-third, "Immovability," there are four phrases; within the twenty-fifth, "Rarity," there are two phrases; within the twenty-sixth, "Emptiness and Quiescence," there are also two phrases; within the thirtieth, "Profound Meaning," there are also two phrases; within the fifty-first, "Equanimity," there are also two phrases; and within the sixty-seventh, "Absence of Narrowness," there are three phrases. All remaining [categories] each constitute one phrase. Therefore, when subdivided, there are one hundred and nine phrases.
Within each and every phrase, there should uniformly be five parts:
first, the enumeration of names; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion; fourth, "it is precisely the Tathāgata"; and fifth, the further analysis of that which is difficult to understand.

However, in the present text, the sequence is somewhat indeterminate: there are cases where the beginning exists but not the end, cases where the end exists but not the beginning, and cases where there is a middle without either beginning or end.

Within the explanations, some consist solely of doctrinal statements, while others employ analogies; these analogies may be either concordant or inverse. Those that are concordant analogies indicate that liberation is likewise, whereas those that are inverse analogies indicate that liberation is not so.

In the pairing of the Dharma and the analogy, the sequence is not fixed: sometimes the Dharma comes first, followed by the analogy and then the application; sometimes the analogy comes first, followed by the Dharma and then the analogy; or sometimes the Dharma is presented first, followed by the analogy, and then the discourse concludes. Thus, the literary structure is indeterminate.
Now, in the first sentence, the names are first listed as "Freedom from Bonds.
Next, their characteristics are explained through two metaphors and two corresponding applications; there is no concluding summary text.

Next, it is precisely the Tathāgata who acts as the differentiator, because he is the liberation of the two vehicles mentioned previously; thus, as in the subsequent passages, he is also identical to *nirvāṇa*, space, the Buddha-nature, definitive bodhi, and all Buddha-dharmas. Since these are analogous to the others, and all other cases are likewise the same, I shall not trouble you with further elaboration; therefore, the preceding phrases refer exclusively to the Tathāgata.

The passage beginning with "Like spring" reiterates this point, first through a simile and subsequently through its application; other instances may be understood by analogy. This is termed "the severance of all conditioned phenomena."

Regarding the phrase "giving birth to all untainted wholesome dharmas," this is the eighty-ninth [section] clarifying freedom from all views. First, their names are listed: "severing conditioned dharmas" clarifies freedom from false views, while "emerging into untainted dharmas" clarifies possessing right view.

Next, I shall explain its characteristics. First, regarding the elimination of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*): "blocking all paths" provides a general clarification of the elimination of outflows; eliminating all the false views held by non-Buddhists is termed "blocking all paths."

To explain this specifically below: if one holds the view that there is a "self," the view that there is "non-self" as emptiness, or the view that there is "neither self nor non-self" as neither existence nor non-existence—though these appear to be true, they must be severed because such fixed attachments do not accord with the principles of the Dharma.
"To sever only attachment, but not the view of self" explains the aforementioned production of untainted wholesome dharmas.
What is called "Buddha-nature" clarifies that which is not severed.
These words are insufficient; if they were complete, one should say, "Understanding the Buddha-nature.
The phrase "The nature is itself true liberation" serves as a general conclusion.
What follows regarding the Tathāgata’s "name is not empty of emptiness" constitutes the ninety-first [section], clarifying how his liberation differs from that attained by non-Buddhists.

First, their names are listed: the liberation of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) is empty, deceptive, and without reality, and is thus called "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā); true liberation is not like that, and is therefore called "not-empty emptiness" (aśūnya-śūnyatā).

Next, I shall explain its characteristics. First, regarding "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*): the statement "emptiness of emptiness is non-existent" explains the meaning of emptiness; "this is the liberation of the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha" points to the person for refutation; "yet that Nirgrantha truly has no liberation" explains emptiness in reference to the person; and "it is truly not thus" clarifies that there is a distinct emptiness.
The composition [of the verse] may be understood accordingly.
It is called "the fruit is not empty" (名果不空). The ninety-first [section] clarifies that it is neither existent nor non-existent;

first, its names are listed. Within these names there is insufficiency; if they were complete, one should say "the name is not empty of emptiness" (名不空空). To distinguish it from the preceding section, it is simply called "not empty" (不空).

Next, the characteristics [of the analogy] are explained. In this explanation, first the Dharma is revealed by means of an analogy: "That jar, when encountering conditions, then breaks" serves to distinguish the Dharma from the analogy.
Within the former section, there are three parts:
first, establishing the analogy to reveal the Dharma; "water, wine, and curd jars" presents the substance of the analogy, while the subsequent portion clarifies the characteristics of the analogy.
Among these, the first section clarifies emptiness and non-emptiness by means of water-jars, wine-jars, and so forth.
The phrase "although there is no water" and so on expresses the meaning of emptiness;

the phrase "it is nevertheless still called a water-jar or the like" expresses the meaning of non-emptiness. It is because the substantial body of the jar exists that it is termed "non-empty," not because the residual water, wine, or other contents exist that it is termed "non-empty."
This is similar in meaning to the previous passage which clarified that although the lamp has been extinguished, the vessel still remains.
The section beginning with "In this way, the vase" clarifies that emptiness and non-emptiness cannot be determined as one-sided.
The passage beginning with "If one says 'empty'" refutes the meaning of other-emptiness (*parābhāvaśūnyatā*).

If one asserts that things are definitively empty, then the substantial entities of a jar—such as its color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility—could not exist; thus, this definitively fixed emptiness is refuted.
"If one says it is not empty and yet lacks water and so forth," this refutes the fixed notion that it is not empty.
Second, by means of the analogy, the dharma is revealed: "Liberation is also like this," which corresponds to the aforementioned substance of the jar.

The lower section corresponds to the analogy: "It cannot be said to be form or non-form" corresponds to the previous point that even when water, wine, and so forth are absent, it is still called a "water jar" or a "wine jar."
"Neither expressible as empty nor as non-empty" combines the previous points regarding the inexpressibility of being empty or non-empty.

The passage beginning "If one says it is empty" combines the previous point that if it were empty, then form, fragrance, flavor, and touch could not exist; and the point that if one says it is non-empty, yet there is no water and so forth.
The section beginning with "By this" concludes [the preceding discussion].
The three layers of dharma and metaphor are explained in detail in relation to one another; therein, first, emptiness is clarified by means of the dharma.
"Emptiness means the absence of the twenty-five existences" clarifies the absence of the fruit of suffering.
“Furthermore, all afflictions” clarifies the absence of the cause of delusion.

“The absence of all suffering and all marks” further clarifies the absence of the fruit; because there is no fruit of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), one is far removed from manifold sufferings and also detached from marks such as impermanence and non-self. Therefore, it is said that there is an absence of all suffering and all marks.
The statement "there is no conditioned activity whatsoever" clarifies that there is no cause of karma; for the two types of karma, good and evil, are termed "conditioned activity.
The first character "wu" (non-/no) runs through all the subsequent phrases.
"Like a jar that contains no curd"—this is the illustration used to apply the analogy.

Next, the text proceeds to clarify non-emptiness in terms of the actual phenomena: "That is to say, there is truly wholesome form, which is permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Here, the various sense faculties and the marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*) are termed "wholesome form."
The phrase "like a jar" and below provides an analogy to apply [the principle].
"Therefore, liberation is like that jar" concludes by showing the identity between the dharma and the analogy.
Thus far, liberation has been analyzed by means of analogies.
People claim that liberation is entirely identical to that analogy; therefore, the following section distinguishes their differences.
"That jar may be destroyed when it encounters conditions" clarifies the dissimilarity between the analogy and the dharma;
"liberation is not so" distinguishes the dharma from the analogy.
The formation of the title can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "named 'Free from Craving,'" the ninety-second [section] clarifies the doubt concerning freedom from craving; because the name is abbreviated, it simply says "free from craving."
First, the names are listed; next, their characteristics are explained.
First, an inverse analogy is established; below, the differences are clarified:
having attained great bodhi, there is nothing further to be sought, and for this reason, one is free from craving.
Regarding the fruit, one attains definitive realization, and thus there is no doubt.
The subsequent conclusion, "is himself the Buddha," further clarifies this point.
"Severing all craving for existence" (the ninety-third [verse]) elucidates his distancing from the causes and effects of birth and death.
First, their names are listed:
"Severing Existence" clarifies the abandonment of the fruit of birth and death, while "Severing Greed" clarifies the abandonment of the cause of birth and death.
Next, their characteristics are explained, with six distinct points:

The first two [phrases] are presented briefly; "severing all marks" clarifies the severance of existence mentioned previously, meaning the severance of various marks such as impermanence and suffering.
"Severing all bonds" clarifies the severance of craving mentioned previously.

The following four sections provide a detailed exposition: "severing all afflictions" clarifies the cause for severing delusions; "all births and deaths" clarifies the result of severing delusions; "all causes and conditions" clarifies the cause for severing karma; and "all retributions" clarifies the result of severing karma. The single character "sever" (斷) from the first phrase runs through all subsequent clauses.
The concluding remarks are omitted.
What follows concerns the Tathāgata and his parinirvāṇa.
From the phrase "all beings" onwards, the ninety-fourth [section] clarifies the departure from fear and the attainment of peace and happiness.
Within this section, there is first an explanation, followed by a conclusion, and finally the mention of the Buddha and others.
For those points that are difficult to understand, they will be analyzed again below.
Regarding the initial part, it begins with the Dharma; however, the text is too brief and insufficient.
If [the conditions] are complete, one should say that all sentient beings, because they fear birth and death, receive the three refuges;

by means of the three refuges, they obtain peace and happiness. Next, this is illustrated through analogies: "The deer fears the hunter" illustrates the arising of fear toward the afflictions of birth and death; "having already escaped" and below illustrate receiving the three refuges; and "obtaining peace and happiness" illustrates what was previously lacking.
The subsequent sections may be understood accordingly.
"Bliss is itself liberation" serves as the general conclusion.
Below, it is shown that liberation is identical to the Tathāgata and other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; however, for now, we shall briefly treat them through seven gates of mutual identity.
"Inexhaustibility" is its dharma-nature, which is space; "certainty" is wisdom. Because these are distinguished as aspects of the same essence, they are mutually identical.
Since this section is thus, the preceding sections should also be understood in the same way; they are not discussed here in full detail for the sake of brevity.
Where there are points that are difficult to understand, they will be further clarified below.
What is difficult to understand?

Previously, it was taught that receiving the three refuges seems to imply they are distinct; yet, it was further stated that liberation is identical to the Tathāgata and so forth, which seems to imply they are one. Since unity and difference are contradictory, this must be explained.

Furthermore, as previously stated, one attains peace and happiness by virtue of the Three Refuges; however, since this might be confused with the experience of pleasure, the following section clarifies their distinction.
There are two question-and-answer pairs:
the first explains the meaning of the unity and diversity of the Three Refuges, while the second clarifies that happiness is not a form of sensation (*vedanā*).
Regarding the first question below: "If nirvana, buddha-nature, and the Tathāgata are definitively one in meaning, why are three spoken of?
This reflects an attachment to the idea of oneness while harboring doubts regarding the three.
Previously, you explained that the seven phenomena are identical; now, however, you cite only four, which is insufficient for this inquiry.
If it were complete, one should ask: since taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is distinct from taking refuge in Nirvana and so forth, how can they be identical?
It is appropriate to respond that these exist; here, one side is cited so that the other may be understood.
The Buddha’s response has three parts:

first, discussing the three in terms of the one; second, from "The name of the existent dharma is one" onwards, distinguishing the three in terms of the one; third, from "The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of one as three and three as one" onwards, praising both the one and the three together to reveal their profundity.
In the preceding section, the first part clarifies that "all sentient beings, out of fear, seek the three refuges," and thus there are three distinctions.
Because of these three refuges, one realizes and knows that Buddha-nature is determinately Nirvana; since what is realized is of the same essence, it is established as one.

In the second section, first the principle is used to demonstrate that the three [categories] are distinct; from the words "Therefore, I... onwards, scriptural citations are introduced to prove their distinctness.
Within the former [part], there is first a general clarification regarding the identity or difference between names and referents (*nāma-artha*) of all phenomena:
when a name is applied to a phenomenon, there are only two possibilities—first, that both name and referent are identical, and second, that both name and referent are distinct.

Dharmas possess both essence and function, as well as general and specific aspects, and similarities and differences. When names are applied based on essence, the general, or similarity, both name and referent are identical.
When names are applied based on function, the specific, or difference, both name and referent are distinct.
The mutual discussion of concealment and manifestation consists of four propositions:
first, name and meaning are both identical;
second, name and meaning are both different, as fully explained above.

The three names share one meaning yet differ in substance; they are designated based on their essence, their totality, and their commonality, and because the meaning is subsumed within the expression, they are said to have "one name.
They follow their functions, their distinctions, and their differences in designation; because the expression is subsumed within the intended meaning, they are said to have "different meanings."
The four meanings share a single name while their referents differ; this can be understood by reversing the previous case.

Now, among these four, two gates are set forth for the time being: "the existence of phenomena where the name is one but the meaning differs" constitutes the third gate, and "the existence of phenomena where both name and meaning differ" constitutes the second gate.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished.
Within the first gate, there is first a restatement of the thesis and then an explanation.
Since the Buddha and others are all eternal, names are applied based on this eternity; thus, by subsuming the essential meaning within its verbal expression, it is said that "the name is one."
The meanings of terms such as "Buddha" differ; here, the expression is subsumed under its intended meaning, which is termed "difference in meaning.
The section beginning with "This is called" concludes [the previous discussion].
In explaining the subsequent gate, first the text is cited, and then it is interpreted.

The meanings of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and so forth each differ; names are assigned based upon these meanings, and thus the names themselves are not the same—therefore, all four are distinct.
"Buddha" is translated as "Awakened," which is its etymological definition.
"The name 'Dharma' means 'non-awakening' (abodha)"; this is neither a transliteration nor an etymological explanation, but rather a term used to distinguish it from the Buddha.
"The name 'Saṃgha' means 'harmony' (saṃghāta)"; this is both a transliteration and an etymological explanation.
"Nibbāna is called liberation" is an explanation of its meaning, not a transliteration of the term.
"Emptiness is called non-virtue" is a word used for distinction; it is neither a transliteration nor an etymological explanation.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty space; it does not correspond to the practice of wholesome deeds, and is therefore termed "non-wholesome.
The term "unobstructed" distinguishes it from others and also defines its characteristic.
The phrase "this is" and what follows serves as the conclusion.
The following section clarifies the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*) based on the preceding meaning, establishing that they are distinct and not one.

Within this demonstration of their distinction through cited scriptural passages, it first presents a former teaching: "Therefore, the three refuges cannot be one," thereby concluding the point of their distinctness.
Regarding the preceding section: first, [the Buddha] instructed Mahāprajāpatī to provide sustenance for the Sangha, which immediately resulted in her taking the Three Refuges.
Mahāprajāpatī was the Buddha’s paternal aunt; seven days after she gave birth, her mother passed away, and Mahāprajāpatī nursed him.

After the Buddha had left the household life, Prajāpatī missed him with longing; she personally wove a golden-threaded woolen cloth, intending to offer it to the Buddha when he returned to the palace.
Later, when the Buddha did indeed return to his kingdom, Prajāpatī presented it as an offering. The Buddha then said to her:
"A gift given out of affectionate attachment does not bring great merit; you should instead make offerings to the Saṃgha."
"If one makes offerings to the Saṃgha, one is making offerings to the Three Refuges.
Therefore, this is cited here.
When Vāseṭṭha asked his question next, the Buddha subsequently explained it by distinguishing three meanings; thus, they are not the same.
The first section distinguished the meaning of unity; the second distinguished the meaning of difference.
From here begins the third section, which concludes by praising both unity and difference to reveal their profundity:
"The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of one as three. This reiterates the preceding latter section regarding the oneness of the Buddha-nature, and explains therein the distinctions of the Three Refuges.
"Explaining three as one" refers to the first section above, which proclaims the Buddha-nature, nirvāṇa, and so forth as being one based upon the three refuges.
"Such meanings are the realm of the Buddhas," etc., praises them to manifest their profundity.

The above clarifies the meaning of the identity and difference regarding the three refuges and so forth within the previously explained liberation; next, it clarifies that the peace and happiness previously attained is quiescence, not sensation.

Kāśyapa first asked, "Regarding what the Buddha has taught—that ultimate peace and bliss is called nirvāṇa—what is the meaning of this? He directly requested its characteristics, seeking to have the nature of tranquil bliss revealed.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, as for nirvāṇa," this refutes the notion that it involves the experience of pleasure.
The Buddha’s response consists of four distinct points:

first, in response to the initial request, he demonstrates that nirvāṇa is exclusively the bliss of tranquility; second, from "severing all" onwards, in response to the subsequent objection, he clarifies that nirvāṇa is not the experience of pleasure; third, from "if one says" onwards, he refutes the claim of experiencing pleasure, thereby establishing the preceding second point; and fourth, from "therefore" onwards, he concludes by defining the aforementioned tranquil bliss as the meaning of nirvāṇa and liberation.
At the beginning, there is first a parable consisting of four points:

First, the parable of emerging from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). "A person" represents the Buddha. In the past, while practicing the causes [of enlightenment], he engaged in karma and afflictions, which is likened to having "eaten. Experiencing suffering, his mind became "oppressed. Seeking to escape the three realms and severing the fetters of karma, he is said to have "vomited out desire. To be truly able to sever them is called "having obtained the vomit. Second, the parable of manifesting transformations in accordance with sentient beings.
Having himself emerged from birth-and-death, he bends down to respond to and follow sentient beings; this is called "returning again."

The third section uses analogies to illustrate virtues through questions: the bodhisattvas practicing together are called "companions"; they inquire whether the Tathāgata’s birth and death have ended, which is termed "inquiry as to whether the illness has been cured"; and they marvel that the Buddha returns to the world, which is termed "returning despite having recovered.

The fourth section uses analogies to illustrate virtues through answers: that all sufferings have already ceased is termed "answering that the illness is cured"; and that he has realized quiescent eternal peace is termed "having attained peace and happiness."

When combined with the next [passage], "The Tathāgata is likewise; he is ultimately far removed from the twenty-five states of existence" corresponds to the first phrase; "forever attains" and what follows correspond to the fourth phrase, that the body attains peace and happiness.
In the second section, the phrase "severing all sensations is called 'no-sensation'" means that the five types of sensation are all severed.
The phrase "such no-sensation is called eternal bliss" is an exaltation intended to reveal its excellence.
Question:
Below it is stated, "By extinguishing impermanent form, one attains permanent form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Why, then, do you say that the Buddha does not experience pleasure?
The commentary states:
There are two kinds of "reception" (vedanā):

first, the reception of objects such as those that are disagreeable or agreeable; second, it is called reception because of the realization of the Dharma and its correspondence with the correct appropriation of the True Dharma.
What is now called "non-existence" refers to the absence of its initial reception;
what is said below regarding "attainment" refers to the acquisition of its subsequent reception. Thus, the two statements do not contradict one another.
The latter two cases can be understood accordingly.
From the beginning, we have only requested that you graciously grant us a further extensive exposition.
This concludes the third major section, which clarifies the characteristics of liberation.
From here on, the fourth section dispels all verbal designations and metaphors.
Why must it be swept away?

Thus far, metaphors have been borrowed and applied by way of analogy to illustrate liberation; however, people might claim that liberation is entirely comprised of these various metaphors. Therefore, the following section sweeps them away.
This section contains two parts:
First, it clarifies that the various metaphors established above are not metaphors but are treated as metaphors;
second, from the passage beginning "How can the Tathāgata make two statements," it clarifies that the metaphors are not metaphors and cannot be definitively stated.
The preceding section has three parts:

first, it clarifies that the aforementioned metaphors are not true metaphors but are used as metaphors; second, from "One who has attained true liberation cannot be matched by any human or deva" onwards, it clarifies the reason why those which are not metaphors are used as metaphors; third, from "Like the incomparable" onwards, it categorically reveals the characteristics of using what is not a metaphor as a metaphor.

Within the first section, the non-exemplification is first clarified; the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata at times, by means of causes and conditions" demonstrates its status as an exemplification.
Within the clarification of the non-exemplification, there are four question-and-answer exchanges.
First, Kāśyapa asks:
"Is non-arising and non-ceasing liberation?
The Buddha replied, "It is.

Kāśyapa II, employing a metaphor consistent with the principle, said, "If non-arising and non-ceasing constitute liberation, then the empty space of the world is also without arising or ceasing; it too should be liberation."
The Buddha replied that it was not so.
The three Kāśyapas asked: "Why is it not so?"
The Tathāgata asked in return,
"Kāla and others, is your voice the same as that of crows and magpies?
The fourth Kāśyapa answered correctly according to reason, and the Tathāgata praised him.
In Kāśyapa’s reply, "No" serves as the general answer.
Below, it is explained in detail through four distinct points:
first, "The cries of crows and magpies cannot be compared to those of the kalaviṅka bird," which clarifies that the inferior cannot be compared to the superior.

Second, from "Kāśyapa said: 'Kālānusārin... onwards, it clarifies how the superior meets the inferior. Within this, Kāśyapa first clarifies being inferior to others, then rebukes the Tathāgata; from "'No different from the *ting* [seed]... onwards, he demonstrates that the Buddha should not be so;
third, from "'The Buddha and space... onwards, he reveals the Dharma by means of a metaphor;
fourth, from "'The sound of the Kālānusārin may be compared to the Buddha... onwards, he distinguishes the metaphor to reveal the Dharma.

The Buddha compared himself to a kalaviṅka bird and not to a crow or a magpie, thereby manifesting the excellence of his voice; because his voice was so excellent, he used it as a metaphor for liberation.
His comparison with empty space is something the Buddha’s praise makes clear.

The preceding section extensively clarifies that [the Tathāgata] is not a metaphor; the passage beginning with "At times, the Tathāgata, by means of causes and conditions" clarifies that he *is* a metaphor.
What is meant by "at times" refers to the causes and conditions for transforming others.
By citing the analogy of space to clarify what is illustrated—the Buddha’s virtues—it is therefore the Tathāgata.
This concludes the first section.
Below follows the second section, which explains the reason why that which is not an analogy is used as an analogy.

"True liberation is entirely without fault" explains that the preceding [statement] is not a metaphor; "for the sake of transforming sentient beings" and below explain that the preceding [statement] is indeed a metaphor, thereby revealing that there were causes and conditions for manifesting the preceding [point].

From here below is the third category, which clarifies the characteristics of taking what is not a simile as a simile. First, its categories are presented: it says, "That which is not a simile is like an incomparable thing that cannot be cited as an analogy," briefly citing what is not a simile;
and "Because there are causes and conditions, an analogy can be cited," briefly citing what constitutes a simile.
The phrase "as in the sūtras" below points directly to the specific instances.

The following section, concerning the manifestation of the Dharma, clarifies that true liberation cannot be illustrated by metaphors, thereby showing it is not a metaphor; the phrase "for the sake of converting sentient beings" below shows how it serves as a metaphor; and the passage beginning with "by means of various parables" explains that all the aforementioned metaphors are in fact non-metaphors used as metaphors.

The preceding section, the first, clarified that the various previous metaphors were not metaphors [in the ultimate sense] yet served as metaphors. From here on, the second section clarifies that metaphors are not metaphors and cannot be definitively stated.
Kāśyapa had previously asked:
"If these were truly metaphors, you would speak of them as exclusively metaphors."
"If it were not an analogy, you would categorically say it is not so.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata provide two kinds of explanations?
Below, the Buddha answers him, clarifying that because dharmas are not fixed, he speaks with non-fixed [provisional] teachings.
The textual divisions are fourfold:
first, the analogy of harming the Buddha, which clarifies that the Buddha’s Dharma-body cannot be definitively described, as it uses what is not an analogy as an analogy;
second, the analogy of harming the mother, which clarifies that the Buddha’s Reward-body cannot be definitively described, as it uses what is not an analogy as an analogy.
3. "For these reasons, I have spoken various parables" concludes the preceding second section; this is done because it follows naturally from the flow of the discourse.
4. "There may also be causes and conditions for which there can be a parable" concludes the preceding first section.
The beginning and middle [of this section] consist of four parts:
first, the Tathāgata establishes a simile; second, he poses a counter-question to Kāśyapa; third, Kāśyapa provides the correct answer; and fourth, the Tathāgata offers praise.
Within the establishment of the simile, he cites that the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* cannot be killed as an analogy to clarify that it is not a [literal] metaphor.
The phrase "desiring to harm incurs guilt" serves as an analogy to illustrate the point.
The initial mention of "a person" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
being internally endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is what is meant by "wielding a sword."
To speak of the true name of anger is "with a mind of hatred";
to desire to use various metaphors to illustrate the Buddha’s Dharma-body while describing its characteristics as being false is "injuring the Tathāgata";
because the Dharma-body is equal and does not change according to appearances, it is said that "the Tathāgata is harmonious and free from the color of anger."
The next rhetorical question is: "Will this person be able to destroy the body of a Tathāgata?
This is the first question. "Does he commit a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya)?
This is the second question.
In Kāśyapa’s response, he first analyzes the characteristics of the analogy and subsequently applies it to reveal the Dharma.
Within the analogy, he first addresses the initial question above to clarify that the Buddha cannot be killed, thereby demonstrating that [the previous case] does not constitute a valid analogy.

The phrase "precisely by an evil mind" responds to the subsequent question; it clarifies that because of an evil mind, the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) is established, thereby manifesting this as an analogy.
Within the preceding section, the initial word "No" is a general response that the Buddha cannot be killed; hence, it says "No."
The section beginning with "For what reason" explains and establishes that [the Tathāgata] cannot be killed.
Regarding the phrase "The realm of the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible," this is an analytical explanation in response to the question.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) refers to the nature of the body; furthermore, the physical limits of a human body are also termed the "body-realm."
The Dharma-body is free from characteristics and is therefore indestructible.
The passage beginning with "Why is this? further explains the reason for its indestructibility, inquiring why the Buddha’s body alone is particularly indestructible.
"By means of being bodiless" clarifies that the body is free from characteristics and is therefore indestructible.
The section beginning with "Only the dharma-nature" clarifies that the body is quiescent in its essence and is therefore indestructible.
From the phrase "this person" onwards, the section concludes with the formation of the "indestructible" (akṣaya).

In the response to the subsequent question, the statement "merely by means of an evil mind one accomplishes the immediate [offense]" (*ānantarya*) means that a transformative intention (*nirmāṇa-citta*) which contradicts the Truth is called an "evil mind"; the accomplishment of the matter described in the metaphorical discourse is called "accomplishing the immediate. The meaning of the "immediate" offense will be discussed separately later.

The following section clarifies the Dharma: regarding the statement, "By these causes and conditions, one draws upon various parables to know the true Dharma," this specifically refers to the latter phrase to clarify that they serve as metaphors.
By means of such an evil mind, one also brings about the causal conditions for the immediate [retribution].
The Buddha employs various parables to enable the great assembly to understand the True Dharma;
yet, regarding the initial [explanation], it should be understood as not being a parable, and thus is briefly left unexplained.
The Buddha’s praise may be understood as before.
In the second section, there are likewise four parts:
first, the Tathāgata establishes a simile; second, he poses a counter-question to Kāśyapa; third, Kāśyapa provides the formal answer; and fourth, the Tathāgata offers his praise.

At the beginning, the "evil person" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); it is called an "evil person" because its manifested characteristics appear to violate the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).

The various metaphors are intended to reveal the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Because the manifested characteristics closely resemble the reality, they are termed "harm"; because the ultimate reality is the source of transformation, it is termed "mother. Since the transformation exists within the three realms of existence, it is said to be "dwelling in the wild fields"; since it exists amidst all manifested characteristics, it is said to be "under the thatch."

The Reward Buddha (*vipākakāya*), through the sustaining power of his great compassionate vow, ensures that the transformation of beings is uninterrupted; this is called "the Mother Sending Food. The Response Body Tathāgata (*nirmāṇakāya-tathāgata*), whose internal conditions are true virtues, is called "Seeing Himself. The arising of the intention to preach is called "Conceiving an Evil Thought. Being fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is called "Whetting the Knife First. The Reward Body Tathāgata, clearly discerning the intent of the transformation, is called "the Mother Knowing Her Son. Following the transformation according to its signs is called "Entering the Cauldron. Using sharp analytical knowledge to extensively explain true virtues according to their metaphorical signs is called "Circumambulating and Cutting the Cauldron. Expounding the mind of holy transformation is called "Cutting Himself and Rejoicing. Recollecting that he has already preached is called "Conceiving the Thought of Killing. The true essence being free from signs is called "Emerging from the Cauldron. Abiding securely in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is called "Arriving at Home."
The meaning can be understood through the counter-question.
In Kāśyapa’s response, he first distinguishes the characteristics of the analogy and subsequently applies it to reveal the Dharma.
Within the analogy, he initially states: "It cannot be definitively said; if one were to say it exists, the mother's body would have to be destroyed."
"If the body were not subject to disintegration, how could one say it exists?
This clarifies that there is no fault [in the opponent's position] and demonstrates that their example is invalid.
The passage beginning with "If one says it does not exist" clarifies that there *is* a fault and reveals that it serves as a valid analogy.

"By these conditions," the following section clarifies the Dharma through analogies; it specifically addresses the latter phrase to demonstrate that there is an analogy, while the former is not discussed in detail.
The Buddha’s praise may be understood accordingly.

From here below begins the third section, which concludes the second [section]. The phrase "For this reason, I have spoken various metaphors for true liberation" establishes the presence of metaphors.

The act of circling a thicket and cutting it all around is termed "speaking various [metaphors]"; the passage beginning with "Although [it is like] immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*... establishes the absence of metaphors.

The first summary at the end states: "There are certain conditions where it is also possible to provide a simile," which establishes the category of "with simile"; "there are certain conditions where it cannot be illustrated by a simile," which establishes the category of "without simile."
From the preceding section, "What is called nirvāṇa? onwards, these are combined as the second part, which elucidates the virtue of liberation.
From here below is the third part, which concludes with a praise that reveals its excellence.
This section contains three sub-divisions:
The first two [verses] praise the virtues of the subsequent liberation; the phrase "therefore, liberation accomplishes such immeasurable virtues" is a concluding praise based on the Dharma.
Because it possesses the aforementioned hundred virtues, it is called "immeasurable."
"The one who proceeds toward nirvāṇa, and the Tathāgata who has attained nirvāṇa, likewise possess such immeasurable merits"—this concludes the eulogy by way of the person.
The Tathāgata is the person seeking nirvāṇa, hence he is called "one who proceeds toward nirvāṇa";
having realized great nirvāṇa and manifested the body of a Tathāgata, he is therefore named the "Tathāgata of Nirvāṇa."
The preceding analysis established that all liberations are identical to the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata likewise possesses such immeasurable merits.
The final phrase concludes the section on the first liberation, stating that because he possesses such qualities of liberation, he is named "Great Nirvāṇa."
From here below begins the fourth section, in which Kāśyapa receives and understands [the teaching].
"I now finally know that the destination reached by the Tathāgata is inexhaustible," he says, reiterating his prior understanding of the place of liberation.

In the preceding extensive explanation of the locus of liberation, Kāśyapa understood that such nirvāṇa is the locus of the Tathāgata, which is eternal and unchanging; therefore, it is now reiterated for his further confirmation.

"I have only now come to know that the Tathāgata’s reach is inexhaustible. Here, "now" refers to the present moment in contrast to the past when this was not known; "inexhaustible" carries the same meaning as previously explained: eternal abiding.
Regarding the statement, "If the dwelling is inexhaustible, one should know that the life-span is also inexhaustible," this refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*).

Because the Dharma is inexhaustible, the person is rendered inexhaustible; this refers to the aforementioned virtue of liberation wherein the Tathāgata is without birth, old age, sickness, or death, which is termed the "inexhaustibility of life."
From this point downward is the fifth section, which concludes with praise and encourages study.
"Excellent, you who are able to protect" is the expression of praise, extolling the preceding understanding and realization.
From "If there are those who desire... onwards is the exhortation to study.
〈Longevity〉: Up to this point, the essential nature of the practice has been clarified; from here on, the second section distinguishes the basis upon which the practice relies.
Within this, the first part correctly clarifies the basis itself, while the subsequent section explains the erroneous and the correct, thereby distinguishing what is not to be relied upon.

In the preceding section, the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) were clarified with the bodhisattva as the person upon whom one relies; this directly answers the previous questions regarding "how one attains greatness to serve as a refuge for the multitude" and "how one who is not actually an arhat is [regarded as] an arhat."
He asked how this was so:
“How does one become such a person of vast capacity who serves as a refuge for the multitude?

Although he has not yet attained equality with the Buddhas and Arhats, because his transformative merit is equal to theirs, I wish to rely upon him; therefore, I now answer him to clarify that there are four types of persons capable of serving as a place of refuge for sentient beings, no different from the Buddha, and worthy of being relied upon.

In the text, the first part correctly clarifies that these four persons constitute the basis of reliance, as the Buddha taught: "relying on four dharmas. The subsequent section, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, provides a comprehensive interpretation, which likewise clarifies the dharmas upon which practice relies.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, clarifying the virtuous conduct and physical characteristics of the four types of persons;
second, from "I now do not rely on these four persons" onwards, exhorting people to take refuge [in others] and instructing them on how to make offerings.
The introduction consists of four parts:

first, a general mention of the four individuals with a collective praise of their virtues; second, a specific enumeration of the four individuals with a collective praise of their virtues; third, a separate citation of each of the four individuals with a distinct manifestation of their virtues; and fourth, a concluding summary of the four individuals with a collective praise of their virtues.

Within the first section, four types of persons are first presented; since these four persons achieve virtue based upon this sūtra, and because they are those proclaimed within this very sūtra, it is said: "In this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, there are four kinds of persons."
Below, he praises his virtue: "Protecting the Dharma, establishing the Dharma, mindfulness, and the True Dharma" constitute the universal practice of the Dharma, which is self-benefit.
Being able to rectify and protect [the Dharma] oneself, so as not to allow others to disparage, slander, or revile it, is called protecting the True Dharma.

As explained extensively above, the ability of the mouth to establish [the teachings] is called "establishing the True Dharma," and the mind’s not forgetting [them] is called "recollection of the Dharma.
From the phrase "capable of much" onwards refers to the practice of benefiting others, which is to say, benefiting others.
"Capable of great benefit" refers to the transformation through supramundane dharmas; "compassionate toward the world" and so forth refer to the transformation through mundane dharmas.
Compassion for the world is the mind of benefiting others, while the section beginning with "serving as the world's reliance" constitutes the practice of benefiting others.
Human beings are the support for all things, and the Dharma is able to bring peace and happiness; since humans and devas can be transformed, it is specifically discussed in relation to them.
Furthermore, out of compassion and loving-kindness for those in the three miserable realms, [the Dharma] serves as a support for the world and provides immediate benefit to humans and devas.
In the second section, the four types of persons are first enumerated.
The phrase "What are they? poses the inquiry, while "There are people who emerge... and so forth, distinguish and list their names.
The meaning of the "four reliances" (catvāri pratisaraṇāni) is explained extensively in a separate chapter; here, we shall briefly explain their names.

Regarding the statement, "There are those who have appeared in the world who possess the nature of afflictions, and they are called the foremost," this refers to persons on the stages of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*). The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states that only after reaching the stage of spiritual lineage does one become a Dharma teacher; since one cannot do so prior to that, we know these individuals are not from before the stage of spiritual lineage.

The subsequent passage declares that only those who have made offerings to the Buddhas five times as many as the sands of the Ganges are fit to be a basis [for this teaching]; therefore, they do not belong to the happy realms (*sugati*).
Since the text states that they possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and are not "eighth-persons" (*aṣṭamaka*), it is clear they are not on the stages (*bhūmi*).

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, manifesting transformations to benefit sentient beings is called "appearing in the world. To have no particular point within the afflictions of the five stages that is fully exhausted is called "possessing afflictions.
Question: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* proclaims that the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is endowed with two kinds of purity. For what reason, then, do you now say it "possesses afflictions"?
The commentary states:
"In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, with respect to the two vehicles, it speaks of the two kinds of purity;
here, in contrast to those on the stages (*bhūmi*), they are called 'possessors of afflictions' (*sākleśa*)."

Regarding the statement, "Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin are called the second": *srotāpanna* is here termed "flowing against the current," meaning one flows against the current of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is also termed "repaying a debt," meaning repaying the debt of the three miserable realms (*apāya*).
Furthermore, it is also termed "cultivating and accumulating the out-flow-free" (*anāsrava*).
Where are these stages located?
There are three types of Srotāpanna:
first, the one who maintains the fruit, at the stage of the final mind of the first bhūmi;
Second is the "comprehensive cause," which includes all stages from the initial mind of the first bhūmi onward;

third is the "progressive direction," wherein everything up to the second bhūmi is termed *srotāpanna*. Combining these two preceding aspects, they are designated as *srotāpanna*; therefore, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) proclaims that the first bhūmi constitutes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner) is here called "one who comes again," as they return and are reborn once more within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); they are also called "abiding in thinness.

According to the Hīnayāna, regarding the cultivation of the path in the realm of desire, among the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*), six have been abandoned and three remain; therefore, it is said that they "abide in thinness."

If one relies on the Mahāyāna, the afflictions cultivated within the three realms can all be attenuated; thus, the *Bhūmi-sūtra* states that the bonds of desire, form, and existence, as well as the bond of ignorance, are all rendered subtle and thin.
As for the stage and position [of this practice], there are three distinctions:
first, the maintenance of the fruit, which resides in the third bhūmi; therefore, the *Bhūmi-sūtra* proclaims that in the third bhūmi, all fetters are attenuated.

Second is the "comprehensive cause," referring to those from the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*) downward who gradually abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation; they are collectively termed *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Third is the "progressive advance," referring to those up to the seventh stage (*saptamī bhūmi*); these three types combined are collectively termed *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Why are these two combined into one?

It is because the functional practice (*prayoga*) of these two individuals is identical; in their service to the Buddha and their understanding of the meaning, they surpass those who are inferior before and after them, and for this reason they are joined together.
"Anāgāmin" means "one who does not return.
According to the Hīnayāna, one is called an Anāgāmin because they will no longer undergo rebirth within the desire realm;
according to the Mahāyāna, one is called an Anāgāmin because they do not return to give rise to the affliction of craving for [the Buddha].
In which stage is this located?
There are three distinctions:
first, the maintenance of the fruit, which resides in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), because the afflictions of craving for the Buddha are severed at this point.

Second is the inclusion of the cause: from the fourth ground upward, they are all equally termed *anāgāmin*, because they cultivate the conforming patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) directed toward the eighth ground;
third is the progressive advancement: extending upward through the ninth ground, the latter two stages are collectively designated as *anāgāmin*.

Because they equally relinquish their functional effort in this state, and because their offering to the Buddha and their comprehension of the meaning surpass what preceded them and exceed what follows, they are considered as one.
As for "Arhat," this name signifies "one who is unattached," because they have severed the causes of existence;
it is also called "one who is non-arising," because they have exhausted the fruits of suffering.
As for the location of its stage,
there are three distinctions:
first, the maintenance of the fruit, which resides in the tenth stage;
Second is the inclusion of the cause: those from the ninth stage upward are all equally termed Arhats.
Third is the progressive advancement: reaching up to the Diamond-like Samādhi, the latter two stages are collectively designated as Arhat because they both reside in the ultimate stage.
In truth, the Buddha is one who highly extols such persons; therefore, they are addressed using the same title as the Buddha.
Since these are all bodhisattvas, for what reason are they instead designated by the names of śrāvakas or ordinary worldlings?

Although this belongs to the stage of a bodhisattva, it is roughly similar to that of the Hīnayāna; thus, it is designated by such a name so that ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles to be converted in the future may understand the Great Vehicle by means of the Small Vehicle.
In the middle section of the praise for virtues, there is a specific praise for benefiting others; this is similar to what preceded it, as the general teaching of the Dharma was not discussed.
From here on is the second part, which specifically cites and praises [the qualities] individually, beginning first with the analysis of the initial basis.
Within this, there is first the question, secondly the exposition, and finally the conclusion.
From the words "not the eighth" onwards, he distinguishes [this stage] from the others; within this exposition, there are four parts:
first, "capable of honoring" and so forth, refers to the practice for one's own benefit—honoring the precepts to distance oneself from evil, establishing the Dharma, and cultivating goodness.
2. From "From the Buddha" onwards is the understanding for one's own benefit (*svārtha-vijñāna*);

3. From "Transforming for" onwards is the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha-caryā*), wherein he teaches the eight factors of enlightenment (*aṣṭa-bodhyaṅga*) to cause them to advance in goodness, and instructs those who have transgressed to repent so that they may abandon evil;

4. From "Skillfully knowing" onwards is the understanding for the benefit of others (*parārtha-vijñāna*), wherein he skillfully masters the protocols of the Bodhisattva’s expedient transformations, which is called "knowing the secret dharma of skillful means (*upāya-guhya-dharma*)."

The term "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) serves as a summary; there are both internal and external ordinary persons, and this refers to the internal ordinary person. Because they have no point of complete exhaustion within the fragmented retributions of the six realms of existence, they are called internal ordinary persons.
In the section distinguishing [the stages] below, the phrase "not the eighth person" distinguishes [this stage] from the preceding one.
Which is the eighth person that is said to be "not"?
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the *srotāpanna* is designated as the eighth, in contrast to the seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*) prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Therefore, that treatise asks: "What are the eight persons? They are the one of firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and the one of firm dharma (*dharmānusārin*). A person of dull faculties who has entered the path of seeing the truths is called one of firm faith; one of sharp faculties is called one of firm dharma.
According to foreign traditions, there are eight further [stages]:
first, the person who has just resolved their mind for enlightenment but has not yet engaged in practice;
second, the person who practices with signs, who loathes and detests birth-and-death (saṃsāra) and delights in cultivating wholesome dharmas.

Third, the practitioner of signlessness (*animitta-carin*) studies the contemplation of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), thereby abandoning both delight and aversion; seeing others commit evil, their mind feels no anger, and seeing others cultivate goodness, they likewise feel no exultation.

Fourth, the practitioner of skillful means (*upāya-carin*), although seeing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), constantly accords with existence (*bhava*) to initiate various virtuous practices; these four abide within the stage of the wholesome destiny (*sugati*).
Fifth is the stage of the cultivated lineage (*śikṣā-bīja*).
Sixth is the lineage of nature;
seventh is the stage of practice through understanding;
eighth is the noble lineage.
Because at the initial stage one has not yet conformed to the lineage of the noble ones (*āryavaṃśa*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), this is not the eighth [person].
The statement, "The person of the eighth stage is not called an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*)," demonstrates that the latter differs from the former.

By saying "not called an ordinary being," he distinguishes it from the initial stage; by saying "called a bodhisattva," he speaks according to their actual characteristics; and by saying "not called a Buddha," he distinguishes it from the subsequent stage.
In the second section on the basis (*āśraya*), there is first a restatement of the topic, followed by an explanation, and finally a summary.
The phrase "not yet attained" and below distinguishes this from others.
Within the detailed explanation, there are six distinct points: the first five concern the cultivation of goodness, while the last one concerns the avoidance of evil.
Regarding the first five [of the six perfections], the former four pertain to self-benefit and the latter one to benefiting others.
Within self-benefit, "if one attains the true Dharma" marks the beginning of one's own portion, for hearing the Dharma is termed "attaining";
"upholding the true Dharma" marks the end of one's own portion, for reciting it is termed "upholding."
"Listening to the Dharma from the Buddha" is the beginning of superior progress; "as it was heard," and so forth, is the end of superior progress—these constitute self-benefit.
From "transforming" [the teaching] onwards is the benefit of others, through which one may be known to have departed from evil.
"This is called" serves as a summary.
In the subsequent section distinguishing the differences, "not yet having attained the second or third dwelling places" distinguishes them from what follows.
Among the four fruits of the path, the *srotāpanna* has not yet attained the dwelling place of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the *sakṛdāgāmin* has not yet attained the dwelling place of the *anāgāmin*.

The phrase "named Bodhisattva and having already received the prediction" distinguishes him from what preceded; he is called a Bodhisattva because he differs from the previous state of an ordinary person, and he is given the Buddha's prediction because he is capable of accomplishing the eight phases of enlightenment and delivering sentient beings.

According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, bodhisattvas even prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) receive predictions from the Buddha; however, it is specifically those on the first stage and above who are able to receive numerous predictions extensively throughout the ten directions, and thus they alone are mentioned here.
Regarding the third section on the middle [stage], it consists first of a restatement, secondly an analysis, and finally a summary.
Within the analysis, there are three parts:

first, an analysis of its characteristics; second, the explanation of its name and meaning starting from "What is the meaning of 'Anāgāmin'? and below; and third, a further praise of its virtues starting from "Abiding and returning" and below.
Within the first section, the refutation of errors is presented first; the passage beginning with "If one says that there is no self, this is possible" clarifies the inclusion of antidotes.
Within the preceding refutation of errors, nine faults are first enumerated, and the conclusion "none of these are possible" summarizes the refutation.
Among these nine faults, the first eight indicate that one’s conduct and virtue are not pure, while the single phrase "speaking of self" indicates that one’s wisdom and understanding are not clear.

Within the first eight phrases, the initial three indicate that evil karma has not been eliminated; the middle two indicate that afflictions have not been exhausted; and the final three indicate that karmic retribution has not been purified.

Regarding the section on karma: first, the phrase "one who slanders the Dharma" refers to slandering the Buddha’s teachings; the passage beginning with "replies that he consents" refers to violating the Buddha’s practice of the Dharma. These two constitute a turning away from what is correct;
the single phrase "accepting external [teachings]" reveals his study of heterodox paths.
Within the afflictions (*kleśa*), "adventitious afflictions" (*āgantuka-kleśa*) arise from the five stages of dwelling.
They are called "adventitious" because they arise later; they are termed "dust" (*rajas*) because they defile and soil.
"The various ancient afflictions" refer to the five stages of dwelling as their ground; they are called "ancient" because they were established first.

Regarding "suffering," the initial statement "if one conceals the relics" means that the Dharma-body has not yet been manifested; "relics" (śarīra) is a name for the body. The Tathāgatagarbha-nature is the Buddha's Dharma-body, and its being covered by suffering is called "concealment."
The two phrases, "afflicted by external illnesses" and "invaded by the four great elements," indicate that the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is not yet purified.
The single phrase, "speaking of self," is not clearly understood.
"All such cases are impossible" summarizes and clarifies their avoidance.

In the subsequent section on "Gathering and Governing," "if one speaks of non-self" reverses the previous speaking of self; "if one speaks of worldly dharmas" reverses the acceptance of external scriptures; and "if one speaks of the Mahāyāna" reverses the slandering of the True Dharma.
Regarding the phrases "allowing to keep" and so forth: "the body one has received contains eighty thousand families of worms" reverses the previous point concerning the *śarīra* (relics).

"Furthermore, it is impossible" reverses the previous point concerning adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*). "Forever free from sexual desire" reverses the previous point concerning the separation from all old [defilements]. "Even in dreams, one does not lose seminal purity" reverses the separation from all former [impurities]. "It is impossible that at the time of death one would experience fear" reverses being afflicted by external diseases or being invaded by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
