At the beginning, "like a king" is a metaphor for the Buddha-Tathāgata; sentient beings whose karmic conditions are exhausted are said to have "contracted an illness"; the cessation of the Sage’s transformative influence is described as "passing away"; a Bodhisattva of the good realms who is destined to succeed the Buddha is called the "heir apparent"; when his transformative virtue is not yet perfected, he is said to be "young and immature"; and being unable yet to undertake the distant transformation, he is called "one who has not yet succeeded."
In the second phrase, the various evil bhikṣus are called “caṇḍālas.

Those whose mouths possess false eloquence are called “abundant in wealth and treasures”; alternatively, because such individuals amass vast assets, they are termed “abundant in wealth and treasures,” which is why it was stated above that they accept and store all manner of impure things.
Because of his great wealth, everyone supported and followed him; thus he was called "One with Many Retinues.

Because of his noble power and alliances, he was called "The Powerful. Because he waited for the legitimate ruler to decline and fall into ruin, he was called "Waiting for Vulnerability. Because he himself became the leader of the multitude, he was called "Usurper of the Throne."

In the third phrase, because the false teaching has not yet spread far and the correct teaching has already been abandoned, it is called "the treatment being of short duration. The passage beginning with "the people of the country" clearly explains the ruin of the assembly.
There are three grades among the multitude, namely: inferior, middling, and superior.
Those of the inferior class cannot bear to witness evil and thus flee to other places; hence it is said, "The people of the country fled far away to other kingdoms.
Those of the middling class have their bodies gathered together but their hearts are alienated; hence it is said, "Those who remain do not even wish to see this king with their own eyes."
Those of superior capacity are able to endure evil upon seeing it; their outward appearance remains unchanged from before, and this is called "not departing from the soil.
First there is the analysis, followed by the analogy; these three parts of the assembly are termed "correctly departing from destruction."

In the fourth phrase, that evil bhikṣu hearing the truth and turning away from it is called "knowing that many people of the country have fled and rebelled"; causing his evil faction to create obstacles is called "dispatching caṇḍālas to guard and patrol all roads."
Within the fifth phrase, there are further four distinct points:

first, the analogy of the sick person who invokes the sages; second, the analogy of the beginner who does not comply; third, the analogy of the harm incurred by non-compliance; and fourth, the analogy of the benefit gained through compliance.

At the beginning and middle [of the narrative], because the periods for moving the sages to respond were each fixed, it says "seven days. The triggering of the spiritual capacity to summon the sages is called "beating the drum"; the manifestation of the response from the sages is called "proclaiming the command. Looking upward to move four individuals to serve as his own preceptors, he thus spoke in this sense: "I request a brāhmaṇa who is capable of acting as my consecration master (*abhiṣeka-ācārya*). A master who can consecrate one's heart and crown with the Dharma is called a consecration master. To transform the people toward goodness and lead them back to that [teaching] is called "granting half the kingdom as a noble title and reward. Furthermore, since his followers would surely assist him together in the future, it is also termed "granting half the kingdom as a noble title and reward."

Second, regarding the initial practice of non-compliance: the phrase "none of the brahmins came" clarifies non-compliance through the body; the section beginning with "each made a statement" clarifies non-compliance through speech.

Third, because he does not follow examples that cause harm, the manifestation of the refutation of those harmful matters is called "speaking these words. Because those who have just begun their practice maintain correctness and do not follow [him], it is said, "there is not a single person who takes me as their teacher. Because they ruin the correct and align with the heterodox, it says, "I must cause" the various Brahmins "to dwell together with Caṇḍālas," and so forth; "dwelling together" clarifies the identity of their persons, while "sharing the same activities" clarifies the identity of their conduct.
Fourth, regarding the analogy of beneficial assimilation, the two explanations for "half the kingdom" and "not in vain" are the same as before.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* explains that the eternal Dharma which it elucidates must ultimately be cultivated together; this is termed "the medicine of immortality produced by incantations, which should be shared and consumed by all."
Second, within the section on the metaphors for propagating the teaching through the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*), there are two distinct parts:

first, the metaphor of the four reliances following the heterodox; second, from "At that time, the youth spoke to the king" onwards, the metaphor of refuting the heterodox and establishing the orthodox.

The first five lines of the preceding section are as follows: first, the analogy of being inwardly endowed with transformative virtue; second, the analogy of manifesting transformations according to sentient beings; third, the analogy of transformations corresponding to the capacities of sentient beings; fourth, the analogy of initial conduct provoking anger and resentment; and fifth, the analogy of transforming oneself into a virtuous teacher, also known as the analogy of the assembly collectively assisting one another.

Regarding the first phrase: the pure conduct of all Buddhas is called "Brahmin," and because they arise through transformation, they are called "sons of the Brahmin"; since their transformations do not occur simultaneously, it is said that there is "one."

The Dharma-body being full and magnificent is called "being in one's early prime"; upholding the precepts without transgression is called "cultivating pure conduct"; the great compassion extending downward to receive beings is called "the mark of long hair"; and being extensively versed in the holy teachings is called "skill in incantations."

In the second line, "going to the king's abode" refers to the manifestation [of the Buddha] in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; "hundred kings" is a figurative expression for the various dispositions of beings. To be able to respond humbly to whatever people seek is expressed as "the king commands me, and I can do it all."

In the third phrase, the transformation that accords with the inclinations of beings is called "the King’s Joy," and the beings' affectionate delight is called "receiving the youth as the consecration master."

In the fourth sentence, "When all the brahmins heard this, they became angry," their inner minds were filled with resentment and aversion; from the words "blaming this" onwards, they expressed their reproach through speech. Since their censure was directed at what is right as if it were wrong, they rebuked him, saying: "O Brahmin, how can you act as a teacher for a candāla?"

In the fifth sentence, the transformation of the good teacher is described as "dividing half the kingdom and giving it to this youth. This may also mean that he was authorized to lead the masses and govern alongside him, which is expressed as "dividing half the kingdom and giving it to the youth. Having transformed together for a long time, it is called "governing the kingdom together for many years."

The preceding section has dealt with the heterodox; now follows the second part, which refutes the heterodox and establishes the orthodox. This section contains four parts: first, the analogy for establishing the orthodox;

second, the analogy for destroying the heterodox, beginning from "At that time, the youth used other miscellaneous [means]"; third, the analogy for establishing the orthodox, beginning from "At that time, the youth reinstated the original crown prince as king"; and fourth, the analogy for expelling the heterodox, beginning from "At that time, the youth managed these affairs."

Regarding the first eight lines of the preceding section: the initial five lines encompass the correct [teaching] and bring it back to oneself; the final three lines employ that correctness to transform others.

Within the former group, the first line addresses resentment toward others and the obstruction of intimacy, manifesting the mind of sentient beings; thus it is called the "King of Speech" (*vāg-rāja*), and it may also be termed "speech" (*vāk*) because it can be communicated through verbal instruction.

"I have abandoned my family dharma to come and serve as the King’s teacher, instructing him in incantations and arts. By stating this, he demonstrates his own benefit to the King; it clarifies that he previously abandoned the True Dharma to follow the heterodox, and that his conversion and instruction in minor dharmas is what is meant by "abandoning the family dharma" to come and serve as the King’s teacher and instruct him in incantations and arts.

"Furthermore, Your Majesty still does not see those who are near": (1) because he harbors resentment toward others and distances himself from them, and has not yet conformed to the practice of the Mahāyāna, he is said to "not see those who are near.
(2) Regarding "he hears what is strange": because he hears with resentment, it is said, "Why do you not become intimate with him? (3) To state his own resentment:

the eternally abiding Dharma realized by the Buddha is called "the Immortal Medicine of the Former King"; because he has not yet practiced it together [with others], it is called "not eating in common."

4. From "The King said, 'Excellent'" below, there is the entrusting of the transformation to the four reliances (*catur-yoni*). Because he rejoices upon hearing the teaching and follows it, he proclaims, "Excellent" (*sādhu*). To manifest that he has not realized the intent of the transformation until now, he says, "Truly I did not know. To entrust the Mahāyāna Dharma-transformation back to the Bodhisattvas, he says, "I pray you, take this and go.
5. From "At that time" below, there is the gathering of the correct [teaching] and its return to oneself. Gathering the Dharma for oneself is called, "taking it and returning home."
The preceding section summarizes the correct practice and applies it to oneself; from the following three phrases onward, one uses the correct practice to transform others.
First, regarding "inviting the great minister to eat together," this is to transform his disciples; because the disciples' afflictions are slight, they are transformed first.
Gathering others through the Dharma is called "inviting ministers"; practicing the Mahāyāna oneself and encouraging others to practice it together is called "sharing food";

when the two disciples exhort the teacher and clarify the matter through reasoning, it is called "sharing with the sovereign," and because they praise the existence of the Dharma upon which he relies, they say, "How wonderful! Great Master, you possess this medicine of immortality.

Third, when the teacher hears their joy and accepts it, encouraging them to likewise attain awakening and understanding, it is called "knowing one's own kin"; lamenting that they did not hear it sooner, they say, "Why did you alone, along with your ministers, consume the nectar of immortality without allowing us a share?"
The preceding first analogy clarifies the penetration of the correct; from here on, the second analogy clarifies the crushing of the heterodox.

Teaching the method for reproaching transgressions based on what was previously explained is called "mixed poisonous medicine"; causing them to hear and accept it is called "administering it to them. When those evil bhikṣus hear that it is being administered to them, they suddenly feel shame, hence the term "for a brief moment. The Dharma operating within the mind is called "the medicine taking effect"; the arising of remorse and shame in the mind is called "confusion and distress. Realizing one's own degradation and retreating from high-mindedness is called "falling to the ground"; because the depth of their remorse and shame is profound, they "lack awareness, like a dead person."
From here below is the third analogy, which clarifies the establishment of the orthodox.

Within this, first, the establishment of the orthodox replaces the heterodox and aligns with that [path to] the good destinies; it is called "establishing the heir apparent and restoring him as king" because the Bodhisattva establishes the stages to rectify and succeed the Buddha’s name. It is termed "restoring" (*huan*) because it returns to the original, correct transformation.
The section beginning with "He spoke these words" rebukes the heterodox and exhorts toward the correct. First, he rebukes the heterodox:

the seat of the True Dharma is, by its very nature, not a place for those who have broken the precepts; therefore, it is said, "It is not according to the Dharma that a *caṇḍāla* should ascend the royal throne. That one who has broken the precepts and is an evil person should serve as the leader of the assembly has never occurred since antiquity; therefore, it is said, "From of old, we have never heard of or seen a *caṇḍāla* acting as king. It is logically impossible for an evil person to govern the masses; therefore, it is said, "There is no such principle as a *caṇḍāla* ruling a state and governing the people."

The following clarifies the exhortation for Bodhisattvas to properly rectify and continue the Buddha’s transformation of beings, which is why it says: "You should now succeed the former king and rule the country according to the Dharma.
From here on, the fourth parable clarifies the expulsion of the heterodox.

"At that time, the youth having managed these matters" refers to the preceding section on managing affairs, which follows the account of his previous life; having finished managing the task of abolishing the heterodox and establishing the orthodox, "he further gave the medicine of liberation to Caṇḍāla" means that the method for repenting sins is called the "medicine of liberation," and bestowing it upon him so that he may repent is called "giving to Caṇḍāla. The joyful state of mind resulting from the removal of sin is described as "awakening. Although he had committed a grave offense, even after he had completed his repentance, he still had to be expelled and kept at a distance from the pure assembly; this is termed "having been driven out."
From here below is the third analogy, clarifying that the four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni) involve no transgression in one’s own practice.

Regarding the phrase, “Although this boy acts thus,” although he performs the aforementioned acts associated with the heterodox, because he proceeds from the heterodox toward the orthodox—thereby establishing both gain and loss—he is called “although” (sui).
To personally act without transgression is called "not yet losing the dharma of a brāhmaṇa.
From here below, the fourth analogy clarifies that the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) are collectively worthy of veneration.

A bodhisattva who has newly begun practice is called a "layperson" (*gṛhapati*). When brāhmaṇas and others behold his skillful transformations, they call him "one who has heard what was to be done. When they marvel at his peerless excellence, they call him "one for whom there has never been before. Under the phrase "praising him as 'good,'" the specific content of their praise is set forth.
Below there are four points of correspondence, which do not follow the previous order:
first corresponds to the first [point];
"guarding the Dharma" and below correspond to the second [point] mentioned previously.
The passage beginning with "At that time, if the Bodhisattva sees... skips ahead to correspond with the fourth section, clarifying the correspondence regarding making offerings;
the passage beginning with "If there is someone who sees one who protects the Dharma" returns to correspond with the third section, clarifying that there is, in fact, no transgression.

Within the first section, the phrase "after my parinirvāṇa" corresponds to the previous account of the king falling ill and passing away, while the crown prince was still too young to assume the succession.

In the second section, the phrase "The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was likewise" corresponds to the following: there was a son of a Brahmin in his early twenties who practiced pure conduct and had long hair and so forth.

"By the power of skillful means, he associates with monks who have broken the precepts in their activities. They go together to the king's residence, and so forth, until they have worked together for many years; the rest is omitted as it does not accord [with the context].
In the third section, there are four distinct parts:

first, an exhortation to make offerings; second, the conclusion that correlates with the preceding statements, beginning with "For this reason"; third, the citation of an analogy as a topical application, beginning with "Just as that"; and fourth, the manifestation of the Dharma by means of the analogy, beginning with "Excellent!"

Within the first section, the phrase "at that time, the bodhisattva" identifies the person being exhorted; this refers to the donor as a "bodhisattva," meaning that among those who are śrāvakas, one who studies the Mahāyāna is the donor.

"If one sees someone who, though having committed many offenses... refers to the person being offered support; "immediately goes" and following is the formal exhortation to provide offerings; "reverently prostrates" clarifies bodily offering; and "the four requisites" and following clarify material offering.
There are three kinds of material offerings:

first, offering what one personally possesses; second, requesting and giving what one does not possess; third, from the passage beginning "for this purpose" onwards, it clarifies that for the sake of making offerings, one may keep eight types of impure items.
Within this, there are four points:
first, it clarifies that one may possess eight kinds of impure items.
What are these eight?
As listed in full in that *Sujāta-upāsaka-sūtra*, they are:
first, the keeping of fields and houses;
second, the planting of roots and sprouts.
Third, to store up rice and millet and occupy supervisory positions to seek profit;
fourth, to keep male and female slaves and subjects;
fifth, to raise herds of livestock.
Sixth, he keeps gold, silver, coins, and treasures;
seventh, he keeps ivory, gold, silver, various engraved jewels, large beds, cotton mattresses, and woolen rugs;
eighth, he keeps all kinds of copper coins, cauldrons, and cooking pots.
One is called "impure" because possessing these eight kinds of things defiles pure precepts.
Second, the section beginning with "Why... provides the explanation.
Third, the section beginning with "At that time... clarifies that there is no offense in possessing them.
4. From "Why" onwards is the explanation.

The preceding section exhorted offerings; from here on is the second part, which concludes the discourse by correlating it with the aforementioned words. "By these conditions" refers to the causal conditions for the Dharma—namely, using these four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) to subdue the heterodox and establish the orthodox.
Regarding the statement, "In this sutra, I have spoken these two verses to cause all bodhisattvas to make offerings to the Dharma":
the latter two [verses] are understood; this concludes the third [section]. Within the fourth section, concerning non-offense through one's own practice, there are four distinct points:

first, citing the offense of slandering to demonstrate that there is no offense; second, from "protecting the Dharma" onwards, clarifying that while there is actually no offense, one incurs the offense of slandering; third, from "there is a bhikṣu" onwards, citing an offense to manifest the upholding [of the precepts]; fourth, from "bodhisattva" onwards, clarifying how upholding differs from offending.
First, the non-offense is clarified; the section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation.

From the preceding phrase "As I have previously said" up to this point constitutes the first section, clarifying that these four persons uphold [the precepts] rather than violating them, and therefore they should be venerated.
From this point downward is the second section, which clarifies that these four individuals are elders and not juniors, and therefore should be venerated.

These four are in fact those who have long practiced; however, in order to transform those who are beginners, I have spoken in my sutras by concealing their true status, saying, "If they are young, they should be venerated. The previous passage reconciled this from the perspective of the teaching, while this passage reconciles it from the perspective of the object of veneration.
"By these causes and conditions," the third section below concludes and correlates the preceding two parts; regarding the first, it concludes:
"Because the śrāvakas do not understand the causes and conditions for the provisional transformation of the four reliances, I do not now speak verses for the sake of the śrāvakas;
because the bodhisattvas do understand them, I do speak verses for their sake."
Within this section, there are two sets of questions and answers:
the first clarifies that these four types of persons together may be supported;

the second clarifies that the four types of persons of reliance possess their fundamental precepts in full, thereby fulfilling the criteria for being worthy of support. This is because the Bodhisattva originally received and practiced precepts that accord with the universal Dharma; since his current conduct accords with those original precepts, they remain fully intact.

In the text, Kāśyapa first asks about the motivation, taking the phrase "such a bodhisattva is extremely lax regarding the precepts" as one sentence; this refers back to the aforementioned matter, equating it with an evil transgression of the precepts, which is termed "extreme laxity.
"Is the original precept still present? constitutes the second sentence, serving as the formal inquiry.
The Buddha first rebuked him, saying, "Why do you act so inferiorly? This is the explanation for what preceded. First there is the question, followed by the interpretation.
Within the interpretation, there are two parts:

first, corresponding to the subsequent phrase, it clarifies that the precepts are fully present; second, from the phrase "slack in regard to the vehicle" (*yāne śithila*) onwards, it corresponds to the preceding phrase to clarify that the precepts are not lax.

In the first part, the initial section clarifies that the precepts are complete because one’s own practice is pure; the section beginning with “like a dyke” clarifies that the precepts are complete because one causes others’ precepts to be pure; and the section beginning with “if there are those who purely uphold the precepts” concludes by clarifying the presence of the precepts.

Within the section on purifying one's own conduct: "The precepts originally received are not lost as they were" clarifies exclusive protection and maintenance; "if there should be... and following clarify repentance after having committed an offense.
Regarding the purification of others, there is first the analogy and subsequently the application.
Within the preceding analogy, it first clarifies through contrast the harm incurred by failing to treat [the problem].
A mound that obstructs water is called a "dyke" (*setu*), which serves as a metaphor for the various dharmas.

The impairment of the various dharmas is called "perforated," and "having holes" refers to this; "water" is a metaphor for the Saṃgha, and the deficiency in the conduct of the Saṃgha is called "leaking.

The section beginning with "Why... provides the explanation, while the section beginning with "If there is... clarifies the benefits of upholding [the precepts] accordingly. Taking the four reliances as the basis and employing the Dharma as the means of governance, when the conduct of the Saṃgha is free from impairment, it is called "the water does not leak out."

Within the section on "Concordance with the Inferior," first is the concordance regarding treatment and benefit: "The Bodhisattva is also like this" corresponds to the aforementioned person; "although they share the same monastic affairs as those [of the Śrāvakas] regarding their precepts, all their disciplinary rules are not like a dam that has been pierced and is leaking" corresponds to water not flowing out.

The subsequent section on "not curing the damage at its inception" uses the phrase "For what reason? (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) to interrogate the preceding and introduce the following; for what reason is the precept not like a dam?
The passage beginning with "If there were none... cites the latter to reveal the former, thereby explaining it through a counter-argument.
"If there are no people who maintain pure precepts" corresponds to the first phrase [of the simile], as there is no one to repair it.
"The Sangha would then suffer decay" and so forth corresponds to the first phrase, where the eaves have holes and water leaks through.

In the third section of the *Sūtra on the Three Bonds*, the phrase "if there is a person who maintains pure precepts" cites the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), while the subsequent phrase "is then able" and so forth concludes by clarifying that the precepts are present.
The following section contrasts with the first phrase to clarify that the precepts are not lax; this section is divided into three parts.
First, a general principle is established: "To be lax regarding the Vehicle is what constitutes laxity; to be lax regarding the precepts is not called laxity."
Being unable to harmonize with the light of the world to penetrate the Great Vehicle is called laxity regarding the vehicle; viewing the Dharma with negligence and indifference is called laxity;

furthermore, contravening the Bodhisattva’s correct precepts of the Great Vehicle is called laxity; and violating the precepts while claiming to penetrate the Dharma is called laxity regarding the precepts.
Because of his intense zeal for the Dharma, he is not called lax; furthermore, because he accords with the Bodhisattva’s Mahāyāna right precepts, he is not called lax.
Second, it is clarified that when a Bodhisattva is not lax regarding the vehicle, he may be said to be not lax regarding the precepts.

To destroy the precepts for the sake of the Dharma is called "not being indolent or arrogant regarding the Mahāyāna mind. Because one made such a solemn vow at the time of originally receiving the precepts—vowing to uphold them as the Great Precepts—it is called the "original precept" (*mūla-śīla*); because it is called the original precept, one does not slacken in regard to the precepts.
Third, from "For the sake of protecting the Dharma" onwards, it clarifies that such a person extinguishes transgressions through the Dharma so that their precepts do not become lax.

Because they "bathe themselves with the water of the Mahāyāna for the sake of protecting the Dharma," they attain freedom from fault. The Mahāyāna they propagate can remove the defilement of transgressions, and is therefore called "water. Protecting the Dharma and extinguishing transgressions is what is meant by "bathing oneself"; because one bathes oneself with this Mahāyāna water, although one may have broken [the precepts], they do not become lax.
The preceding section exhorted one to make offerings; this second part below teaches how to examine [the recipient]. One might ask:
"Since they have already been examined previously, why labor to examine them again?
The commentary explains:
In the former case, Māra transformed himself into a semblance of reliance, coming with evil to disrupt the correct; therefore, one was taught to examine.
Now, these four reliances may likewise be violated by those who break the precepts, using the correct to masquerade as the false; thus, they must also be examined.
Kāśyapa first made his request, and the Tathāgata subsequently gave the instruction; following the words "Kāśyapa," Kāśyapa again received and understood it, offering praise.
Within the request, the initial statement, "Among the assembly of monks there are four kinds of persons," was somewhat vague regarding the Dharma explanation.

Those who are mature internally but immature externally, those who are mature externally but immature internally, those who are both immature internally and externally, and those who are both mature internally and externally—these four types of persons are explained through the analogy of the *āmra* (mango) fruit to illustrate their confusion.
"By what means can one recognize those who break the precepts and those who uphold them? Thus he requested the Buddha’s instruction.
In the Buddha’s teaching below, it says: "By means of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they can be easily known. This summarizes the teaching on the method of verification.

Regarding the section "What is the cause," this is the method of verification according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*). It first poses a question and subsequently provides an analysis; it discusses the general principles of verification and the verification of teachings, asserting that one must rely on the extensive scriptures of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) to definitively determine what is right and wrong.

To verify conduct, one must apply four types of observation: living together, long-term association, wisdom, and investigation; these are the four. Living together and long-term association verify physical conduct, while wisdom and investigation verify mental conduct.

The body has the distinction between that which is difficult to know and that which is easy to perceive; that which is easy to perceive is known through cohabitation, whereas cohabitation alone is insufficient without prolonged association.

Within the mind, there is likewise the distinction between the difficult and the easy; that which is easy to recognize is known through the verification of wisdom, while if wisdom does not comprehend it, one must apply analytical observation.
Verifying the mind in accordance with the teachings is called wisdom; investigating and seeking through reasoning is termed observation.
In the following text, one is instructed to examine their conduct through four types of observation, among which there are three similes.
First is the simile of the farmer, which instructs one to examine them by living and dwelling together for a long time.
The second forest analogy teaches through wisdom;
the third medicinal herb analogy teaches through observation.
Within the first of these, the initial analogy—extending up to the phrase "called a pure field"—illustrates communal dwelling.

The Sangha is like a field because it can produce merit; those who plant merit are like "farmers. Providing for the Sangha to generate merit is like "planting rice seedlings. Evil conduct within the Sangha is like "weed and tares"; selecting out the evil to provide for the good is called "weeding. Superficial observation that mistakes the coarse for the fine is called "observation with the physical eye."

The passage beginning with "Named 'Pure Field,' until its ripening" uses a metaphor to clarify long-term coexistence. Just as the awn of grain or the *pāṣa* weed among rice cannot be distinguished until they have matured, when they finally differ; so too is it with these subtle evils, which are difficult to recognize and only become known as distinct after a long period of coexistence.

When combining these with the following section next, first combine the initial portion: "These eight matters can defile the Saṃgha. This corresponds to the preceding passage on weeds and chaff. Possessing the eight types of impure items is termed the "eight matters"; just as weeds defile a field, they are said to defile the Saṃgha.

"If one can remove [defilements]" corresponds to "cultivating and removing"; "if one observes with the physical eye, one immediately knows it is pure" corresponds to observing with the physical eye being named a "pure field."
"If there is one who maintains [the precepts]" below combines the latter section with the preceding, leading up to "each becomes distinct.

From "maintaining the precepts or breaking them; when one does not commit evil" onwards, it distinguishes that which is difficult to differentiate because it has not yet matured. From "if the evil is manifest" onwards, it properly combines the matured state where grass and grain are distinct. "If the evil is exposed, then it is easy to know" combines the grass as being distinct from the grain. "Like the *sūna* (awned rice)" and following provide an analogy to illustrate this point.
"The same applies within the Saṃgha" means that grain should be kept separate from weeds; because the Saṃgha is like a pure field, it is said "the same applies.
"If one stays away from impurity" clarifies the avoidance of faults; the eight types of impure things that can cause harm are called "the dharma of poisonous snakes."

The section beginning with "This is named" concludes by praising and manifesting its excellence; the section beginning with "should be" clarifies that it merits offerings; and the section beginning with "not with the fleshly eye" clarifies that only those who have long dwelt [in the Dharma] are able to recognize it.
In the examination through wisdom, there is first the analogy and then the application.
Within the analogy, there are four parts:

first, the analogy of the intermingling of the false and the correct; second, from "its fruit ripens" onwards, the analogy of the ignorant spreading [the truth] erroneously; third, from "the foolish and deluded" onwards, the analogy of the ignorant person who cannot distinguish; and fourth, from "the wise person" onwards, the analogy of the wise person who can distinguish.
In the beginning and middle [of this passage], "kāra" (迦羅) is a metaphor for a monk who has broken the precepts; because such a breaker of the precepts is numerous, he is called "many trees.

"Cinduka" (鎮頭) is a metaphor for those who rely upon the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*); because their reliance on the transformative teachings is not uniform, they are called "one," yet because their reliance on the transformative teachings is identical to that of the heterodox, they are called "fruits that resemble one another and cannot be distinguished."

In the second section concerning the confused transmission due to ignorance, the basis and the person of false views are described according to their own understanding; the one who initiates the teaching is called "When the Fruit Ripens.
"There was a woman" is a metaphor for the person who transmits the confusion.
The term "woman" has many meanings; herein, it is used specifically as a metaphor for that which is perverse and devoid of wisdom.

To include both the perverse and the correct is called "gathering them all. Because the perverse is predominant while the correct is scarce, it is said that "of the *cintā* there is but one part, while of the *kāra* there are ten parts. When the perverse and the correct are confusedly transmitted, it is called "the woman does not know. To proclaim this among the multitude is called "going to the market to sell."

In the third phrase, "foolish children" is a metaphor for those who receive [the teachings] indiscriminately; because children lack wisdom, they are used as a comparison, and their failure to recognize [the truth] is the same as before, thus termed "furthermore not distinguishing."
"Abandoning the correct and taking the deviant" is termed "buying kāla"; falling into the three evil realms due to receiving deviant teachings is termed "devouring at the end of life.

In the fourth phrase, "the wise" is a metaphor for those capable of discernment; knowing that the foolish person has suffered harm by accepting the deviant, it is said "hearing this matter. Because they have inferred where [the fruit] was obtained from, it says, "From where did you bring this fruit?"

The answer regarding the location where it was heard is called "indicating the direction and place. Because the wise know that there is much that is false and little that is correct therein, they say: "In this direction there are many *kāla* [trees], and only one *ciñcā*."
"Discarding the perverse and not accepting [it]" is called "laughing and departing.
Among these, one should only combine the first, third, and fourth, but not the second.

In the first section, the phrase "entering into impure practices within the great assembly is likewise" corresponds to the Kara Forest; this text is abbreviated, for if it were complete, it should state: "those who accept and store the eight kinds of impure things are likewise," as there are many in that assembly who do so.
"These eight dharmas" correspond to many trees;
"only one who maintains the precepts and does not accept impurity" corresponds to a single tree named *cūta*.
"Knowing that they maintain what is not the Dharma, yet remaining in the same practice without parting from them" corresponds to the similarity of the result.
"Just as that forest" and below provide the illustration to apply [the analogy]; this concludes the first section.
Next, combining the second and third [cases], the foolish do not distinguish between them.

"There was a lay follower (upāsaka)" is combined with the ignorant child; "seeing that these people mostly acted contrary to the Dharma and were not respectful" is combined with the failure to purchase the kāra fruit; and "having eaten it, his life came to an end" refers to failing to honor and support these four types of persons worthy of reliance (catur-śaraṇa).

In the analogy, the encounter with what is taken indiscriminately is revealed; in the application, the error of discarding everything together is clarified. Both cases involve a failure to distinguish, and thus they are presented as alternatives.
The following section corresponds to the fourth [case], where the wise person is able to distinguish; herein are four propositions:
first, the instruction to inquire carefully, "Does the Buddha permit the keeping of the eight impure things?"
Second, if he says that it is permitted, one should further instruct him to be questioned as follows: "Is such a person allowed to participate in the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā*?
Third, if he says that they are permitted, one should again instruct him to receive the scriptures in order to verify his statement.
"Having been asked thus, they all said that the Tathāgata permitted these eight things," citing their erroneous answers.
Below, the instruction for examination follows:
"'The bhikṣus at Jetavana said that gold and silver were permitted by the Buddha to be kept,' citing past erroneous speech; 'or they said they were not permitted,' citing past correct speech."

The phrase "there are those who listen" refers back to the former heterodox individuals; "these are those who do not listen" refers back to the former orthodox individuals. The expression "not associating with them" and so forth clarifies the correct expulsion of the heterodox; "not dwelling together with them for the recitation of the precepts or the *pravāraṇā* ceremony" clarifies that their Dharma is different; and "not even drinking from the same river" and so forth clarifies that their practical affairs are different.
"How can you say that the Buddha permitted you to keep [these things]?"—this uses the past to challenge the present.

The four teachings admonish and exhort: "Although the Buddha, the God among Gods, may accept them, you members of the Saṃgha should not keep them. This corresponds to the first response above, which exhorted not to accept them oneself: the Buddha may accept them for the sake of benefiting others, but the Saṃgha, acting for its own sake, should not keep them.

The passage beginning with "If there is one who experiences" provides a subsequent response by contrasting the inferior with the superior; it clarifies that those who experience [suffering] should not associate, first exhorting them not to associate.
The passage beginning with "If they speak together" clarifies that associating causes harm, first through the Dharma and subsequently through a simile.
In the examination and verification, first the analogy is established, followed by the application, and finally the exhortation.
Within the analogy, according to the application, there should be three parts:

first, the analogy of the intermingling of the false and the correct; second, the analogy of the fool who cannot distinguish between them; and third, the analogy of the wise person who can distinguish them.
In this present passage, only the first two [analogies] are provided, while the third is omitted.

Within the first section: "the city" is a metaphor for the assembly; "a man selling medicine" is a metaphor for the Dharma-preacher; "exquisite sweet medicine produced from the Snowy Mountains" is a metaphor for the preaching of the True Dharma as it emerges from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; and "also selling miscellaneous medicines" is a metaphor for preaching false teachings. Because false words accord with worldly sentiments, they are called "sweet-tasting"; because false doctrines masquerade as the truth, they are called "resembling."

Regarding the second type of fool who does not distinguish within the parable: "The people wished to buy [the medicine] but did not recognize it" refers to their failure to distinguish at the beginning; "when they came to the sale of the medicine," and so forth, refers to their failure to distinguish in the interim. This consists of the initial question and the subsequent answer.

Regarding the phrase "this person," [the text] gives them false teachings, which is termed "using mixed medicines"; because it praises what is not correct as being correct, it says, "This is the sweet medicine of the Snowy Mountains."
"Selling at the time" refers to taking up a dark and obscured mind that fails to discern the heterodox from the orthodox; hence it is said, "the fleshly eye cannot distinguish well.
Hearing the teaching and receiving it in faith is called "buying and carrying it away."

Regarding the phrase "He further said," it means that at the end [of his life], he did not distinguish between right and wrong, taking what is incorrect for what is correct; thus he said, "I have obtained the sweet medicine of the Snowy Mountains.

Within this section, there are two parts; first, the correspondence with the initial segment: "If the assembly of śrāvakas" corresponds to the previous city. Even those who rely on the four reliances (caturniśraya) are called śrāvakas, because these four reliances appear in the world to transform sentient beings as śrāvakas.

"The Sangha of Designation" corresponds to those in the city who sell poisonous drugs; they lack the actual virtue of a monk yet are falsely given the name "monk," hence they are called the "Sangha of Designation.
"The True Sangha" corresponds to those who sell the wondrous medicine of the Snowy Mountains; these people of the four reliances truly possess monastic virtue and are thus called the "True Sangha."

Regarding "the harmonious Saṃgha," it is a convergence of similar flavors; when the heterodox and the orthodox intersect, it is called the harmonious Saṃgha, and there are no other persons [distinct from them].

From the phrase "if one maintains the precepts" onwards, this corresponds to the second section of the preceding text, which clarifies the distinction between the ignorant and the wise; first the correspondence is established, and then the application follows.
The section beginning with "Who is the upholder" constitutes the third segment, which combines what was previously omitted to clarify the capacity for discernment.
"Who upholds and who destroys" is distinguished according to their conduct;
"who is genuine and who is counterfeit" is distinguished according to the person.
This enumerates what is known.
The phrase "only those with the divine eye can discern" clarifies their capacity for knowledge; that is to say, only those of the three vehicles who possess the pure divine eye are able to know.
The three phrases within the exhortation are:
first, it clarifies that one should not provide alms, prostrate to, or make offerings to those who will break the precepts in the future;
second, it clarifies that one should likewise not provide alms, prostrate to, or make offerings to those who accept and store impure things.

The third admonition regarding the precepts states that those who have broken the precepts should not be revered or prostrated to simply because they wear the kashaya; since the transgression of breaking the precepts is so grave, this case is singled out for emphasis.
From this point downward is the third section: the summary understanding and praise.
"Excellent" (sādhu) is an expression of praise.

The remaining words constitute the summary understanding: "expounding the reception of the true self" is the summary understanding through the discourse on the Dharma; "like a vajra," etc., is the summary understanding through the discourse on similes.
The preceding section has correctly clarified the basis of the person through direct questioning; from here on is the second section, which provides a reconciliation with the past.
Since the terminology of the past teachings and the present person differ, they must be reconciled, which also clarifies the dharma upon which their practice relies.
Kāśyapa asked first; within his question, he first raised the previous teaching that [the Dharma] is not for four kinds of persons, posing a challenge to those persons.

In the preceding section, "one should rely on the four dharmas" summarizes the former statement; from "what are they? onwards is the specific explanation; and from "in this way" onwards is the conclusion.
The Buddha descends for the sake of the assembly; therein, one should first explain the meaning of the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*), as discussed in a separate chapter.
This passage has two parts:

first, the distinction that the Dharma is identical to the person in order to form the assembly. Since the Dharma currently under discussion is identical to these four persons, those who rely on the present Dharma likewise rely on these four persons.
Because the Dharma previously analyzed was distinct from the four types of persons, one relies on the person of the present rather than the Dharma of the past.
Second, the Dharma is distinguished from the person for the sake of reconciliation; since person and Dharma are distinct, the person is the fleshly eye and the Dharma is the wisdom-eye.
The preceding section consists of two parts:

first, distinguishing the four reliances by deriving their function from their essence; second, from "Furthermore, relying on the meaning" onwards, distinguishing the four reliances by seeking the cause based on the fruit.
Within the first section, there is first the exposition and later the conclusion.
In the exposition, the reliance upon the Dharma is clarified first; since the Dharma is the essence of the Great Parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, it is expounded first.

Next, the meaning based on the substance is explained. "Meaning" refers to the dharmakāya, liberation, and prajñā—all the various virtues. Since these virtues exist in dependence upon the substance, they are discussed next.

Next, the reliance upon wisdom is explained. "Wisdom" refers to the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas; because the application of the knowledge contained in the *āgamas* arises based on this merit, it is discussed next.

Fourth, the reliance upon sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is explained. "Sūtra" refers to the Mahāyāna teachings of all Buddhas; because these are spoken based on wisdom, they are explained next.
Regarding the first section, "Relying on the Dharma," there are four distinct parts in the text:
first, the explicit teaching that one should rely on the Dharma and not on persons;

second, from the passage "the four kinds of persons as described above" onwards, the distinction between the authentic and the spurious, clarifying that the aforementioned instruction not to rely on persons refers to not relying on false persons, and does not mean not relying on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

3. "That which relies on the Dharma is the Dharma-nature" and below clarify that one relies on the person and not on the Dharma; that is, one relies on the aforementioned person who is the Dharma-nature itself, rather than relying on the aforementioned Dharma which is the person.

4. "If a person breaks the precepts for the sake of benefiting others" and below distinguish the false from the true, clarifying that the aforementioned reliance on the person refers to relying on a person who is truly the Dharma-nature, and does not mean relying on a person who has broken the precepts.
Within the first section, the reliance upon the Dharma is first elucidated; there are four distinct points:
first, the manifestation of the essence of the Dharma, which refers to the Great Nirvana;

second, from the word "all" onwards, it clarifies that the Great Nirvana is identical to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). All Buddha-dharmas are as previously described regarding Nirvana: the *dharmatā* is its beginningless *dharmatā*. By manifesting this fundamental *dharmatā*, Nirvana is established; therefore, it is identical to the *dharmatā*. This is to distinguish it from the Nirvana of the cessation of fetters through remedial means, which is why it is said to be identical to the *dharmatā*.

Third, the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is identical to the Tathāgata; because the Dharma manifests to form the person, it is identified with him. It is identified with the Tathāgata to distinguish it from the *dharmatā* realized by the followers of the Hīnayāna, and furthermore, it is identified with the Tathāgata to clarify that the Buddha is identical to the Dharma and thus a reliable refuge.

Fourth, the Buddha is identical to the eternal; since the Tathāgata is the Buddha and the Buddha is identical to the *dharmatā*, he is therefore eternal and unchanging. This eternity must be taught to distinguish him from the impermanent transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Tathāgata.

The passage beginning with "If it is further said" clarifies not relying on persons: Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas claim that the Buddha is impermanent and do not perceive the Dharma-nature; because they do not perceive this nature, one should not rely upon them.

Within the second section, which distinguishes the authentic from the spurious, the first part clarifies that these four types of persons are the Dharma upon which one may rely. The passage beginning with "If there is anyone who can fully understand" illustrates the superior by means of the inferior to clarify that these four are reliable; specifically, it cites the five stages of bodhisattvas in the good destinies as a comparison for these four persons.

Regarding the first part of the middle section, the statement "the four persons who appear in the world as previously described should be relied upon" correctly clarifies that they are worthy of reliance.

The passage beginning with "Why? provides the explanation; therein, it first raises an objection: if it was previously stated that one should rely on the Dharma and not on the person, for what reason is it now said that persons may be relied upon?
The subsequent explanation has two parts:

first, it clarifies that such individuals can rely upon because they are able to understand the profound meaning; second, from the passage "These four persons are themselves the Tathāgata" onwards, it clarifies that they can rely upon because they are able to decipher the esoteric teachings.

Regarding the initial statement in the first section, "skillfully understanding the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata," this refers to knowing the aforementioned *Nirvāṇa* [sūtra] which says, "One can know that the Tathāgata is permanent and unchanging," and so forth—thus knowing the permanence of the Buddha mentioned previously. This follows the sequence of the original and then reverses it; although there were four phrases previously, for now we shall explain "knowing" by contrasting the very beginning and the end.

Within the section on "Knowledge of the Lower [Realms]," the first part clarifies that "the four types of persons are themselves named Tathāgatas. The section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation, consisting first of a formal inquiry and subsequently the resolution.

"Able to understand the secret language" clarifies that their understanding is identical to that of the Buddha; "and able to speak" clarifies that their speech is identical to that of the Buddha. Because they are identical to the Buddha in these respects, they are named Tathāgatas.

To illustrate the mediocre by means of the inferior, one first presents the inferior: "If there be a person" refers to those of the five grades within the state of the happy realms; "able to know the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury" means knowing the aforementioned *Nirvāṇa*; and "knowing that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging," etc., means knowing the aforementioned eternity of the Buddha. Having first followed the sequence and subsequently reversed it, the text now cites the inferior to illustrate the superior: "Even such a person as this may yet be relied upon, how much more so the four types of persons."
The third section concerns relying on the person rather than the teaching, and its text contains three pairs of contrasts:
first, the superior person and the dharma, where it says, "Relying on the dharma means relying on the *dharmatā*; not relying on the person means [relying on] the *śrāvaka*";

second, using the aforementioned dharma as the person upon whom one relies, namely, "the *dharmatā* is the Tathāgata"; and third, using the aforementioned person as the dharma realized, namely, "the *śrāvaka* is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)," because the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle involve the constant flux of impermanence and are thus called "conditioned."

Regarding the three knowledges (trividyā), as previously mentioned, there is the sense that persons and dharmas may be either reliable or unreliable. Because the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, he is reliable; because conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are impermanent, they are unreliable.

Within the fourth section, "Distinguishing the False from the True," the phrase "if a person violates the precepts" clarifies their lack of practice; "preaching that the Buddha is impermanent for the sake of gain and support" clarifies their lack of understanding. "Such a person should not be relied upon; this meaning is definitive, hence it is called the 'definition'"—this clarifies that those who rely on a person as a refuge should rely on the Tathāgata, and not on such a person who violates the precepts.
Regarding the clarification of "relying on the meaning and not on the words," there is first a presentation and then an explanation.
First, the reliance on the meaning is clarified, which begins with an analysis and concludes with a summary.
Within the analysis, there are six parts:
The first three are the three aspects of *nirvāṇa*: "the meaning is called awakening" (*bodha*) refers to *prajñā*;

because *prajñā* observes and illuminates, it is called awakening. "Awakening to the meaning is called not being weak or inferior" refers to *vimukti*; because all obstructions and burdens have been exhausted, one is not weak or inferior.
To say "not being weak or inferior is called fulfillment" refers to the *dharmakāya*; because the *dharmakāya* is perfectly complete, it is termed fulfillment.

The latter three are the merits of the Three Jewels: "The meaning of fulfillment is called the Tathāgata’s permanence" refers to the Jewel of the Buddha; "The Tathāgata’s permanence is itself the permanence of the Dharma" refers to the Jewel of the Dharma; and "The permanence of the Dharma is itself the Saṃgha" refers to the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
The section beginning with "This is called" concludes [the preceding].
From "What is it? onwards, the non-reliance on words is elucidated, consisting first of a question and subsequently of an exposition.
Within this exposition, there are three parts:
First, that which is "worldly," namely various treatises with flowery and ornate rhetoric, is not to be relied upon;

second, that which is "as spoken by the Buddha" yet is actually false and heterodox sutras falsely claiming to be the Buddha's word is not to be relied upon—this may also be understood as the Buddha’s teaching in other sutras that one must not rely upon the immeasurable heterodox sutras of the worldly;
third, from "Furthermore, he proclaims" onwards, the words that slander the Buddha are not to be relied upon.
"Thus" may serve as the conclusion.
Within the explanation of relying on wisdom (*jñāna*) rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is first a presentation and then an exposition.
The exposition consists of four parts:

First, the statement "The wise one is precisely the Tathāgata" clarifies reliance upon the Buddha’s wisdom; second, from "If there is... onwards, it clarifies non-reliance upon the consciousness of the śrāvaka; third, from "If one knows that the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body" onwards, it clarifies reliance upon the bodhisattva’s wisdom; fourth, from "If one sees the Tathāgata’s body of expedient means" onwards, it clarifies non-reliance upon the consciousness of the ordinary person.

In this [passage], the first part clarifies that one should not rely on consciousness; the section beginning with "If there should be... clarifies that neither persons nor teachings are to be relied upon.
How does this sentence differ from the second [point] mentioned previously?
The preceding section revealed delusion regarding the Truth; this section clarifies the response to that delusion.
According to the *Liaoyi jing* (Sūtra of Definitive Meaning), the discussion proceeds by first presenting the subject and subsequently analyzing it.

In this analysis, it is shown that the Hīnayāna is not to be relied upon because its followers do not realize the ultimate meaning, whereas the Mahāyāna is to be relied upon because its teachings are of definitive meaning.

The text contains seven pairs of contrasts. The first six clarify the distinction between teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and those of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); the final pair clarifies the distinction between what is reliable and what is unreliable.

Within the first six pairs, the first two concern the clarity or lack thereof regarding the cause—namely, the former as understanding and the latter as practice; the next one concerns the fruit; the following one concerns the cause; and the final two concern the fruit.
Regarding the fruits, the former refers to *bodhi* (enlightenment) and the latter refers to *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, among the six, the first two refer to the cause, the next one to the fruit, the next one to the teaching, and the final two to the meaning.

In the seventh pair, the first part clarifies that the Hīnayāna is not fully realized and thus cannot be relied upon; the statement "the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle should not be relied upon" precisely clarifies this non-reliance.
The section beginning with "Why" provides an explanation, first posing a question and then offering a resolution.
Within the explanation, there are four points:
the first clarifies that the Hīnayāna is provisional and incomplete, first through doctrine and then through analogy.
Second, the passage beginning with "The Śrāvaka vehicle is like the first plowing" clarifies that one should not rely upon it;
third, "This is called the 'provisional meaning'" concludes the first point;
fourth, "Therefore, one should not rely on the Śrāvaka vehicle" concludes the second point.
The next section, "Clarifying that the Mahāyāna is to be Relied Upon," consists of four distinct points:
First, "The Mahāyāna Dharma should be relied upon" directly clarifies that it is to be relied upon;

second, from "Why? onwards, it clarifies the great definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) to establish the preceding point that it should be relied upon. This is done by first posing a question and then providing an explanation, clarifying that "the Buddha, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, skillfully taught the Mahāyāna through the power of skillful means. Because it exhaustively penetrates the profound and provides definitive resolution, it should be relied upon.
3. "Therefore, one should rely [on this]" concludes the first [point];
4. "This is called the definitive meaning" concludes the second.
The phrase "These four are thus" and below summarizes them all.
In the second section, first is the reliance on meaning, where "meaning" refers to the merit of the fruition;
second is the reliance on the Dharma, where "Dharma" refers to the *dharmatā*;
third is the reliance on wisdom, where "wisdom" refers to the practice of the Saṃgha.
The fourth [section] relies on the Sūtra; "Sūtra" refers to the teaching.
Among these four, the first two explain the reliance in terms of the fruit, while the latter two do so in terms of the cause.
Since the meaning constitutes the essence of the fruit, it is explained first; since the fruit is established based upon the Dharma, the Dharma is analyzed next.
Wisdom is the essence of the cause, and thus it is clarified first; since the cause is established through the Dharma, the Sūtra is explained afterward.
Furthermore, since the preceding fruit is accomplished by means of the cause, wisdom must be understood;
since the preceding Dharma must rely upon the exposition of the teaching to be manifested, the Sūtra must be discussed.

In this text, the first two points are discussed together in one section: first, the reliance on the meaning is clarified; second, the reliance on the Dharma is clarified; third, the non-reliance on the person is clarified; and fourth, the non-reliance on the words is demonstrated.

According to the preceding principle, the "endowments" (*sambhāra*) should likewise be six; however, here only four are mentioned—the Dharma-body, liberation, wisdom, and the Tathāgata—omitting the [Dharma-]Dharma and the Sangha.

The initial statement, "Furthermore, 'meaning' (artha) is named 'uprightness,'" refers to the Dharma-body; because the body is free from crookedness, it is called upright. "'Uprightness' is named 'radiance'" refers to Prajñā; because wisdom is free from the obscuration of darkness, it is named radiance. "'Radiance' is named 'not inferior'" is itself liberation. "'Named Tathāgata'" refers to the Jewel of the Buddha.

The subsequent section further elucidates this: “Clarity is named wisdom” distinguishes the essence of *prajñā*; “Rectitude is named eternal abiding” reveals the meaning of the *dharmakāya*. Because it eternally dwells in the body and does not change with time, it is called “substantial rectitude.”

Next, the reliance upon the Dharma is explained: “The Tathāgata is eternal; this is called relying upon the Dharma. This serves as a general heading, which is then specifically elucidated below. Regarding the characteristics of the Dharma, it is eternal and boundless; that which is unchanging is termed “eternal.”
The meaning is manifold and its substance is vast; therefore, it is called "boundless.

From the phrase "inconceivable" downward, the text addresses sentient beings to explain the Dharma: first, it clarifies that while it is "not existent, it can nevertheless be seen," thereby demonstrating that the Dharma is not non-existent. The preceding section on the inconceivability within non-existence clarifies the departure from mental characteristics (*citta-nimitta*); the phrase "cannot be grasped or bound" clarifies the departure from material characteristics (*rūpa-nimitta*). Because its substance is truly not non-existent, it is "visible."
"If there is one who says it is invisible, that which [he teaches] should not be relied upon" clarifies non-reliance on the person.
"Therefore," and below, is the conclusion.

"If one proclaims impermanence with eloquent words, that which [is taught] should not be relied upon" clarifies non-reliance on the words; if even the sublime is difficult to rely upon, how much more so the coarse and vulgar?
The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes [the argument].
Regarding the third reliance, it first clarifies reliance upon wisdom, consisting of an initial citation followed by an exposition.

"The Sangha is eternal, unconditioned, and immutable" is the wisdom of realization (*adhigama-jñāna*); "not storing impure things" is the wisdom of the teaching (*śāsana-jñāna*). From "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion clarifies that one should rely [upon this].
The following passage also clarifies that [the Saṃgha] does not rely upon consciousness. "Not relying upon consciousness" serves as a general heading, after which its characteristics are explained:

"If anyone should say that consciousness acts and consciousness receives, and that there is no harmonious Saṃgha"—this cites erroneous consciousness; because it clings to the real and slanders the conventional, it is erroneous.
The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: "Harmony is called non-existence. Since that which is non-existent lacks permanence, where could there be a Saṃgha?
The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes by establishing the lack of reliance.
Within the section on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the definitive is explained first, followed by the non-definitive.

Regarding the definitive, the "definitiveness of meaning" is explained initially: through such practices as "knowing contentment," one understands that even regarding the Tathāgata’s teachings given according to specific needs (*yathārhata*), one does not give rise to attachment; this refers to understanding the meaning of the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, even concerning the Buddha.
The section beginning with "This is called" concludes [the preceding].

The section beginning with "If there is one who can" clarifies reliance on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); relying on the two aforementioned definitive names is termed "capable of abiding. That which is the excellence of the basis within the Tathāgatas and so forth is termed "having already attained abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes [this point].
Next, we clarify that [the *aniyata-sūtras*] are not to be relied upon, first by citing the text and subsequently by explaining it.

In the explanation, the initial section clarifies within the context of the "Dharma of Meaning" (*arthadharma*) that the *aniyata-sūtras* cannot be taken as a basis; the section beginning with "If there be someone who says the Tathāgata out of compassion... explains within the context of the "Dharma of Practice" (*pratipattidharma*) that the *aniyata-sūtras* cannot be relied upon.
In the first part, there are two sections: first, a detailed exposition on the lack of definitive understanding; second, a conclusion regarding non-reliance [on such teachings].
Within the exposition on the lack of definitive understanding, there are four distinct textual divisions:
first, citing sūtras of provisional meaning from the past.
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the sūtras," this refers to what was taught in the ancient Hīnayāna sūtras.
As for "all are burned," it is because the ancient teachings state that the three poisons burn all sentient beings, hence they are called "burned," as explained in the passage below;
alternatively, the ancient teachings also state that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds, and thus they are called "burned."
It is taught that all phenomena are burned by that [fire]; therefore, they are called "all. The same applies to categories such as impermanence and suffering.
The section beginning with "This is called" is the conclusion; because the term "all" is spoken without qualification, it is termed "indefinite" (*apariniṣṭhita*).
Second, the section beginning with "Why" explains the non-definitive meaning.
The phrase "For what reason" interrogates the preceding statement to introduce the subsequent one: for what reason are all things such as burning considered non-definitive?

Because they cannot understand such meanings, these are explained in response to them. Relying on the arising of the mind, one cannot understand the various meanings such as "burning" and so forth; because this is restricted to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called "not understanding."

3. The section beginning with "Causing all" clarifies the harm resulting from lack of understanding; "Causing them to fall into Avīci" specifically clarifies that harm. Because it causes others to rely on [such views] and even leads them to slander the Buddha—whereby impermanence, suffering, and so forth become slanders against the Vaipulya sūtras—they consequently fall into Avīci.

The section beginning with "Therefore" provides an explanation. Within it, first the reason for his current fall is questioned; the phrase "because of attachment" answers that question. It means that upon hearing the teaching that all things are impermanent, burning, and so forth, he dogmatically clings to them and asserts that the Buddha is likewise [subject to these conditions]; hence, it is called "attachment."

4. Regarding the passage beginning with "One who burns all is called the Tathāgata," the characteristics of non-comprehension are explained; first the explanation is given, followed by the conclusion, the structure of which is clear from the text.
The phrase "should not rely" concludes the point that one should not rely [on such views].

The following section, which clarifies that sūtras of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*) cannot be relied upon by means of the practice of the Dharma, first presents the opposite case—sūtras of complete meaning (*nītārtha*) that can be relied upon—in order to highlight the former’s inadequacy.

The passage beginning with “If there are those who speak of [appropriate] time and [inappropriate] non-time” reverses the preceding point regarding complete meaning to correctly clarify the nature of incomplete meaning.
The preceding four statements are as follows:

first, regarding persons, it refers to sūtras of explicit meaning; second, it concludes the basis for reliance; third, from "If one possesses the precepts" onwards, it generally refers to sūtras of explicit meaning concerning the Dharma-teachings; fourth, it concludes what may be relied upon.

At the beginning, the passage "If one says that the Tathāgata, out of compassion and knowing the proper timing, speaks of the light as heavy and the heavy as light" briefly clarifies the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
At that time, there were four distinct categories, as will be fully explained below.

Within this period, if there is a donor who is wealthy but not a protector of the Dharma, and who does not offer pure gifts, yet [the recipient] accepts and keeps all manner of impure things, the Buddha declared this to be grave; the opposite of this is termed light.
The following provides a detailed exposition, which consists of four parts:
first, regarding whether there are donors among the disciples—if there are heavy objects, they are prohibited; if there are none, their possession is permitted.
Second, "even though there are no donors"—in times of abundance, they are prohibited; in times of scarcity, their possession is permitted.
Third, although one may not be preserving the Dharma during times of scarcity, the Tathāgata prohibits it; yet for the sake of preserving the Dharma, he permits its possession.
Fourth, although one may be preserving the Dharma, if one does not rely on pure offerings (śuddhadāna), the Tathāgata prohibits it; however, through pure offerings, he permits its possession.
Among these four, that which is prohibited by the Tathāgata is called a "heavy" teaching, and that which is permitted by the Tathāgata is called a "light" teaching.
"These four dharmas are to be relied upon" concludes the clarification of what may be relied upon.

Within the section on the definitive meaning according to the provisional teachings, the phrase "if there are precepts, etc., that do not contradict the four" means they do not contradict the preceding four; "they should also be relied upon" concludes by clarifying that these may indeed be relied upon.
Within the section that correctly clarifies the non-definitive meaning, there are also four points.

First, the non-definitive is clarified by means of human speech: "There is a time; there is no time. This reverses the second [point] above; "time" refers to a period of scarcity, while "no time" refers to a period of non-scarcity.
The phrases "having protection" and "not having protection" are the reverse of the third [point] mentioned previously.
The remaining two lines are omitted and not translated; because it is stated that "the Tathāgata permits the acceptance and possession of impure things," this is called "incomprehensible.
Second, from the words "speaking thus" onwards, the conclusion clarifies the lack of reliance.
3. From "If there are precepts" onwards, it clarifies the lack of understanding with respect to its teachings;
4. From "In this way" onwards, it concludes by clarifying that it is not a reliance, designating those three collections as the "Three Divisions."
The preceding discussion has reconciled the Dharma with the person; from here on, the text distinguishes the Dharma as distinct from the person.
Within this section, first the person is clarified as distinct from the Dharma, and second, from the words "As for the Dharma" onwards, the Dharma is explained as distinct from the person.

In the first part of the preceding section, the statement “I am for the sake of those with the fleshly eye, not for those with the wisdom-eye” precisely clarifies the distinction between different dharmas; since those with the fleshly eye do not recognize the Dharma, it is for their sake that the reliance upon persons is taught. The phrase “therefore” below serves as a conclusion: because those with the fleshly eye do not recognize the Dharma, I now teach them the four reliances regarding persons.

Within the subsequent discussion on the distinction between the Dharma and the person, the characteristics of the Dharma-body are explained as being manifest such that they cannot be perceived by the fleshly eye, but are visible only to the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Of the two preceding sections, the first was distinguished in detail, while the latter was omitted for brevity.
Among the śrāvakas, those who study the Mahāyāna are called those with the fleshly eye (māṃsacakṣus), while all bodhisattvas are called those with the wisdom-eye (prajñācakṣus).

The following clarifies the heterodox and the orthodox, answering the previous question: "How does one know when Māra creates obstacles for the assembly? How does one distinguish between what is spoken by the Buddha and what is spoken by Māra?"
For what reason is this explained?
There are three meanings in the explanation:
first, to clarify that these four types of persons can subdue the heterodox and penetrate the orthodox, thereby serving as a refuge for sentient beings.
Second, to clarify the reason why sentient beings must rely [on the right], the Sūtra states that one should rely on four types of persons because there are four Māras;
third, it desires to cause people to recognize what is false so as not to follow it, thereby departing from that which is not to be relied upon.
The text consists of three parts:

first, a brief enumeration of the four māras at the request of Kāśyapa; second, a detailed exposition of the four māras at the request of Kāśyapa; and third, Kāśyapa’s understanding and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s discourse, followed by the Tathāgata’s praise.

At the beginning, the question "The four persons mentioned above should rely [on this]" arises first, followed by the Buddha’s answer, "As I have taught, you should rely [on it]," which directly answers the preceding question.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: because there are four māras who delude and confuse sentient beings, one must necessarily rely upon the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
The section beginning with "What are they" defines the four māras; first there is the question, followed by the explanation.

In other places, it is frequently taught that there are four kinds [of Māras]: the afflictions (kleśa), the aggregates (skandha), death, and the celestial Māra (devaputra-māra). Here, however, the four are explained solely with reference to the celestial Māra.
What are these four characteristics?
Regarding the analysis of the single meaning: Māra and his disciples constitute one pair, and the sūtras and vinaya he preaches constitute another pair; these together form four types.
Among these four, the first two are Māra and humans, while the latter two are Māra and the Dharma.

The citation of the person’s response addresses the question: "How does one know that Māra creates obstacles for the assembly? The citation of the Dharma’s response addresses the question: "How does one distinguish between what the Buddha has spoken and what Māra has spoken?"

Furthermore, another classification holds that all four types are explained in relation to persons: first, the māra of preaching the sūtras; second, the māra of preaching the vinaya; third, the māra of receiving the sūtras; and fourth, the māra of receiving the vinaya.
In the second broad section, Kāśyapa first asks, "As the Buddha has said, there are four kinds of Māras," thereby citing the Buddha’s previous words and then proceeding to pose his questions.
Based on the response provided therein, the inquiry is insufficient; there should have been three questions:

first, asking by what forms the various māras corrupt and disrupt the True Dharma; second, asking how one may distinguish between the teachings of the māras and those spoken by the Buddha; and third, asking how one may recognize those who follow the māras and those who follow the Buddha’s teachings.
Among these three, the first asks about his demonic teacher, the second asks about the Dharma, and the last asks about his disciples.

Furthermore, the first asks about the confusion regarding his physical form, the middle one asks about the confusion regarding his preaching, and the last asks about the confusion regarding his reception [of followers].
However, in the present text, only the latter two [questions] appear, while the first sentence is omitted; yet, according to the requirements of the response, it must necessarily be supplied.
