Below, when the Buddha provides his answer, he first addresses the one question that was previously missing—namely, "When Māra destroys the Dharma, he speaks these words"—and subsequently addresses the two questions contained within the preceding text.

Within the first section, the phrase "seven hundred years after my parinirvāṇa" clarifies the time when the Dharma will be destroyed; the mention of "this Māra Pāpīyān" identifies the person who destroys the Dharma; and the phrase "gradually destroying my Dharma" correctly clarifies the destruction of the Dharma itself.
From "For example" onwards, the characteristics of the disintegrating dharma are elucidated; first the simile, then the application.
Within these two [sections], the first is general, the second is specific, and the last is the conclusion.
Within the latter section, the first is the detailed exposition, followed by the conclusion.

The ten pairs within the *Guang*: first, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox based on the Buddha’s descent from heaven; second, clarifying the orthodox from the heterodox based on the Tathāgata’s manifestation of walking seven steps; third, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox based on the matter of the heavenly deities’ reverent offerings; fourth, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox based on the matter of the Tathāgata’s taking a wife; fifth, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox based on the establishment of the precepts; sixth, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox based on the Tathāgata’s various skills; seventh, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox by contrasting the Great and Small [Vehicles]; eighth, clarifying the heterodox and orthodox based on the Buddha’s body; ninth, distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox based on the matter of observing or violating the precepts; and tenth, clarifying the heterodox and orthodox by reference to the teachings of the internal and external paths.

Among these ten, the first four concern events prior to his attainment of enlightenment; the next one concerns an event after his enlightenment; the next one clarifies both the matter of his enlightenment and his transformation of others; and the final four again clarify matters subsequent to his enlightenment.
Within these ten points, each first clarifies the explanation of the heterodox and the orthodox, corresponding to the initial question;
subsequently, they distinguish the recipients of the teaching, corresponding to the latter question.
Regarding the first pair, there is first a discussion of the demonic teachings, which is divided into three sections:
First, it is said that the Tathāgata was born due to craving;
second, it clarifies that after being born, he was not honored by the world;
third, it asserts that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood solely through practicing the asceticism of giving, without cultivating other virtues.
Next, it is explained that the Buddha’s teaching merely reverses the first statement: it clarifies that the Buddha’s birth was not caused by desire.

Regarding the second pair [of statements], the claim that the Buddha’s taking seven steps immediately after birth is an unreliable manifestation is deemed heterodox, whereas the claim that the Buddha’s manifestation is reliable is deemed orthodox.

In the third pair, it is said that when the Buddha was first born, he entered a celestial shrine; those who do not revere the deities therein consider this heterodox, while those who revere and serve them consider it orthodox.

In the fourth pair, it is said that while the Buddha was at home, his greedy mind led him to take a wife and truly experience sensual pleasures, which they consider heterodox; conversely, they consider it orthodox to say that the Buddha ought to have acted in such a way.
In the fifth pair, it is stated that the claim that the Buddha permitted the keeping of impure things is heterodox, while the statement that the Buddha prohibited them is orthodox.
In the sixth pair, it is stated that the claim that the Buddha did not possess various skills is heterodox; herein there are six points:

first, it is said that the Tathāgata entered a temple of the devas for the sake of making offerings to the devas. The phrase "the reason for entering" below cites the orthodox to reveal the heterodox; the phrase "if one says no" below refutes the heterodox to reveal the orthodox. If one claims that the Tathāgata entered the temple of the devas to discipline the devas and humans, and asserts that this is not so, such a statement contradicts reason and is termed "impossible."
Second, it is said that the Tathāgata cannot enter into the various treatises of non-Buddhists to understand their deportment, literature, and arts;
third, it is said that the Tathāgata cannot reconcile servants who are quarreling;
fourth, it is said that the Tathāgata is not honored by men and women, kings and ministers.

The fifth [position] asserts that the Tathāgata does not know how to compound all medicinal herbs; herein, first it clarifies his ignorance, next it clarifies that he is called "Tathāgata" precisely because of this ignorance, and finally it clarifies that if he were to know, he would fall into false views.
The sixth asserts that the Tathāgata can only abide in the middle way and is unable to fully employ various skillful means to accord with the world.
The following section explains that the Tathāgata is called "Correct" because he possesses various virtues; this also consists of six points:

First, it clarifies that when the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, he manifested entry into a celestial temple, which reverses the first point mentioned previously.

Second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata left the household life to practice the Way within the systems of non-Buddhist studies, mastering their deportment, literature, and arts, which reverses the second point mentioned previously.
The Tathāgata’s possession of the three vidyās (三明) can reconcile strife and conflict, reversing the third point above;
the Tathāgata’s possession of the four vidyās (四明) is revered by the world, reversing the fourth point above;

fifth, from the phrase "is also able to demonstrate" (亦能示) onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha conforms to the world and is also able to manifest the compounding of various medicines, yet this is not false view, reversing the fifth point above.

Sixth: The section beginning with "For the sake of delivering" clarifies that the Buddha, in order to deliver all sentient beings, employs various skillful means and accords with worldly conventions; he does not merely abide in the middle way. This reverses the sixth point mentioned previously.
In the seventh pair, holding that the Small [Vehicle] is not the Great is termed "false," while knowing that the Great is external and the Small is internal is considered "correct.
Within the false, there are two types:

first, holding that the Small is not the Great; second, as stated below in the passage "This person further says: 'I shall accept such sūtras and vinayas,' thus learning the Small and abandoning the Great."
The beginning and middle sections further comprise two parts:

first, clinging to the *Vinaya* of the Lesser Vehicle while rejecting that of the Greater Vehicle; second, from the passage "The Tathāgata previously taught the ninefold canon" onwards, the exclusive clinging to the sūtras of the Lesser Vehicle while rejecting those of the Greater Vehicle.
There are five points in the Vinaya:

First, citing what the Buddha previously established; that is, the Tathāgata formerly proclaimed in the Hīnayāna Vinaya the five categories of offenses, both light and heavy, as well as the *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgressions), all of which are inherently grave. Therefore, they are cited here now, and because they equally invite great suffering, it is said they are "all grave.
Second, from the words "Our Vinaya" onwards, one cites the minor rules to belong to oneself.
3. From “I have long endured” downward, he manifests his own faith and acceptance, while resenting the other’s lack of faith;

4. From “I shall” downward, he clings to the small and abandons the great: he regards the precepts of the Hīnayāna as his own discipline (*sva-vinaya*) and the precepts of the Mahāyāna as your discipline (*yuṣmad-vinaya*); therefore, he now says, “How could I abandon my own discipline to follow your discipline? 5.
From “Whatever you possess” downward, he pushes the Great Vehicle into the category of the heterodox, saying that your discipline is what was taught by Māra.
The sutra consists of three parts:

first, it clarifies how Māra’s followers cling to the Lesser Vehicle and deny the Great; second, from "In a future age there shall be... onwards, the Buddha rebukes them to reveal their faults; third, from "I have also taught... onwards, it clarifies that his own teaching of the Great Vehicle exposes their errors.
The first part contains six sections:
first, citing the ninefold division of the scriptures to prove that there is no Vaipulya;
second, citing the Tathāgata’s immeasurable minor sūtras to prove that there is no Vaipulya.
3. From "If there were such" onwards, it is inferred that the Vaipulya sutras were taught for the sake of Devadatta;
4. From "Such as these" onwards, it is inferred that they were taught for the sake of Māra—first inferring and then explaining;
5. From "Such words" onwards, it is inferred that [these teachings] exist in other sutras but are absent from one's own sutras.
Sixth: "My own Sūtras and Vinaya" refers to the false citation of the Buddha’s words below to prove what is incorrect.
This concludes the first section. The second section concerns that in future ages there will be such evil bhikṣus; this is the Buddha’s reprimand revealing their faults.
Within the third section, there are three distinct points:
first, the Buddha himself reveals his own past transgressions through the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*), stating that the Vaipulya sutras exist;
second, from the passage beginning "If there is a person," it clarifies the attainment of those who are correct.

Third, from "If there are those who say... onwards, the faults of the slanderer are clarified; first, the nature of their slander is explained, followed by the conclusion regarding the offense incurred.
The preceding section was the first: clinging to the Small Vehicle and rejecting the Great Vehicle; from here on is the second: studying the Small Vehicle while abandoning the Great Vehicle.
"I shall receive and uphold such sutras and vinayas" explicitly clarifies the training in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);

the section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation. Contentment and few desires are the path within the cause; the eradication of afflictions is cessation within the cause; wisdom is the path within the fruit; and *nirvāṇa* is cessation within the fruit. These four preceding types are collectively termed wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
"The sūtras and vinayas of the Hīnayāna take this as their basis and are called the causes of wholesome dharmas; because they are wholesome causes, I now uphold them.
To say "one who speaks thus is not my disciple" is a rebuke intended to expose the fault.

Next, the correct [teaching] is distinguished: "If there are those who say that the Tathāgata, for the sake of deliverance, preached the Vaipulya sūtras, they are truly my disciples"—this correctly reveals what is right. "If there are those who do not accept the Vaipulya sūtras"—from here below, the heterodox is censured to reveal the correct. "Sūtras and Vinayas such as these were spoken by the Buddha"—this concludes by clarifying the aforementioned correctness. "If it is not like this, it was spoken by Māra"—this concludes by clarifying the aforementioned heterodoxy. Below, the acceptance of [these teachings by] people is clarified.
In the eighth pair, it is stated that to claim the Buddha is not accomplished through immeasurable virtues is termed "erroneous.

Within this, the first part clarifies that the Tathāgata is not accomplished through immeasurable virtues, but has attained only the dharma of emptiness; the section beginning with "proclaims" clarifies that his teaching of non-self does not conform to worldly conventions, and therefore he speaks provisionally of being accomplished through immeasurable virtues.

The section beginning with "Thus" concludes the discourse, explaining that the Buddha is fully endowed with immeasurable virtues and is thus designated as "Right. Having first provided the analysis and subsequently the conclusion, the following section clarifies the receiving of the precepts.

In the ninth pair, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox is clarified in terms of the observance and violation of precepts. The text is divided into four sections: first, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox regarding non-violation;

second, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox regarding the meaning of violation, beginning with the passage "Furthermore, some say there is no *pārājika*"; third, the question-and-answer section further clarifying the meaning within non-violation, beginning with "Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: 'As previously stated, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature'"; and fourth, the section further clarifying the meaning within the aforementioned violation, beginning with "If one commits a *duṣkṛta*, [the retribution is] eight million [kalpas] in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the distinction between the erroneous and the correct; second, the clarification of those who receive [the precepts].

Regarding the distinction between the erroneous and the correct: to claim that one has committed an offense when one has not is called "erroneous"; to state that one has not committed an offense when indeed none was committed is termed "correct."
In these two passages, there is a distinction between the "deviant" and the "correct.

In the former, within the context of explaining what is deviant, it is said that those of the Lesser Vehicle who are contented are considered to be without offense; yet, because this lack of offense is described as being an offense, it is termed "deviant.

In the latter, within the context of explaining what is correct, it is said that those of the Great Vehicle who possess right view are considered to be without offense; because this lack of offense is described as being truly without offense, it is termed "correct. In reality, however, both principles apply universally.
Regarding the first category of wrong views, the section first clarifies that there is no offense; from "If one says this person incurs guilt" onwards, it refutes those [wrong views] in contrast.

Within the former section, there are four parts: first, a brief clarification that there is no offense; second, the explanation beginning with "Why..."; third, a detailed clarification that there is no offense; and fourth, the explanation beginning with "Why...".

Regarding the first summary, the phrase "there may be a bhikṣu who has not, in fact, committed a pārājika offense" precisely clarifies non-offense, as explained in the following passage: there are bhikṣus who have few desires and are content, dwelling in secluded places; people, believing them to be noble ones (ārya), prostrate to and praise them, yet the bhikṣus do not accept this honor—this is called "not having actually committed an offense."

The passage beginning with "the multitude" clarifies that those people of wrong views claim this bhikṣu has actually committed a grave offense; the passage beginning with "in this way" shows how the Tathāgata, through reasoning, demonstrates that he is without offense.
In the second explanation, first there is the inquiry: "For what reason do I say that there is no offense? Below this, it provides the response.

Within this, offenses are cited to demonstrate the absence of offense: "I have always said that if one commits even one of the four *pārājikas*, it is like breaking a stone," which specifically cites the transgression; "If one claims for oneself to have attained superhuman states," and so forth, distinguishes the characteristics of the offense; "For what reason," and so forth, explains and clarifies those characteristics; and "Such a person," and so forth, concludes the nature of the transgression, meaning that one has withdrawn from the Dharma of the supramundane noble ones.
Within the third section, which extensively clarifies the absence of offense, there are five distinct parts:

first, explaining how a bhikṣu with few desires and contentment dwells in a secluded place; second, explaining how the king and his ministers claim he is an arhat; third, from the words "The bhikṣu hears" onwards, explaining how the bhikṣu does not accept [the claim]; fourth, explaining how the king and his ministers further claim he is an arhat; and fifth, concluding that there is no offense.

The first section is clear. In the second section, the initial thought is that the person has presently attained arhatship, while the subsequent praise concerns the fact that this person shall attain bodhi in the future.
In the third section, the text is further divided into three parts:
first, revealing that one has not yet attained the fruits of the path in the present, and thus exhorting the king not to speak [of such things].

Second, from "I only wish" (*vande*) onwards, it clarifies the fault of lack of contentment and requests that the King not speak [of it]. Within this, first, there is the request that the King not speak; from "one who is not content" (*atṛpta*) onwards, it clarifies the characteristics of lack of contentment;

and from "I now" (*aham idānīm*) onwards, it clarifies the fault of lack of contentment. Third, from "the practice of contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi-caryā*) onwards, it cites the attainment of contentment to manifest one's own joyful acceptance. Within this, first, it clarifies that the attainment of contentment is praised by the Buddha; from "therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, it clarifies one's own joyful acceptance; and again, from "contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*) onwards, it clarifies the characteristics of contentment.

In the fourth section, the King first laments that his teacher has attained arhatship; he then announces this to the people of the country so that all may know it together. From the words "For this reason" (*tasmāt*) onwards, the people, having heard this, join together in praise.

In the fifth section, the first part praises the person’s own pure conduct; the passage beginning with "by these causes and conditions" shows how they can generate merit for others; and the section beginning with "in this way" concludes that there is no offense.
The preceding section, the third, extensively clarifies that there is no offense; the passage beginning with "Why... provides the explanation, which is clear and can be understood.

Having clarified above that there is no offense, the following section contrasts this with the wrong view: if one says that such a person who is free from offense commits an offense, that is the teaching of Māra.
To clarify the central meaning, there is first the exposition and then the conclusion.
Within the exposition, there are four parts:

first, stating that the body possesses a nature; second, from "Although this... onwards, demonstrating that there is no offense; third, from "There was a bhikṣu who had just left the household life... onwards, reflecting on the attainment of Bodhi; fourth, from "Such a person, although not yet having attained... onwards, returning to clarify that there is no offense.

The first three phrases at the beginning clarify that a bhikṣu expounds the Buddha’s secret treasury, stating that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature; because this nature exists, one attains bodhi upon severing the fetters of afflictions.
Second, from "If a king... onwards, the Dharma is revealed through hypothetical questioning, consisting first of the questions and then the answers.
Within the questions: "Bhikṣu!
Will you become a Buddha? is the first question; "Do you possess buddha-nature? is the second question.
In the response, "I now certainly possess the Buddha-nature" answers the latter question first, while "whether it is perfected or not remains yet to be examined" answers the former question.
3. From "The King said" onwards, the King hears and understands, and the bhikṣu confirms it.
This concludes the first section.
In the second section, it is clarified that asserting the existence of a self-nature (*svabhāva*) is consistent with reason and does not constitute a grave offense.
The third [point] is easy to understand.
Within the fourth section, there are three distinct statements:
first, it clarifies that although such a person has not yet realized the fruit [of the path], they obtain immeasurable merit because their bodhicitta is vast and great.

Second, from "Suppose" (*yadi*) onwards, it demonstrates that there is no offense. This is done by hypothetically citing false speech as a category to refute [the objection]: if that person were to incur an offense, then all bhikṣus would be the same as him; if one considers that those who have attained the fruits of realization should likewise be guilty of offenses, yet in fact none are guilty, then this case is the same.

Third, the section beginning with "Why" provides a dual explanation of the preceding two points. Within this, it first asks, "For what reason does that person obtain merit and no transgression? Then, from "I, while dwelling... onwards, it uses its own case as an analogy to clarify the point: by citing its own dwelling in cultivation and its present attainment of *bodhi*, it analogically demonstrates that the other person will likewise certainly attain the fruit, thereby establishing that their mindfulness is free of transgression. The passage "In the past, he was always far removed from impure things" and so forth clarifies the cultivation of the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). "He also knows for himself" and so forth indicates the presence of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*). "Therefore, I have now attained *bodhi*" establishes the fruit of self-benefit; "Possessing great compassion" establishes the fruit of benefiting others. Since that person is identical to oneself and shall likewise attain *bodhi*, one reflects upon oneself as being destined to attain *bodhi*. Thus, in accordance with this principle, one obtains merit and is free of transgression.
The preceding section has extensively analyzed [the topic]; from "In this way" onwards is the conclusion, which can be understood as referring to receiving offerings.
Above, the first part defined the heterodox and the orthodox by focusing on non-offenses; below, the second part defines the heterodox and the orthodox by focusing on offenses.
To claim there is no offense when one has committed an offense is called "deviant";
to acknowledge an offense when one has committed an offense is considered "correct.
Within the preceding section on deviance, the first part provides the analysis and the latter provides the conclusion.
The analysis consists of five parts: first, the teaching that there is no retribution for offenses;

second, from "If one says the Buddha taught that sexual intercourse is permissible," onwards, it clarifies that sexual misconduct is not a transgression; third, from "Or committing the four [grave offenses]," onwards, it clarifies that various offenses do not obstruct liberation; fourth, from "The Tathāgata spoke of *duṣkṛta* (misdeeds)," onwards, it clarifies that while offenses have retribution, this is merely the Buddha’s means of intimidating people and lacks ultimate reality; fifth, from "From *pārājika* down to *duṣkṛta*," onwards, it clarifies that the five categories of precepts were not established by the Buddha.
Below, in the section on the Middle Way, these five points are inverted; one should carefully note them.

Within the first section, the initial statement clarifies that there is no offense, while the subsequent passage beginning with "If a bhikṣu commits such [an act]" explains the absence of retribution for the offense.

First, an objection is raised: "If those who violate these [precepts] fall into hell, then since the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) have no precepts to violate, they should all equally be reborn in heaven.
The section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation, and the section beginning with "Therefore" provides the conclusion.
In the second section, there are four distinct points:

first, citing the Tathāgata’s permission for bhikṣus who have left the monastic life to engage in sexual intercourse as proof that it is not an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); second, from "Furthermore, one should... onwards, clarifying that engaging in sex according to former laws is not one's own fault; third, from "When the Tathāgata was... onwards, clarifying that such sexual conduct does not obstruct rebirth in heaven or liberation, thereby supporting the first point; fourth, from "Throughout antiquity and today... onwards, concluding the second point.
In the third section, it is clarified that no offense whatsoever obstructs liberation; this is evident from the text and requires no further explanation.

In the fourth section, the Buddha’s past teaching regarding the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing)—that one falls into hell for eight million years of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven—is cited. This was merely intended to instill fear in people and does not indicate an actual retribution; he spoke only of the *duṣkṛta* as a representative case, and other offenses are to be understood by analogy.

In the fifth section, it is clarified that the various offenses of the five categories were falsely fabricated by Vinaya masters who, under false pretenses, claimed they were established by the Buddha; the phrase "speaking thus" concludes this by distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox.
The correct explanation has three parts:
first, clarifying that there are karmic retributions for transgressions, which reverses the first [point] above;
second, from "I also say in the sūtras that there are [retributions]" onwards, clarifying that all transgressions are established by the Buddha, which reverses the fifth point above.
3. From "If one does not uphold the precepts, how can one see? onwards, it clarifies the liberation from karmic obstacles of sin; this reverses the third section mentioned previously.
The remaining two sections are omitted and not reversed.
The first part consists of five sections:
First, it clarifies that the retribution for various offenses is limitless, exhorting people to guard against them.
Second, from the passage beginning with "There was a Vinaya master," it clarifies that one should not associate with those who proclaim there is no retribution for offenses.

3. Regarding the passage beginning with “As the Buddha said,” the following cites the Buddha’s past words to establish the preceding point that [a person] cannot be relied upon. First, he cites those past words:
“If one exceeds one” means that at the time of reciting the precepts, one has recited beyond one precept.
Regarding the phrase "called lying": at this time, the concealment of one's transgressions is called "silent lying.

Regarding the phrase "not seeing the consequence": it means that this lying does not bring about future suffering, which is called "not seeing the consequence"; because one does not see [the result], all transgressions are concealed, which is called "there is no evil one does not commit."

From the words "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion is drawn that [the person] is beyond being associated with; for one who does not perceive the consequences of such a future life regarding the sin of silent falsehood will fail to refrain from committing any evil whatsoever.
It was previously declared that there is no karmic retribution for [such acts] and that one should not associate with them.
This concludes the third section.
Fourth, from the phrase "my Dharma" onwards, the light case is cited as an illustration of the heavy case to establish that there is indeed guilt in the preceding matter.

"The purity within my Buddha-dharma is such" refers to the minor offenses; since even the *duṣkṛta* offense of lying by remaining silent is not permitted, it is said, "The purity of my dharma is such."
From the phrase "How much more so" (*kā punar vādaḥ*) onwards, the light case is used as an illustration for the heavy case to establish that there is a grave offense.

Regarding the five points from "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, they conclude with an exhortation to guard [the precepts]: first, it exhorts one to protect them; then, from "If such dharmas as these are not maintained," it rebukes those who do not protect them.
The preceding first section contains five sentences clarifying the retribution for transgressions;
the second section is self-evident.

Within the third section, the phrase "If one does not uphold the precepts, how can one see the nature? explicitly clarifies that various transgressions can obstruct liberation. The passage beginning with "All sentient beings" clarifies that one attains liberation only by departing from transgressions. The section beginning with "The ninefold canon" resolves doubts and reveals the Dharma.
What is the nature of this doubt?
In the former teachings, it was not said that there is a "nature" (prakṛti); how then can it be said that by upholding the precepts one perceives this nature?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:

Because the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*) lacks the Vaipulya [sūtras], it does not speak of the existence of the nature (*dhātu*). Although the sūtras do not mention it, the principle actually exists; therefore, by upholding [the teachings], one attains vision.
The following clarifies the recipient of the teaching, distinguishing the orthodox from the heterodox.
From this point downward is the third section, which further elucidates the meaning of the preceding "absence of offense. It consists of two question-and-answer pairs:

the first pair further elucidates the meaning of the "correct" portion within the first section, while the second pair further elucidates the meaning of the "erroneous" portion within the first section.
What was not yet fully understood in the preceding section that necessitates further clarification?

It was previously stated that those possessing the *gotra* (spiritual lineage) shall attain *bodhi*, and that they do not commit grave offenses; since it was proclaimed that those with the *gotra* do not commit such offenses, this must now be explained, and thus it is discussed again here.
Furthermore, although it was previously declared that there is no offense, the nature of what constitutes an offense has not yet been clarified; therefore, it is now being explained again.
Among the "perversions" mentioned previously, what remains unexplained that necessitates this further elucidation?

It was previously stated that a bhikṣu who dwells in fewness of desires and emptiness does not commit an offense when praised by others; however, the meaning of "committing an offense" was not yet clarified, and thus it must now be analyzed.
In the preceding dialogue, the non-offense was first explained, while the section beginning with "If there are those who cannot speak in this way" clarifies the cases where an offense is committed.
There are three ways in which there is no offense:

first, there is no offense in speaking of existence; second, from the passage "For example, suppose someone were to speak of the great ocean" onwards, there is no offense in speaking of non-existence; third, from the passage "There are heterodox teachers" onwards, there is no offense in proclaiming that which is neither existent nor non-existent.
At the beginning, he first asks: "From what cause does this arise? [The answer is:
It arises from the fact that the nature (*prakṛti*) was not mentioned among the ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-dharma*) previously cited.

Since it was stated above that all sentient beings possess this nature, yet it has never been mentioned in the ninefold scriptures, if one were to speak of its existence, would this not contradict the holy teaching (*āgama*)? How, then, could such a person avoid committing a *pārājika* offense?
The Buddha answered him below; although this is not explicitly stated in the sutra, what was said accords with reason, and therefore there is no offense.

Regarding the second section on "speaking of non-existence without offense," it first provides a simile, then applies it to the case at hand, and the passage beginning with "Why? provides the explanation.
In this commentary, the first part clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles do not know the Buddha-nature; for this reason, it is said that they do not commit any transgressions.
The section beginning with "Such an object" demonstrates that this nature is known only by the Tathāgata, thereby explaining the reason why the Two Vehicles do not know it.

The passage beginning with "If a person does not" clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles do not know their own nature because they have not heard the secret treasury; the section beginning with "What is" defines and reveals this secret treasury, namely, the Vaipulya sutras.
In the third section, it first clarifies that Buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent; the passage beginning with "If there are those who say" explains that there is no transgression.

Within the former part, the initial statement, "There are certain heterodox teachers who speak of annihilationism or eternalism," sets forth the false to reveal the correct. The subsequent section, "The Tathāgata does not [speak thus]," distinguishes the correct from the false; thus, the absence of transgression is evident.
The first part clarifies non-offenses; the second part discusses offenses. Within this, there are three sections:
first, clarifying offenses in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*);
second, from "I have already accomplished" onwards, discussing offenses in relation to *bodhi*; [and third, discussing offenses in relation to the stages].

3. Regarding the passage beginning with "By this meaning," it is because people do not understand that they falsely grasp [the rules] and thus commit offenses. This praises the inconceivability of the Dharma, causing people to look upward and reflect upon it, so that they may abandon their transgressions and achieve observance.

Regarding the initial statement, "To be unable to speak in this way is called an offense": it means that while one does not say that Buddha-nature truly exists within the body, to claim it is definitively non-existent because it is not seen due to the obscuration of delusions is called a grave offense.

In the second section, the statement "If one says, 'I have already accomplished awakening'" expresses the presence of the effect within the cause. The passage beginning with "For what reason" explains the meaning of its existence, while the passage beginning with "By these conditions" concludes that it exists; this reveals the characteristics of the offense. The passage beginning with "One should know that" concludes by clarifying that there is indeed an offense, as it proclaims that the fruit of expedient awakening already exists within the cause; therefore, it constitutes an offense.

The section beginning with "For what reason" explains the meaning of the offense; the statement "those with the potential who have not yet cultivated [the path] do not attain bodhi" is cited to demonstrate what is incorrect.

In the third section, the phrase "For this reason, the Buddha-dharma is extremely profound and inconceivable" indicates that because people do not understand it, they falsely grasp at it and thereby commit an offense; thus, the Dharma is profoundly deep and inconceivable.

Next, to clarify the meaning within the section on "wrong views," Kāśyapa first requests that the matter be explained by means of a hypothetical case: "There was a king who asked. This is because in the preceding passage, the king praised a bhikṣu, yet the bhikṣu did not accept it and thus did not violate the precepts; therefore, in this present context, the text returns to the statement that the king asked.

In the preceding section, it was stated that a bhikṣu who dwells in emptiness with few desires is not considered to have violated the precepts even if he does not accept [offerings], yet how can it be permitted for him to fall into the offense of claiming superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*)?

Below, the Buddha provides a clarification; therein, first, he directly addresses the previous question by explaining that some bhikṣus, for the sake of gain, feign virtue and thus commit the offense of claiming superhuman qualities.

From the passage beginning "Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who act for the sake of establishing... onwards, he distinguishes the genuine from the counterfeit, clarifying that such [genuine] individuals do not commit the offense.

Regarding the offenses, the first section clarifies feigning virtue for the sake of profit so that others may recognize one as a *bhikṣu* seeking alms; the passage beginning with "Such a bhikṣu is greatly deluded" illustrates feigning virtue for the sake of profit, while the section beginning with "desiring to make others know oneself to be an *ārya*" concludes the offense.

In the section clarifying non-transgression, the first part serves as a general teaching on the Dharma, demonstrating that the Noble Ones are without transgression; the passage beginning with "Furthermore, I also possess nature" serves as a general proof of the Dharma, explaining that there is no transgression because one possesses nature within one's own person; the phrase "Acting thus" concludes the section.
The first five points of the beginning are:
first, to establish the True Dharma by dwelling in a place of empty stillness, desiring to lead others to regard oneself as a sage;
second, to cause others to respect and have faith [in oneself].
Third, because others respect and trust him, they all come to rely upon him;
fourth, because they have come to rely upon him, he causes them to initiate practice so as to penetrate the True Dharma;

fifth, "illuminating and extolling" refers to the subsequent stage where, due to others relying on him for transformation, he causes them to give rise to understanding and thereby penetrate the True Dharma—meaning he causes sentient beings to understand the meaning of the gravity and lightness of what the Buddha has taught.
In the second section, there are three distinct points:

first, for the sake of instructing others, he speaks of his own possession of the nature that attains fruition: "I also possess Buddha-nature within my present body" clarifies the existence of the present cause; the passage beginning with "There is a sutra named... clarifies the future attainment of fruition; "I shall attain the Buddha-way" refers to attaining the fruit of Bodhi; and "exhausting the fetters of affliction" refers to attaining the fruit of Nirvana.
Second, from "Extensively for... onwards, he speaks of others possessing the nature.

Third: The passage beginning with "I and you" clarifies that because both oneself and others possess the nature of existence (*dharmatā*), one should fulfill the causes for Buddhahood and achieve the fruit of Buddhahood. The phrase "I and you shall both abide in the stage of the Tathāgata" clarifies the possession of the causes for Buddhahood—namely, abiding in the path of the ten stages—and the subsequent attainment of the fruit.

Within this, the first section clarifies the attainment of the fruit of *bodhi*; the section beginning with "immeasurable" concerns the attainment of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; and the section beginning with "having spoken thus" summarizes that there is no transgression.

The following fourth section further clarifies the meaning of the preceding discussion on transgressions. Within this, the initial statement—"One incurs a *duṣkṛta* [offense], and for eight million years in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven one falls into hell; how much more so for a *sthūlātyaya*?"—inverts the previous explanation regarding the "evil" [consequences] where it was said that a *duṣkṛta* results in falling into hell for eight million years as a means of instilling fear in people through the Tathāgata’s teaching. Therefore, it is now clarified that such a fall actually occurs and is not false.
By citing a minor case to illustrate a major one, it is said: "How much more so for intentionally committing a sthūlātyaya.
Here, the term *sthūlātyaya* refers to grave offenses in general, not merely to preparatory acts.

Regarding the passage "This Mahāyāna" and below: the five categories of offenses mentioned above in the section on "refuting the heterodox" were not originally established by the Buddha; this [text] clarifies that all offenses were indeed established by the Buddha. First, the precept against stealing was established; next, the precepts against killing, drinking alcohol, and false speech; and finally, the precept against sexual misconduct was established.
Because the questions and answers regarding the prohibition of sexual misconduct are presented again for further clarification, they are placed later.
Within the prohibition against stealing, there are three distinct sections:

first, a general statement on *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) exhorting others not to associate with such persons; second, a detailed exposition in three parts beginning with "What is... (*katamaḥ*); and third, a general condemnation revealing the faults beginning with "A bhikṣu such as this is called one who is groundless" (*evamrūpo bhikṣur amūlakaḥ*).
Within the prohibitions against killing and so forth, the textual characteristics are clear.

Below, the prohibition against sexual misconduct is established; this is the inverse of the aforementioned practice of committing sexual misconduct as a non-fault, clarifying that it is indeed a fault.
First, there is the formal prohibition; following "Kāśyapa said," there is a question-and-answer section that further elucidates it, consisting first of the question and then the answer.
In the response, first the initial question is directly answered to clarify that one does not incur an offense in a dream.
Below, the teaching is presented in five distinct points:
first, one should cultivate the perception of impurity regarding sexual desire.
Second, he taught that one must not give rise to thoughts of desire toward women;
third, he taught that if one dreams of engaging in sexual intercourse, one should give rise to a sense of remorse;
fourth, he taught that bhikṣus should give rise to the perception of revulsion toward food, for since food is a cause of lust, he taught them to feel revulsion toward it.
Fifth, if a lustful mind arises, one should instruct them to abandon it quickly.
The phrase "In this way" below concludes [the section].
Below, the receiving of persons is clarified.
In the tenth pair, first the false and the correct are distinguished, followed by a discussion on receiving [the precepts].
External teachings are termed "false," while internal teachings are called "correct.
Within the false, there are four types:
First, it is said that non-Buddhists take asceticism and heterodox teachings as the true path;
second, it is said that the Tathāgata permits the ordination of evil persons and those without roots of goodness;

third, it is said that the Tathāgata permits the possession of various impure things. Regarding these, the first part clarifies what he permitted, while the section beginning with "except for this" clarifies how heterodoxy differs from orthodoxy by addressing what he did not permit.
The four statements that the Tathāgata said plants and trees all possess life-span are of these four kinds,
which are taught by Māra. Below, in the exposition of the correct [view],
only three phrases are translated in reverse, while the second phrase is omitted and not translated.

"I also do not permit [the practices] from 'constantly standing on one foot' up to 'harmful life-taking, incantations, and arts,' which correspond to the first section above; from 'Kojū' (軻具) onwards corresponds to the third and fourth sections above."

Within this, first, the heterodox is criticized and the orthodox is revealed; from "I only permit" onwards, the orthodox is distinguished from the heterodox; "I only permit the eating of the five kinds of flavors" and so forth correctly correspond to the third [point]; "I say that the four great elements have no life-span" correctly corresponds to the fourth; and from "If there is... onwards is the conclusion.
The preceding ten pairs have extensively distinguished between the heterodox, the orthodox, the teachings of Māra, and the teachings of the Buddha; what follows serves as a general conclusion.

From "Kāśyapa said" onwards is the third section, which, following Kāśyapa’s reception [of the teaching], consists of the Tathāgata’s praise of longevity. Taken together with the preceding, this constitutes the first part, clarifying the practice of cultivation performed in accordance with conditions.
From here below is the second section, which clarifies the practice of entering realization through relinquishment.

Within this section on realization, the first part correctly elucidates the practice of realization itself; the subsequent portion, beginning with "Sentient beings of meager merit do not see it," clarifies the basis upon which realization relies, which is similar to what was explained above.
Within the explicit exposition of realization, there are three distinctions:

first, the chapter on the Four Truths, which discriminates the characteristics and leads toward reality; second, the chapter on the four inversions, which discriminates the erroneous and returns one to the correct; and third, from "Do the twenty-five states of existence have a self? onwards, which involves relinquishing characteristics to enter realization.

The initial clarification of the Four Noble Truths answers the previous question, "In what way do those who have disciplined their minds joyfully expound the Truths? Now, this detailed exposition of the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) Four Noble Truths elucidates the Buddha’s intention for conversion; thus, it is called the "Joyful Expounding of the Truths."
What is the purpose of the exposition on the truths?

The truths are the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is their ultimate reality (*tattva*). Because one wishes to lead sentient beings from these characteristics toward that reality, it is necessary to expound the truths.
The meaning of the Four Noble Truths has been explained in a separate chapter.
Within this [chapter], the Tathāgata first extensively analyzes the truths, and subsequently Kāśyapa receives and understands them.
Regarding the initial section, there is first a detailed exposition followed by a summary.
Within the section on "Distinctions," there are four parts: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Regarding the clarification of suffering, the text is divided into two sections:
first, defining the distinction between characteristics and reality; second, from the words "If a person" onwards, clarifying the distinction between reality and characteristics.

Regarding the first section, the previous statement that "suffering is not called a Noble Truth" correctly clarified its difference from reality; now, this teaching proclaims that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* constitute the reality of suffering. Since the characteristics of suffering are not real, suffering itself is not a truth.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation; first, it raises the question: "For what reason do I say that suffering is not a truth? From the words "If one says... onwards, the erroneous view is refuted to reveal the correct teaching.
If that which is a painful matter were the Noble Truth of Suffering, then since cattle and other beings experience suffering, they too would possess the Noble Truths.
Question: Do these beings not indeed possess the Noble Truths?
The commentary states:
Although these entities are in fact identical, because what is perceived by their respective faculties is not true, one may say they are "not [identical].
As stated in the following passage: "There is suffering, there is truth, and there is reality. Yet, if even suffering is not the truth, how could it be reality?
Within the section defining the actual characteristics of difference, the right and wrong of phenomena are revealed by way of the ignorant and the wise.
The essential meaning consists of two parts:
first, defining what is wrong from the perspective of the ignorant; second, clarifying what is right from the perspective of the wise.
The text contains three pairs of contrasts:

first, it clarifies the delusion and awakening, as well as the loss and gain of the ignorant and the wise; second, it demonstrates their respective harms and benefits; third, it concludes by doubly refuting what is not [the truth].
Within the first pair, delusion comes first, followed by awakening.
Within the section on delusion, there are two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of that delusion; second, the clarification of the faults inherent in delusion.
Regarding the delusion, the phrase "if a person does not know the profound realm of the Tathāgata" refers to being deluded regarding the realm of the Tathāgatagarbha and Buddha-nature.
"To not know the Tathāgata’s subtle and secret Dharma-body" means to regard it as a body of nutriment rather than the Dharma-body; this is delusion regarding the Buddha's Dharma-body.
"To not know the Tathāgata’s moral power and majesty" is delusion regarding the Buddha's reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Alternatively, one may interpret the preceding phrase as being deluded regarding the Buddha’s mind, and the subsequent phrase as being deluded regarding the Buddha’s virtues.
Question:
Since the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and its moral qualities are not of the nature of suffering, why is being deluded about them termed "delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering"?
The commentary states:

Although these are not the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), they are nonetheless the reality of suffering (*duḥkha-tattva*); therefore, to be deluded regarding them is called being deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
What is the meaning of this?
The true nature of suffering is the *tathāgatagarbha*; this *tathāgatagarbha* is the essence of all ordinary beings and Buddhas.

From the perspective of the Buddha, it is primordially and eternally pure; outside of the *garbha*, not a single instance of birth and death can be found. Therefore, the *tathāgatagarbha* is itself the Buddha-body and itself the Buddha-virtues.

To speak in general terms, that Tathāgatagarbha is shrouded by delusion; yet this shrouded garbha is, from its very foundation, identical to the Dharmakāya at the time it is later revealed. It is described as the cause of Buddhahood and as Buddha-nature. Thus, this Buddha-nature is non-dual and indistinguishable from ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and the Buddha’s Dharmakāya. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "There is suffering, there is truth, there is reality," and so on, up to "there is the path, there is truth, there is reality. This ultimate truth is precisely the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature and space (*ākāśa*), because they are without distinction.

Now, it is taught that the Buddha’s body and the various qualities of a Buddha constitute the reality of suffering; to be deluded regarding this reality of suffering is called "delusion regarding the truth of suffering" (duḥkha-satya), and the same applies to the remaining truths.
What follows clarifies that such delusion is itself termed "suffering."
This section generally clarifies the state of delusion: because one is deluded regarding the Truth, suffering arises;

therefore, it is called "suffering. The passage beginning with "Why? provides the explanation: "Because of not knowing, one perceives the Dharma as non-Dharma and non-Dharma as Dharma. This clarifies that there is a cause for suffering; "not knowing" is another term for delusion.
Deluded regarding the Buddha’s Dharma-body, they claim it is a body of nutriment and not the Dharma-body; therefore, this is called "seeing the Dharma but not the non-Dharma.
Birth-and-death is empty and non-existent, which constitutes the non-Dharma; yet, by falsely grasping it as existent, they are said to "see the Dharma."

The passage beginning with "One should know that" clarifies the existence of the fruit of suffering; "will certainly fall into the evil realms" refers to the fruit of the three miserable destinies; and "revolving in birth and death" refers to the fruit of the human and celestial realms.
The preceding pair concerns the causes and effects of collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*);

"the increase of all fetters" further clarifies the cause of suffering, while "undergoing much pain and affliction" further clarifies the fruit of suffering. The subsequent pair concerns the causes and effects of individual retribution (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka*).
Furthermore, the former may be understood as the fruit of *pariccheda* (segmented existence), while the latter is that of *pariṇāma* (transformation).
Within the section on awakening, the first part correctly clarifies the nature of awakening itself, while the subsequent part clarifies the attainment of awakening.

Within this section on awakening, the phrase "If one knows that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change" refers to seeing with the eyes; "or hearing the sound of the two characters 'eternally abiding'" refers to seeing through hearing.
The Dharma is eternally constant, and its abiding is an eternal retribution.
Within this clarification of attainment, the initial section provides a formal exposition, while the passage beginning with "I, in the past" cites the self as evidence.

Regarding the preceding section: the initial statement, "If it enters the ear but once, one is immediately born in the heavens," refers to being freed from the sufferings of the three miserable realms; the subsequent passage beginning with "later liberation" refers to being freed from the sufferings of the human and celestial realms.

It is only at the time of subsequent liberation that one can realize the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding; from the beginning to the end, the passage starting from "having realized" and below refers to tracing back from the end to the beginning.

Within the section citing one's own realization, the phrase "I, due to ignorance regarding the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi), transmigrated through birth and death" reversely cites the state of delusion; the section starting from "beginning from today" and below inverts this to reveal the attainment of clarity. The text is slightly incomplete; if it were full, it should state: "Beginning from this very day, I have attained true wisdom, and by means of this true wisdom, I have emerged from birth and death."
The first part clarifies delusion and awakening; the second part clarifies loss and benefit.

"If one knows thus, this is truly practicing the contemplation of suffering, which brings great benefit" clarifies the benefit of the preceding awakening—seeing the true nature of suffering is called truly practicing the contemplation of suffering. "If one does not know," and so forth below, reveals the loss resulting from the preceding delusion.
In the third section of the conclusion, first the realization of what is correct is concluded, and subsequently the delusion regarding what is incorrect is concluded.

Next, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is clarified; it is first presented and then explained below. Within the explanation, this is further demonstrated by contrasting the ignorant and the wise.
The text contains three pairs of contrasts:

first, the clarification of delusion and awakening, loss and gain regarding the ignorant and the wise; second, the clarification of harm and benefit; and third, the conclusion concerning right and wrong.
Within the first pair, delusion is presented first, followed by awakening.

Within the context of delusion, the initial statement, "not giving rise to true wisdom regarding the true Dharma," clarifies delusion regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The *tathāgatagarbha* nature is that true Dharma; failing to awaken to it through the mind is termed "not giving rise to wisdom."
The section beginning with "Accepting impure things" clarifies the faults of delusion regarding existence (*bhava*).

Within this, the portion up to "not knowing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)" clarifies the cause for the accumulation of existence; the portion "accepting impure things, namely slaves and servants" clarifies their lack of practice; and the portion beginning with "being able to declare what is contrary to the Dharma to be the Dharma" reveals their lack of understanding.

To claim that what is not the Dharma is the Dharma and so forth is to fail to understand the practice of the Dharma; by reason of this, one does not know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and does not recognize the principles of the Dharma.

The section beginning with "Because of not knowing" clarifies the existence of the fruit of accumulation (*saṃskāra-phala*). First, it clarifies the experience of suffering; from "not attaining" onwards, it demonstrates the loss of happiness. "Not attaining birth in heaven" signifies the loss of worldly happiness, while "and [not attaining] true liberation" signifies the loss of supramundane happiness.

Regarding "Awakening," the initial phrase "if there is profound knowledge" clarifies the realization of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); because one knows the true nature of origination, it is called "profound knowledge. The section beginning with "not destroying" clarifies that awakening has its attainment:

"not destroying the True Dharma" clarifies the absence of the cause of origination; "by this cause" and following clarify the absence of the fruit of origination; "attaining birth in the heavens" indicates the absence of the fruits of the three miserable realms (*apāya*); and "as well as right liberation" indicates the absence of the fruits of the human and celestial realms.
In the second pair, only the delusion and its impairment are clarified, while the awakening and its benefit are omitted.

The passage beginning with "If there are those who do not know the locus of the truths of suffering and its origin, yet claim that the True Dharma is not eternal," etc., restates the aforementioned delusion by naming the *tathāgatagarbha* as the locus of suffering and its origin; the section from "For this reason" onwards explicitly clarifies its impairment.
In the third section of the summary, first the realization of what is correct is summarized, and subsequently the delusion regarding what is incorrect is summarized.
Next, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) is elucidated.
This contains four parts:
First, the extinction of dharmas; second, the analysis of cultivation with respect to persons; third, the conclusion of the preceding dharmas; fourth, the conclusion of the preceding cultivation.
The first section is self-evident.
Within the second section on cultivation, both delusion and awakening are clarified, and the text contains two pairs [of concepts]:
First, it clarifies the delusion and enlightenment, gain and loss of the ignorant and the wise; second, it clarifies harm and benefit.
Within the first pair of contrasts, delusion is presented first, followed by enlightenment. Regarding delusion:

"If there is one who practices the dharma of emptiness" correctly clarifies the nature of that delusion; "called unwholesome" and below manifest the loss inherent in that delusion; "this is unwholesome" provides a general clarification of the loss of delusion—because grasping at emptiness while contravening reality, it is called unwholesome.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: to say that "all dharmas are extinguished" contradicts the Buddha’s true virtues; since it is taught that extinction refers only to the unconditioned state of the exhaustion of fetters, to claim that all [virtues] are extinguished is to slander the absence of true virtues. Thus, "all are extinguished."
"To destroy the Tathāgatagarbha" means to contradict the true nature of the Buddha by asserting that there is only emptiness and no reality; for this reason, it destroys the Tathāgatagarbha.
"To practice in this way" and below reiterates the point to conclude the refutation of the error.

Next, the realization [of this] is explained. Within this, first, one is taught how to enter [the path] so as to bring about awakening and understanding; from the words "If one generates... onwards, it clarifies that there is attainment within this realization.

Regarding the first part of the middle section, the initial statement, "Those who cultivate the cessation of suffering oppose the non-Buddhists," distinguishes the correct from the heterodox. It demonstrates that knowing the essential nature of cessation to be the *tathāgatagarbha* is what constitutes this opposition; it is called "opposition" because it differs from the non-Buddhists' unilateral grasping at emptiness.

The section beginning with "If one says 'cultivation'" refutes the heterodox to reveal the orthodox. First, it refutes by citing the heterodox cultivation of non-Buddhists; the section beginning with "If there is someone who says" establishes the correct teaching through principle. Because the essence of the *pitaka* is not empty, it is said to "exist."
What is meant by "having characteristics"?

As it is said in the sutras, the single Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is the Tathāgatagarbha; this Tathāgatagarbha is the true consciousness-mind (*tathatā-vijñāna-citta*). Within this true mind are contained all the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—namely, the dharmas of wisdom, samādhi, supernormal powers, liberation, and so forth—just as within the deluded mind there are contained all the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This mind and these dharmas share the same essential nature; they are neither separate nor different.
The Tathāgatagarbha possesses this meaning, and for that reason it is said to "exist.
Although the essence of the garbha exists, it is obscured by afflictions and cannot be perceived;
yet once the afflictions are severed, it will certainly and inevitably be attained—therefore, one knows it exists.
Just as a person who was lost can see the correct direction once they have regained their bearings, it is therefore called "existence.

The following clarifies the attainment through awakening: that is to say, if one gives rise to the mind that knows the *tathāgatagarbha* for even a single moment, by virtue of these causes and conditions, the delusive phenomena of birth and death cannot act as an obstruction; one realizes and knows the true dharma of Buddha-nature without hindrance, which is termed "attaining complete mastery over all dharmas."
In the second pair, there is first harm and subsequently benefit.

Regarding the harm: "If one cultivates the Tathāgata’s secret treasury as being selfless, empty, and quiescent" cites the previous delusion; taking that principle of emptiness to be the Tathāgata-garbha is called "cultivating the secret treasury as selfless and empty."

The phrase "wandering through birth and death and undergoing suffering for immeasurable eons" precisely clarifies that there is harm; because one grasps at emptiness and slanders reality, one remains in birth and death and is said to undergo all manner of suffering.

Within the section on "benefit," the phrase "if there is one who does not act in this way" restates the previous realization; "seeking reality by reversing emptiness" is termed "not acting in this way," while "the afflictions are eliminated" correctly clarifies that there is benefit.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: because one knows the treasury [of the Tathāgatagarbha], one realizes that delusion is fundamentally non-existent, and thus swiftly extinguishes affliction.
The preceding second section extensively distinguishes its cultivation; this is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
This is the third section, which concludes by clarifying the preceding teaching.
The passage beginning with "If one can... constitutes the fourth section, which concludes by clarifying the preceding practice.
"If one can act thus, they are my disciple" concludes by clarifying what constitutes awakening; the passage beginning with "If there are those who... concludes by identifying the errors of delusion.

The path also consists of four parts: first, clarifying the Dharma of the path; second, distinguishing cultivation according to persons; third, concluding the preceding Dharma; and fourth, concluding the preceding cultivation.

Regarding the first part, "the path" is used as a general heading. "That is, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and right liberation" points to the essence of the path. Within this, they are further distinguished: the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Sangha constitute the conditions for the path, while right liberation is the actual essence of the path; this refers specifically to conditioned liberation.
In the second section on cultivation, both delusion and awakening are discussed together, with delusion preceding awakening.
Within the discussion of delusion, the first part explicitly clarifies the nature of that delusion; the section beginning with "By this cause" clarifies the faults inherent in such delusion.

In the first part, the initial statement, "There are sentient beings with perverted minds who say there is no Buddha-dharma," etc., clarifies what they slander; the section beginning with "the flow of birth and death" below demonstrates their own tenet, proclaiming that everything is merely birth and death, like an illusion or a transformation. The phrase "cultivating and accumulating this view" concludes by clarifying their delusion, for their lost direction is thus made known.

Within the section on awakening, the passage beginning with "If one can resolve the mind to see" etc., clearly elucidates the nature of that awakening; the section beginning with "Riding upon this" etc., clarifies that there is attainment through awakening.
Within this, the former portion first makes the distinction, while the latter portion, starting from "For what reason," cites oneself as evidence to demonstrate that awakening is beneficial.
Within this, first the preceding point is questioned to introduce the subsequent one: "For what reason does the view of permanence cause one to obtain karmic retribution according to one's wishes?

By stating "In the past, through the four inversions," etc., the text highlights the harm to manifest the benefit; from "Now it has been extinguished" onwards, it correctly clarifies that there is indeed benefit.
"This is called the Truth of the Path" constitutes the second section, which concludes by clarifying the aforementioned dharma.

The passage beginning with "If there is anyone... constitutes the fourth section, which concludes by clarifying the aforementioned practice; it first concludes the delusion regarding what is not [the path] and subsequently concludes the awakening to what is [the path]. Since only the Path should be concluded, and because the subsequent includes the preceding, the statement "truly seeing and cultivating the dharma of the Four Noble Truths" serves as the final summary.
This can be understood through interpretation.

From here below is the second section, "Distinguishing the Deviant and Returning to the Correct," which answers the previous point regarding the perfect accomplishment of the correct and good by proclaiming the four inversions; it is discussed with the aim of causing sentient beings to abandon the deviant and return to the correct.
In this passage, the initial section provides the analysis, while the latter part records Kāśyapa’s comprehension.
Within the analysis, the opening statement, "As for the four inversions," serves as a general heading.
Since there are actually eight inversions, why does it speak of only four?
Because there are four pairs, the following provides a detailed analysis.
First, the two inversions of suffering and pleasure are clarified; first the inversion of pleasure is explained, next the inversion of suffering is explained, and finally they are summarized.

Among these, the perversion regarding pleasure (*sukha-viparyāsa*) differs slightly from that found elsewhere. In other contexts, it is simply said that taking the suffering of birth and death as pleasure constitutes the perversion of pleasure. Here, however, it is taught that being deluded regarding the Buddha’s true bliss and falsely grasping it as suffering is a great sinful suffering; to take this sinful suffering as a cause for pleasure, hoping thereby to experience happiness, is what is called the arising of the perversion of pleasure within suffering.
Within this passage there are six phrases organized into three pairs:

first, it clarifies that sentient beings delusively reckon the Buddha’s bliss as suffering; second, it explains that such inverted minds constitute the suffering of transgression—these two form one pair.

Third, it explains why the Buddha is considered suffering, thereby establishing the initial phrase; fourth, it describes how the aforementioned suffering of transgression is taken to be bliss—these two form another pair.

The fifth [section] refutes the [false] view that the Buddha’s bliss is suffering; this constitutes the first phrase. The sixth [section] concludes by stating that the prior calculation of suffering as bliss is an inversion (*viparyāsa*); these two form a pair.

Within the first phrase, "To take what is not suffering as suffering is called an inversion" serves as a general heading, while the subsequent text explains its characteristics—namely, that it is not suffering—and how the Tathāgata resolves the delusions therein.
To give rise to perverted conceptions means to claim that the Buddha is impermanent; this clarifies what has been established, namely that because he is impermanent, he is suffering.
In the second sentence, "If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent" reiterates the aforementioned perverted conception, while "is called great sinful suffering" concludes it as being suffering.
This is a transgression that serves as the cause for suffering; therefore, it is called "the suffering of transgression.

In the third sentence, the phrase "If one says that the Tathāgata abandons this body of suffering and enters nirvāṇa" cites cessation to prove suffering, while the words "this is called" and following constitute the conclusion.

In the fourth phrase, [the text states]: "If I were to say that the Tathāgata is eternal, that would be the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi), which entails immeasurable faults. Fearing that what is pleasant is actually suffering, one should—according to the following passage—"take suffering as pleasure," meaning one takes that inverted state of fault and suffering to be pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "for this reason," it means that the Buddha is said to always possess immeasurable faults.
"Therefore, one should say the Buddha is impermanent"—to say the Buddha is impermanent is what accords with reason; for this reason, it further says, "If one speaks thus, I shall accept it as true."

In the fifth statement, "That the Tathāgata is impermanent is itself suffering" establishes the meaning of suffering. This refers to the aforementioned Tathāgata relinquishing his body and entering nirvana, which is considered impermanence; because it is impermanent, it is suffering.
Alternatively, impermanence is the conditioned nature of arising and ceasing, which is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); therefore, it is said to be suffering.
"If suffering exists, how can pleasure arise? This refutation challenges the Buddha’s teaching on pleasure, asserting that Buddhahood is suffering.

In the sixth statement, "To perceive pleasure within suffering is called an inversion" means that to falsely grasp at the sinful suffering of perversion as being pleasure is therefore termed an inversion.
Next, the perversion of suffering is explained. The general heading is stated: "To conceive the idea of suffering regarding that which is pleasant is called a perversion.
This is followed by a detailed exposition consisting of three parts: first, the delusion of reckoning suffering where there is pleasure;

second, the identification of what is deluded, stating "Pleasure is the Tathāgata"; third, the clarification of what is established, stating "Suffering, O Wayfarer, is the impermanence of the Tathāgata"; and finally, the conclusion by restating the preceding points with the words "If one says... and so forth.

Second, the refutation that pleasure is established as suffering: by reversing the premise that "the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding is called pleasure," he establishes it through concession; then, by raising the objection, "If I were to say it is eternal, how could I also enter nirvāṇa? he refutes it.

Third, the refutation of the claim that non-suffering constitutes Buddhahood rather than pleasure: by raising the opponent's position, "If you say it is not suffering," and then raising the objection, "How can one abandon the body to attain extinction (parinirvāṇa)? he refutes it.

The preceding section provides a detailed explanation; the passage beginning with "because suffering arises within pleasure" serves as the conclusion. The phrase "this is called the first inversion" summarizes the preceding two points, referring to the arrival at the first pair among the four pairs.
In the second pair, it is stated in general that "perceiving the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is called inversion.
Next, its characteristics are explained; therein, only the misapprehension of the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is clarified.
The points discussed above have been explained at length; now they shall be summarized.

The statement, “To speak of impermanence is called not cultivating emptiness,” clarifies why one who perceives impermanence does not cultivate emptiness. The phrase, “therefore their lifespan is short,” precisely defines impermanence.
Because one does not realize emptiness and follows the flux of existence, one's life is short; this clarifies that which is deluded.

The section beginning with "If there is someone who says" clarifies what is established [as the view]; the section beginning with "This is called" provides the conclusion. The phrase "the second inversion" serves as the general summary.
In the third pair, "the notion of self in what is non-self, and the notion of non-self in what is self—this is called perversion" serves as the general heading.
The following explains its characteristics; first, the perversion of self is clarified: "Worldly people also say there is a self," which specifically identifies the perversion of self.

The Buddha-nature is likewise: by citing what is correct, it reveals what is erroneous. The passage beginning with “Although worldly people... clarifies how the erroneous differs from the correct; the section beginning with “This is then... provides the conclusion.

Next, the following clarifies the inversion of the absence of self: the statement “In the Buddha-dharma there is a self, which is precisely the Buddha-nature” identifies that which they are deluded about.

The section beginning with "What the world says" clarifies what is established; "The world says there is no self" correctly explains the arising of inversion; the section beginning with "This is called" provides the conclusion; and the section beginning with "If one says" cites scriptural testimony to prove its non-existence.
Judging by these words, the emptiness that negates characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is certainly not the Buddha-nature.
The section beginning with "is called" concludes [the preceding discussion], and the phrase "this is called the third" provides a general conclusion for the whole.
In the fourth pair, the statement “the perception of purity in the impure and the perception of impurity in the pure are inverted dharmas” serves as a general heading.

What follows provides a detailed analysis. Within this, first, the notion of purity where there is impurity is clarified; the passage beginning with “purity is the Tathāgata, who is eternal,” etc., explains the object of their delusion, while the section beginning with “if anyone says,” etc., demonstrates their established position.

The following clarifies the inversion regarding the pure: "To perceive the impure as pure is called an inversion" serves as a general heading, while the section beginning with "If anyone says... provides a detailed exposition thereof.

The statement, "If one says there is not a single impurity within the body," correctly clarifies the arising of inversion. The passage beginning with, "Because there is no impurity, one will certainly enter [it]," cites the end to reveal the beginning, thereby establishing the meaning of purity; the fruit of *nirvāṇa* is called the "place of purity."

The phrase "As the Tathāgata has said" below serves to destroy defilement and reveal purity; the phrase "is named" below provides the conclusion; and the phrase "is called the fourth inversion" concludes it as a whole.
The understanding [of this] can be inferred: to show that he is the same as a beginner, he says, "From before, all were called wrong views."

From here below begins the third section: the relinquishing of signs and entry into realization, which answers the aforementioned question, "How does one perform wholesome deeds? Great Seer, please explain this now.
What was that question?
The term "explanation" (*śeṣa*) has three meanings: First, it refers to a question concerning practice:

"If ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles all perform wholesome deeds yet do not attain *bodhi*, how is it that a bodhisattva practices wholesome deeds and is able to attain *bodhi*? Below, the Buddha instructs him: abandon existence and non-existence, enter the Middle Way, and by practicing wholesome deeds in this manner, one will attain *bodhi*.

Second, it is a question posed in relation to the fruit: "If there were a fruit to be obtained in the future, it would be necessary to cultivate wholesome deeds; [but since there is none, why practice?]"

"If nothing can be attained, how can one perform wholesome deeds?"—in the Buddha’s response below, he clarifies that all sentient beings currently possess the Buddha-nature and will certainly attain the fruit, just as a child in the womb is certain to be born before long; one need only cultivate wholesome deeds.
