describes the skillful means of contemplative inquiry; the passage beginning with "removing the skin" correctly elucidates the contemplation of the bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*).
In the second section, there are three distinct parts:
first, "Furthermore, he forms this thought: 'the color and appearance of the bones,'" etc., which correctly contemplates the color of the bones;
second, from "'Such a color of bone is also not-self'" onwards, which clarifies non-self, first stating that it is not-self and then explaining why with the words "For what reason," etc.

3. "When one contemplates in this way, one immediately attains severance" and below explains the benefits of contemplation, which can eliminate desire for form (*rūpa-rāga*). Within this third section, the text is divided into two parts: first, contemplating that the various skeletal marks are established based on the conventional (*prajñapti*), beginning with a general statement, followed by a detailed enumeration, and concluding with a summary; second, [the contemplation of] their impermanence. Regarding the first part: the general statement is as follows: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Next is the detailed enumeration: "The head bone, the two jaw bones, the two eye sockets, the two ear bones, the nose bone, the upper jaw bone, the lower jaw bone, the seven vertebrae of the spine, the forty-five ribs, the two collarbones, the two shoulder blades, the two arm bones, the two upper-arm bones, the two forearm bones, the two hands, the two thigh bones, the two knee bones, the two shin bones, the two feet, and the spinal column. This enumerates the thirty-two skeletal members. Finally is the summary: "These are collectively called the 'internal body. This concludes the first part. Second, the contemplation of their impermanence: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as impermanent. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all subject to birth and death, arising and ceasing moment by moment, and are therefore collectively termed "impermanent. This concludes the second part. Third, the contemplation of their impurity: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as impure. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all foul-smelling and repulsive, and are therefore collectively termed "impure. This concludes the third part. Fourth, the contemplation of their selflessness: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as selfless. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of a master, devoid of a self, and devoid of a person; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "selfless. This concludes the fourth part. Fifth, the contemplation of their suffering: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as suffering. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all subject to the three types of suffering and are therefore collectively termed "suffering. This concludes the fifth part. Sixth, the contemplation of their emptiness: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as empty. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of a permanent substance, devoid of a master, devoid of a self, and devoid of a person; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "empty. This concludes the sixth part. Seventh, the contemplation of their signlessness: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as signless. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of characteristics, devoid of signs, and devoid of appearances; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "signless. This concludes the seventh part. Eighth, the contemplation of their wishlessness: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as wishless. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of desire, devoid of attachment, and devoid of craving; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "wishless. This concludes the eighth part. Ninth, the contemplation of their detachment: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as detached. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of grasping, devoid of clinging, and devoid of attachment; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "detached. This concludes the ninth part. Tenth, the contemplation of their cessation: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as ceasing. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all subject to destruction, subject to disintegration, and subject to extinction; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "ceasing. This concludes the tenth part. Eleventh, the contemplation of their non-arising: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as non-arising. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of production, devoid of birth, and devoid of origination; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "non-arising. This concludes the eleventh part. Twelfth, the contemplation of their non-origination: "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the internal body, they observe it as being composed of bones, bound together by sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and they contemplate them as non-originating. This means that within the internal body, there are thirty-two skeletal members, which are collectively termed the "body. These are bound together by nine hundred sinews, covered by skin, flesh, and blood, and are collectively designated as the "internal body. Furthermore, these are all devoid of causes, devoid of conditions, and devoid of origination; they are merely a collection of conditioned phenomena and are therefore collectively termed "non-originating. This concludes the twelfth part. Thirteenth, the contemplation of their non-existence: "Furthermore

Second, from "Attaining this contemplation" onwards, the benefits of the contemplation are clarified; it can sever the three desires, first by general mention and subsequently by detailed enumeration.
Within the fourth section, there are five distinct points: first, the color of the bones fills the ten directions;

second, five-colored light issues forth from between the eyebrows; third, one sees Buddhas within the light; fourth, the Buddha questions me regarding the mark of self (*ātman*); fifth, the mind that clings to marks is destroyed, and as the Buddha-mark is realized, [the light] ceases.

Within the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), the passage beginning with "Because [the Buddha] thought, 'I am consciousness,' he did not teach it to me" expresses a doubt following the preceding [section]; the section beginning with "Furthermore, he contemplates consciousness" correctly clarifies that the arising and ceasing of the mind is not the self.

Within the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), the initial contemplation on non-self (*anātman*) serves to dismantle and detach from the "feeler. The subsequent section, beginning with "In what place does desire arise," serves to dismantle and detach from the mind that feels.
Within the dismantling of the feeler, there are three distinct textual sections:

first, contemplating that exhalation and inhalation are not the self; second, the passage "If consciousness is not the self, perhaps exhalation and inhalation might be the self," which follows a prior doubt; and third, "Furthermore, one contemplates that exhalation and inhalation are wind," which explicitly clarifies their non-self nature.

Second, one observes that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are not the self. Regarding "wind is one of the four great elements," one traces from the preceding to the succeeding; this is subsumed under the wind element among the four great elements. By investigating with the question, "Among the four great elements, which is the self? one seeks the reality and correctly realizes that the nature of earth is not the self—that there is no self.

Third, one observes that form and mind are not the self. First, an explanation by way of principle (*dharma*) is given: "In this entire body, there is absolutely no self," clarifying its absence in terms of ultimate principle; "Only the conjunction of mind and wind manifests [the body]," demonstrating its conventional existence. This is followed by an analogy and then the application to the subject at hand.

Within the refutation of the feeling of sensation (*vedanā*), it is asked: "In what place does this craving arise? This refutes and separates from pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*); since pleasure coexists with craving, if there is no place for craving to arise, then there is likewise no pleasure.

"If one is reviled," and so forth, [this section] refutes the separation from painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*). Since suffering coexists with anger, if there is no place for anger to arise, then suffering will likewise not exist.
Within this, there are two parts;
the first is the refutation of anger by means of reviling, which consists of three distinct sections:

1. By contemplating the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one is able to destroy anger: "If one is reviled, where can anger arise? This is because the person who reviles is empty; and "this body of mine consists of thirty-six impure and foul substances," etc., because the person being reviled is empty.

2. By contemplating the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one is able to destroy anger: "Upon hearing the revilement, one should reflect: 'What sound is it that sees me being reviled? This is a general inquiry. "No single sound can revile," etc., is the specific explanation of the absence of reviling; because speech and meaning cannot be established when analyzed into their constituent moments, there is no reviling.
3. From "For this reason" onwards is the summary of what is improper: for the sake of the two preceding reasons, one should not be angry.
Second, regarding the refutation of anger, there are two distinct sections:

first, observing that this beating arises because of one's own body and thus one should not be angry with another. Within this, there is first the principle (*dharma*), followed by the analogy (*upamā*), and finally the application (*upanaya*).

Within this teaching, first one reflects on from where the impulse to strike arises; next, one recognizes that it is caused by the hand, the weapon, and one's own body. From the words "I now" onwards, one uses reasoning to restrain oneself, realizing that one ought not to be angry with another.
Second, from the words "If I do not endure, my mind will scatter," onwards, one understands that patience must be maintained for fear of increasing future suffering; herein there are five phrases.

The preceding section extensively explained the skillful means of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the phrase "having performed this contemplation, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness" clarifies the completion of the foundations of mindfulness.

The preceding section clarified the practice; the following section clarifies what is accomplished. The phrase "attaining the stage of endurance" (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) provides a general clarification of what is accomplished, while the subsequent portion explains its specific characteristics.

First, the passage beginning with "Enduring afflictions and also enduring cold" clarifies the ability to endure suffering; it briefly omits the endurance of karma. The section below "This is called" serves as the conclusion.

The preceding portion is the first part, which correctly explains the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Below this is the praise of the excellence of the sutra, which consists of three pairs of textual units:
first, Kāśyapa asks, "For one who has not yet attained immovability (*akopya*), could there be causes and conditions by which they might break the precepts? and the Buddha replies, "There are."
The second Kāśyapa replied with respectful assent and asked, "What is this?
The Tathāgata explained it for him, providing three points within that explanation:

First, he clarified that there are causes and conditions by which a bodhisattva may break the precepts yet cause other sentient beings to receive and uphold this sutra, and to preach it extensively for others so that they do not regress from Bodhi; at such a time, breaking [the precepts] is permissible. Kāśyapa said, "To break the precepts for the sake of the sutra" demonstrates the excellence of the sutra, and furthermore, it is intended to lead people to break the precepts in order to propagate the sutra.
2. From "At that time, the bodhisattva should form this thought" onwards, there is the instruction on generating the intention to refute;
3. From "By means of this cause" onwards, there is the conclusion establishing the attainment of refutation.
These two pairs are completed.

Mañjuśrī elucidates this principle that one who violates the precepts does not fall into hell; the Tathāgata confirms this, first offering praise therein with the words "I recall in the past," and subsequently providing scriptural evidence for its establishment.

Within this, first, there is an extensive citation of past events concerning the killing of a Brahmin for the sake of protecting the Mahāyāna, stating that "from that time onward, he has not fallen into hell. From the words "protecting" (*yong-hu*) onwards, the passage concludes with an exclamation praising how the protection of the Dharma possesses great power, enabling people to uphold it.
The phrasing is thus, yet the meaning remains unresolved. Previously, Kāśyapa asked, "Can one who has not yet attained immovability break the precepts? and the Buddha replied, "Yes.

Mañjuśrī then stated that such a person, though breaking the precepts, does not fall into hell. Now, the Tathāgata cites the example of the seer Śyāma killing a Brahmin without falling into hell to substantiate this prior point. However, it is subsequently stated that Śyāma dwelt on the stage of *parama-preman* (the stage of supreme affection). Since this stage of supreme affection is vastly different from the aforementioned state of "not yet abiding in immovability," how can this serve as proof?
The commentary states:

herein, one does not intend to take the relative status or rank of their positions as the proof; rather, one takes as proof the fact that they have upheld the Dharma and committed no transgressions regarding the precepts.
Practicing in opposition to the protection of the Dharma applies in meaning to both the superior and the inferior levels; even the realization of a Buddha would not be hindered by this.
Next, the practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*) is explained, which contains two parts:
first, clarifying the essence of the practice; second, from the term "stainless" (*vimala*) onwards, praising the sutra and exhorting others to study it.
The preceding section further divides into two parts:
first, that which is cultivated during the causal stage; second, from "then one abides in the ground of fearlessness" onwards, that which is accomplished during the resultant stage.
Within the cultivation of the causal stage, there is first the analysis, followed by the conclusion, and finally the explanation of its name.
The analysis consists of two parts:
first, manifesting reality through words to lead people toward entry;
second, from "The Tathāgata, approaching parinirvāṇa, skillfully turns [the wheel]" onwards, brushing away words to manifest quiescence, leading people to relinquish attachment.

The preceding section has three parts: first, the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths; second, from "One who knows the conventional truth is said to possess middle-level wisdom" onwards, the clarification of the contemplation of the two truths; and third, from "Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: 'What is the meaning of the ultimate truth? onwards, the clarification of the contemplation of the single reality.
Contemplating these three stages through the practice of clear wisdom constitutes the sequence for entering into contemplation.
Regarding the preceding Four Noble Truths, one should first explain the meaning of the Four Noble Truths and then interpret the text; the meaning is as discussed in a separate chapter.
Within this passage there are ten points:
first, a general enumeration;
second, the listing of four names.
3. "Suffering is oppressive" and below briefly explain its meaning;
4. "Suffering is manifest" and below briefly discuss its characteristics;
5. "There are three types of suffering" and below briefly discuss its essence.
Sixth, from "The two with outflows" (*sāsrava*) below, there is a brief classification of the distinctions between the causes and effects of defilement and purity;
seventh, from "The eight characteristics are called suffering" (*duḥkha*) below, there is an extensive discussion according to their characteristics;
eighth, from "That which is born has the characteristic of emerging" (*jāta*) below, there is an elucidation of contemplation based on the [Four] Truths.
9. From "These Four Noble Truths were taught in sequence by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones" onwards, the benefits of the teaching are summarized;

10. From "In the past, at one time, the Buddha was in Śiśumāragiri" onwards, the vastness of the Truths is revealed, showing that they encompass all phenomena exhaustively, and may also be termed the distinction between the Great and the Small.

Among these ten sections, the first seven directly clarify the Dharma of the Truths; the next one discusses contemplation; the ninth section concludes by explaining the benefits; and the eleventh section demonstrates that what is contemplated is fully encompassed and exhaustive.
"Four" is stated as a general enumeration, while "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and so forth list their specific names.
Within the third section, regarding the statement "suffering is oppression," there are two interpretations:
first, in terms of coarse suffering, it is called "suffering" because it arises from internal affliction when the mind is oppressed by adverse objects.

Secondly, with respect to subtle suffering: conditioned phenomena arise and perish, mutually pressing and urging one another; this is called "oppression. Because they are constricted and lack peace, it is termed "suffering."

Regarding "the accumulation that gives rise [to suffering]," it means that suffering which is yet to come begins to grow; because it is produced extensively and ultimately brought to completion, it is called "growth.
Regarding "the characteristic of cessation," it means that suffering is stilled and accumulation is halted; therefore, it is called "cessation."
Regarding the "characteristics of the Mahāyāna," when discussing its path, "void-penetration" (xu-tong) is the primary meaning.
If one discusses the vehicle (yāna), "conveying-penetration" (yun-tong) is the meaning.

When its essence is penetrating, it is called the Path; when its function is penetrating, it is called the Vehicle. By borrowing that functional penetration to manifest the essential penetration, it is therefore termed a "Vehicle."
What is discussed here is the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), which distinguishes it from the Lesser Vehicle; for this reason, it is called "Great.
All of these are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the meaning of the Truths, and are therefore termed "characteristics."

In the fourth section, "the manifestation of suffering" refers to the characteristic of suffering wherein, having arisen according to its respective portion in any given world-age, it does not arise again thereafter.
Regarding the "characteristic of the turning toward origination" (*samudaya-parivarta-lakṣaṇa*): the characteristic of origination is that it gives rise to subsequent suffering.
Regarding the "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*): the characteristic of cessation is the state where the causes and effects of birth and death have been extinguished and eliminated.
Regarding "The Path can eliminate": the characteristic of the Path is its ability to eliminate the phenomena of the causes and effects of birth and death.
In the fifth section, "Suffering has three characteristics" is stated as a general heading, followed by the enumeration of their names.
Regarding these three types of suffering, there are four ways of explaining them.

First, distinguishing them according to their conditions (*pratyaya*): the conditions are divided into internal and external. The internal mind’s pursuit of objects is termed "internal," while all else is termed "external."
Externally there are adverse and favorable conditions: weapons, staves, and the like are adverse;
one's own body, life, wealth, and kinsmen are said to be favorable.
Among these external factors, adverse conditions can give rise to internal affliction; therefore, they are called suffering.
From these conditions of suffering arises the mind of suffering; because suffering gives rise to suffering, it is called "external.

Within the external, favorable conditions are capable of producing pleasure, while their destruction produces suffering; because the destruction of conditions leads to affliction, it is called "suffering."
The practice of seeking causes within the inner mind leads to affliction; this arising of affliction through such practice is called the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Second, distinguishing by way of conditions and essence: the nature of the mind is itself suffering, and because suffering is added upon this suffering, it is called "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
What kind of suffering is added?
That which was previously described as the three types of suffering in relation to their respective conditions is collectively termed "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

The fact that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) must inevitably perish is called "suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); this very conditioned flux is termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*), and the instability of the nature of these formations is called "suffering of formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Third, regarding the differentiation of the three types of suffering based on the three kinds of impermanence: with respect to the limits of the impermanence of conditioned existence (*pariccheda-anityatā*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is proclaimed.

The nature of the mind is itself suffering; when this inherent suffering is further compounded by the coarse suffering of the temporal divisions of the three periods, it is called the "suffering of suffering. Furthermore, by means of the coarse suffering of the temporal divisions of the three periods, the suffering of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-duḥkhatā*) is also revealed and termed the "suffering of suffering."

Regarding the contemplation of impermanence, it is taught as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); because that contemplation of impermanence involves shifting, flowing, and disintegration, it is called the suffering of change. Thus, what was previously [discussed] under the second category—the two sufferings of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) and change—here, within this present category, is designated by the same name: the suffering of change.

Regarding that very nature which is unestablished and impermanent, it is taught as the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Because the four characteristics share a single substance and arise in mutual dependence, they are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*). These formations, being a hollow accumulation, lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because their intrinsic nature has no stability, they are called the suffering of conditioned formations. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To penetrate the five aggregates of clinging as empty and non-arising—this is the meaning of suffering."

Fourth, the various characteristics of faults are revealed to clarify the three types of suffering. To reveal suffering by means of suffering is called "suffering upon suffering" (duḥkha-duḥkhatā), which refers to revealing subtle suffering by means of coarse suffering.
Suffering manifested through impermanence is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Suffering manifested through non-self is called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Because all phenomena are without self and are a hollow assemblage of causes and conditions, they are termed "formations."
The meaning of *duḥkha* (suffering) is as explained above; *samudaya* (origination) and *nirodha* (cessation) may be understood accordingly.

The meaning of the Path (*mārga*) is manifold; briefly stated, it consists of the three trainings. With morality (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) serving as the equipment for the Path, wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes its essential substance.

Within the sixth section, first the cause and effect are elucidated with respect to the contaminated (*sāsrava*), next they are elucidated with respect to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and finally the truths (*satya*) are analyzed.
The sequence proceeds from the defiled to the pure because of the principles of aspiration and revulsion;
it proceeds from the fruit to the cause because it follows the method of retrogressive contemplation.
In the seventh section, suffering is divided into eight types, first mentioned and subsequently enumerated.
Arising is termed "birth"; because there is suffering at the time of birth, it is called "the suffering of birth.
Decline and transformation are termed "aging"; because there is suffering at the time of aging, it is called "the suffering of aging."
That which violates and damages [the body] is called "sickness"; when one is sick, there is suffering, which is termed "the suffering of sickness.
The disintegration of the aggregates is called "death"; at the time of death, there is distress, which is termed "the suffering of death."
Furthermore, the very nature of birth and so forth is suffering; therefore, they are called "the suffering of birth," up to "the suffering of death.
The separation from what is beloved is called "parting from the loved"; because this separation causes affliction, it is called "the suffering of parting from the loved.
The forced encounter with what is disliked is called "meeting with the hateful"; because this encounter gives rise to affliction, it is called "the suffering of meeting with the hateful."
When what is desired is not attained as named, and one fails to obtain it through seeking, the resulting affliction caused by that seeking is called "the suffering of not obtaining what is sought";
the intense burning of the five aggregates is called "the suffering of the five flourishing aggregates."

Furthermore, within the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*), the seven types of suffering previously mentioned are called the "five aggregates of intense suffering" (*pañca-upādāna-skandha-duḥkha*); strictly speaking, they should rather be called the "intense suffering of the five aggregates.

In the context of the Path (*mārga*), one specifically speaks of the fruit-merit as the Path; whereas in the previous fifth [section], its cause was specifically discussed, here the fruit is specifically discussed. Thus, regarding the implicit and explicit expressions, the underlying principles are equal.

From here below, the eighth section distinguishes the contemplation according to the Truths (*satya*). First, one contemplates the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Within this, there is first an extensive exposition of the eight types of suffering, followed by a clear exposition of the contemplation itself.

Regarding the former, the initial mention of "birth" (*jāti*) presents its characteristics to generally reveal the meaning of birth; what follows provides a specific exposition, first stating the heading and subsequently listing the details.

Regarding the phrase "at the beginning," the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the commencement of a single retribution; therefore, it is called the "beginning. Since retribution arises, it is termed "birth" (*jāti*).
Regarding the phrase "until the end," name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is designated as the "end" in relation to what precedes it.
Regarding the term "increase" (*vṛddhi*): it refers to the aforementioned name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) increasing to become the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
These three [stages] occur within the womb;

those occurring after birth can be known through experience. Regarding the term "species" (*jāti*): from the time after birth until old age and death, every successive new arising within a single lifetime is called "birth."
Next, the suffering of aging is explained, first by way of inquiry and then by way of analysis.

Within this, the first two [points] distinguish between the coarse and the subtle: the continuous process of decline and transformation from beginning to end is called "aging moment by moment" (*kṣaṇika-jarā*); the state where the roots of a single lifetime reach maturity as its term approaches is called "aging throughout one's life" (*ātyantika-jarā*).

The latter two are distinguished according to specific periods: the process of decline from birth up until the prime of youth is called "aging of growth" (*vivardhana-jarā*); that which occurs after the years have declined is called "aging of decay" (*vināśa-jarā*).
Next, the suffering of illness is discussed, following the method of first posing questions and then providing analysis, with the exposition increasing in numerical detail.

First, the phrase "the four great elements are mutually unbalanced" provides a general explanation of the suffering of illness; this is subsequently divided into two parts: first, the presentation, and second, the enumeration, which can be understood from the subsequent analysis.
Next, this is divided into three parts, each of which has two gates.
The first three are distinguished according to causes and conditions, presented first by general heading and then by specific enumeration.

Illnesses invited by past causes are termed "karmic retribution"; contracting illness and suffering due to encountering adverse conditions in the present is termed "not being free from adverse counterparts"; and illnesses arising at the transition of seasons are termed "the shifting of times."

The latter three are designated as "feeling" (*vedanā*) in terms of their causal conditions; they are analyzed according to three meanings, first presented and subsequently explained, such that the text is clear and intelligible.
Next, the suffering of death is elucidated, first presented and subsequently explained, with its enumeration increased.
The initial statement, "giving up the body," provides a general explanation of the suffering of death.
This is subsequently divided into two parts: first, the introduction, and second, the enumeration.
Below, its characteristics are analyzed; the phrase "the end of life has three aspects" cites the subject to introduce the number.
Their names are listed as follows:
when the primary retribution has perished while the secondary environment still remains, it is called "the end of life, not the end of merit";
when the secondary environment has been destroyed while the primary retribution still remains, it is called "the end of merit, not the end of life."
When both the basis and the primary [condition] have perished, it is called "the exhaustion of merit and life-force.
The phrase "there are three external conditions" cites the number to introduce the topic; the subsequent analysis will be clear.
Thus far, the two methods of numerical increase have been distinguished.
This is further divided into three parts: first, the introduction; second, the enumeration; and third, the exposition, which may be understood accordingly.
It concludes with the summary: "Thus, death is called the great suffering."
Next, the separation from what is loved is explained; first there is the question, followed by the exposition.
Discussing it in terms of its broad categories and specific divisions: "the destruction of that which is loved" provides a general explanation of separation from what is loved.
This is subsequently divided into two parts: first the presentation, and then the analysis.
In the section "Discriminating Examination," the text is subdivided into many parts; in the section "This is Called," it provides a conclusion.

Within the context of association with the hated and disliked (*apriya-saṃprayoga*), the text first poses questions, then provides explanations, and finally elaborates by increasing the number of categories.
"Unpleasant association" provides a general explanation of encountering enemies.

It is subsequently divided into three parts: first, the introduction; second, the enumeration; third, from "In this way, the three realms are analyzed and compared," the text follows with numerous specific divisions; and finally, from "In this way," it concludes.
Within the section on "the unattainable," the structure is evident: first the question, next the exposition, and finally the conclusion.
Within the section on the "five aggregates of clinging," there is likewise first the question, next the exposition, and finally the summary conclusion.
The following clarifies the contemplation of suffering, which is divided into four sections:

first, the contemplation of the characteristics of suffering; second, the reconciliation and integration; third, the contemplation of the reality of suffering; and fourth, from the passage "All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" onwards, the repeated reconciliation and integration.
In contemplating the characteristic of suffering, one first contemplates the suffering of birth, which is divided into three sections:
first, clarifying the faults of birth; second, distinguishing the contemplation based upon it; and third, a general conclusion.
The three subsequent sentences:
First, it clarifies that the suffering of birth is able to serve as the root of the [other] seven;

second, from "Now, aging and decline" onwards, it cites the broad pervasiveness of birth to establish it as the root. Within this, it first cites aging to manifest birth, and from "The three realms of existence" onwards, it distinguishes how birth differs from aging.
Third, the conclusion from "Therefore" onwards.
Within this contemplation, there are six parts:
first, explaining how the Bodhisattva fears death and relinquishes life.
2. The Parable of the Two Boys: To clarify that Bodhisattvas differ from those who practice near-attainment by seeking birth and avoiding death;
3. The Parable of the Food Seller: To show that they differ from ordinary beings who create causes for the sake of birth;
4. The Parable of the Poisonous Tree: To clarify that the suffering of death is vast and pervasive, making birth something to be loathed.
The fifth, the analogy of filth and excrement, clarifies that the suffering of death is vast and long-lasting, establishing that birth is to be loathed;
the sixth, the analogy of the precipice, clarifies that the mixed, false pleasures of birth cause people to become greedy and deluded, establishing that birth is to be feared.
In the beginning and middle [of this section], there is first the principle (*dharma*), next the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and finally the application (*upanaya*).
Within the principle, the statement "Sentient beings have their minds shrouded by perversion; they crave birth and loathe death" cites the general case to reveal the noble [truth].
"Bodhisattvas are not like this; they perceive the faults [of existence] from the very beginning," which demonstrates the distinction between the noble and the ordinary.
Within the parable, there are also two parts:

first, the analogy for the Bodhisattva’s revulsion toward death and renunciation of birth; second, from "At that time, the two women again led each other to a certain poor [man]" onwards, the analogy clarifying the ordinary person’s craving for life and attachment to death.
The preceding section further contains two parts:
first, a metaphor for the beginning of a bodhisattva’s contemplative practice, wherein one loathes death and craves life;
second, from the passage "The woman replied, 'You are utterly deluded,'" onwards, a metaphor for the completion of contemplation, wherein both birth and death are abandoned.
The preceding section further divides into two parts:
first, the analogy for birth through craving; second, from "Outside the gate" onwards, the analogy for an evil death.
Within the analogy for birth through craving, there are four distinct points:

1. The analogy of the manifestation of signs throughout one's life; 2. The analogy of discerning the name of birth, beginning with "The master sees"; 3. The analogy of discerning the capacity for birth, beginning with "The master asks"; 4. The analogy of craving and delighting in birth, beginning with "The master hears."
At the beginning, the metaphor of "like a woman" illustrates the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*); because arising accords with human sentiment, it is described as a woman.

When future arising intends to emerge and enter into the present aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*), it is called "entering another's house. Furthermore, when these ordinary phenomena intend to emerge and enter into the body of a Bodhisattva, it is called "entering another's house."

Being born with a beautiful appearance is called "the woman’s exquisite countenance"; having all faculties fully developed is called "her features are circular and lovely"; and being naturally accompanied by manifold pleasures is called "adorned her body with necklaces."

In the third sentence, the Bodhisattva, as the subject, regards the arising [of the name] as "seeing" (*darśana*) and the examination of the arising as "inquiring" (*paripṛcchā*). Because he examines the name of the arising and investigates its affiliation, he asks: "What is the name, and to whom does it belong? (*kiṃnāmā kaḥ pratisaṃyuktaḥ*).
The manifestation of the characteristic of arising within the mind is termed "Answer"; it is provisionally designated by the name "I am Devadatta.
In the third sentence, the Bodhisattva’s re-examination is termed "The Master’s Question"; because it examines the functional capacity of arising, it asks, "What is done at the point of arrival?"

Because the characteristic of arising manifests in the mind, it is said that "the woman answers"; because the dependent retribution follows wherever one is born, it is said that "upon reaching any place, she can provide various gold, silver, and so forth."

In the fourth phrase, the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the mind and perception of its generative capacity is called "having heard"; the arising of craving is called "joy"; knowing that the arising is due to virtue, he says, "It is by my merit that you have come"; and because he performs wholesome deeds seeking rebirth, he says, "I burn incense and scatter flowers as offerings."
From here below, the second section, the parable of a miserable death, also contains four parts:

first, the parable of the manifestation of the signs of death; second, the parable of inquiring about the name of death following the phrase "having seen [them], he asks"; third, the parable of inquiring about the function of death following the phrase "he asks why it is named 'darkness'"; and fourth, the parable of the Bodhisattva’s revulsion toward death following the phrase "the master asks."

Regarding the beginning of the text, the phrase "further seeing a woman outside the gate" means that after the arising of contemplation, one separately perceives the signs of death; thus it is called "outside the gate. Because she belongs to the category of those born into existence, she is described as a "woman."

The wretchedness of the signs of death is called "the ugliness of form"; the decay and extinction of pleasurable things is called "the tattered state of clothing"; the pursuit of all sufferings is called "various impurities and grime"; the withered and haggard appearance of the physical form is called "wrinkled and cracked skin," its color becoming as pale as mugwort.

In the second line, the act of looking is termed "seeing"; because one examines the name of the object and infers its affiliation, it says, "Under what category does it fall? To whose house does it belong? The manifestation of the realm of death before the mind is termed "answering," and "My name is Darkness" is used as a provisional designation.

In the third line, because one seeks the meaning by inquiring into the name, it asks: "For what reason is it called 'darkness'? The woman's answer below correctly explains the power of death: as soon as the signs of death appear, one suddenly abandons all external resources; therefore, it is said that "it can cause all the family's wealth and treasures to decline and waste away."

In the fourth phrase, the Bodhisattva’s contemplative vision is called "having heard"; his cultivation of clear wisdom is called "possessing the power of benefit. He rebukes the fault of death, hence saying, "If you do not depart, I shall sever your life. His contemplation of emptiness and the breaking of [delusory] existence is what is meant by "severing life."
The above constitutes the first stage of contemplative practice, wherein one develops revulsion for birth and death.
From here on follows the second stage, the completion of contemplative practice, wherein both birth and death are abandoned.
This section contains four parts:

1. The analogy of life and death following one another; 2. From "The master returns and inquires about his merits" onwards, the analogy of the certainty of birth and death; 3. From "The master then says, 'If there were... onwards, the analogy of revulsion toward both birth and death; 4. From "The master sees... onwards, the analogy of the joy of liberation from [suffering].
The first three sentences of the beginning are as follows:

First, the girl replies, "You are utterly foolish. This is a reprimand of her feelings by means of the Dharma; she is called "foolish" because her desire to avoid death and seek life does not accord with the principles of the Dharma. She is called "lacking wisdom" because she does not know that severing the cycle of birth is what removes old age and death.
Second, from the section where "the master asks" onwards, he uses worldly feelings to examine the Dharma through analogy.

Third, the "Woman’s Reply" below illustrates the principle of the Dharma through a metaphor for the mind. Because birth arises prior to death, she says, "My elder sister. Because birth and death follow one another, she says, "We always move and stop together. Because the cessation of death must first involve the severing of birth, she says, "If you drive me away, you must also drive her away."
In the second analogy, "The Certainty of Birth and Death," the passage—"The master returns and asks Guṇakāśikā:
'There is a woman outside who says she is your younger sister; is this true or not?'"—examines the Dharma through human emotion. When "Guṇakāśikā replies:
'She is indeed my sister,'" the Dharma subsequently manifests within the mind.
Within this, the first part clarifies that the law of death follows birth; because it follows, she is called "sister.

Next, it clarifies that birth and death follow one another without separation. The section beginning with "wherever they dwell" clarifies that the karmic activities of birth and death differ from one another. The section beginning with "if they love me" clarifies that the meanings of love and hatred do not belong exclusively to one side.

In the third analogy, which illustrates the simultaneous loathing of both birth and death: "If there are such things as good and evil" refers to both birth and death together—birth being good and death being evil;
"I do not desire either" expresses the simultaneous loathing of both birth and death;
and "let each depart as it pleases" signifies the simultaneous rejection of both birth and death.

"At that time, the two women together returned to their dwelling. Having departed from both birth and death, they abandoned their status as holy ones and returned to their dwelling as ordinary people.
Regarding the fourth phrase, "seeing [them] depart, her heart rejoiced," the meaning is clear and self-evident from the text.
The upper part of the analogy represents the bodhisattva, while the lower part represents ordinary beings who, driven by craving, undergo birth and death.
Within this, there are four phrases:

first, the statement that "the two women again went together to a poor household" illustrates how birth and death pursue ordinary beings; because they lack the wealth of merit, it is called a "poor household."

2. From "The Poor Man Sees" onwards, the analogy clarifies that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) undergo both birth and death; from "Upon first seeing him, he was joyful and immediately invited him" onwards, it shows their creation of karma to seek [happiness].
3. From "The Words of Merit" onwards, the noble one reproaches the ordinary being by comparison: "I am driven by others; for what reason do you also invite me to stay? 4. The poor man says:

"May you remember me": the following section distinguishes between the ordinary person and the noble one. Because birth follows the sentiments of ordinary beings, it is called "may you remember me. Since ordinary beings crave birth and consequently undergo old age and death, it says, "Therefore, you should likewise revere them. "For this reason, we both request" concludes the response to the preceding challenge.

In the section on "conjunction," first the conjunction of both the Bodhisattvas and the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) in their shared aversion is established; from the passage beginning "The foolish ordinary person" downward, the conjunction of both in their shared experience of receiving [birth] is established.

From here below is the second part, concerning the difference in their near-activities (*upavicāra*), namely seeking birth and avoiding death; this consists first of a simile and subsequently of its application.

In the analogy, there are four statements: First, the analogy of the beginner seeking birth: The bodhisattva who has newly begun to cultivate pure conduct is called a "Brahmin youth. Being tormented by suffering is called "being pressed by hunger. Seeking birth among humans and devas amidst various forms of death is likened to "seeing an amra fruit in the midst of filth and immediately picking it up. Here, the filth symbolizes old age and death, while the fruit symbolizes birth.

Second, the analogy of the long-practitioner’s reproach: The bodhisattva of noble conduct is called a "wise man. Because he loathes that seeking of birth, he rebukes him, saying: "O Brahmin, your lineage is pure; for what reason do you take this fruit from within human excrement?"

3. From "The boy heard" (*kumāraḥ śrutvā*) onwards begins the parable of the Bodhisattva’s initial practice regarding the purpose of birth. Feeling shame for having previously sought birth is called "feeling remorse upon hearing" (*śrutvā hrītaḥ*). Manifesting that one's inner mind actually does not crave birth is called "I will not eat. Desiring to rely on birth to eliminate old age and death is called "washing clean.

Having eliminated old age and death, abandoning both [birth and old age] together is called "casting it away again. 4. From "The wise man said" (*vidvān āha*) onwards is the parable of the long-term practitioner’s renewed rebuke. "You fool! is a direct rebuke. "If you cast it away, you should not have taken it in the first place" is a reproach used to manifest his folly.

In the section on "Correspondence" (*yōu*), the passage beginning with "The bodhisattva is also like this" corresponds to the second and fourth phrases, while the section beginning with "Just as that wisdom" provides a simile to apply [the correspondence].

The passage beginning with "Ordinary people delight in birth and loathe death" corresponds to the first and third phrases, while the section beginning with "Just as that child" provides a simile to apply [the correspondence].
From here below is the third section, concerning how one differs from ordinary beings by not creating the causes for rebirth; first the analogy, then the application.
Within the analogy, there are two parts:
first, the analogy of a bodhisattva who knows that birth entails death and thus does not create the causes for it.
Second, the section beginning with "Then he spoke" uses an analogy to illustrate how ordinary people, being ignorant, create karma for the sake of rebirth.
Within this, there are four parts:

first, an analogy for a person who raises the result to examine and seek it; second, the passage beginning with "There was a man from afar," which uses an analogy to illustrate how a bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching, inquires with scrutiny; third, the passage beginning with "The host of eaters replied," which uses an analogy to illustrate how the speaker praises birth and distinguishes death; fourth, the passage beginning with "When that person heard," which uses an analogy to illustrate how the bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching, develops weary detachment.

Regarding the first sentence: the place where the fourfold assembly gathers is called a "crossroads. "A person" is a metaphor for the one who preaches the Dharma; "vessel" is a metaphor for the teaching. Fully explaining the fruits of joy for humans and devas in the future is called "filling it with food. Explaining that those beings possess physical beauty, strength, peace, and happiness throughout their lives is called "endowed with color and fragrance. Encouraging people to practice the causes to support those fruits is called "wishing to sell it."

In the second sentence, "a person" is a metaphor for a bodhisattva practicing the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*). Having long wandered through birth and death is called "coming from afar"; having no pleasure with which to satisfy oneself is called "hunger and emptiness"; being weary and exhausted by suffering is called "emaciation and weakness. Hearing it said that the bliss of that fruit is abundant and complete is called "seeing that the food possesses color, fragrance, and flavor"; examining what was said is called "pointing to it and asking, 'What is this?'"

In the third sentence, the phrase "The Master of Food replied, 'This is the supreme food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor'" praises its excellence. The section beginning with "If one eats this" distinguishes the benefits according to the person; that a person receives the name "born from that" upon eating it is expressed as "eating this food. "Obtaining form and obtaining strength" clarifies that there is pleasure, while "being able to eliminate hunger and thirst" demonstrates the absence of suffering. Having many devas and humans as one's retinue is termed "obtaining the sight of devas."
The preceding statement, "Lamenting that birth has but one affliction, namely the end of life," demonstrates that there is death.
In the fourth line, "Having heard this, the person immediately thinks:
'I do not need form,' etc., seeking no future birth" and "nor do I need death," expressing weariness with the prospect of dying.
The following clarifies how ordinary beings create karma for the sake of birth:

"Having said this—'Once this food has been eaten, if one’s life comes to an end, what is the use of selling it?'"—this metaphor clarifies that the Bodhisattva questions the purpose of his actions: since one who takes birth must inevitably die, what is the use of encouraging others to seek [birth]?

The response of the "Master of Food" illustrates the intended meaning through a parable. "The wise do not buy" distinguishes the noble ones from ordinary people; "only the ignorant do not know, so give much and buy it from me" reveals the difference between ordinary people and the noble ones. That ordinary beings do not realize that birth is inevitably followed by death is termed "the ignorance of the foolish"; their practice of many wholesome causes in pursuit of such birth is termed "giving much in exchange."

Within this synthesis, there are two parts: first, the synthesis with the wise person who knows the fault and does not seek [the gem], and from "The foolish ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana-bāla*) downward, the synthesis with the fool who does not know it and offers a high price.
From here below is the fourth section, which cites the vastness and pervasiveness of death to establish that birth is to be loathed.
Within this, first the analogy of the poisonous tree is presented; the application of this analogy can be understood accordingly.
From here below is the fifth section, which cites the vast duration of death to establish that birth is to be loathed.
First the analogy of excrement is presented, and the subsequent application [of the analogy] can be understood.
From here on, the sixth section clarifies how various delusions arise, which delight people in their greed or result in what is fearsome; first the analogy, then the application.
The three phrases within the analogy are as follows: first, the analogy for the arising of mixed delusive pleasure.

"The precipitous bank" symbolizes the bodies of humans and devas; it is called "precipitous" because they are on the verge of falling into the three miserable realms. Within those births, the obstruction of the mind by ignorance and darkness is called "covered with grass. Being drawn by the passions of delusive pleasure in those places of birth is called "having much ambrosia at the edge of the bank. Cultivating causes and receiving their fruits is called "having food. The prolongation of celestial retribution is called "a lifespan of a thousand years. Abiding therein without suffering is called "permanently removing illness. Receiving many blessings is called "peaceful and secure happiness."

Second, the analogy of the ordinary person’s craving and delusion: Seeking that pleasure is called "craving its flavor"; not knowing that such pleasure leads to falling into the three miserable realms is called "not knowing there is a deep pit below"; performing good deeds while seeking [pleasure] is called "wishing to take it up first"; being unaware that one's life has ended is called "stumbling with the feet"; and falling headlong into the three miserable realms is called "dying in a pit of dust. Third, the analogy of the Bodhisattva’s renunciation.

In the section on "Application," the phrase "The Bodhisattva is also like this" and so forth applies the third line [of the verse]. The statement "He does not even desire to accept exquisite food from the heavens, much less that of humans" uses the superior to illustrate the inferior; because the dharma is expressed by means of a metaphor, it is referred to as "food."

The phrase "ordinary persons" corresponds to the second line; the passage from "they even swallow iron balls in hell, how much more so for humans and devas" uses what follows to illustrate what precedes it.
The preceding section clarified the faults of arising, the subsequent section discussed contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), and the following section concludes both.

"By means of such analogies and countless others, one should know that arising is suffering" concludes the preceding discussion on the faults of arising; "this is called a bodhisattva abiding in nirvāṇa," etc., concludes the preceding discussion on contemplative practice.
Next is the contemplation of the suffering of old age, which consists of an initial inquiry, followed by an exposition, and finally a conclusion.
Within the exposition, there is first a brief summary, and from "For example, like a pond" onwards is the detailed explanation.
The three phrases within the summary are as follows:
first, clarifying what aging causes, namely such things as "causing hiccups and upward gasping";

second, clarifying what it destroys, namely the eight kinds of things such as "courage," where "advancement" (*jin*) refers to diligence (*vīrya*) and "retention" (*chi*) refers to maintaining the precepts (*śīla*), or alternatively, to being able to remember and uphold them.
The three types of actions performed by old age are the three matters of "causing one to become hunched-backed, indolent, and lazy.
In the detailed exposition, there are fifteen similes in total that collectively reveal the faults of old age.

Within the section on the "conjunctions" (*saṃyojana*), the initial statement, "By means of such analogies and other immeasurable [teachings], one should know the suffering of old age," concludes the object of observation previously examined; the phrase, "The bodhisattva practices," etc., concludes the subject capable of observation previously examined.
Next, one contemplates the suffering of illness, which consists of an initial inquiry, a detailed exposition, and a concluding summary.
Within the exposition, there are three parts:
first, five successive sections that extensively reveal the faults of illness;

Second, from "the causes and conditions of illness" onwards, the six types of causes and conditions for the arising of illness are clarified. "Suffering and affliction," and so forth, constitute the immediate conditions (*pratyaya*); "destroying the life-preserving bag" and "pulling down the bridge" constitute the remote causes (*hetu*). Because these transgressions commit such acts, illness presently exists.
Third, from "furthermore, it can" onwards, that which is damaged is clarified; there are six such things damaged.
Regarding the concluding summaries, first the suffering of illness is summarized, followed by the summary of the contemplative capacity.
Next, the suffering of death is contemplated; within this, there is first the question, then the exposition, and finally the summary.
In the "Discourse on Death" (*Maraṇavibhaṅga*), there are first twelve successive sections that extensively reveal the faults of death; below these, ten phrases explain the characteristics of death.

"Death" is the name for that which harms the body and is thus called a "perilous place. Having nothing by which to sustain oneself in order to cross over it is called "lacking provisions. Passing away once and for all is called "the destination is far. Having no one to escort one is called "being without a companion."

Once a body has been received, it proceeds moment by moment toward death without pausing for even an instant; this is called "constant movement. Because its proximity or distance cannot be measured, it is called "not knowing the limit.

Alternatively, one may say that because ordinary beings receive bodies and die constantly, it is called "constant movement," and because the extent [of these deaths] is difficult to measure, it is called "not knowing the limit."
Once one has entered the stage of death, it is difficult to emerge from the state of dullness and torpor; thus it is called "profound and deep.
As the sense faculties perish and the six consciousnesses become useless, it is said to be "gloomy darkness without a lamp of light."
When life ends, one dies without any point of departure; therefore, it is called "entering through no gate.
Death does not leave the body; thus, it is called "having a location."
At the final thought-moment, when life comes to an end and there is no further perception, it is called the "place of no pain.
Worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness; this is called "incurable."
That which is difficult to delimit is called "having no place of rest.
That which inevitably shifts when the time arrives is called "not being able to escape.
That this person, upon the death of the body, does not extinguish another aggregate (skandha) is called "being indestructible."
When people of the world see it, there are none who do not feel sorrow and fear; thus it is called "Seeing Sorrow and Poison.
It is extinguished and ceases to exist, and no further distinct form or foul color can arise; thus it is called "Non-Foul Color."
That which causes those who see it to be struck with terror is called "that which instills fear.
That which ends with the finality of the body is called "abiding by the side of the person.
That whose timing is difficult to discern is called "unconsciousness."
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first fetter returns to the suffering of death, while the subsequent fetter contemplates the mind.
Within the separation from what is loved, there is first a question and then an exposition; the text on the fetters is omitted.
The initial summary of the *Madhyamaka-vibhāga* states: "Now, [I shall explain]" below follows the detailed exposition.
Within the summary, there are three points:
first, a general clarification that the separation from what is loved is the root of all suffering.
Second, from "As it is said" onwards, the specific explanation that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the root of all suffering.

First, the verse is cited: "From craving, craving arises; from craving, fear arises. This directly clarifies the root of suffering. [The commentary continues: "If one is free from craving, what would there be to crave?"
"What is feared? reverses [the previous point] to clarify the root of suffering; "with craving as the causal condition" below reiterates this further.

Third, from "separation from what is loved means the end of life" onwards, it specifically clarifies that separation is the root of all sufferings, first explaining separation and subsequently clarifying the suffering of birth.

In the extensive version, the phrase "I shall now analyze and reveal" serves as a general heading; from "the past" onwards, its specific characteristics are correctly explained. First, past events are cited; then, from "the Bodhisattva still remembers the past" onwards, the past is used as an analogy for the present.
Regarding the encounter with those one hates and dislikes, first there is the inquiry, next the analysis, and finally the summary.
Within the analysis, there are two parts:
first, contemplating the encounter with the hateful, which consists of an initial teaching, followed by a simile, and then an application; second...
Second, from "Just as a person" onwards is the cultivation and relinquishment [of attachment], consisting first of a simile and subsequently its application.
Within the section on "seeking and not finding," there is first a question and subsequently an exposition.
In the exposition, "seeking everything exhaustively" is the general statement, while "there are two kinds" and below is the specific analysis.
"The five aggregates of clinging" can be understood; "this is called the Truth of Suffering" serves as the general conclusion.

From here on is the second section, which reconciles the Truth of Suffering: since what was taught in the past was that there is pleasure, while what is taught now is that there is suffering, the present and the past appear contradictory; therefore, they must be reconciled.
Kāśyapa asked first; within his question there are three parts:

first, he restates what the Buddha taught—that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all suffering—and directly affirms that this is not otherwise; "the abundance of the aggregates" is the general principle, and thus he specifically restates it;
second, from "Why... onwards is the explanation; third is the conclusion.
Third, from "As in various sutras" onwards, there is an inquiry requesting a reconciliation.
The first section is self-evident.
In the second section, which provides the explanation, "For what reason? poses the inquiry, and the subsequent passage offers a refutation in response.
Within this, the first part clarifies that ordinary beings possess happiness, while the verses clarify that noble ones (ārya) possess happiness.

Regarding the happiness of ordinary beings, it reverses the previously explained suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) to demonstrate that happiness exists within all five aggregates.

“Formerly, when it was said, ‘Māṇava, if form is suffering,’ and so forth, this clarifies that there is pleasure within form; this is explained in terms of seeking [pleasure], first by way of negation and then by way of affirmation.

‘As it was told to the bhikṣus that there are three feelings,’ and so forth, clarifies that there is pleasure within feeling. ‘As the Buddha previously said, “If a person cultivates wholesome deeds, they will obtain pleasure,”’ this clarifies that there is pleasure within volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, ‘as the Buddha said that within the good realms, the six types of contact experience pleasure,’ commentators differ on this point: if one follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, contact belongs to the aggregate of volitional formations; if one follows the explanation in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, which takes perception (*saṃjñā*) as contact, then this sentence clarifies pleasure in terms of perception. As for the visual consciousness perceiving forms and so forth, there is pleasure within the aggregate of consciousness.”

The Noble One possesses joy within the Middle Way: the first two verses concern the cause of the Hīnayāna; the next one and a half verses concern the cause of the Mahāyāna; the subsequent half verse concerns the fruit of the Hīnayāna; and the final verse concerns the fruit of the Mahāyāna.

Within the causal stage of the Hīnayāna, the first verse clarifies the joy of maintaining ethical discipline; the subsequent half-verse clarifies the joy of cultivating wisdom; and the final half-verse clarifies the joy of cultivating meditative concentration.
In the Mahāyāna context of the causal stage, the first verse concerns benefiting others, while the latter half concerns self-benefit.
Among the eight great awakenings, only few desires, contentment, and wisdom are specifically mentioned, while the remainder are omitted for brevity.
The two fruits, great and small, can be understood from the text.

In the third section, "The characteristics of bliss as described in various sūtras have such a meaning" cites the Buddha’s former words; "as the Buddha now says" introduces his present speech; and "how should this be consistent with this meaning? poses a dual inquiry by contrasting the present and the past: since the former teaching asserts that there is bliss, how can it be consistent with this present meaning of suffering?
The following section clarifies the assemblies, first enumerating them and then presenting the assemblies themselves.
Within this text, there are four distinct parts;
the first assembly concerns the experience of pleasure through the six types of contact, from "the eye seeing beautiful forms" up to "mental intention."
2. “Kāśyapa said: ‘That person does not experience pleasure from even a single blow’” reconciles [this] with the teaching on the existence of pleasure within form (*rūpa*) given to Mānava;
3. “There are three feelings” and below reconcile the previous three feelings;
4. “Kāśyapa said: [and so forth].

If one speaks in accordance with worldly convention, is this not false? This section below reconciles the previous point that those who cultivate goodness receive happiness, and it also reconciles the "holy and noble happiness" mentioned in the verse.
Within the first segment, there is first a brief exposition, followed by a detailed one.

"All sentient beings mistakenly give rise to the notion of pleasure amidst lower suffering," and so forth; this reconciles previous statements. Because the characteristics of affliction in the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*)—which involve arising and ceasing—are subtle, it is termed "lower suffering."

“Ordinary beings have not awakened to this suffering; within this very suffering, they perversely give rise to the notion of pleasure. Therefore, when I previously taught that there is pleasure in the six contacts and even pleasure in the mental faculty’s engagement with agreeable phenomena, what I say now is no different from that original teaching. By bringing the present into accord with the past, I show that because they perversely conceive of lower-grade suffering as pleasure, the suffering spoken of now is no different from the lower-grade suffering in which they were formerly deluded.”

Furthermore, as I now teach the perception of suffering based on those lower forms of suffering, it does not contradict the adventitious perception of pleasure; therefore, I say they are not different.
The passage beginning with "Kāśyapa said" is its detailed exposition.
First the objection, then the explanation.
The objection consists of three points:

first, an objection based on using the subtle to challenge the coarse; second, an objection through a counter-argument using pleasure, beginning with "If, moreover, someone were to ask this"; third, an objection that examines the principle by adhering to the facts, beginning with "If one perceives pleasure within suffering."

Regarding the first objection: it argues that by means of the subtle arising and ceasing of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), one should cause the coarse and heavy eight types of suffering within the three miserable realms to all produce happiness; this is the nature of that objection.

In the text, the initial statement, "As the Buddha has taught, one gives rise to the perception of pleasure within inferior suffering," cites the Buddha’s prior words. From the phrase "arising in the inferior" (*hōshō*) onwards, the subtle is used to categorize the coarse: among the three miserable realms (*trāya*), the eight heavy sufferings are the most debased and inferior, and are thus termed "inferior. Having heard the Buddha’s previous teaching that the perception of pleasure can arise even within such subtly inferior suffering, Kāśyapa then interrogates the Tathāgata, wishing to know whether the debased and inferior suffering of the three miserable realms can likewise give rise to the perception of pleasure; therefore he says, "Arising in the inferior"—that is, inferior birth, aging, sickness, and so forth—should also give rise to pleasure.
"The 'inferior' refers to the three evil realms," and so forth; this section below explains their inferior characteristics, revealing them by contrasting them with the middling and superior.
At first glance, this point appears somewhat difficult to resolve, but upon careful analysis, it is not difficult.
What is not a valid objection?
That which the Tathāgata calls "minor" is designated as such because suffering is subtle; since coarse pleasure is not manifested, the perception of pleasure arises.
As for what Kāśyapa cites as being called "inferior and base," this suffering is coarse and heavy and stands in direct opposition to pleasure; how, then, could the perception of pleasure arise?
Because it was not a valid objection, the Buddha did not answer; this should be recorded and understood.
Regarding the second objection, he provisionally raises another question and requests the Buddha’s teaching as an answer.

If the Tathāgata were to say that inferior suffering gives rise to pleasure, and another were to counter by asserting that everything is entirely pleasure, yet sentient beings perceive the notion of suffering within inferior pleasure, the notion of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure within middling pleasure, and only the notion of pleasure within superior pleasure—how would you answer?
In the third objection, Kāśyapa, acting as the interlocutor, challenges the reasoning:

"If the Tathāgata says that suffering produces pleasure, [one might argue] that no one has ever been seen who, while undergoing a thousand punishments, would give rise to a perception of pleasure at the very first stroke. Since a perception of pleasure does not arise at the first stroke, how can it be said that suffering produces pleasure?"

Since pleasure does not arise in lower states of suffering, it is clearly understood that worldly people experience pleasure in places where pleasure exists; because pleasure arises in such places, they are not entirely suffering.
The Buddha then answers this: of the three preceding objections, he only responds to the latter two, for the first is not a valid objection and thus is not answered.
In the text, the Tathāgata first confirms Kāśyapa’s third objection with this seal-word, using it to resolve the difficulty raised in the preceding second sentence.
"Just so, just so" summarizes his statement, while "as you have said" and the following lines explain it in detail.

What you have said—that pleasure does not arise from the first degree of inferiority—is indeed logically correct; because pleasure does not arise from the first degree of inferiority, it lacks the characteristic of pleasure. Since the characteristic of pleasure is absent, how can you challenge me by saying that suffering arises from pleasure?

The section beginning with "For what reason" correctly resolves the objection raised in the third preceding sentence. By stating "For what reason," it interrogates the previous point to introduce the subsequent one: since there is no characteristic of pleasure, for what reason do I say that pleasure arises within superior suffering?

Explaining this in contrast to what follows: "It is just as if that person were due to receive a thousand punishments, yet having received only one, he immediately attains release and conceives the notion of pleasure. For this reason, I say that one falsely conceives of pleasure in a place where there is no pleasure; "no pleasure" here carries the same meaning as the aforementioned "lower suffering."
From here begins the second assembly, in which Mānava is told that there is pleasure within form (*rūpa*).

At the outset, Kāśyapa first raises an objection against what preceded and initiates the subsequent discussion: "That person does not produce pleasure through a single stroke; rather, it is because he has attained liberation that the perception of pleasure arises."
The Buddha seals this as being identical to the assembly at the summit.

As for the phrase "therefore," it refers to the arising of joy from the state of liberation; thus, when he previously told Mānava that among the five aggregates there is joy within the aggregate of form, it was true and not false. This is because the five aggregates of humans and devas have attained freedom from the coarse and heavy suffering of the three miserable realms, and thus their joy is not false.
Because the former was treated briefly, it was referred to simply as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
because this section is comprehensive, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are discussed collectively.
From here on, the third section correlates these with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*); this passage consists of four distinct parts:
