Below, the conception of a self is clarified; first it is presented in general, and then it is specifically revealed in eight successive sections:
the first uses the eyes and other faculties—the instruments of the self—to prove the existence of a self, first establishing the doctrine of the self and subsequently refuting non-self.

Second, the existence of a self is established by means of the characteristic of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*): "There is a self" is stated briefly; from "How is this known? onwards, the question and answer provide a brief exposition; from "What kind... onwards, the question and answer provide a detailed exposition; and from "Therefore... onwards, the conclusion is made.
Third, the existence of a self is established by means of the capacity for specific cognition: first it is stated, then it is expounded, and from "Therefore... onwards, the conclusion is made.
Fourth, from "Grasping the sickle" onwards, the existence of a self is established by means of having functional activity.
Fifth, at the time of birth, the desire for milk and so forth proves that habitual tendencies from previous lives have not perished, thereby establishing the existence of a self;

sixth, the fact that objects such as jars, clothing, and vehicles benefit people through their combination establishes the existence of a self—this is first briefly indicated, then explained under the section beginning with "For example," and finally concluded under the section beginning with "Therefore";
seventh, by means of negation, the existence of a self is established—first asserting the self, then refuting non-self, and finally restating and concluding the proof.

Eighth, the existence of a self is established by means of its companions. First, it was briefly indicated; next, from "How so? onwards, it is explained; and from "In this way" onwards, it is concluded.
Having extensively discussed the matter above, the section concludes with the summary: "For this reason, even the non-Buddhists proclaim that the self possesses ultimate truth."
The Buddha refutes this from below; the text is divided into four parts:
first, an extensive censure; second, an extensive refutation; third, a reiterated censure; and fourth, a concluding refutation.

At the beginning, the Tathāgata offers a general rebuke, stating, "If there were permanence, bliss, self, and purity, one would not be a śramaṇa," and so forth. From the words "For what reason? onwards, the Tathāgata provides a detailed rebuke, first posing a challenge and subsequently providing an exposition; within this section, there are twenty-two sentences in total.
In the second section on refutation, the four preceding views are refuted in successive order.
Within the refutation of the eternalist view, there is first a general refutation, followed by a specific refutation, and finally a concluding summary of the refutation.
In the previous general refutation, [the Buddha] rebuked their thesis by stating, "These non-Buddhists are deluded and inverted, claiming that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent.
He negated their thesis by stating, "It is impossible for conditioned phenomena to be permanent."
"I observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent" overturns what was established.
Within the specific refutation, "How do you know this? interrogates the preceding statement to introduce the subsequent one; the following section then provides the actual refutation.
There are eight points to be refuted, as extensively analyzed above:
first, establishing permanence by means of the fact that one does not lose the experience of desirable or undesirable karmic retributions;
second, establishing permanence by means of the fact that the causal conditions of the karma of killing are not destroyed.
Third, one realizes permanence through single-minded mindfulness without forgetfulness;
fourth, one realizes permanence through the non-extinction of what is conceived;
fifth, one realizes permanence through the growth of habitual karma.
Sixth, by the increase of calculation and arithmetic, one realizes permanence;
seventh, by the increase of reading and recitation, one realizes permanence;
eighth, by the fact that all jars, garments, vehicles, mountains, rivers, and the great earth remain similar and do not perish, one establishes and proves the existence of permanence.
In this passage, the Tathāgata first refutes the first two [theses] and next refutes the eighth; the five middle ones he refutes together in a single section.
Within the refutation of the first two, there are four distinct textual parts:
first, it clarifies that because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from conditions, they are entirely impermanent.
Second, from "Buddha-nature" onwards, the permanence is revealed;
third, from "By this meaning" onwards, the first [point] is concluded;

fourth, from "These non-Buddhists do not see the nature" onwards, in contrast to the previous two, it is clarified that the non-Buddhists do not attain the permanent dharma, and all that they can express is entirely impermanent.
The first part has two sections:
first, a general clarification that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and are therefore entirely impermanent;

second, from the passage "Of these various heterodox paths, not a single dharma... onwards, a specific clarification that among the things heterodox practitioners conceive as permanent, there is not a single dharma that does not arise from conditions, and is thus impermanent.

Non-Buddhists often reckon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to be permanent; yet among the phenomena of the five aggregates, how could there be a single dharma that does not arise from conditions?
Therefore, they are impermanent.

In the second refutation, it is first clarified that the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is permanent, and subsequently, by means of the analogy of the Buddha-nature to the Three Jewels (*triratna*), it is shown that the Three Jewels are likewise all permanent.
The first ten phrases of the preceding section are as follows:
First, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is without arising and without cessation, and is therefore eternal;
second, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature neither goes nor comes, for it is immutable.
Third, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is not subsumed within the three periods of time, because it does not undergo flux or transformation;

fourth, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither produced by causes nor produced without cause: it is not produced by causes because it is not generated by them, and it is not produced without cause because it is realized through the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*);

fifth, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither an action nor an agent: the nature of the Buddha-nature is called "non-action" because it does not arise as *nirvāṇa*, and it is called "non-agent" because it does not cause others to produce the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Sixth, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither with signs nor signless: because all signs are eternally severed, it is not "with signs"; because the gates of the Dharma-realm are complete, it is not "signless.

Seventh, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither a name nor nameless: when discussing reality according to reality, no name can be found apart from reality, so it is not a "name"; when designating the nature through conditions, the nature is manifested by the name, so it is not "nameless.

Eighth, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither name nor form: because it does not correspond to the four aggregates, it is not a "name"; because it does not correspond to the aggregate of form, it is said to be not "form."
Ninth, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither long nor short, because it is free from the characteristics of form;
tenth, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is not subsumed by the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, for it is truly unlike them and thus cannot be contained by them.
"Thus it is called 'permanent'"—this serves as the general conclusion.

Below, the Buddha-nature is categorized as being identical to the Three Jewels. Within this, first, the nature is identical to the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is identical to the Dharma; and the Dharma is identical to the permanent.
Subsequently, the meaning of permanence is identical to the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is identical to the Saṃgha; and the Saṃgha is identical to the permanent.

From here below begins the third section, which concludes the first [section]. Within this, it is first clarified that all phenomena arising from conditions cannot be called permanent. From the passage beginning with "These various outsiders," it is clarified that among the things considered permanent by the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there is not one that does not arise from conditions; therefore, they are impermanent.

From here below is the fourth section, clarifying that the various non-Buddhists do not perceive the eternal Dharma; all that they describe as eternal is merely false speech, for there is no true eternity.

The passage beginning with "All ordinary beings" skips ahead to refute the eighth [point]; therein, it first clarifies that what the non-Buddhists conceive is in fact not eternal, and from the word "space" onwards, it cites the eternal to manifest this [truth].

In the first part of the middle section, the initial portion restates their conceptualization; from "it should be known" onwards, it clarifies that [existence] is not permanent; and from "all that exists" onwards, it sets forth the phenomena that are impermanent.
In this section, which cites the permanent to clarify the impermanent, there are five distinct points:
first, it clarifies that space is permanent because it is unconditioned; here, the term "space" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and not to the physical void;
second, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature is permanent because it is unconditioned.
Third, emptiness is identical to nature;
fourth, buddha-nature is identical to the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the unconditioned is identical to the eternal;
fifth, the eternal is identical to the Dharma, the Dharma is identical to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha is identical to the unconditioned, and the unconditioned is identical to the eternal.

"Conditioned phenomena are of two kinds," and so forth, refutes the prior calculation of permanence regarding the five intermediate phrases. Within this, first the phenomena are divided into two categories, and subsequently, based on these two, their calculated positions are refuted.

In the first part of the middle section, the statement "conditioned phenomena are of two kinds" serves as a general heading; "material and non-material phenomena" specifically list their names, while the following portion explains their characteristics.
"Non-form refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). Here, the six consciousnesses are the mind, while perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others are the mental factors.
"Form refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there are fourteen types of form:
the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and the four great elements.
According to the *Abhidharma*, there are eleven types of form (*rūpa*):
the five sense organs, the five objects, and the non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
For what reason, then, is only the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) specifically discussed here?

Relying solely on the *Tattvasiddhi*, "great" (mahat) is both the effect of the sense-object and the cause of the sense-faculty; because one knows the effect by citing the cause, the sense-faculty is not mentioned, and because one knows the cause by citing the effect, the sense-object is not mentioned.

If one follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the fundamental basis of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*); therefore, they are singled out for mention. Since mentioning the root encompasses its branches, other elements are not mentioned.

If one follows what Buddhadeva established—namely, that matter consists solely of the four great elements and there is no further derived matter beyond them—one now speaks as if in agreement with that Buddhadeva.

Below, we shall refute his positions based on these two [views]: by refuting the third, fifth, sixth, and seventh [positions] through the impermanence of mind, since those four are calculated based on the mind; and by refuting the fourth position regarding the non-extinction of what is conceived, since this one is calculated based on matter.
Within the initial section concerning the mind: "The mind is called impermanent" serves as the general heading; "Why? introduces the explanation; and "Because of this... provides the conclusion.

In the commentary, the initial phrase "For what reason" interrogates the preceding section to introduce the subsequent one; the passage beginning with "The nature is... cites the latter to clarify the meaning of the former: that the mind is impermanent.
First, four gates are opened:
the first gate concerns their nature, clarifying that although the essential natures of the six consciousnesses are identical, their names differ, and thus they are impermanent;
the second concerns their objective conditions, clarifying that the objects conditioned by the six consciousnesses are each distinct.
The third [section], "Correspondence," clarifies the dharma-realm associated with the six consciousnesses;
the fourth, "Discrimination," clarifies that through various analytical approaches, the mind is not permanent.
The following is explained in sequence according to this gate: "The nature of eye-consciousness differs, up to and including mind [consciousness] differing" expands upon the first gate;
"the object-field of form differs, up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*) differing" expands upon the second;

and "the association with eye-consciousness differs, up to and including the association with mind-consciousness differing" expands upon the third. The factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*); that which is co-present with eye-consciousness does not reach other consciousnesses, and this is termed "difference in association. The same applies to all others.

"If the mind were permanent, the visual consciousness alone should perceive all objects. This section, which expands upon the fourth [point] below, contains eleven successive arguments (*paryāya*). Of these, the first five arguments refute the permanence of the mind through further reasoning; the next three arguments directly refute the preceding position; the next two arguments again refute the permanence of the mind through further reasoning; and the final argument directly refutes the preceding position.

Regarding the first five [points]: first, the permanence of the mind is refuted by the fact that a single consciousness cannot independently perceive all phenomena; second, the permanence of the mind is refuted by the principle that it can be destroyed through causes and conditions; third, the permanence of the mind is refuted by the diversity of the various gates of remedial practice; fourth, the permanence of the mind is refuted by the distinctness of the mental natures of sentient beings; fifth, the permanence of the mind is refuted by the multiplicity of conceptual discriminations.

At the beginning, the statement, "If the mind were permanent, the visual consciousness alone should perceive all phenomena," refutes the opponent's doctrine of permanence; for that which is permanent does not cease, and therefore it should perceive all phenomena independently.
Furthermore, I shall examine visual consciousness; the others will be omitted for brevity.

The phrase "visual consciousness is distinct" below naturally reveals its impermanence, while the passage beginning with "because phenomena arise moment by moment in similarity" explains why ordinary people falsely conceive of it as permanent.

In the second sentence, it is briefly indicated that "it is also called impermanent because it can be destroyed by various causes and conditions. The term "differentiation" (viśeṣa) refers to destruction; because the causes and conditions for the various consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, are distinct, they are said to be differentiated. Furthermore, that which can be broken and extinguished is termed "destruction" (bhaṅga). Since the eye-consciousness and other such consciousnesses arise dependent upon conditions and do not arise when conditions are lacking, they are termed "destroyed. This will be explained in detail below.
In the third section, there are four distinct points: First, it clarifies the causes and conditions for the impermanent destruction of formations.

The phrase "the mind is called impermanent" briefly sets forth the thesis; because the mind engaged in contemplative practice can destroy the various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) of birth and death, this contemplation itself is termed "destruction. Since the causes and conditions of all formations lead to their destruction and these conditions are ever-changing, the mind is impermanent—this is detailed in the following passage beginning with "That is to say.

Second, from "If the mind were permanent" onwards, it refutes the opponent's calculation of permanence. If it were permanent, it would remain fixed; therefore, one who cultivates the perception of impermanence cannot even attain the contemplation of suffering, emptiness, and non-self, let alone attain the contemplation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

3. From "By this meaning" onwards, the second point is concluded to clarify the fault of the non-Buddhists' adherence to permanence: because those who calculate [things] as permanent are stubbornly attached to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and cannot contemplate the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are unable to apprehend permanence, bliss, self, and purity within the teachings of the non-Buddhists.
4. From "Good son" onwards, the first point is concluded to clarify that the mind and dharmas are definitively impermanent.

This concludes the third section. In the fourth section, the statement “the nature of the mind differs, and thus it is called impermanent” is briefly presented as a heading; what follows below provides a detailed exposition. First, it clarifies that the minds of all noble ones (ārya) differ. Next, the passage beginning with “The minds of all non-Buddhists (tīrthika) are of three kinds” clarifies how the minds of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) who possess right view differ. Then, the passage beginning with “When all non-Buddhists address the minds of those they confront, there are three kinds” clarifies how the minds of ordinary persons with right view differ when contrasted with those non-Buddhists. Within this, the differences among the minds of the non-Buddhists themselves have not yet been clarified and will be discussed separately later.
The minds of ordinary beings with right view are of three kinds:
first, the mind that performs karma; second, the mind that experiences retribution; and third, the mind of afflictions.
Within the mind that performs karma, the phrase "there are three" indicates the number, and their names may be understood from the enumeration.
“Associated with pleasure” and so forth refer to the mind that experiences retribution;
“associated with greed” and so forth refer to the mind of affliction (*kleśa*).

Next, it clarifies that the minds of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are distinct: “The characteristics of all non-Buddhist minds are also different” briefly indicates this, which is then specifically explained below. “That is to say, association with delusion is different” and so forth refer to the mind of affliction; “the mind of advancing and ceasing is different” refers to the mind of action (*karma*).

In the fifth statement, "If the mind were permanent, it likewise would be unable to differentiate various forms," the permanence of the mind is refuted by means of its manifold differentiations. Being permanent implies being immobile; how then could it differentiate the various kinds of forms?
The phrase "that which is called blue" and so forth brings forth the object of conceptualization (*vikalpya*).
The preceding five phrases separately refute the permanence of the mind by means of other arguments; the following three phrases directly refute the aforementioned attachment.

"If the mind were permanent, the dharmas of recollection should not be forgotten"—this refutes the third preceding argument for permanence based on mindfulness. If it were permanent, it should remain fixed; for what reason would there be forgetfulness?
When what has been contemplated is forgotten, one realizes it is impermanent.

"If the mind were permanent, whatever one recites and studies should not increase"—this refutes the previous seventh [point] regarding the increase of recitation and study; [the mind] should remain fixed and constant, so for what reason would there be increase?

"If the mind were permanent, one should not say that it 'has already acted' or 'is now acting. This refutes the previous sixth point regarding the increase through calculation. Within this, first the opponent's doctrine of permanence is refuted: even within the context of calculation, when the counting is finished, one says "it has already been done"; while counting, one says "it is being done"; and before counting, one says "it is to be done. Since a permanent phenomenon is fixed and unchanging, how could there be such things as "having already acted" or "acting now"?
The passage beginning with "If there is that which has been done or is being done" correctly demonstrates impermanence.
The following two lines further refute the permanence of the mind through other arguments: if the mind were permanent, it would not differentiate between enemies, kin, and neutral persons;
if the mind were permanent, one should not speak of "my property" or "another's property," nor of birth or death.

Next, the previous position is further refuted: "If the mind were permanent, even though it performs actions, those actions should not increase. This refutes the fifth previous point regarding the increase of action; for how could there be increase if a permanent phenomenon is fixed and unchanging?
The section beginning with "By this meaning" concludes the refutation as a whole.

Next, the impermanence of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) is proclaimed to refute the fourth misconception—that what is conceived does not perish. Within this, first, the preceding is concluded and the subsequent is introduced: "I have now proclaimed impermanence within these non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*); their meaning has already been made manifest" is the conclusion of the preceding; "Furthermore, I shall explain the impermanence of matter for you" is the introduction of the subsequent.
Next, this is explained in detail through ten successive sections: 1.

First, that which originally does not exist is born now, and having been born, it returns to extinction; therefore, it is impermanent. Within this section, the first part provides a general summary, followed by a specific exposition based on the internal and external, and the portion beginning with "Therefore" concludes the argument.
2. From the section beginning with "All that exists," it is shown that internal and external forms undergo transformation according to time; therefore, they are impermanent.
Third, because internal and external flavors differ, they are impermanent;
fourth, because internal and external powers differ, they are impermanent;
fifth, it is explained that internal and external appearances each differ, and thus they are impermanent—here, for brevity, only the internal is discussed.
Sixth, because the internal and external fruits of retribution differ from one another, they are impermanent;
seventh, because the names of the internal and external differ, they are all impermanent;
eighth, because internal and external forms disintegrate and then reunite, they are impermanent.
9. Because internal and external forms arise gradually according to time, they are impermanent;
10. because internal and external [forms] undergo change through cessation, they are impermanent.

From the passage beginning with "Ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*) below, the reason why ordinary persons conceive of permanence is explained: because they perceive similarity and [see things] arising in a continuous succession, they therefore conceive of permanence.
The preceding section was the second part, which extensively refuted the attachment to permanence. The passage beginning with "By this meaning" concludes it as a whole.

"Impermanence is suffering" refutes the prior attachment to pleasure; "Suffering is impure" refutes the prior attachment to purity. "I have already answered because Kāśyapa previously asked" refers back to the extensive explanation above: within the previous analogy of the herd of cows, the Tathāgata, in response to Kāśyapa’s question, extensively clarified that non-Buddhists ultimately lack permanence, pleasure, self, and purity; therefore, he points to and reveals this here.
Next, the refutation of the self: "All conditioned phenomena are without self" is a general refutation; below, it is refuted specifically.
There are eight ways of conceiving a self, as extensively debated above:
first, there is the conception of a self through the instruments of its use, which testify to the existence of a self.
Second, because there is the characteristic of a self, one knows there is a self; this refers to such acts as looking up and down.
Third, because there is specific cognition, one definitively knows there is a self; for instance, seeing a person eating fruit, saliva is produced in one's own mouth.
Fourth, because there is the function of a self, one knows there is a self; this refers to such acts as grasping a sickle.
Fifth, because of habitual tendencies from previous lives, one clearly knows that there is a self;
sixth, because all things combine to benefit the self, one clearly knows that there is a self;
seventh, because of negation, there is a self.
Because there are eight companions, there is a self.
In this present passage, the refutation is based on names and strictly refutes five propositions—namely, the second, third, fifth, seventh, and eighth.
Applying this principle, all eight propositions are refuted; however, they are not in sequential order. They are recorded in four pairs:
in the first pair, the first proposition is refuted first, followed by the fourth;
in the second pair, the seventh is refuted first, followed by the eighth.
Regarding these pairs: the third pair first refutes the sixth and subsequently refutes the fifth;
the fourth pair first refutes the second and subsequently refutes the third.

Within the first pair, one first refutes the "instruments of the self," which refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Among these six, the first five are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), while the mind (*manas*) is a mental phenomenon (*cittadharma*); therefore, we now refute all phenomena collectively by means of these two categories: matter and mind.
"Form and non-form"—these two dharmas are briefly enumerated.

Below, the refutation of the self is undertaken; therein, the non-self nature of form-dharmas is first clarified, beginning with an initial enumeration, followed by an explanation, and concluded with the phrase "for this reason" and so forth.

The following clarifies the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*): "neither form nor self" is briefly stated as a heading, while from "why" onwards it is explained that because the mind arises from conditions, it is therefore not the self.

The phrase "by means of focused mindfulness" below transcends and refutes the fourth [type of] self-activity; the title "In this regard, the Tathāgata is not to be grasped" serves as the formal refutation. By taking that focused mindfulness and recollective conceptualization within the notion of permanence to refute the activity of the self, for what reason is this so?
Since the faculty of focused mindfulness and recollection is also something produced by my own actions, the refutation of the self first proceeds by means of focused mindfulness.

Initially, it raises the point that direct non-mindfulness and the nature [of things] are not the self; then, under the section beginning with "If one takes focused mindfulness as the nature of the self," it raises a false objection to refute [the claim].

Below, he further refutes the self by means of recollection (*smṛti*). "If one knows there is a self through recollection" raises the opponent's position; "if there is no recollection, there is no [self]" reverses that position. From "as it is said" onwards, he extensively cites the absence of recollection to refute the existence of a self. First, he cites a matter of common worldly inquiry, and below, he clarifies the refutation of the self: since one does not inquire about a self that exists, and yet one does inquire, there is no self.
In the second pair, first, regarding the refutation of the existence of a self based on the negation of the seventh [category], there are two parts:
first, the refutation of its existence through the Buddha’s negation; second, the failure of non-Buddhists to negate the self.
In the first part, the initial section restates the opponent's thesis and refutes it by stating, "Because [the self] is negated, one knows it does not exist.

The subsequent sections elaborate on this point. Within them, the first portion clarifies that the existence of a self is not negated: "Just as Devadatta never says he is not [Devadatta]," this is cited as an illustrative example; "I am likewise; I never negate [myself]," this is the formal argument based on the principle itself. The final portion clarifies that because there is indeed a negation [of the self], one definitively knows there is no self.

In the following section on "Clarifying the Non-existence of Self through Non-refutation," the phrase "If one were to know there is a self because of refutation" restates the opponent's thesis; the subsequent statement, "Since you do not refute it now, there must certainly be no self," takes up that very meaning and uses it to dismantle the position.

In order to refute the eighth position—that there is a self because it has companions—the author first restates the opponent's thesis: "Because there are no companions, there should be no self. He then briefly reverses their statement; for since a true self has no companions, that which possesses companions should not have a self.

The following section extensively elucidates this point. Within it, the fact that the true self (*ātman*) has no companion is first clarified through passages such as, "That which has no companion is the Tathāgata," which serves to illustrate the principle. The phrase, "I am likewise; truly, there is no companion," directly clarifies that the true self of the Tathāgata has no companion. The subsequent section beginning with "For this reason" concludes by showing that companionship is not the self.

Within the third pair of arguments, the sixth point—that the combination of various phenomena benefits the self—is first refuted. Non-Buddhists grasp at the worldly expression that "the combination of phenomena benefits the self" and insist upon the existence of a fixed self; therefore, it is now refuted to demonstrate that this is merely a conventional designation and lacks any substantial reality whatsoever.
Within this, first the initial thesis is restated, and subsequently it is refuted:

"In the midst of non-self phenomena, there is also the designation 'self'" demonstrates that the name lacks reality; "like a poor and lowly person" and following cite examples by analogy to clarify this;
"as when one says 'I die'" and following refute the notion that the name possesses reality; "as when people say 'I die'" cites the common usage of worldly people.
He said, "If I were to die, I would be killing myself. Examining the reality based on the name:
"If the various non-Buddhists, upon hearing the words 'it benefits me,' immediately claim there is a self, then just as they say 'I am dead,' I too should die.
If I were to die, this 'I' would be a self that can be killed; therefore, it is said: 'I.'"
"If they were to kill me, yet I am incapable of being killed"—this is a synonym for "reality" (tattva).
"'Conventionally named, 'they kill me'"—this is a designation that lacks substantial reality. "'Like a short man'"—the following provides an illustrative example to clarify this.
"'By this principle'"—the following concludes that there is no self.
The following section refutes the fifth ingrained habit of clinging to a self (*ātman*). First, it restates the opponent's position, and then proceeds to refute it directly.

By raising the example of "if there were a self, one should not grasp filth and excrement," it employs a reductio ad absurdum. The section beginning with "for this reason" concludes the proof of non-self (*anātman*), establishing that because one grasps filth and excrement, one certainly knows there is no self. The section beginning with "all living beings" explains why even infants seek milk, and the section beginning with "therefore" provides the conclusion.

In the fourth pair of arguments, the second [position]—which seeks to prove the self by means of its characteristics—is first refuted. Within this, the initial step is to restate the thesis to be established, followed by its refutation.
"The self does not exist because it possesses characteristics" constitutes the first gate; "even that which lacks characteristics does not exist" constitutes the second gate.
The passage beginning with “If a person, while sleeping, neither advances nor halts” and so forth, reveals that the latter gate [of the preceding section] is both signless and non-existent.

The passage beginning with “If by advancing, halting, bowing, or looking up” and so forth, reveals the former gate; therein, first, the analogy of a wooden man is raised to refute [the self], and subsequently, the true self of the Tathāgata is raised as a contrast to reveal that the true self is signless, clarifying that signs are not the self.

This section refutes the third [argument] which attempts to prove the self through specific cognition. First, it restates the thesis; then, from "because of recollection" onwards, it explains why various sentient beings produce saliva.

Next, it proceeds to refute the self: therein, it first clarifies that saliva is not the self, and subsequently clarifies that the true self is not saliva, pleasure, joy, and so forth. The section ending with "for this reason" provides the conclusion.
The preceding section has completed the refutation; from here below begins the third part, which again offers a reprimand.
Within this, first is the principle (*dharma*), second is the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and third is the application (*upanaya*).

Regarding the principle: first, it clarifies that the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) themselves possess no knowledge; second, it clarifies how the non-Buddhists, within the Buddha’s teaching, seize a mere fragment and falsely reckon it as eternal and so forth; and finally, it clarifies that the non-Buddhists truly cannot know the eternal, blissful, self, and pure (*nitya-sukha-ātma-śubha*).

In the analogy, "like a blind person not recognizing the color of milk" illustrates one's own ignorance; "it is just as if," and so forth, illustrates grasping only a small portion of the Buddha-dharma and falsely calculating it to be permanent, and so on. Within this, four phrases specifically illustrate the false establishment of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; "even though they hear," and so forth, illustrates that in reality they do not know permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

In the section on "Combining," the phrase "non-Buddhists are likewise" corresponds to not recognizing the milk; the passage from "vainly speaking of sound and so forth" onwards corresponds to ultimately failing to obtain the true color of the milk.

The section beginning with "For this reason" constitutes the fourth segment, which reiterates the refutation: because that which is established by the non-Buddhists is incorrect, it is within our Buddha-dharma alone that there exists true reality (satya), and not among the non-Buddhists.
The preceding exposition on the Four Truths and the two truths as one reality constitutes the first section, wherein words are used to manifest reality so that people may realize and enter it.
From here on, the second section sweeps away words to manifest quiescence, leading people to relinquish their attachments.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, Mañjuśrī takes up a characteristic and offers praise to initiate the discourse; second, the Tathāgata addresses him to refute and dispel that notion; third, Mañjuśrī clarifies the purpose of his inquiry and explains it for the sake of others.

At the beginning, having heard the profound exposition of the four truths, the two truths, and the single reality, Mañjuśrī’s mind was deeply moved; thus he offered praise, which consists of three points:

first, taking the form of the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa; second, taking the form of the Tathāgata turning the wheel of Dharma; and third, taking the form of further turning the unsurpassed wheel.

In the past, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment at Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the Four Truths; now, as he enters parinirvāṇa, he speaks of them once more. Therefore, it is praised that the Tathāgata, approaching parinirvāṇa, turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma anew, thus making such distinctions regarding the True Truths.
The Buddha’s refutation and dismissal [of these views] consists of three parts:

first, the dismissal of the mark of the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa; second, from "If there is one who conceives of a self as being the Buddha" onwards, the dismissal of the mark of turning the wheel of Dharma; and third, from "All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, have all dualities" onwards, the dismissal of the mark of further turning the unsurpassed [Dharma].

At the beginning of this section, the Buddha rebukes him for perceiving the Tathāgata as subject to extinction, saying, "Why do you now conceive of the Tathāgata as entering nirvana? This rebuke for grasping at cessation follows from the fact that, although the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding has been repeatedly clarified above, Mañjuśrī’s current statement appears contrary to what preceded; therefore, the Buddha offers this censure.
"The Tathāgata is truly eternal and does not enter parinirvāṇa" clarifies that the Buddha does not perish.
In the second section, there are four distinct parts:
first, it clarifies that the Buddha is without attachment and does not undergo transformation.
1. The section beginning with "If one says it is permanent" clarifies that the Buddha-body is permanent, and therefore there is no transformation; 2.

The section beginning with "For example, depending on the eye and conditioned by form" clarifies that while conventional designations are spoken, the attainment of Buddhahood does not involve transformation; 3.
The section beginning with "Space is neither born nor produced" clarifies that the essence of the Buddha is quiescent, and therefore there is no transformation.
The first and second [sections] further contain four parts:

first, showing how worldly people conceive of a self within the fruit; second, clarifying that the Buddha does not; third, showing how worldly people conceive of a self within the cause; and fourth, clarifying that the Buddha does not.
The first six phrases consist of five instances of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and one instance of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*).

Within the view of self, the first phrase generally refers to the arising of mental activity based on both persons and phenomena. When it says, "If one reckons me as the Buddha," this is reckoning the self with respect to the person; when it says, "I shall attain bodhi," this is reckoning the locus with respect to the phenomenon, because one takes that bodhi as what is attained by the self, and thus calls it "mine" (*mama*).
The following two [statements] specifically concern the arising of conceptualization within phenomena (*dharma*). The former sentence concerns *nirvāṇa* and gives rise to the conceptualization:
"I am the phenomenon," whereby one conceives of the phenomenon as the self;
and "the phenomenon is mine," whereby one conceives of the phenomenon as what belongs to the self.
Because one grasps at dharmas as being what has been attained by oneself, it is called "mine" (*mamāyita*).
The latter phrase refers to the conceptualization regarding awakening;
"I am the Way" is the conceptualization of the Way as the self.
"The Path is my possession" (mama): one reckons the Path as that which belongs to oneself; because one takes the Path as what is practiced by "me," it is called "my possession.
The following two [conceptions] arise specifically among human beings:
"I am the World-Honored One" (bhagavān), wherein one reckons that World-Honored One as the very essence of one's own self.
"The Blessed One is what belongs to me"—thus one conceives that Blessed One as "mine";
"I am the śrāvaka"—thus one conceives that śrāvaka as the essence of the self;
"the śrāvaka is what belongs to me"—thus one conceives that śrāvaka as "mine."
There are four stages of the noble ones:

śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and buddha. By mentioning the highest and the lowest, the middle is omitted for brevity; alternatively, one may say that a buddha is a śrāvaka, because he is reckoned among the fruits [of the path], and because he causes all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way, he is called a śrāvaka.
Regarding the first five types of self-view, the thought "I am able to preach the Dharma, whereas others cannot" constitutes the conceit of "I-am-ness" (asmimāna).
In the second section, it is clarified that the Buddha is eternally free from these; this is evident from the text and can be understood accordingly.

From here below is the third section concerning the conception of a self within the causal framework. Within this, the first part clarifies the conception of the body as the self; the passage beginning with “I am faith” and following concerns the conception of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) as the self.

Regarding the body, there are three propositions: first, conceiving the six sense faculties, such as the eye, as the self; second, conceiving the six objects of the senses, such as form, as the self; and third, conceiving the four great elements, such as earth, as the self.
Within the practice (*caryā*) there are also three stages:
first, reckoning faith, confidence, and extensive learning as the self is the deluded practice of skillful means;
next, reckoning the six perfections such as giving (*dāna*) as the self is the delusion regarding the essence of the practice.
Subsequently, calculating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as "self," one becomes deluded regarding the Dharma.
In the fourth section, it is clarified that the Buddha is eternally non-existent; this is evident from the text and can be understood accordingly.
The preceding four sections together constitute the first part, clarifying that the Buddha is free from attachment and does not himself undergo transformation.
From here below is the second section, clarifying that the Buddha-body is eternal and thus undergoes no transformation; this may be understood from the text.

The third section clarifies transformation within the realm of the provisional and false. Within this, the first five repetitions clarify that transformation within the provisional and false is not something the Buddha alone undergoes;
the subsequent summary and praise clarify that such transformation is the exclusive domain of the Buddha, unknown to the two vehicles.
What is the distinction between the first five?
If one wishes to differentiate them individually:

the first clarifies that [the nature] is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); the second is not arising; the third is not emerging; the fourth is not acting; and the fifth is not creating. Generally speaking, however, these five together reveal a single meaning.
At the beginning of the text, there is first a parable, which consists of three parts:

first, the presentation of the illustrative matter; second, the clarification that it is actually non-existent, starting from the phrase "the eye does not think"; and third, the clarification that it exists as a conventional designation, starting from the phrase "in this way, etc."

Next, the [text] provides a combined explanation of the Dharma. First, it correlates the initial phrase: "The Tathāgata is also like this" identifies the speaker; "by means of the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment" identifies the Dharma taught; "awakening to all dharmas" identifies the wisdom of the speaker; "by means of the throat," etc., indicates the basis for the arising of speech; "words and sounds" refers to the expressions used by the speaker; and "for Kātyāyana" identifies the person to whom it is addressed.

"The first teaching is called 'turning'" correctly clarifies what is being taught; "for this reason, it is not called the Wheel-Dharma" correlates with the second [point] above; the third single phrase is omitted and not correlated.

To summarize its characteristics: non-transformation is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Tathāgata. This non-transformation is the true nature of the Dharma, and the nature of the Dharma is the very essence of the Tathāgata.
The textual structure of the remaining four sections is analogous to this; their concluding praises may be understood accordingly.

From here on, the fourth section clarifies that the Buddha-body is quiescent and therefore undergoes no transformation. However, the intent of this passage is to clarify that the Buddha is not subject to birth, emergence, and so forth;

it employs the analogies of empty space and *buddha-nature* to illustrate this. First, regarding empty space, it is clarified that it is neither born nor emerges. "Birth" (*jāti*) and "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) are distinguished in relation to causes for the production of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*): the initial arising is called "birth," and the final manifestation is called "emergence. "Production" (*kṛti*) and "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) are distinguished in relation to conditions: the initial formation is termed "production," and the final completion is termed "creation. "Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is the general category.
Next, following the discussion of the Tathāgata, we proceed to the Buddha-nature.
From here on is the third section, which refutes and eliminates the further-ascending aspect of the unsurpassed; it contains three parts:
first, the elimination of the further-ascending; second, the elimination of the unsurpassed; and third, the summary and censure.
Within the first section, how is "repetition" (punarukta) refuted?
If it were a single teaching that was proclaimed again and again, it could be called repetition; however, since the present and the past are entirely distinct, how can one speak of repetition?
Within the Chinese text, there are eight sections that distinguish the differences:
first, the distinction of "speech" (yu), where "speech" refers to the teaching; this is first introduced, then enumerated, and finally explained as can be understood;
second, the distinction according to "desire," wherein formerly one sought the Small [Vehicle], while now one seeks the Great [Vehicle].

Third, the distinction according to the faculties: formerly they were of medium capacity, whereas now they are of superior capacity; ordinary persons of inferior capacity are unable to hear the Truths, and therefore [the teaching] is not for them.
Fourth, the distinction in the arising of practice;
fifth, the distinction in the attainment of benefit.
Sixth, the distinction of the host who invited [the Buddha];
seventh, the distinction of what was taught;

eighth, the distinction of distance: formerly, when sounds were emitted, they were heard as far as the Brahma Heaven; now, when sounds are emitted, they are heard throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers.

From here on begins the second section, which dispels the notion that [only] this is supreme. It clarifies that everything spoken by the Buddha is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*); how then can one exclusively praise only the present teaching as being supreme?

Within this, first there is a general clarification that all that the Tathāgata has taught, both past and present, is the Wheel of Dharma. Under the heading "Like a Holy King," the meaning of the wheel is specifically revealed in three parts: (1) explaining the wheel in terms of both the eradication of evil and the production of good;

(2) focusing exclusively on the eradication of evil; and (3) focusing exclusively on the production of good. In each case, a metaphor is established first, followed by the application to the subject, which may be understood accordingly.

The third section below concludes with a general rebuke: "Therefore, you should not now praise the Tathāgata as if he were turning the wheel of Dharma for the first time. Mañjuśrī previously stated that turning the unsurpassed wheel is what constitutes praise; yet all that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught throughout the past and present is the wheel of Dharma, for it extinguishes evil, gives rise to good, and benefits sentient beings. Thus, one should not exclusively praise the present teaching as being unsurpassed.
Furthermore, because what was taught in the past and present are entirely distinct, one should not say that the Buddha is now turning the wheel of Dharma anew.

The preceding section [up to this point] constitutes the second part: the Tathāgata’s refutation and dismissal [of the objection]. From here on, Mañjuśrī clarifies the purpose of his inquiry; "I am not ignorant of what is meaningless" demonstrates that he has already understood it himself; "the reason why I ask" below clarifies that it is for the sake of others; and "I have known for a long time" below reveals the characteristics of his own understanding.
The preceding section constitutes the first part, which extensively expounds upon the practice of wisdom; the phrase "this is called" concludes it.

The section beginning with "Kāśyapa said" explains the meaning of that name through two rounds of question and answer. These primarily address the Buddha’s own interpretation, as the textual structure makes clear; the final round of question and answer, however, applies universally to all.
Kāśyapa asked first; if this were the practice of a Buddha, it would not be the practice of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Below, the Buddha provides the explanation, first discussing it from the perspective of the Buddha: because these are what the Buddha has realized and what the Buddha has taught, they are called "Noble Practices" (*ārya-caryā*). "These World-Honored Ones abide in nirvāṇa" refers to the Buddha’s realization; "opening up, showing, and distinguishing" refers to the Buddha’s teaching; the section beginning with "by means of this" concludes [the argument].

The following section provides further exposition: it is called "noble conduct" (*ārya-caryā*) because it is what is heard and practiced by the śrāvakas and others. The phrase "having heard [this] by the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas" refers to their hearing; the phrase "they are then able to practice it accordingly" refers to their conduct; and the words "therefore it is called" conclude the section.

The preceding section clarified the practices of the causal stage; next, we clarify the accomplishments of the resultant stage. This refers to attaining the ground of fearless sovereignty: because all faults have been extinguished, one attains fearlessness; because sublime virtues are perfectly fulfilled, one attains sovereignty.
Fearlessness and mastery are first accomplished at the initial stage (the first bhūmi); they gradually increase through the remaining stages until they reach their ultimate fulfillment in Buddhahood.

In this text, the first part clarifies the attainment of the stage of fearlessness, while the subsequent part clarifies that the Bodhisattva attains mastery. The passage beginning with "The accomplishments of the Bodhisattvas are thus immeasurable, how much more so those of the Buddhas" employs the inferior to illustrate the superior.

In the preceding section, the attainment of the stage of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya-bhūmi*) is first elucidated; from the passage beginning "If there are those who abide... onwards, the characteristics of fearlessness are explained; and from the passage beginning "Attaining the twenty-five samādhis... onwards, the remedies for fearlessness are clarified.
Within these characteristics, it is clarified that one is free from six kinds of fear:

first, by stating "fearless of greed, anger, and delusion," one is freed from the fear of afflictions; because one is free from a greedy mind, one does not dread the inability to sustain oneself, and for this reason, it is also called being free from the fear of non-sustenance.
Second, by being fearless of birth, old age, sickness, and death, one attains freedom from the fear of death.

The third is the fearlessness of not falling into the hells and other realms, which is the removal of fear regarding the evil destinies (*durgati*). The fourth, from the passage "There are two kinds of evil" onwards, is the removal of fear regarding evil karma;

since evil karma is the root of all evil reputations, and without its root there is no end, it is also called the fear of various evil reputations. First, the number two is raised, followed by the enumeration of the two names. Within the six destinies, one can create karma in all of them, but because humans and *asuras* create the heaviest karma, they are singled out for mention. Below, their characteristics are explained, specifically highlighting human evils. "There are three" raises the number, listing the *icchantikas* who slander the sutras as committing grave offenses. The sins of the five heinous acts (*ānantarya*) are not restricted to humans alone, as they exist partially in other destinies as well; therefore, they are omitted here. Below, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva has severed these and is thus fearless.
The fifth section, "Fearless Among Śramaṇas," and those following clarify the departure from the fear of the majesty and authority of the great assembly;
the sixth section, "Fearless in Receiving the Twenty-five Existences," clarifies the departure from the dread of the cyclic flow of birth and death.
Among the six [topics], the first five are the same as those in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, while the last one is not found there.
The preceding section provides an extensive analysis; the passage beginning with "Therefore" serves as the conclusion.

Within the treatment of fearlessness, the first part clarifies the essence of the samādhis, while the section beginning with "If a bodhisattva enters these kings of samādhis and wishes... clarifies their function.

Within the essence of samādhi, the initial statement—“The bodhisattva attains twenty-five samādhis and destroys the twenty-five states of existence”—serves as a general heading. As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, one attains these samādhis upon entering the first stage (bhūmi), and thereby shatters all states of existence.
Question:
Since birth and death are not yet exhausted at the first stage (bhūmi), how can one destroy the twenty-five states of existence?
Answer: [The commentary] says:
Birth and death are of two kinds:
first, the segmented (paricchinna), and second, the transformative (pariṇāma).
Within the segmented type, there is the distinction between the good realms and the evil realms.
The residual karmic energy of the evil realms is exhausted at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Within the good realms, there are both coarse and subtle [afflictions]: the coarse are exhausted at the first stage, while the subtle persist until the Buddha-stage.
Because the first stage is free from the coarse, it is said to be able to destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
To discuss this in detail, it is fully and extensively analyzed in the chapter on the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Following that extensive exposition, the conclusion provides a summary and praise: "This is called attaining the twenty-five samādhis and severing the twenty-five states of existence" (*bhava*)—this is the summary.

"This samādhi is named the King of Samādhis" is a praise of its excellence; because it is the most excellent among all samādhis, it is called "King. Because it is such a king, within each and every instance, it fully encompasses immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Within the function of samādhi, the five phrases may be understood.

Next, to clarify mastery: "The Bodhisattva, having entered this King of Samādhis, attains the stage of mastery" reiterates what preceded to introduce what follows, thereby clearly manifesting that attainment.
Below, its characteristics are defined; according to the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, there are ten masteries (*vaśitā*):
first, mastery over life, which consists of maintaining it at will;
second, mastery over the mind, which consists of entering into immeasurable samādhis with mastery.
Third is mastery over objects, manifesting immeasurable pure lands at will;
fourth is mastery over karma, dwelling for as long as desired throughout present and future lives;
fifth is mastery over birth, manifesting birth at will in all worlds.
Sixth is mastery over vows, attaining Buddhahood at will in all times and places;
seventh is mastery over faith and understanding, manifesting Buddhas filling all worlds;
eighth is mastery over the miraculous, transforming all Buddha-lands according to one's mind.
Ninth is mastery over phenomena, wherein boundless illumination of the Dharma manifests and enters according to one’s will;
tenth is mastery over knowledge, which possesses the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Herein, the mastery of a single lifetime is briefly elucidated, consisting first of the principle, second of the metaphor, and finally of the application.

The following section addresses the hells to manifest the characteristics of his birth: first, it clarifies that he was born in hell for the sake of sentient beings; next, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva is not born there due to karma, thereby demonstrating the difference in cause; finally, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva does not undergo great suffering, thereby demonstrating the difference in result.

Within the context of using the inferior to illustrate the superior by descending to a lower level, the phrase "that which is accomplished by a bodhisattva is still ineffable" first cites the inferior, while "how much more so for a Buddha could it be expressed" illustrates the superior.
The preceding section was the first, which extensively elucidated the practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*). From here below is the praise of this sutra to inspire others to practice and study it.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, manifesting the excellence of the sutra through its causeless purity; second, clarifying the benefits of upholding it through Kāśyapa.

Regarding the first part of the preceding section: first, the King of the Immaculate Treasury cites the merits of the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas mentioned previously, using comparison and measurement to reveal the superiority of this sutra; subsequently, the Buddha confirms and completes this teaching.

In the first part of the preceding section, the phrase "there was a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbha" distinguishes him from all other persons; "possessing great majesty," and so forth, manifest his various virtues; and "immediately from his seat," and so forth, initiates the request for skillful means. From this point downward is the formal request: having set forth what he himself understands, he requests the Buddha’s confirmation and thus makes his petition.

"Regarding what the Buddha has said—that the immeasurable virtues accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are truly ineffable"—this summarizes the preceding words of the Buddha. "In my own mind, I still think it is not as this sutra [describes]"—this expresses his own understanding. From "For what reason" onwards, he explains that because this sutra can give rise to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not equal it.
Question:
This sutra is its verbal teaching, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is its realized fruit. Since the teaching is shallow while the realization is deep, why is *bodhi* not superior to this sutra?
The commentary states:

In this context, the teaching that specifically proclaims the Buddha-nature and elucidates the Dharma-body is designated as the "Sūtra. That which is elucidated consists of the causes and effects of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*); that which is produced consists of the causes and effects of skillful means (*upāya*). Intrinsic purity is the root, while skillful means are the branches. Since the branches do not equal the root, the merits of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not reach [the level of] it.
In accordance with the subsequent Buddha’s response, the meaning is as follows:
first, the latter Buddha offers praise; next, he confirms those words, saying, "So it is, so it is, just as you have spoken"; finally, he recounts what was said.

Within this section, other Mahāyāna sūtras are further cited to be compared with this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in order to manifest its superiority, thereby establishing the point that the remaining qualities [of other teachings] do not equal it.
This is presented first through the Dharma (the teaching), second through a simile, and finally through the application (the synthesis).

Within this Dharma, the phrase "although these various Mahāyāna sūtras have accomplished immeasurable merit" generally cites other sūtras, while the section from "wishing to compare" onwards specifically refers to this present sūtra to demonstrate their inferiority.
In the analogy, there are six stages from milk to clarified butter (*ghṛta*), though although all six stages are mentioned, the intent lies in the *sarpis* (clarified butter).
"Clarified butter arises from *ghṛta*" indicates arising from the lower to the higher; "clarified butter is supreme" clarifies that the higher surpasses the lower.
The phrase "if there is one who takes it" below clarifies its ultimate meaning: it is superior because it cures extensively, as "all ailments are eliminated";

it is superior because its virtues are complete, as "all medicines enter into it"—meaning that within a single *sarpis* (clarified butter), all medicinal potencies are present, hence it is said they "all enter."

Within the section on "Concordance," there are likewise six stages from the Buddha up to Nirvana, which correspond sequentially to the preceding [sections]. The phrase "The Buddha is also like this" corresponds to the ox mentioned above.
This teaching takes the *saṃbhogakāya* as the Buddha.
"From the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of the scriptures" is likened to a cow producing milk; this refers to all the sūtras and dharmas of the Hīnayāna as the twelve divisions.

"Emerging from the Sūtra" is likened to milk producing curd; this clarifies that the Mahāyāna teaching is the Sūtra, and that it is called "emerging" because it relies upon the Hīnayāna to open up and manifest the Mahāyāna.

Within the Mahāyāna, when subdivided according to its specific categories, there are likewise twelve types; however, in this general sense, it is called *sūtra*. The latter four categories are all Mahāyāna; among them, the teaching that explains phenomena (*vastu*) is termed *sūtra*, meaning it expounds upon all matters such as generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Regarding the phrase "from the Sūtras emerge the Vaipulya," this corresponds to the production of ghee. Within the Mahāyāna, those teachings that proclaim the principle of emptiness through the deconstruction of all marks are called Vaipulya sūtras; they are said to "emerge" because they reveal the underlying principle by means of specific events.
This refers to the teaching that the giver, the recipient, and the material gift are unapprehendable, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the Prajñāpāramitā emerges from the Vaipulya Sūtras," it is like extracting clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Ultimate realization of emptiness—the wisdom that realizes the truth by departing from all signs—is called *prajñā*. Because this wisdom arises based on the principle [of emptiness], it is said to "emerge."
To explain the teaching according to its practice, it may also be called "produced from the *Prajñā-sūtra*"; however, this *prajñā* is precisely the capacity for awakening mentioned previously.

To say that "nirvāṇa is produced from *prajñā*" is equivalent to saying that the *amṛta* (clarified butter) is produced; since *prajñā* is the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), it realizes and brings forth the nirvāṇa of the beginningless *dharmatā*, and is therefore said to "produce" it. To explain the teaching according to its reality, it may also be called "produced from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*."

In the text, the initial statement "emerges from the Great Nirvāṇa" establishes the analogy for the Dharma; "just like *sarpis* (clarified butter)" cites the metaphor to introduce the subject. *Sarpis* serves as the metaphor for the nature (*dhātu*), while "the nature is the Tathāgata" clarifies the Dharma by means of the metaphor. This refers to the Tathāgata of the Dharmakāya and not to the Saṃbhogakāya; since the merits of the Saṃbhogakāya do not equal those of this sutra, it is not identified with that body.
The section beginning with "By this meaning" praises the Dharma through a common analogy; it praises only the Tathāgata and briefly omits praise for the nature.

Just as all medicinal herbs enter into that *amṛta* (clarified butter), so too is the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata: all merits enter into it. Therefore, it is said that "the merits of the Tathāgata are immeasurable and boundless."

From here begins the second section, which demonstrates that because Kāśyapa clearly upholds [the teaching], it is beneficial; herein, Kāśyapa first makes a vow to propagate the sūtra, which the Buddha subsequently endorses.
This section contains three parts:

first, Kāśyapa receives the Buddha’s previous words and reveals the excellence of the sūtra; second, from "Thus have I heard" onwards, he clarifies the folly of those in the world who do not study it; third, from "I, at this time" onwards, he vows to propagate and disseminate it.

Among these, the first section—beginning with the desire to personally transcribe, recite, and master the text, and stating, "I shall flay my skin to make paper," and so forth—demonstrates the depth of his affection for the Dharma and reveals the extraordinary excellence of the sutra.
From "Then" onwards, he transforms others and causes them to uphold [the teaching], first explaining it for their sake.

From "If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached" onwards, he gathers them and causes them to accept it; herein there are six phrases: the first phrase is gathering through giving (*dāna-saṃgraha*);
the second is kind speech (*priyavāditā*); the latter four are beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*); *samānārthatā* (common purpose) is omitted for brevity.

Within the context of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), first, from "toward ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*) downward, one uses intimidation and coercion to compel them to read; second, by means of respect and service toward those who are haughty, one causes them to study; third, by means of refutation and subjugation of slander, one causes them to read; fourth, through affection and praise, one causes them to study.
The Buddha first offers praise: “By means of this virtuous mind of yours,” and so forth, clarifying that upholding [this teaching] is beneficial.

Within the preceding praise, “Excellent! is the general praise; the five subsequent phrases beginning with “You are exceedingly... are the specific praises. Cherishing it from the outset is called “loving the Mahāyāna”; craving it for one’s own possession is called “desiring the Mahāyāna”; being able to correctly receive it is called “accepting the Mahāyāna”; becoming attached to the flavor of the teachings received and not relinquishing them is called “savoring the Mahāyāna”; and having faith in the teachings of the flavors one savors, respecting them, and practicing in accordance with them is called “believing in the Mahāyāna,” extending even to making offerings.

Within the section on the benefits of upholding [the teaching], the first part correctly elucidates those benefits; the passage beginning with "In the past" below cites past precedents to provide proof.

Within the former, the phrase "By means of the causal conditions of your virtuous mind, you shall surpass immeasurable bodhisattvas and attain enlightenment" clarifies the benefit of surpassing others in realization; the passage beginning with "You, moreover, shall likewise be like me" clarifies the benefit of surpassing others in teaching.
In the section on citing examples as proof, there are three distinct parts:
first, clarifying what one has practiced; second, clarifying what one has accomplished; and third, using oneself as a model for others.

Within the clarification of what was practiced, the initial portion first cites one’s own past asceticism as the object of testing: "When I performed such asceticism" and below, it clarifies that the examination itself constitutes the means of testing. This contains three sub-sections:
First, Śakra first sees [the transformation] and is struck with wonder, desiring to go and test it;
second, from "At that time, Śakra immediately transformed himself" onwards, he actually goes to test it;
third, from "At that time, the rākṣasa returned to his original form" onwards, having finished the testing, Śakra restores his own physical form and departs after offering a confession.

The preceding section has four parts: first, the initial sight and the resulting astonishment; second, from "They immediately together... onwards, the praise for what was done; third, from "At that time, among the assembly there was a certain deva... onwards, the evaluation of the deed performed; and fourth, from "Such a matter is truly difficult to believe... onwards, the clarification that it must be verified through testing.
The first two sections may be understood as before.
In the third section, three individuals evaluate it:
first, a celestial son speaks of seeking the place of the Emperor; second, a seer advises him not to seek it; and third, Śakra, seizing upon these words, offers praise.

Regarding the second section on persons: first, the individuals are identified; next, what they have said is explained. First, he exhorts them not to worry; then, he compares them to the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists; finally, he clarifies the purpose behind the bodhisattva’s ascetic practices.

The passage beginning with "In the world there are great beings for the sake of sentient beings" generally enumerates all that Bodhisattvas do; the section beginning with "As I understand it" below uses these cases as analogies for others.
Within Śakra’s praise, the phrase “as you have said” restates what was previously mentioned. The three subsequent lines beginning with “this person” express affirmation:

first, it clarifies that this person can gather in sentient beings through wholesome dharmas; second, the line beginning with “there is the Buddha-tree” clarifies that they can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings; third, the line beginning with “this person will become a Sugata in the future” clarifies that they can benefit themselves.
From here below is the fourth section, clarifying the necessity of verification and testing;

this text is divided into four parts: first, clarifying its difficulty of belief; second, permitting a journey for verification and testing; third, again clarifying its difficulty of belief; and fourth, again verifying and testing.

The first part of the middle section first provides a general explanation of what is difficult to believe; the section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation; and the section beginning with "Great Seer!
I have seen such things" provides the conclusion.

Within the explanation, it is stated that immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings resolve their minds on Bodhi, yet seeing only slight causes and conditions, they waver from Bodhi—this explains the difficulty of belief.
The following uses analogies to clarify this, consisting of two analogies and two applications.

Within the second section, which grants permission to go and test him, the phrase "I must now go myself to test him" constitutes the formal grant of permission for the test. The section beginning with "to know whether he is capable" sets forth the actual testing; herein, first the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy, and finally the application are presented. The statement "this ascetic is likewise" is the general application (*upanaya*).

The section beginning with "Although I... distinguishes the two aspects: observing the precepts and profound wisdom correspond to the two wheels of a chariot and the two wings of a bird. Observing the precepts constitutes merit (*puṇya*), while profound wisdom constitutes liberation (*vimukti*). To have practice without liberation cannot lead to the fruit; it is like a one-wheeled chariot that cannot transport a load, or a bird with only one wing that is incapable of flight.
In the third section, which further clarifies the difficulty of belief, two analogies are first presented, after which the application to the subject matter can be understood.

In the fourth section, which further clarifies the granting of a trial, [the Buddha] first commands the Great Sage to seek a joint test; from the words "For example" (*tadyathā*) onwards, it clarifies the necessity of testing, first through analogy and then through application: just as gold must undergo three tests, so too is ascetic practice.
"Below the passage 'Śakra' [it is said that he] manifested a terrifying form, spoke of terrifying food, and urged him to give quickly by pointing out terrifying matters; these are the three trials."
Regarding the second section, the "Verification through Proper Progression," there are two topical divisions. First, the division concerning the examiner, which consists of five distinct parts:
first, Śakra manifests a terrifying form;
second, from the passage beginning with "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) onwards, he teaches the delightful Dharma.
3. From "Great Brāhmaṇa, you should not question me now" onwards, the "frightening food" is explained;
4. From "If you can sacrifice your body and listen attentively" onwards, the "lovely Dharma" is explained;
5. From "Having spoken this verse, he said this" onwards, [the Buddha] urges him to give quickly and reveals the frightening matter.
This section concludes directly without further explanation; it should be carefully noted and understood.
Second, regarding the text of the examination, it is divided into four parts:
first, upon hearing the first half-verse, his heart gives rise to joy.
2. From "Immediately rising from his seat, he raised [the bowl] with his hand" onwards, he seeks out the person who recited it;
3. From "At that time, I again spoke to the rākṣasa, saying:
'If you finish reciting the verse, I shall become your disciple for the rest of my life'" onwards, he seeks the latter half of the verse.
4. From "At that time, I reflected deeply" onwards, this constitutes the verse on the relinquishing of the body.
Within this section, the first part clarifies Śakra’s recitation of the verse, while the latter part clarifies the Bodhisattva’s joyful state of mind upon hearing the verse.

Within the discourse spoken by Śakra, the first part clarifies how Śakra transformed himself into a rākṣasa and went to the Snowy Mountains to initiate the teaching on skillful means; from "Eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) onwards, it correctly clarifies the recitation of the verses; and from "Having spoken this half" onwards, he stands still so that [the beings] may behold him.

Within the joy arising from hearing the verse, there is first the explanation of the Dharma, followed by the presentation of eight similes, and finally the application [of these similes], which may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the second section, "Seeking Out the Speaker," there are four distinct parts:

first, seeking the speaker by tossing his hair and looking around—"Who spoke that verse? briefly seeks the speaker; "At that time... and below, he sees only the rākṣasa; "Who opened [the door]? and below, he extensively searches for the speaker; and "I, at that time... and below, he sees only the rākṣasa.

1. From "Again he thought" onwards, [the Bodhisattva] recognizes him as a rākṣasa; first, he doubts what the other has said; from "Furthermore" onwards, he doubts his incapacity; from "I [heard] you" onwards, he again doubts what was said.
2. From "I shall now go" onwards, he proceeds to inquire; first, he thinks of asking; next, he goes there in person; finally, he asks the question directly. 3.
From "When I have asked this, he will answer me" onwards, the other hears it and refuses or evades.
In the third section, concerning the seeking of the latter half-verse, the Bodhisattva makes six requests and the Rākṣasa gives six replies:
First, he requested that the verse be spoken so that he might become his disciple; the Rākṣasa declined, citing his hunger and refusing to speak it.
Second, he asked what his food was; the Rākṣasa, fearing that humans would be terrified, refused to speak of it immediately.
Third, the Bodhisattva asked again, and the rākṣasa then spoke;
fourth, he requested that verses be recited, and [the rākṣasa] promised to sacrifice his body, yet upon hearing this, the other did not believe;
fifth, the Bodhisattva manifested his own true capability, and upon hearing this, the rākṣasa gave his ear and consented for him to proclaim the teaching.
Sixth: "At that time, having heard these matters," and so forth, he offered a seat and made a renewed request, whereupon the other then preached for him.
Within this, first the verses were formally preached; following the verses, the prose exhorted him to sacrifice his body. The text is all intelligible.
In the fourth section, concerning the relinquishing of the body through verses, there are six distinct points:
first, hearing the verses and reflecting deeply upon them, copying them everywhere;
second, from the words "thereupon," the desire to relinquish the body.
