King Śreṇika previously cited examples to demonstrate that one who has committed evil through body, speech, and mind will inevitably fall into hell; this is called "believing in cause and effect."
The passage beginning with "If there is... clarifies that because he possesses faith, the King’s offense is not grave and is not beyond remedy.

This differs from the case of an icchantika; it is not grave because he has faith through which he can be saved, and thus it is not incurable. Within this section, the text first cites the grave to highlight the light, and the passage beginning with "Great King, you are now not an icchantika" clarifies how the light differs from the grave.
The preceding section has four parts:
first, it clarifies that icchantikas commit sins without repentance, thereby manifesting their grave illness;

second, from "Such persons as these" onwards, it clarifies that they are incurable, consisting of an initial presentation of the principle (dharma), followed by a simile, and finally an application (conclusion).
3. From "How so? onwards, the text identifies that person by referring back to the first section;

4. From "That which even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot [cure]" onwards, it further clarifies the incurability in relation to the second section, first presenting the point and subsequently explaining it.
Having finished the preceding praise, the following section is the second part, which indicates the place where the King shall pass away.
The phrase "As the King has said, there is no one who can cure him" restates the King's previous words; what follows is the actual indication.
The text also consists of five parts: first, a listing of the Buddhas' names;

second, from "Without a Teacher" onwards, a praise of the Buddhas' virtues; third, from "Now" onwards, an indication of the Buddhas' locations; fourth, from "And for" onwards, an elucidation of what the Buddhas have taught; fifth, from "O King, listen now" onwards, an exhortation for the King to follow them.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text]: the statement "named Siddhārtha" translates here as "Accomplished Benefit.
In the second section of praises, the initial portion extols his own virtues, while the passage beginning with "Great Compassion" extols his benefit for others.
From the middle [of the text], the initial statement "attained by oneself without a teacher" is a general praise.

What follows below elucidates this specifically: "the physical body adorned with the marks and signs" praises the Buddha’s merit, while "possessing the powers and fearlessnesses" praises the Buddha’s wisdom.
In the section praising altruism, "Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion" praises the altruistic mind, while from "Born in Accordance with Virtue" onwards, it praises altruistic conduct.
Conduct is divided into three types of action:
"Born in Accordance with Virtue" and so forth praise the Buddha’s bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

The phrase "speaking at the proper time" and so forth praises the Buddha’s vocal karma; within the Buddha’s vocal karma, "speaking at the proper time and not speaking at the improper time" means that his speech can respond appropriately to the capacities of sentient beings.

"Truthful speech" culminates in the single word; the essence of speech is pure. "Truthful speech" and "pure speech" clarify the absence of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*): when a thing accords with its name, it is called "truth"; when it accords with its characteristics, it is called "pure. "Wondrous speech" clarifies the absence of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). "Meaningful speech" and "Dharma-speech" clarify the absence of frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*): speech that benefits people is called "meaningful speech," and speech that accords with the Dharma is called "Dharma-speech. "Single speech" clarifies the absence of divisive speech (*paiśunya*). "Causing [beings] to be free from affliction" means speech that benefits all things.
"Knowing the faculties and dispositions" and so forth praise the Buddha’s mental karma (*manas-karman*): knowing the roots and natures of beings, he understands the mental capacities of all things.

Knowing the medicinal teachings below, "skillfully penetrating all according to what is appropriate" refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*); "his wisdom is lofty" and so forth refer to the Buddha’s true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). His rank is ultimate and his name is exalted; because his wisdom can exhaust all phenomena, it is called profound and vast. Because this wisdom can extinguish hindrances, it is like a vajra that shatters all evils.
The section below indicates the location.

Within the explanation of what was taught, the phrase “preaching various dharmas for immeasurable monks” serves as a general heading; next, it is specifically elucidated. The passage beginning with “If the King hears” clarifies that what the Buddha has spoken is appropriate for the King.

Regarding the initial statement within this section, "if there is existence or non-existence": from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called existence; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called non-existence.
Furthermore, one may also explain that ultimate truth is called existence because it possesses real nature (*dharmatā*);
conversely, conventional truth is called non-existence because it lacks true reality.
The "conditioned" is birth-and-death; the "unconditioned" is nirvāṇa.
The "outflowing" is the truth of origination; the "outflow-free" is the truth of the path.
The "fruits of afflictions" constitute the truth of suffering; the "fruits of wholesome dharmas" constitute the truth of cessation.
“Form” refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); “non-form” refers to the remaining aggregates.

Since the ultimate truth is distinct from these, it is said to be “neither form nor non-form. “Self” refers to *nirvāṇa*; “non-self” refers to saṃsāra. Since the ultimate truth is distinct from these, it is said to be “neither self nor non-self.

This applies similarly to categories such as “neither world nor non-world,” and so forth. The Three Vehicles are “vehicles”; the mundane world is “non-vehicle. Since the ultimate truth is distinct from these, it is said to be “neither vehicle nor non-vehicle.”
To perform an action oneself and subsequently experience its fruit oneself is called "self-performed, self-experienced.
To perform an action in the present life and experience its fruit in another life is called "self-performed, experienced by another.
To maintain that there is no cause in the present and consequently no retribution is called "no-action, no-experience."

Ultimate truth is free from characteristics and can eliminate karmic obstacles; therefore, it is said: "When the King heard that there is no action and no recipient [of karma], his grave offenses were immediately extinguished.
From this point downward is the fifth section, which exhorts the King to take refuge and follow [the teaching]. This passage is divided into three parts:
first, citing thirteen types of people who attained benefits and accomplished their goals as a model to exhort the King.
2. From "The Great Compassion is Universal" onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha’s compassion is universal, thereby removing the King's doubts;
3. From "Suppose for a month one constantly [offers] clothing" onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha is supreme among all conditions, giving rise to the King's resolve to depart.
In the preceding section, the text first presents specific instances and concludes with a summary exhortation.

Within the presentation: first, five successive passages clarify the Buddha’s ability to benefit others; next, one passage cites Maudgalyāyana’s capacity to benefit others to manifest the Buddha’s greatness; following that, four passages further clarify the Buddha’s benefits; then, one passage cites Śāriputra’s capacity to benefit others to manifest the Buddha’s greatness; and finally, two passages further clarify the Buddha’s benefits.
The concluding exhortation may be understood as before.

In the second section, first there is a brief clarification that the Tathāgata’s compassion is universal and the True Dharma is vast and expansive; from the phrase "enemies and kin alike" onwards, thirteen further sections extensively manifest this universality of compassion.
In the third section, there are five successive comparisons and evaluations used to manifest the Buddha’s superiority, ensuring that the King will certainly depart.
Thus far, the third part has featured Jīvaka praising the King and showing him where he should go;
from here on, the fourth part concerns how, due to the King’s sense of shame and his inability to bear facing the Buddha, the multitude collectively exhorts him.
The text contains three pairs of themes:

first, the contrast between the King and Jīvaka, which clarifies the Buddha’s supreme dignity; [the King], mindful that his own transgressions were grave, did not dare go to see him, until his father-king came to exhort him.

Second, upon hearing his father’s exhortation, the King’s sense of remorse and shame was so profound that he fainted and fell to the ground; the Buddha’s light touched him to receive and encourage him, which is also termed "encouragement through guidance."
The three kings were still fearful of battle and did not dare to see the Buddha; Jīvaka urged them repeatedly.
At first, it was explained that the reigning king would not go, and later the father-king offered his exhortation.

The King did not depart from the midst [of the assembly], but first praised the sublime purity of the Tathāgata and his assembly of disciples; with the words "I, now," and those following, he expressed his own shame at not having gone.
The first five phrases are as follows:
first, it clarifies that both the Tathāgata and the assembly of disciples are well-disciplined, meaning their minds are harmonious and supple.
Second, both the Buddhas and their assemblies are pure; this refers to the purity of the body.
Third, both the Buddhas and their assemblies are tranquil; this refers to the tranquility of speech. These praise the presence of virtue.
Fourth, it clarifies the absence of greed; this refers to the severance of craving.
The five types of knowledge are free from affliction, for anger and ignorance have been extinguished; this knowledge is devoid of evil. Regarding the middle section of the latter part:

first, he reflects on his own heavy transgressions and does not dare to see the Buddha; in the passage beginning with "If I were to go," he fears that going would be inappropriate; and in the passage beginning with "Although you urge me," he concludes that he will not go.
Within the King’s exhortation, he first cites the extinction of the Dharma to urge [the Prince] to depart quickly;
subsequently, he cites the suffering of hell to terrify him into certain departure.

In the former section, the initial eleven phrases clarify that the Dharma is about to perish; the six phrases beginning with "Great Terror" clarify that evil is about to arrive; and the phrases beginning with "The Buddha-Sun" clarify that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be no remedy for the King’s transgressions.

Regarding the seven subsequent lines: the first line clarifies that the King’s body bears grave offenses and is certain to enter the Avīci Hell; the middle five lines distinguish the characteristics of Avīci; and the final line beginning with "I only pray" serves as a concluding exhortation.
In the analysis of the middle [section], the first sentence explains the name and reveals the fault. Generally, there are four meanings of "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*):
first, uninterruptedness of rebirth, wherein one who casts off their life among humans immediately enters Avīci, with no dwelling place in between;

second, uninterruptedness of physical form, wherein the great city of Avīci is eighty thousand *yojanas* in extent, and when a single person enters it, their body fills it entirely, and likewise when all people enter, their bodies do so as well, with no empty space remaining in between.
Third, there is the uninterruptedness of lifespan: once born therein, one’s lifespan lasts for an entire kalpa without interruption.

Fourth, there is the uninterruptedness of suffering: once born therein, the experience of suffering continues in succession without even a momentary interval of pleasure; therefore, it is called "uninterrupted" (Avīci).
Now, for the time being, this shall be explained according to the latter meaning.
Second, from "Suppose" (*jāsu*) onwards, the physical characteristics of the body are distinguished; this refers precisely to the uninterrupted nature of that bodily form.
Third, from "The Cold Hells" (*han diyu*) onwards, the light cases are cited to manifest the heavy ones.
4. From "The four directions" downward, the characteristics of their suffering are distinguished.
5. From "Committing one transgression" downward, the determination of cause and effect is distinguished.
According to the *Abhidharma*, the duration of each [rebirth] is one kalpa, corresponding to the gravity of the offense.
What is now being explained occurs within a single kalpa, differing only in the degree of gravity; what is taught in the *Āgama* sūtras is identical to this.
In the second pair, King Śreṇiya first heard the exhortation and fell down in distress; when the Buddha saw him, he touched him with the light of compassion and offered him encouragement.
In the first part, King Śubhavyūha, upon first hearing this, was struck with alarm and fear, looking up to ask who it was;
his father-king then replied and earnestly admonished and exhorted him;
in the final part, having heard this, King Śubhavyūha felt remorse and shame, fainting and falling to the ground.
There are three reasons why King Ajātaśatru fainted and fell to the ground:

first, he feared that the Buddha would soon pass into parinirvāṇa and his own sins could no longer be remedied; thus, when the Tathāgata saw Ajātaśatru fainting and prostrate on the earth, He granted him the promise to remain in the world.
Second, he was terrified that the sufferings of hell were about to descend upon him.
Feeling deep shame before his father, he fell to the ground in a faint.
Within the illumination of the Buddha’s light, he was first granted permission to remain in the world as a king, and subsequently illuminated by that light.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the Buddha, seeing King Śibi faint and fall to the ground, grants that he shall remain in the world for immeasurable kalpas;
second, the dialogue and detailed explanation.
Regarding the statement "dwelling for immeasurable kalpas" mentioned previously, there are two interpretations:

first, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the King of the World was unaware that the Tathāgata dwells eternally, and thus fell into a swoon; the Buddha now manifests this to enable him to know the Buddha’s permanence, and for this reason it is said that he dwells until immeasurable kalpas.
Second, regarding what should be explained, there are two points within this:
first, it is spoken as a provisional hypothesis for the sake of the worldly king; if the worldly king’s grave offenses were not extinguished, the Buddha would remain for immeasurable kalpas;
if those offenses were extinguished, there would be no need for the Buddha to remain.

Second, this is explained by way of analogy with the lineage of worldly kings. The lineage of worldly kings is vast and inexhaustible; likewise, the Tathāgata remains constantly in the world for their sake and does not enter parinirvāṇa. For this reason, it is said that he abides until immeasurable kalpas have passed.
In the course of the dialogue, Kāśyapa first asks, "Since the Tathāgata acts for the sake of immeasurable multitudes, why do you speak specifically of Ajaśatru?
The Buddha’s response has two parts.

First, he addresses King Ajātaśatru specifically: "Within this assembly, there is no one who says that I have definitely entered parinirvāṇa; it is only King Ajātaśatru who believes I have entered it. Therefore, he speaks specifically for his sake.

Second, regarding the explanation by way of classifying the category of King Bimbisāra: "When I said it was for Ajātaśatru, it was actually intended for the entire class of kings like him," and not for King Bimbisāra alone.

Within this, the first part first restates the preceding words to demonstrate that [the interlocutor] has not yet understood; the section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation; and the section beginning with "The Tathāgata’s secret words are inconceivable" concludes by praising and revealing their profundity.
In the explanation, first the question is raised as to why it is called "esoteric" (*mi*), which is then answered below.
Within this, there are six sections: the first four address the person, and the latter two concern the Dharma.
Regarding the first four [cases], it is clarified that "those who act" refers generally to all beings, whereas "Ajātaśatru" specifically discusses King Ajātaśatru and his kind.
What is the distinction between these four instances?

The initial term "for" (wei) refers generally to all ordinary, mundane sentient beings; the term "Ajātaśatru" (A-jie-shi) is cited as an example to encompass all sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes.

In the second section, it clarifies that those who act do so for the sake of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) sentient beings; "conditioned" is a general term encompassing both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). First the term is raised and subsequently explained.
Regarding Ajātaśatru, he is cited as a representative example to include all sentient beings fully possessed of afflictions (*kleśa*).

In the third section, it clarifies that those for whom [the teaching] is intended are sentient beings who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature; prior to the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*), they are collectively termed "those who do not see. Alternatively, because Bodhisattvas from the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) downward have not yet seen it with their eyes, they are also collectively termed "those who do not see. This follows the method of stating the conclusion first and then providing the explanation: those who see the Buddha-nature are not called "sentient beings," and therefore [the teaching] is not for them.
As for "Ajātaśatru," this refers to Ajātaśatru as a representative example to include all those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
In the fourth section, it clarifies that those who acted were the two assemblies of Ānanda and Kāśyapa;
as for Ajātaśatru, this refers to King Ajātaśatru taking the consorts and concubines of the royal harem and all the women of Rājagṛha.

Although the latter two sections both distinguish [the meaning] by means of the Dharma and persons, the first section explains it in relation to those who are to be converted (*vineya*), while the latter section explains it in relation to those who convert (*vināyaka*). Within these two sections, the term "world" (*loka*) is analyzed according to three distinct meanings for the sake of clarifying its differentiation from "non-Aśa" (*a-jña*).

Regarding the previous section, first we shall definitively establish the meanings of these three characters. That which is called "wei" (for) refers to Buddha-nature; it is called "wei" because it is intended to cause sentient beings to perceive Buddha-nature.
That which is called "A-jie" (Aja) is named "non-arising.
"Shi" is a Sanskrit term, translated here as "enemy."
Next, we discuss this in terms of persons; persons are either deluded or awakened.
If we consider the deluded, the meaning of "non-arising" is associated with their nature, because for a deluded person, there is no nature of non-arising.
If we consider the awakened, the meaning of "non-arising" is associated with their resentment, because for one who has attained awakening and understanding, resentment does not arise.

In this passage, the initial section first provides an analysis based on delusion: "Because their nature is non-arising, the enemy of afflictions arises" demonstrates that such deluded people lack the remedy and possess obstructions; "The enemy of afflictions arises, yet they do not see the Buddha-nature" demonstrates that such deluded people possess obstructions and lack the remedy.

Next, regarding the realization of those who have awakened, the statement "because afflictions do not arise, one sees the Buddha-nature" demonstrates that such a realized one is free from obstructions and possesses the remedy; the statement "because of seeing the nature, one abides in nirvana, which is called non-arising" demonstrates that such a realized one possesses the remedy and is free from obstructions.
Because one perceives the Buddha-nature, afflictions do not arise; thus, abiding in nirvana, it is called "non-arising. Therefore, he is named Ajātaśatru—this serves as the general conclusion.
Next, regarding the explanation of how he can transform others, we shall first determine the meaning of three characters therein.
"Aja" means "unborn," and that which is unborn is Nirvana.
Regarding the statement, "The world is named for worldly dharmas, yet it is called undefiled by names," what is the meaning of being called "undefiled"?
If the Buddha were in the world and possessed attachment himself, he would be called defiled; because he has departed from such states, he is called undefiled.

Next, this meaning shall be explained by reference to the Buddha: if the Buddha were in the world and defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, he would have had to abandon the world and enter nirvana immediately.
Because the Buddha exists in the world, the eight worldly dharmas cannot defile him; therefore, throughout immeasurable kalpas, he remains constantly in the world and does not enter nirvana.
The eight dharmas are as described above.
The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes [the preceding discussion].

The subsequent summary and praise consists of two parts: first, the direct praise of the essential characteristic as "inconceivable secret language"; second, the praise of the perfected speech he has taught—such as "Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha"—as being inconceivable.
From here below is the second section, in which the Buddha’s light touches [the king] to provide encouragement; herein there are four parts:
first, the Buddha enters samādhi and emits light that shines upon the king, whereby the king awakens and his sores are healed;
second, a question-and-answer session to discern the source of the light.
The third section consists of the question-and-answer clarifying the purpose of the light’s appearance;
the fourth explains the meaning of the term "light.
The first part may be understood [as previously explained].
The second section contains two questions and answers:

first, the king, suspecting that the light was something other than [the Buddha's], questioned Jīvaka; because the king feared his own transgressions, he did not believe that the Tathāgata’s light had shone upon him, and thus he asked this question. Jīvaka replied that it was not so.
Second, the king asked who had emitted it, and Jīvaka answered that it was the Buddha’s light.
There are four distinct points:

first, it clarifies that this light is emitted by the Buddha; within the body of the Buddha’s dharma-gate of equality, the manifestation of the *āgama* light is termed "emission. Although the Buddha’s light is eternally constant, the King has only now seen it, which is why it is said to be "emitted.
Second, it distinguishes the true nature of the light: this light has no root, and so forth, up to being neither white.
The radiance of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) appears for the sake of deliverance;
the fourth, the mark of the whisk, reveals reality. Although this light is thus, it is in fact invisible, even to the point of not being white.
Within the third section, there are two questions and answers:

At first, the King asked Jīvaka, "For what reason did that God among Gods emit light? Jīvaka replied, "It was for the sake of the King," speaking thus because he feared the King might rejoice excessively.

The phrase "beginning with the king" below clarifies the reason for this: because the king previously stated, "There is no good physician in the world who can cure my body and mind," this light was emitted first to treat the king's body and subsequently his mind; by analogy, one should seek out and eliminate true afflictions through such practice.
From the words "The King said" onwards, he again asks with astonishment, "Does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, also think of me? He asks this because he does not expect it.
Kātyāyana’s answer is precisely for this purpose, and within it there are two parts:

first, clarifying that the Buddha acts specifically for the King because the King is ill; second, from the words "The Buddha does not regard sentient beings [with partiality]" onwards, clarifying that the Buddha acts for the King because the King possesses virtue.

The preceding section first provides an analogy: "one person" represents the Buddha; "seven sons" represent bodhisattvas at the six stages as well as sentient beings of the lineage who have previously attained a favorable rebirth; "one son contracting an illness" represents sentient beings of the lineage who have previously attained a favorable rebirth giving rise to karmic afflictions; "the parents' heart is not unequal" represents the Buddha’s impartiality; and "yet the heart is more inclined toward the sick one" represents the Buddha’s particular compassion for sentient beings burdened by transgressions.

Next, the text combines [the analogy] to clarify the Dharma: "The Tathāgata is also like this" corresponds to the parents mentioned previously; "toward all sentient beings he is not unequal" corresponds to "not being unequal"; and "yet his mind is particularly focused on the one who has committed an offense" corresponds to "his mind is especially directed toward the sick son. As for the person who has seven sons, one of whom falls ill, that portion is omitted here and not combined.

The following section elaborates upon this: "Laxity in mindfulness of the Buddha" clarifies what was previously emphasized as partial, while "not relaxing the mind's equanimity" highlights the minor to reveal the major.
From the words "What is... onwards, the state of non-laxity is revealed, first by way of a question and subsequently by way of an explanation.

As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) constitute the first two; the pure mind of the first ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) constitutes the third; the tracks of practice from the second ground upward constitute the fourth; the certainty of the eighth and ninth grounds constitutes the fifth; and the ultimate state of the tenth ground constitutes the sixth.
The passage on the "bodhisattva in the sixth stage who is not negligent" indicates that negligence occurs prior to the sixth stage.

Within the section clarifying the presence of wholesome qualities, the first part explains how the Tathāgata does not differentiate among the lineages and natures of sentient beings when gathering and transforming them, while the latter part explains that the Tathāgata reflects upon them because he possesses such wholesome qualities.
The one who speaks these words clarifies that the King’s goodness is such that he has become a Buddha.
From here below, the fourth section explains the meaning of the name "Light": Jīvaka first identifies this as the Tathāgata’s moon-like radiance (*candrakānta-prabhā*).

Below, this is further analyzed, following the format of question and answer in six successive stages (*ṣaḍ-anupūrvakrama*). Of these, the first five explain the moon, while the last one explains craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Within the first five, the first three explain it in terms of the arising of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*): the first initiates the initial mind like the moon; the second advances the intention for practice like the moon; and the last brings about final accomplishment like the moon. In all cases, the analogy is established first, followed by the application to the subject, as can be understood.

The latter two [verses] are explained in terms of their extinction of evil. The former phrase takes the metaphor of the moonlight gradually fading to illustrate how this samādhi gradually extinguishes afflictions; the latter phrase takes the metaphor of the moon’s ability to dispel heat to illustrate how this samādhi can eliminate afflictions. Thus, it first establishes the metaphors and subsequently applies them to reveal the Dharma.
The explanation of "love" (tṛṣṇā) can be understood.
In the third pair, King Śreṇika first manifested that he would not depart, and Jīvaka subsequently exhorted him.
Within the former [section], there are four phrases:

First, it clarifies what was previously heard—that the Tathāgata does not associate with evil people; herein, the initial teaching, followed by four similes, and finally the application [of the meaning] should be understood.
Second, from "I shall... onwards, it clarifies that [the Buddha] has already departed [from evil].
Third, from "I observe... onwards, it is a self-assessment of how the Tathāgata does not associate with evil people.
4. From "Therefore" onwards is the conclusion that [the Buddha] has not departed.
Within Jīvaka’s exhortation, he first urges the King to focus his mind on seeking the Buddha; he first cites six similes, and below, he exhorts him to emulate them.
"Even the Tathāgata... and below introduces the Buddha preaching the Dharma for those icchantikas to remove the King's doubts and fears;
herein there are three parts: first, citing the Tathāgata preaching for the icchantikas to enchant the King, clarifying that there is a proper purpose in doing so;

second, the King hears this and asks in astonishment, "I have heard that icchantikas do not believe, do not hear, and do not contemplate, yet they attain the meaning; for what reason does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma for them? By saying they do not believe, it means they lack the skillful means of practice; below, it clarifies their lack of practice. By saying they do not hear, it means they lack the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); by saying they cannot contemplate, it means they lack the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and by saying they do not attain the principles of meaning, it means they lack the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Jīvaka provides an extensive analysis of this, in which he first presents the analogy, next applies it to clarify the Dharma, and finally explains the reason why the Tathāgata taught it.
Within the analogy there is an extreme abundance of detail, whereas the corresponding prose is extremely concise; thus, it is difficult to align the two perfectly.

Furthermore, as for the various analogies, they may be taken partially, in full, or entirely; since it is not necessarily the case that they are taken in their entirety, it is difficult to achieve a perfect correspondence. For now, this shall suffice as a rough approximation.

There are five sections within this passage: first, the analogy of the icchantika severing their roots of goodness; second, from "The relatives of various households" onwards, the analogy of investigating how goodness brings about the attainment of sainthood; third, from "At that time, the good physician immediately reflected" onwards, the analogy of the Buddha observing the capacities of sentient beings; fourth, from "Having reflected thus, he immediately dispatched messengers" onwards, the analogy of responding to capacities to transform beings; fifth, from "He said to the patient, 'My illness is grave'" onwards, the analogy of temporarily setting aside [the teaching] through skillful means.
The first part has two sections:
first, when the deluded mind is not yet clear, it is described as "a dream"; second, when the deluded mind is fully resolved, it is described as "having finished dreaming. Regarding the former:

"a person" is a metaphor for one who has severed the roots of goodness; the arising of evil and false views is called "contracting a severe illness," and the state where the deluded mind is not yet clear is described as "dreaming at night."
There are two kinds of wholesome states:
first, those acquired through effort (*upāya*), and second, those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
When the wholesome states acquired through effort are severed, only those acquired by birth remain; therefore, it is called "ascending to the Single-Pillar Palace."
The mind’s craving for the five desires is called "consuming ghee"; because the body constantly dwells therein, it is called "anointing the body.
The body residing in adverse conditions is called "lying in ashes"; because the mind gives rise to anger toward objects, it is called "eating ashes.
The mind focusing on the principle that there is neither cause nor effect is called "clinging to a withered tree. The mind...
To be accompanied by doubt, wavering, and indecision is called "walking, standing, sitting, and lying down with monkeys.
For the mind to dwell amidst evil is called "sinking into mud and water. To fall away from all wholesome qualities is called "falling from towers, palaces, high mountains, and trees.
To adorn one's body with the qualities of shamelessness and lack of remorse is called "clad in blue and yellow."
"Red and black garments" refers to the mind being fully given over to committing evil. "Delighting in song and dance" refers to unwholesome thoughts manifesting in the mind.
Unwholesome thoughts that harm the wholesome are like crows, vultures, and foxes, whose primary activity is to prey upon and kill; therefore, they are used as metaphors.

Falling away from faith and wisdom is called "the falling out of teeth and hair"; having no precepts to shield the body is termed "nakedness"; because the mind takes evil objects as its conditions, it is said to be "pillowed upon a dog"; sinking into all manner of afflictions is called "lying in filth," or alternatively, being constantly submerged in the three evil realms without the intent to seek escape is "lying in filth."

To associate closely with those who have severed their roots of goodness is called "walking, standing, sitting, and lying down with the dead. Because their mental conduct gradually becomes identical, it is called "holding hands. To swallow and destroy wholesome dharmas is called "devouring. Because they form the causes for the evil realms, it is called "snakes filling the road. To wander toward and enter the three evil destinies is called "passing through them. To be bound by inverted craving is called "embracing a woman with disheveled hair. Using the false precepts of non-Buddhists as a means of self-protection is called "using *tāla* leaves as clothing. To initiate cultivation based on the false teachings of non-Buddhists is called "riding a donkey cart."
Turning one's back on the good and heading toward evil is called "wandering directly south"; since the south is the direction of fire and is the most malevolent, it is taken as a metaphor.

A resolute and perverse mind is called "having already dreamed," the withering and destruction of wholesome dharmas is called "mental distress," and the intensifying of a perverse mind is called "the illness increasing further."

In the second analogy concerning how even a minute good deed can induce the state of a noble one (*ārya*): the past wholesome karma of a person who has severed their roots of goodness is called "family and relatives," because it gives rise to present goodness, it is termed "sending a messenger. The arising of goodness that induces the state of a noble one is called "the physician who restores life. When wholesome conduct is incomplete, it is called "having physical deficiencies"; when the five faculties are not fully equipped, it is called "having impaired faculties"; when obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "covered in dust"; when lacking a sense of shame and dread of blame (*hrī-apatrāpya*), it is called "wearing tattered clothes. Relying on the remnants of wholesome dharmas from past Buddhas to give rise to this present goodness is called "riding an old cart. The manifestation of the noble mind through the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is called "the physician who speaks"; because the induction of the noble state is immediate, it is called "speaking swiftly. The desire to have the Tathāgata ride upon the former Dharma to go and provide instruction is called "quickly mounting the carriage."
In the third analogy, the Tathāgata’s observation of capacities, there are five distinct points.

The first point uses the metaphor of observing that present wholesome [roots] are subtle and inferior; thus it says, "seeing that the signs and characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are inauspicious. Because this inferior wholesome [root] cannot counteract the chronic illness, it is said to be "difficult to cure."
"Divining the day" is a metaphor for observing the mind that initiates action, as the mind is distinguished by its periods of goodness and evil;
"divining the stars" is a metaphor for observing the underlying dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are formed;
"divining the time" is a metaphor for observing the mind of aspiration and desire.

Looking down at the analogy of merit means observing the five faculties, such as faith, which are acquired through birth; although the preceding conditions may have ceased to exist, if these faculties are acquired at birth and one's roots of goodness have not been severed, they can still be healed. However, if they are absent, there is no way to save them; therefore it is said: "If they are absent, what benefit is there even if one is fortunate?"
In the fourth section, the analogy regarding the manifestation of transformations according to the capacities of beings, there are four distinct parts:

first, the analogy of the Tathāgata ascending to Tuṣita Heaven, wherein he observes the capacities and ailments of beings; this is presented with specific instances followed by a summary, yet it is difficult to discern and hard to reconcile.

Second, from the passage "If I do not go, I am not a true teacher" onwards, the analogy concerns the Buddha descending to Jambudvīpa to observe the capacities and ailments of beings; here too, specific instances are followed by a summary, and the matter is likewise difficult to discern.

3. The passage beginning with "At that time, he immediately enters the patient’s house" is a metaphor for observing the conditions and illnesses of beings at the time of renunciation; entering the house of illness refers to first practicing what is to be cultivated within the teachings of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika-dharma) prior to renouncing the world. 4.

The passage beginning with "Having seen this, the physician asks the nurse" is a metaphor for preaching after attaining enlightenment by observing the capacities [of beings]; herein, there is first a specific analysis, followed by a summary of the difficulty of treatment beginning with "At that time, the skilled physician sees such... and so forth.
Within this section, there is first the questioning, then the smelling, and finally the touching.

Regarding the initial questioning, it serves as an analogy to illustrate that mental activity is indeterminate; the Bodhisattva who is personally transformed is like a caregiver for the sick, and the Tathāgata provides complete answers in response to his inquiries.
Next, smelling illustrates the uncertainty of verbal expression: smelling represents evil speech, while fragrance represents virtuous words.
Finally, touching illustrates the uncertainty of physical conduct.

In the fifth analogy, "Temporarily Relinquishing Authority," the Tathāgata addresses the bodhisattva who was personally transformed by him, declaring his intention to further migrate and transform in another realm; this is called "Speaking to the Illness."
I am now occupied with urgent affairs; hereafter, my transformation and deliverance shall be called "Coming Again.
According to what each can endure, I bestow upon them worldly dharmas, which is called "Granting Whatever Is Needed Without Restraint."
Leaving him behind and proceeding toward extinction is called "returning home.

His arising of subtle goodness that induces the state of a noble one is called "having arrived. The Tathāgata, knowing that he was not yet capable of receiving transformation, did not immediately approach him; therefore, He informed the messenger:

"My work is not yet finished, and furthermore, the medicine has not yet been compounded. This clarifies that his remaining methods for transformation were not yet complete, which is termed "the work is not yet finished," and that the Buddha had not yet assessed the disciple's capacity to bestow the Dharma, which is termed "the medicine has not yet been compounded."
The analogies are difficult to identify and cannot be fully correlated;
even where a correlation exists, it cannot be definitively established. Next, we shall correlate them in order:

"The World-Honored One is likewise" correlates with the physician mentioned above; "the group of icchantikas" correlates with both the first and the second [analogies] mentioned previously; "skillfully knowing their faculties and natures" correlates with the third above; and "preaching the Dharma for them" correlates with the fourth above.
The following clarifies the reasons why the Tathāgata preached [this teaching], first posing questions and subsequently providing explanations.

Within the explanations, the first part clarifies that it was taught in order to quell the slanders of others; for if the Buddha had not spoken, others would have claimed that the Buddha lacks compassion.

The latter part clarifies that it was taught for the benefit of icchantikas; therein, the initial section explains how it causes them to produce wholesome roots, while the subsequent section, beginning with "For example," explains how it delivers them from the three miserable realms.
Regarding the arising of wholesome states, the first section clarifies how the arising of wholesome states differs for icchantikas, for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma;
from the phrase "furthermore, there are two" onwards, it cites differences in their faculties to demonstrate the distinct ways in which they generate these states.
First, the preceding section introduces the subject, followed by the enumeration of two names.
Below, it clarifies that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for them; in general discussion, icchantikas are said to possess three types:
the first is the superior type, who, upon hearing the sutras and Dharma in the present, is slightly able to give rise to faith.

The second is the middling grade: although they do not believe the sutras and teachings when hearing them in the present, they do not slander them, and are thus able to produce roots of goodness for the future.
The third is the inferior grade: they do not believe when hearing them in the present, and furthermore, they slander and reject them.
Now, of the three faculties mentioned previously, only the first two are cited; the third, lack of faith, is not mentioned here as the Buddha does not preach for its sake, and thus it is omitted.

In the subsequent section on the faculties, there is first a general citation, followed by a detailed listing, then an explanation of how that person’s production of wholesome roots differs, and finally a conclusion regarding the Tathāgata’s non-vain preaching of the Dharma.

This section clarifies the extraction from the sufferings of the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*). It first provides a parable, followed by its application (*yoga*), and concludes with the Buddha’s discourse beginning from the words "Therefore.
Below this is the fifth section: King Ajātaśatru accepts the exhortation and goes to the Buddha to repent. This section contains three parts:

(1) the preparatory account of his departure in a grand carriage to the Buddha as the cause for extinguishing his transgressions; (2) the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma to eliminate the king’s sins, beginning from "At that time, the Buddha addressed Ajātaśatru"; and (3) his taking leave and returning to the palace.
The beginning and middle have four parts:
first, having accepted the exhortation to go but not yet setting out immediately, Jīvaka urges him on;
second, he immediately orders his subordinates to prepare the carriage and proceed toward the Buddha.
Third, while on the road and descending the path, he heard two voices and his heart was filled with alarm; the Tathāgata granted him the means to attain a mind of certainty.
Fourth, when the Four Kings arrived at the Twin Trees, the Tathāgata looked upon them and charged them with a command, thereby dispelling the kings' doubts.
The first part has two sections:
first, the worldly king is exhorted and chooses a time to grant permission for his departure;
second, "if it is so that the Tathāgata truly intends this," meaning he truly intends to preach the Dharma for those who have abandoned all roots of goodness (icchantikas).
Second, Jīvaka’s exhortation and encouragement, which consists of four points:
first, clarifying that the Buddha-dharma does not select specific times or days;
second, since the King’s illness is grave, one should not wait for an auspicious time—first citing worldly affairs and subsequently using them as a basis for the exhortation.
Third, the three [disciples] approach the Buddha and receive equal benefits;
fourth, the exhortation to go.
Within the second section, there are five distinct points:
First, he commanded his ministers to prepare everything;
second, the ministers replied that all was ready;
third, they prepared the carriage and proceeded toward the Buddha.
Fourth, the great assembly in Kuśinagara all beheld him;
fifth, the Buddha praised his good friend, first praising him and subsequently explaining [the reason].

In the third section, it is first shown that upon hearing the two words, the king’s mind was struck with alarm; from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata grants permission to bring about a resolute mind.

In the first part of the preceding section, there is first an explanation of hearing two statements: hearing that King Piliyakkha died after being consumed by fire, and that the bhikṣu Kokālika was reborn alive in the Avīci hell—this constitutes the first statement.

King Prabhāsa, having murdered his father, heard the Buddha’s prophecy that he would be consumed by fire; he thereupon boarded a ship and entered the ocean of the rear garden to escape it, but the fires of Avīci immediately reached into the sea and drew him away.

The bhikṣu Kokālika was a disciple of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; at one time, he slandered these two masters, claiming that both had committed grave offenses, and consequently fell into the Avīci hell.
"Having heard that Sunakṣatra went to the Buddha and had his offenses extinguished"—these are the words of the two [kings].

From "I now," below, it clarifies the kings' terror as they seek to share one elephant with Jīvaka; [the text] says, "If I should fall, I hope you will save me," and "If I should fall, I hope you will catch me. Thus, first they request, and subsequently they explain.
While the Tathāgata was granting his consent to settle the king's mind, the Buddha first addressed the assembly, saying: "King Śreṇiya has a doubt; I shall resolve it for him.
What is the meaning of this?
When King Śreṇika heard these two statements earlier, he immediately conceived a doubt:

he did not know whether the Tathāgata would be willing to grant him salvation so that he might become like Sunakṣatra, or whether he would fail to save him so that he might fall into the Avīci Hell like Devadatta or Kokālika.
According to what follows, "seeing the Buddha" means the removal of doubt and the attainment of certainty; the intention of "doubt" is precisely this.
When the Buddha descends and accepts the command, causing [the practitioner] to know that the Buddha definitely intends to provide salvation, this is termed "settled mind."
Regarding the section "Holding All," the following questions and answers provide an analytical explanation.
Prior to this, he [the interlocutor] asked: "Since all phenomena are not fixed, why do you speak of them as fixed?"
The Buddha first offers praise and subsequently provides an analytical explanation.

The passage "I have brought about a resolute mind for the King of the World" generally clarifies the act of establishing certainty; the section beginning with "For what reason? specifically reveals this establishment of certainty, consisting of a prior question followed by its resolution.
The explanation consists of four parts:

first, by means of the King’s doubt being indeterminate, one classifies all phenomena as indeterminate; since the King’s doubt can be destroyed, one should know that all phenomena likewise lack any fixed characteristic.
Second, from the words "Therefore" onwards is the conclusion: because this mind of doubt in the King can be destroyed, I act as the World-King to establish a mind of certainty.

3. From "One should know" below, the king’s unsettled mind is used as an analogy for the unsettled nature of the offense; herein, first the king’s unsettled mind is clarified, and from "If that king’s mind were determined" below, the mind is used as an analogy for the offense to clarify its unsettled nature—first by way of negation and then by way of affirmation;
4. From "Therefore" below, the conclusion is drawn.
Fourth, from here below, the king arrives at the twin trees; the Tathāgata addresses him with his final instructions, removing the king’s doubts.
This section contains four parts:
first, the king arrives at the twin trees and gazes upward at the Tathāgata’s marks and signs, which are exceptionally sublime and wondrous.
1. The Tathāgata’s entrustment of his final charge, which removed the King’s state of doubt; 2.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva’s address to Sarvasattvaparigraha, clarifying that the Buddha had already made a definitive decision for the King; 3.
The Worldly King’s joy, wherein he prepared offerings for the Buddha, paid homage, and withdrew to stand aside.
The first section may be understood as it stands.
Within the second section, there are four phrases:
the first is the Tathāgata’s utterance of a call.
Regarding the eight kinds of voice, as described in the *Brahmāyu Sūtra*:
first, the most excellent voice, which is pure and elegant;
second, the easily understood voice, wherein whatever is spoken is distinct and easy to comprehend.
Third, the harmonious voice, in which the high and low tones attain the middle;
fourth, the gentle voice, whose sound is soft and pleasing to hear;
fifth, the unerring voice, in which speech is free from error or confusion.
Sixth, his voice is not feminine, but is powerful and resonant;

seventh, it is a voice of venerable wisdom, for his speech is free from timidity—just as the World-Honored One’s speech is free from timidity when addressing those possessed of wisdom, so too is the Buddha’s voice;
eighth, it is a deep and far-reaching voice, like the roll of thunder.
Fearing that the king might become displeased if they did not immediately announce their names, they addressed him collectively as "Great King.
When the two kings heard this, they were startled and filled with doubt, asking, "In this assembly, who is the Great King?"
"I am a sinner without merit; the Tathāgata should not address me as 'Great King'.
(3) The Tathāgata repeated his name to call out to him.

(4) When the world-king heard this, his doubts were dispelled and he was filled with joy. First, "joy" clarifies his state of gladness; from "truly knowing the Suchness" (*tathatā*) onwards, it clarifies the dispelling of his doubts.
The third point is thus understood.
In the fourth section, King Śreṇiya first manifests his joy, then offers worship, and finally pays homage before withdrawing to stand aside.
From this point on, the second part follows: the Buddha preaches the Dharma for him, thereby eliminating the king’s transgressions.
Within this, the Tathāgata first gave his permission for the discourse, which is now correctly expounded.
This exposition consists of three parts:
first, the teaching on the arising of the king’s sense of shame through contemplation.
Second, from "I myself have invited calamity by creating this grave [offense]" onwards, the characteristics of sin are refuted and eliminated to remove the King’s clinging mind;

third, from "For example, nirvana is neither existent nor non-existent" onwards, the true nature of sin is clarified, causing the King to contemplate and enter into the correct cessation of his own offenses.
Within the first section, the Tathāgata first provides the instruction, and subsequently Ajātaśatru attains realization regarding the nature of birth.
Within the Tathāgata’s instruction, the benefit of contemplation is clarified first; from the words "if not bound" onwards, the loss resulting from non-contemplation is clarified.

There are four sections within this [chapter on] "Benefits": first, the instruction on contemplating the body; second, the clarification of the benefits of that contemplation; third, the instruction on contemplating the mind; and fourth, the clarification of the benefits of that contemplation.

Within the section on contemplating the body, the text first provides a general heading: "An ordinary person should constantly contemplate twenty matters," and subsequently explains them individually.

Among these twenty matters, the first fourteen phrases contemplate that the body lacks ultimate (paramārtha) happiness and is replete with various sufferings; the latter six contemplate how one has already become deluded or inverted.

The preceding fourteen phrases are grouped into four sets. The first two contemplate that, having already [realized] the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no bliss; "this body of mine is empty and devoid of the outflow-free" means there is no outflow-free fruit; "empty and devoid of the roots of goodness" means there is no outflow-free cause. The next two contemplate that the body is fully possessed of all sufferings:

"I have not yet attained harmony within this cycle of birth and death" indicates the presence of the cause of birth and death; being unable to abandon evil is called "not yet harmonized. "Falling into a deep pit, fearing nothing" indicates the presence of the fruit of birth and death; sinking into the three miserable realms is called "falling into a deep pit," and since taking birth among humans or devas is entirely suffering, for this reason one fears nothing.

Next, in contrast to the preceding [section], regarding the teaching on the ultimate bliss, one gives rise to the mind of seeking: one seeks the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) by asking, "By what skillful means can one see the Buddha-nature? and one seeks the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) by asking, "How should one cultivate meditative concentration to see the Buddha-nature?"

Furthermore, while the preceding phrase sought the practice that follows existence (*bhava*), how does one cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to seek entry into the practice of tranquility (*śānti*)?

The following eight points contrast with the former by teaching the generation of revulsion through the presence of all sufferings; therein, the first seven teach the contemplation of heavy suffering, while the final phrase teaches the contemplation of profound suffering.

Within the preceding seven [categories], the teaching that "birth and death are constantly suffering, and are impermanent, non-self, and impure" instructs one to contemplate the general faults of birth and death; the section beginning with "the eight difficulties" instructs one to contemplate the specific faults of birth and death.
"The eight difficulties that are hard to escape" refers to the fault of obstructing the Path; "constantly being pursued by enemies," and so forth, refers to the fault of saṃsāra.

Within this, the first two clarify the faults of saṃsāra among humans and devas. "Constantly pursued by enemies" clarifies the shared obstruction: the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are the enemies, and because they are fixed upon birth, it is said they constantly pursue one. "No dharma can block existence" reveals the absence of a remedy.
The final three phrases clarify the faults of transmigrating within the three miserable realms: "not yet escaped from the three evils" refers to the fruits of the three miserable realms;
"possessing evil and false views, not having crossed the turbulent ford" refers to the causes of the three miserable realms.
To possess evil and false views is to have afflictions;
to have not yet crossed the turbulent ford is to have evil karma.
Since false views and the five heinous crimes are the certain causes for the three miserable realms, they are singled out for mention.
The preceding section elucidated heavy suffering; the statement "birth and death are boundless, and one has not yet reached their limit" clarifies profound suffering.

Thus far, it has been shown that there is no ultimate bliss (*paramārtha-sukha*) and that all manner of sufferings are fully present. Below, six sections clarify how beings are already deluded or inverted; within these, the first four establish general principles, while the latter two clarify the state of being deluded or inverted in relation to those principles.

Regarding the first four [points]: "Not performing various karmas, one does not obtain their retribution" clarifies that there is no absence of cause; "There is no self who acts and another who receives the retribution" clarifies that there is no extraneous cause; "If one does not create the cause of happiness, there will ultimately be no fruit of happiness" clarifies that there is no inverted cause; and "If one has performed karma, the fruit is never lost" clarifies that there is no absence of result.

Regarding the latter two [of the four truths], one is born because of ignorance and likewise dies because of it; by being deluded regarding the aforementioned principle, one undergoes the fruit of birth and death. Throughout the past, future, and present, one constantly practices heedlessness, and by being deluded regarding the aforementioned principle, one creates the causes of birth and death.
The phrase "The ordinary person is permanent" concludes the preceding section as a whole.
The first part above was the formal exhortation to contemplate the body; from the words "Practicing this contemplation" onwards, it clarifies the benefits of such contemplation.

The passage "At that time, one sequentially contemplates the arising of the mind" below teaches the method for contemplating the mind; "Sequentially contemplating the characteristics of the mind’s arising, abiding, and ceasing" teaches the contemplation of the mind itself.

The passage beginning with "Next, the contemplation of cessation" and so forth teaches the method of contemplating the mind; the section beginning with "Having contemplated arising and ceasing, one already knows the characteristics of the mind" clarifies the benefits of contemplation; the section "Knowing the mind, one reaches the precepts and ultimately does no evil" clarifies the departure from evil causes; and the section "There is no fear of death" and so forth clarifies the departure from the fruits of suffering.
The preceding section clarifies the benefit of contemplation; the subsequent section, beginning with "If one is not bound," clarifies the loss incurred by non-contemplation.
The above constitutes the Buddha’s teaching, while the following clarifies how the Worldly King understood and felt remorse; the text is explicit and thus easily understood.
From here below is the second section, which refutes and dispels the King’s attachment to the notion of a transgression; this passage is divided into two parts:

first, the refutation based on the circumstances of killing his father; second, the refutation based on the mind, beginning with the passage "Sentient beings are either mad or ordinary," and so forth.
The preceding section has four parts:
first, King Śreṇika maintains that there is a fixed determination of guilt, such that one is certain to fall into hell;
second, the Tathāgata briefly refutes this, which is also called "refutation by analogy."
The first three are the King’s Comprehension;
the fourth is the Tathāgata’s Extensive Refutation, also called the Correct Refutation.
Regarding the first, there are six statements:
"Bringing calamity upon oneself" is the first phrase, signifying that by clinging [to self], one incurs offense;
"Committing these grave evils" is the second phrase, signifying that by clinging [to them], the offense is certain to be heavy;
"The Father King" is the third, signifying the certainty of having a father.
"Being innocent" is the fourth [point], maintaining that the father was without fault;
"to have perversely committed the act of killing" is the fifth phrase, maintaining that there was a definite act of murder;
"these twenty matters, whether one contemplates them or not, will certainly lead to falling into hell" is the sixth phrase, maintaining the certainty of falling into hell.
These six statements will be refuted individually by the Buddha below; they should be carefully noted and understood.

From "The Buddha told" onwards, the Tathāgata provides a brief refutation. By stating that "the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are impermanent and lack any fixed determination," he refutes them by generalizing the principle. When [the King] asks, "Why do you say I am certain to fall into Avīci?", this constitutes a formal rebuke; among the preceding six statements, the latter ones are used here to deliver the rebuke.

From here on, the third section concerns the King’s understanding and realization. [He thinks: "If all phenomena lack a fixed nature, then my crime of killing must also be unfixed. Thus he uses the phenomenon to categorize the crime. Then: "If killing were fixed, then all phenomena would not be unfixed. Thus he uses the crime to categorize the phenomenon.
The preceding sentence follows the same category, while the subsequent sentence opposes it.
From the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata provides a detailed refutation; he first offers praise and subsequently performs the refutation.
Praise is necessary because the King previously attained understanding, and refutation is necessary because the King previously held attachments.
Within the section on praise, "Excellent! is the general praise; from "The Buddhas" onwards is the specific praise; and from "Therefore" onwards is the conclusion.

Regarding the refutation in the subsequent section, there are six points to be refuted, as previously stated: from the self as clung to which invites calamity, up to the certainty of falling into the Avīci Hell.
The textual analysis is divided into three parts:
first, refuting the [notions of] a fixed father and a fixed killing among the previous six points, thereby refuting entry into hell based on these two;

second, from the passage "Sentient beings commit sins, which are generally of two kinds" onwards, refuting the [notion of] one's own self inviting calamity and creating such grave evils among the previous six points, thereby refuting entry into hell based on these two.

3. "The former kings created [their own karma] and received it themselves" and below, there is a second refutation of the previous argument that one invites calamity upon oneself, as well as a refutation of the notion of innocence; thus, by means of these two refutations, one enters hell.
Since the hells are what is feared, all three points are therefore refuted.

Within the first section, first the fixed nature of the father is refuted; below the passage "Ordinary beings [regard] this form," the fixed nature of the killing is refuted; and below the passage "If form were the father and could be killed," entry into hell is refuted.

Within the first section, the phrase "As the King has said, my father the king was innocent, yet you have perversely committed an act of rebellion against him" restates the King's previous words; this serves as the refutation of the father. The subsequent portion, beginning with "Which one is it? and so forth, constitutes the formal refutation of that father.

Within this, first he interrogates his father by means of the three categories of dharmas—the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). Under the section beginning with "If form is [the father]," he specifically interrogates and refutes the real father by means of the five aggregates:
"If form is the father, the other four aggregates should not be [the father]"—this uses form to refute mind;
"If the four are the father, form should also not be [the father]"—this uses mind to refute form.
"If it were the case that form and non-form combined to constitute the father, such a thing is impossible. This [statement] refutes the notion of the father by means of both form and mind together.

The section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation: because "there is no combination of the natures of form and non-form," it is impossible for form and mind to combine to constitute the father.
Within the refutation of killing, the argument specifically targets form (*rūpa*), because form possesses substantial resistance (*sapratigha*) and is thus susceptible to being harmed.

The phrase "Ordinary people falsely conceive of form as a father" cites their specific misconception; the subsequent statement, "Such a form-aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) likewise cannot be harmed," provides a general refutation of that position. The word "likewise" (*api*) is used because the [form-aggregate] shares the same quality of being indestructible.
The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation. Within this, it first asks, "For what reason is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) also indestructible? and subsequently answers it.
The explanation consists of four points:
first, dividing form into ten categories—the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) constitute these ten.
As stated in the *Abhidharma*, there are eleven types: the five faculties, the five objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*);

whereas in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, fourteen are mentioned: the five faculties, the five objects, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). For what reason, then, are only ten types specifically mentioned here?
The commentary states:
Within this sutra, the four great elements are subsumed under the sense-object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*); therefore, they are not discussed separately.

As for those unmanifest forms (*avijñapti-rūpa*), within this sutra they are merely material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) that lack the characteristic of form; because they constitute the hidden characteristics of the body, they are not mentioned.

Second, within the ten [bases], one is excluded and nine are set aside: "Only the single category of form (rūpa) is visible, tangible, and even subject to being bound," whereas the remaining nine are not so; therefore, they may not be killed.

Only the single category of form—namely, the object of the eye—is said to be "visible" because it is illuminated by the eye; it is said to be "graspable" because it can be seized and held. It can be weighed for its lightness or heaviness, measured for its length or shortness, pulled and dragged, and even bound; therefore, it can be killed.

According to the *Abhidharma*, the characteristic of form (*rūpa*) is visible; the shape of form is measurable, as its squareness, roundness, largeness, or smallness can be quantified; and thus the nature of form can be maintained, pulled, and bound.
Because it possesses qualities such as substantiality (*dravya*), it may be called "tangible.

According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, visible form (*rūpa*) is solely that which is visible; however, that which can be touched, held, measured, pulled, or bound is "conventionally designated form" (*prajñaptirūpa*), subsumed under the object-field of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Now, for what reason is it said that "form (rūpa) is visible" and so forth, up to "it can be bound"?
The explanation states:

This teaching is largely consistent with the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā). The characteristic of form is visible; the shape of form is measurable; the nature of form can be maintained, pulled, bound, and weighed. Since the sensation of heaviness cannot be distinguished apart from form, these characteristics are collectively designated as "form."

3. Regarding the passage beginning with "Although it is visible," the author refutes the notion of "seeing" and so forth by means of that single form (*rūpa*). The phrase "although it is bound by being visible" above restates what has been analyzed.
There are six clauses above; since the first and the last are cited, only "visible bondage" is mentioned.
If discussed in terms of coarse characteristics, the characteristic of form is visible and even subject to binding; yet when minutely analyzed, it does not exist.
Since this discernment of existence encompasses non-existence, one says "although."

Regarding "the nature does not abide," the subsequent section negates existence to reveal non-existence: the nature of form is impermanent; it exists for only a single moment, undergoing initial arising, subsequent abiding, final alteration, and ultimate cessation; therefore, it is said not to abide.
Because it does not abide, it cannot be perceived, and so forth, up to being impossible to bind.

Fourth, from "the characteristics of form" (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) onwards, the conclusion is established that there is no killing: since the essential nature of form is thus non-abiding, and so forth, up to being impossible to bind, how could it be killed?
The following section refutes the [notion that] the first two [elements] enter hell; it consists of six distinct points:

First, by selecting one from among the ten material elements and excluding the other nine: "If form were the father, such that he could be killed or harmed and thereby incur the retribution for sin, then the remaining nine should not be so; if the nine are not [the father], then there should be no sin."
Second, regarding a single form (*rūpa*), it is explained that there is the sense of being "slayable. First, three numbers are raised; next, three names are listed;
finally, they are analyzed. Within this, it is first clarified that the past and present cannot be slain, beginning with the initial citation and followed by the explanation.
Past form has already ceased and is therefore incapable of being killed;
present form appears only momentarily, ceasing of its own accord in every moment, and is therefore incapable of being killed.
The following section addresses the future to clarify the sense in which killing is possible, by way of preventing [future form] from arising.
3. From "In this way" onwards, the preceding arguments regarding what can be killed and what cannot be killed establish that form (*rūpa*) is indeterminate.
4. By means of the indeterminacy of form, the indeterminacy of killing is established.
Fifth, because killing is not determinate, its retribution is not determinate.
Sixth, since the retribution is not determinate, it refutes the claim that one enters hell; for if the retribution is not determinate, how can you say that one is "certainly" to enter hell?
From here below begins the second section, which refutes [the claim that] one brings calamity upon oneself by committing grave evils, thereby entering hell based on these two points of refutation.

First, the gravity of the offense is established; then, from "If he commands his attendants to execute the king immediately" onwards, the refutation of bringing calamity upon oneself is presented; and from "Bimbisāra previously committed evil" onwards, the refutation of entering hell is presented.

Regarding the breaking of the gravity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), first, in general, it is stated that the actions performed by all sentient beings are of two kinds; next, the two names are listed; and finally, their characteristics are distinguished: actions performed by mind and speech are light, while those performed by body, speech, and mind are explained as grave.

The following section distinguishes the king’s actions based on these two [factors], stating that "the retribution obtained for one who intends in the mind and speaks with the mouth, but does not act with the body, is light. This clarifies the previous point regarding lightness.

Below, the king is tested: "Great King, in the past you did not command the killing with your mouth, but merely said 'cut off his feet'"; thus, the king's offense is lighter than even that which was previously deemed light—how can it be said to be heavy?

If one breaks through this self again in the future, one will invite calamity; what was previously called "inviting calamity" is here termed "incurring offense," though the meaning is identical while the phrasing differs.
First, he directly refutes it: "If the King were to incur offense, then the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would also incur it. Below this, he uses the Buddhas as a category to refute the claim.
Within the direct refutation, the principle of "the heavy case illustrating the light" is employed to establish that the King is without fault.

"If [the executioner] were commanded to behead the King while he was standing, yet waited until he was seated before executing him, he would still not incur guilt"—this is the citation of the heavy case.
This means that one cannot cut off the head of the seated king, because the seated king did not command his execution.
"How much more so when the king did not command it—how could one incur guilt? This is an illustration of the lightness [of the offense].

Even among those sentenced to death, one who merely rises from his seat is not yet considered guilty; how much less so when the King on that former day merely spoke of lopping off a foot and did not issue an order to kill—how could he incur the guilt of patricide?
In this context, one merely refutes the sin of actual killing; it does not say that by amputating the foot, one becomes free from sin.
Why must one resort to such an analogy? The King maintains a further objection:
"Because I am the one who amputated the foot and thereby caused my father's life to end, I cannot be free from the sin of actual killing."

The Buddha now refutes this by analogy: if a king incurs the fault of killing because his father’s life was ended by the amputation of his feet, then the Buddhas would also incur the fault of killing, as they likewise have the causal conditions for it.

Although the Buddha had a specific cause for this killing, he incurred no offense; yet although the king had a specific cause for his actual killing, how could he avoid the guilt of that very act of killing?

In the text, the initial statement, "If the king commits an offense, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should also commit an offense," briefly cites a parallel case to refute [the opponent's position].

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation; it first poses a question and then answers it below, clarifying that because the Buddha has a causal basis even for killing, he should indeed incur an offense.

In this context, it is not intended to clarify that the Buddha incurs guilt; rather, by citing the Tathāgata, it is shown that although he had the conditions for killing, he incurred no guilt, thereby establishing that the King of the World, despite having the conditions for killing, did not incur the formal offense.
The text contains four statements:
first, it clarifies that the former kings attained their status as kings because they made offerings to the Buddhas; this follows the sequence from cause to effect.
Second, from the phrase "If one does not [act]" onwards, it clarifies that because one acts as a king, one may be killed; this is expressed through the reverse order to highlight the point.
3. From "If you were to kill your father, you would incur guilt" onwards, the king is compared to the Buddha in order to cause the Buddha to incur guilt;
4. From "If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, incurs no guilt" onwards, the Buddha is compared to the king in order to establish that the king incurs no guilt.
The Buddhas may also commit acts of killing for specific reasons without incurring sin; why then do you alone incur the specific fault of killing?
Next, [the author] refutes the certainty of his descent into hell by citing the example of that former king to undermine his argument.
When the former kings committed sins, they repented and did not enter [hell]; why then must Your Majesty, having now felt remorse and shame, certainly enter it? This passage contains four parts:

first, explaining how she was like those women who in the past roamed for hunting and killed sages; second, explaining how the sages, upon their deaths, gave rise to anger and subsequently made evil vows; third, the king hearing this and feeling remorse and shame; fourth, citing the case of the worldly kings as an analogy.

If even this king, being thus, was still able to receive [the retribution] lightly and did not enter hell, how much more so for one who is not like him—such a person would surely have to undergo the karmic fruit in hell.
There are two meanings to this explanation:
first, distinguishing the case based on the cause; the former king’s past mental intention to inflict harm and his verbal command to kill were grave offenses.
"Worldly King, although your mind today harbors thoughts of harm, you have not commanded with your mouth that he be killed; therefore, your offense is light.
If even the grave sins of a former king were reduced to a light retribution through repentance, how much more so for a king who has done no such thing?"
It is not the case that a former king, having personally commanded a killing by word of mouth, would necessarily undergo the retribution of hell.

Second, to distinguish the case by way of its result: if a former king committed a transgression and subsequently gave rise to shame and regret, a worldly king who commits a transgression would likewise give rise to a mind of remorse;

if a former king committed a transgression and, through repentance, received a lightened punishment and did not enter hell, then by analogy with him, why should a king alone be no different, such that he must exclusively undergo the retribution of hell?

From here below begins the third section, which doubly refutes both the claim that one invites calamity upon oneself and the claim of being innocent; it further demonstrates that based on these two points, one enters hell.
