Just as it cannot be said that a worldly person who has already reached their destination is still "going," so it is in this case: the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already attained *nirvāṇa*, and since they have not heard the Dharma, it cannot be said that they hear it.

The phrase "having departed, one does not arrive" illustrates the latter part of the statement. Just as a person on a road cannot be said to have arrived while they are in the process of going, so it is here: once one has already heard, one cannot hear again that which was unheard.

In the second analogy, "arising" is used as a metaphor for hearing, while "non-arising" is a metaphor for the meaning of not hearing. "Having arisen, it does not arise" serves to illustrate the subsequent phrase: just as when those marks of arising produce various phenomena, one cannot say they arise from non-arising, so too, once hearing has been attained, one cannot declare that one hears what was not heard. "Non-arising, non-arising" corresponds to the preceding phrase: just as space cannot arise and is therefore correctly termed "non-arising" and cannot be said to arise, so too, that which cannot be heard is correctly termed "not heard" and cannot be said to be heard.
In the third analogy, "attaining" is used as a metaphor for hearing, while "not attaining" is a metaphor for not hearing; "having attained yet not attaining" corresponds to the subsequent phrase.

Just as among those fourteen dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there is a "possession" (*prāpti*) that is neither form nor mind and is capable of possessing all phenomena—taking this now as an analogy—when those various possessions possess their respective phenomena, it cannot be called "possessing what was not possessed. How much more so in this case: once one has attained the capacity for hearing and retention (*śrutadhara*), it cannot be said that one is "hearing what was not heard."

The phrase "not-attaining not-attaining" serves as a category to clarify the preceding statement. For example, dharmas that cannot be attained, such as the horns of a rabbit, are correctly termed "not-attained"; they cannot be described as "not-attaining-attaining. By this analogy, dharmas that cannot be heard are correctly termed "unheard," and one cannot say they are "unheard-heard."

The preceding establishment of metaphors—“having heard, one does not hear; not having heard, one does not hear, and it is likewise so”—is applied to reveal the Dharma. “Having heard, one does not obtain” cites the subsequent phrase to apply it to the preceding metaphor, while “not having heard, one does not hear” cites the initial phrase above to apply it to the preceding metaphor.

In the first statement of the third pair, the argument refutes the existence of "hearing" based on the time when one has not yet heard; it clarifies that this is merely "not-hearing-not-hearing," and not "not-hearing-hearing."

The latter phrase addresses the time when one does not hear; it refutes the notion of "not hearing" to demonstrate that there was previously hearing. Having previously possessed hearing, one subsequently attains the state of a sage and hears what is to be heard; this is not a case of hearing what was previously unheard.

Regarding the first part: "If the World-Honored One hears what was not heard" means that it is definitively established that even before hearing, the Tathāgata already possessed the nature of hearing; this is called "hearing what was not heard."
Next, the objections are set forth; these objections consist of three stages.

First, an objection is raised from the perspective of ordinary beings prior to the stage of practice: "If there were already those who had heard [the Dharma] even before they had heard it, then all sentient beings who have not yet attained bodhi should already possess it; those who have not yet attained nirvana should already have attained it; and those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature should already see it."

Second, a challenge is raised regarding the bodhisattvas of the ten stages: if they have already heard [the teaching] even before now, why is it said that "although the bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature, they have not yet attained clear realization"?
Third, he raises an objection regarding the Buddha: if there were already those who heard [the Dharma] before [the Buddha] had heard it, from whom did the Tathāgata originally hear it in the past?
If there were a source from which he heard it, why did the Tathāgata state in the *Āgamas* that he had "no teacher"?

Regarding the first statement in the middle section of the latter part, "not hearing what was not heard": this definitively establishes that at the time when the Tathāgata had not yet heard, there was no nature of hearing; thus it is called "not hearing what was not heard."
Now, the following objection is raised: What is the intent of this objection? It is as follows:

If the Buddha-Tathāgata originally had no hearing at all when he had not yet heard [the Dharma], and only later attained Bodhi and perceived the Buddha-nature; [then how could he have been omniscient from the beginning?]
When all sentient beings have not yet heard [the Dharma], they likewise possess no hearing; they should thus be identical to the Buddha in attaining Bodhi and perceiving the Buddha-nature.
That all sentient beings do not attain Bodhi and do not perceive the Buddha-nature can be explained as being fundamentally without hearing.

Because the Buddha has attained Bodhi and perceived the Buddha-nature, he clearly hears what is primordially present; because he hears what is primordially present, when the Buddha causes others to hear, they hear that which was heard from the beginning, not hearing what was previously unheard.
*Nirvāṇa-gi-ki*, Scroll Six. On the twentieth day of the fifth month of the third year of Ōei, the supplementary transcription including the characters for *kaku* (加) and *shū* (修) was completed.
Recorded by Kenpō, Provisional Great Sōjō and Dharma Seal.
*Nirvāṇa-gi-ki*, Scroll Seven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingying Monastery during the Sui Dynasty.
Having above refuted the arguments concerning "hearing" and "not hearing," the second section below distinguishes the characteristics of actual difference,
clarifying that [the Dharma] cannot be heard.
However, for now, let us clarify that Nirvāṇa as a single dharma cannot be heard; other cases may be understood by analogy.
This section contains two parts:
first, clarifying that Nirvāṇa cannot be heard because it differs from form and sound; second, clarifying that Nirvāṇa cannot be heard because it is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Regarding the first two lines:
the first raises the coarse to illustrate the subtle, clarifying that visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) can be seen and heard.
As for the statement, "All dharmas of form are either visible or invisible," there are three types of form:
First, that which is visible and resistant, namely the objects of the eye;
second, that which is invisible and resistant, namely the forms perceived by the ear, nose, tongue, and body;
third, that which is invisible and non-resistant, namely the unmanifest form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Among these three types, the first can be seen, while the others cannot; therefore, they are called "delusions" (*moha*).
Furthermore, among the objects of form (*rūpa*), that which is present can be seen, whereas those of the past and future cannot; thus, these too may be called "delusions."
"Sound is also like this; as for delusion, it may be heard or not heard"—that which is present can be heard, while that of the past and future cannot.
Second, to distinguish the subtle from the coarse, it clarifies: "The Great Nirvana is not the same as form or sound; how then can it be said that it can be seen or heard?"
The latter middle section also has two parts:
first, investigating through the sounds of the three periods of time to clarify that nirvāṇa cannot be heard.
Regarding the phrase "the past has already ceased and cannot be heard": since the sound of the past has already perished, it cannot be sought out so as to hear nirvāṇa therein.
Regarding the phrase "In the future, even when seeking its arrival, it is not heard": because future sounds have not yet arrived, one cannot seek them and hear Nirvana.

Regarding the phrase "When listening in the present, it is not called 'hearing'": at the time of present listening, the ear merely hears sound; one has not yet been able to seek out that sound and grasp Nirvana. Therefore, even at the time of listening, it cannot be called hearing Nirvana.

Regarding the phrase "Having heard, the sound ceases and is no longer heard": once listening is finished, the sound ceases and there is no further grasping or seeking; therefore, one likewise cannot hear nirvāṇa.

Second, by investigating the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of nirvāṇa through the three periods of time, it is shown that nirvāṇa cannot be heard. The passage "Neither past, present, nor future" precisely clarifies that the essence of nirvāṇa does not belong to the three periods of time. The section beginning with "If it is not [of] the three" clarifies that it is ineffable to speak of hearing it. The section beginning with "How can one say" concludes that this is not the teaching of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
Above, the first section consists of King Guṇarāja’s objection; below, the Buddha praises him. “Excellent! is the general praise, while “You now,” and so forth, is the specific praise.
Within the specific praise, there are two parts:
first, praise for his understanding; second, praise for what he shares in common.

In the section on understanding, the passage beginning with “You know that all dharmas are like illusions and mirages” praises his understanding of emptiness; “like traces drawn upon water” praises his understanding of impermanence; “like foam and bubbles” praises his understanding of non-self; and “neither suffering nor pleasure” praises his understanding of suffering.
There is no pleasure, for it has the characteristic of suffering;
there is no suffering, for it is the reality of suffering.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The thorough penetration of the five aggregates as empty and without arising is the meaning of suffering."

Question: Up to this point, King Guṇa has challenged the Buddha regarding the meaning of "hearing" and "not hearing. For what reason does the Tathāgata now praise his knowledge of illusion and so forth? Answer:

Because King Guṇa previously understood that all phenomena are illusory, impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and that when sought throughout the three periods of time, they entirely lack the reality of being heard; therefore, the Buddha offers this praise.
Next, he praises what they have in common, clarifying that it is as known and seen in the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).
As for where King of Virtue himself resides—is it like the Ten Stages?
The following explains that King of Virtue has long since accomplished the merit of Bodhi, transforming immeasurable beings and causing them to abide in Bodhi.

From the first bhūmi upward, all are said to have accomplished the merits of bodhi; however, the present King of Virtue may be a Buddha manifesting as one dwelling in the stage of learning, or he may be one who has reached the culmination of learning, yet his understanding is the same as that of other bodhisattvas in the ten abodes; therefore, it is said that he is "like" them.
Just as the sutras praise the Buddha, and just as that which is spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time remains unchanging, this case is also similar to that.
For what reason does the Tathāgata not answer within this?
Some say it is because a guest has arrived.
There is no guest who does not receive an answer; the Sage’s transformative influence is unhurried and relaxed—how could there be such an obstruction?

It is simply that the Buddha employs skillful transformation, intentionally withholding this answer to simultaneously benefit the newly arrived bodhisattvas and others; for this reason, he does not respond.
From here begins the second section, in which Vimalacandra poses questions and the Tathāgata provides answers.

This section contains six parts: first, Vimalacandra’s prior manifestation of light-signs; second, the identification of the source of that light; third, Vimalacandra’s arrival and his making of offerings to the Buddha; fourth, the exchange of questions and answers regarding the phenomena of coming and going; fifth, the exchange of questions and answers concerning the Dharma; and sixth, Vimalacandra’s joyful reception and understanding of the Dharma upon hearing it.

The distinctions between these passages can be understood as follows: Because the Sage’s transformation has its source, he first manifests signs; because those signs have what they derive from, he next analyzes them; because the manifestation of signs requires a response, he next describes the coming of the body; because the appearance of the coming obscures the truth, he next brushes it away; because the coming is for the purpose of revealing the Dharma, he next analyzes the Dharma; and because attaining the Dharma satisfies the mind, there must be a realization and understanding.
First, the characteristics of the light are distinguished.

"At that time, within the great assembly" clarifies the place where the light appears; "in an instant" clarifies the moment the light appears; "there was a great radiance" indicates the actual manifestation of the light; and the phrase "not blue" and those following reveal the specific characteristics of the light.

The Bodhisattva Vaidūrya emits from within his body—the body of the realization of equality—the light of the Āgamas, enabling people to behold it; therefore, the great assembly perceives blue though it was not blue, and so on, perceiving that which was not seen.
"The great assembly transcends light, their bodies and minds are joyful" clarifies the benefit of the light, first through the Dharma and subsequently through an analogy.
Question:
For what reason does the emission of boundless light cause this assembly to feel fear, while the emission of light from the lapis lazuli causes this assembly to feel joy?
This is because the Buddha’s transformations differ according to what is appropriate for those being converted. How do they differ?

To manifest that the Sage has entered extinction for the sake of boundless future generations, he desires to cause this assembly to perceive the world as unstable, thereby inducing fear in the multitude.

As for this light emitted by the lapis lazuli now, it is intended to manifest the Dharma so that the multitudes may realize and enter it; because a supreme benefit is about to arrive, it causes the assembly to rejoice.
From here on is the second section, which distinguishes the source of the light, and the text is divided into two parts:

first, clarifying that this light issues from within the realization of equality; second, clarifying from the perspective of its transformative appearance that it comes from the side of the lapis lazuli in the east.

Regarding the preceding section, the first part initially employs silence to manifest quiescence; from "At that time, the World-Honored One questioned Mañjuśrī" onwards, words are used to reveal reality.

Within the initial section employing silence, Mañjuśrī first poses a question, but the Buddha remains silent and does not answer as to where the light comes from. Because it is quiescent and beyond words, he manifests it through silence.
The Buddha’s realization is profoundly deep; thus, he first manifested [the truth] through silence, and Mañjuśrī attained awakening to the meaning of quiescence from the Buddha.
Therefore, next, Kāśyapa asked a second time, but Mañjuśrī did not answer; Kāśyapa then again attained awakening to it from Mañjuśrī.
Therefore, next, Anantamati asked a third time, but Kāśyapa did not answer; Anantamati then again attained awakening to it from Kāśyapa.
Therefore, when the King of Pure Abodes asked his fourth question, Anantamati did not answer;
since this was a realization shared by all the noble ones, even after five hundred such inquiries, he remained silent and did not respond.
To manifest the Middle Way through words, the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata first questioned Mañjuśrī" elaborates upon this through seven statements.
The first six statements reveal reality by means of reality itself, clarifying that there are no causes or conditions.

The final phrase clarifies the reality through its phenomenal aspects, demonstrating that there are causes and conditions: because one attains the lamp of Bodhi by extinguishing ignorance, this light exists.
What precedes has clarified reality; what follows distinguishes the transformative [teaching].
Within this, the Tathāgata first instructs that one must not enter the primary [truth], and it should be explained by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
From the passage beginning "Mañjuśrī," the following is distinguished, which contains three parts:
first, this clarifies that matter; second, that clarifies this matter; third, the concluding response to the Tathāgata.
This section clarifies that within it, there are four distinct parts:

first, clarifying the matters concerning the people of that land; second, clarifying the master of that transformation; third, from "Wherever they dwell" onwards, clarifying that what was taught therein is no different from this; and fourth, from "Vaidūryanirbhāsa asks Pūrṇacandraprabha" onwards, clarifying that the questions asked therein are no different from these.
Within this section, there are five distinct textual divisions: first, the description of the affairs of the people of this world by the Buddha Candraprabha;

second, the description of the presiding teacher of this [assembly]; third, from "Great Compassion and Purity" onwards, the description that what is being taught here is no different from that [previous assembly]; fourth, from "There is a bodhisattva there named Prabhāsa" onwards, the description that the questions asked here are not different from those [previously asked]; and fifth, from "The Buddha now answers" onwards, the account of his exhortation to Vairocana to come to this place.
Question:
For what reason does this [text] not exhort one toward that?
There are five reasons for this explanation:

First, because the sentient beings of that land have past causal conditions with this Buddha, they are exhorted to come here; whereas these beings do not necessarily have such conditions with him, and thus he does not exhort them to go there.

Second, because it is appropriate for the sentient beings of this land to see those beings come to request the Dharma and thereby obtain benefit, they are exhorted to come here; whereas it is not necessarily appropriate for those beings to be here, and thus he does not exhort them to go there.

Third, he wishes to cause those bodhisattvas to come and lead these beings to be born in the Pure Land, so that the benefit of their transformation may be vast; therefore, he exhorts them to come here, as there would be no such benefit if these beings were to go there.

Fourth, because he wishes for those newly practicing bodhisattvas to come to this evil world to increase their compassionate vows, he exhorts them to come; since there would be no such benefit for this assembly if they were to go there, he does not exhort them to go.
Fifth, if King Śīla had been able to provide spiritual benefit there, the Buddha would have exhorted him to go; however, as this was not the case, it is not discussed here.
"Regarding 'That Vaiḍūrya' below, this is the third section; Mañjuśrī brings forth that Vaiḍūrya to provide a concluding response to the Tathāgata.
This concludes the second [section].
As for the third major section, it can be understood that the Vaiḍūrya arrives to make offerings to the Buddha."
From here below is the fourth section of questions and answers, which dispels the characteristics of coming and going.
The Buddha first poses a test question: "Does that which has already arrived come, or does that which has not yet arrived come?"

In the response below, first the absence of coming is clarified with respect to the body; next it is distinguished with respect to phenomena (*dharma*); finally, it is revealed through the mind, showing that because all faults have been exhausted, there is no coming.
Regarding the opening statement, "World-Honored One, neither having arrived does one come, nor not having arrived does one come," there are two interpretations:

first, it is explained in terms of the impermanence of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Reaching this [state] is called "having arrived," while perishing along the way is called "not having arrived."
Regarding those who have arrived, they are newly born in this place and do not come from elsewhere; therefore, they are not called "coming.
Regarding those who have not arrived, they perish while still on the road and do not reach this place; therefore, they also do not "come."

Second, this is explained from the perspective of the permanence of the true body (*dharmakāya*): as for whether the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has arrived or not, it has never moved from its original state of true, eternal quiescence; therefore, it does not come at all.

"I observe that this principle has no coming at all"—this serves as the general conclusion. Since both "arriving" and "not arriving" are equally without coming, it is said to be "entirely non-existent. Next, distinguishing by way of phenomena (*dharma*):

"If conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) were permanent, they would not come," which is explained in the same manner as follows; "If they were impermanent, there would likewise be no coming," which is explained as previously stated. Here, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are designated as "conditioned formations."
The following section clarifies the meaning through the mind, consisting of eight distinct phrases.

The first three remove the faults of ordinary beings; thus, there is no coming or going. The first removes the view of self, the next removes arrogance, and the last removes grasping at formations—or, alternatively, the grasping at the two [views of] self is termed grasping at formations.

The latter five remove the faults of the two vehicles: the first two and the last one are faults of being deluded regarding the Great Vehicle, while the middle two phrases are faults of clinging to the Lesser Vehicle.
From here below is the fifth section, the analysis through question and answer regarding the Dharma. This section contains two parts:
first, the desire to inquire and request permission to listen, which is granted by the Tathāgata; second, the actual inquiry by Vimalakīrti, to which the Tathāgata provides the analysis.
In the first part of the preceding section, Vimalakīrti first wishes to inquire;

he requests the Buddha’s permission by saying, "Set this matter aside. He says "set it aside" to suspend the previous discussion on the meaning of neither coming nor going, as its explanation would be inexhaustible. By saying "I wish to ask something," he expresses his own intention; with the words "only grant your compassionate favor," he requests the Buddha’s consent to listen.

The Buddha granted his permission, saying: "Ask as you wish" means he truly permitted the questioning; "Now is the very time" urges them to ask quickly; and from "I shall... onwards, he grants his consent to explain it later.
The following section provides an explanation: "Therefore," I say that now is precisely the right time, because a Buddha is difficult to encounter and the Dharma is difficult to hear.
"Buddhas are difficult to encounter, like the Udumbara flower"—this refers to the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
“The Dharma is likewise difficult to hear,” and so forth; this means that the Dharma is difficult to hear.
Within this, it first clarifies that even the minor teachings are difficult to hear—just as the Buddha is difficult to encounter—and for this reason, the word “likewise” (*api*) is used.
"The Vaipulya among the twelve divisions of scripture is even more difficult [to encounter]" clarifies that it is extremely rare to hear.
From "For this reason" onwards, there is a summary exhortation to listen with single-minded devotion.
Within the Tathāgata’s response to Vairocana’s formal inquiry, the text is divided into two parts:
First, Vimalakīrti himself asked about hearing and not hearing, and the Tathāgata explained it;
second, Vimalakīrti asked on behalf of others about arising and non-arising, and the Tathāgata elucidated it.
How is this known?
The subsequent text clarifies it itself.

Thus, in the section on Vairocana’s realization, it says: "I have received from the Buddha the explanation of 'hearing' and 'not hearing,'" which shows that hearing and not hearing pertain exclusively to oneself; and "furthermore, causing eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to know 'arising' and 'non-arising,'" which clarifies that arising and non-arising pertain exclusively to others.
Question:
Why is it that hearing and not hearing pertain exclusively to oneself, while birth and non-birth pertain exclusively to others? Answer:
When hearing and not hearing are analyzed in relation to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), their meaning is profound and deep; therefore, they pertain exclusively to oneself.

The distinction between "arising" and "non-arising" clarifies the characteristics of the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because its meaning is coarse and proximate, it is taught predominantly for the sake of others.

In reality, there is nothing among the questions asked that is not for the sake of others; however, this distinction is made to differentiate between the practices of self-benefit and benefit for others.

Question: Since both the equal and the differentiated practices exist, for what reason does one not first practice for the sake of others? There are three reasons for this explanation: 1. One’s own roots of goodness are not yet firm; if one were to teach others first, they would become discouraged and lose heart. 2. If one’s own afflictions have not been severed, one will be unable to sever the afflictions of others. 3. If one has not attained the various stages of realization (bhūmi), one cannot lead others to attain them. For these reasons, one must first cultivate oneself before benefiting others. Furthermore, if one were to benefit others first, one would fall into the error of seeking fame and profit, which would cause one to regress from the path. Therefore, it is said that one should first practice for oneself and only then for others. This is why the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "One who wishes to save all sentient beings must first discipline themselves. Thus, the sequence of self-benefit followed by the benefit of others is established. This is the first meaning. Furthermore, there is a second meaning: although the Buddha’s compassion is impartial toward all sentient beings, he did not manifest his appearance in the world during the era of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) because at that time, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties and great wisdom, and could achieve liberation through their own power. Consequently, the Buddha remained in the Tuṣita Heaven and did not descend to appear in the world. It was only during the era of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) that he manifested his appearance. This is because during the Semblance Dharma, sentient beings’ faculties were dull and their wisdom weak; they required the guidance of a teacher to achieve liberation. Therefore, the Buddha appeared in the world to guide them. This is the second meaning. Furthermore, there is a third meaning: the Buddha’s original vow was to bring all sentient beings to ultimate liberation. However, if he had manifested his appearance during the era of the True Dharma, sentient beings would have been liberated so swiftly that the Buddha’s vow would have been fulfilled prematurely. To ensure that his vow would be fully realized, he waited until the era of the Semblance Dharma to manifest his appearance. This is the third meaning. For these reasons, it is said that one should first practice for oneself and only then for others. This is the third meaning. First, regarding the sequence of practice: one must first practice for oneself before being able to benefit others; therefore, one acts for oneself first. Second, regarding what has been heard or not heard:
the Bodhisattva Vaidūrya previously inquired about this in his own land, and now, responding to that request, he asks first.
Third, regarding what has been heard or not heard as the fundamental substance of the initial virtue: because it relies upon what was established above, he asks about it first.

Question: If it is said that the sequence for initiating practice must first be for oneself, why did the Tathāgata, in his instructions to King Vairāṭa, advise first acting for others and only later for oneself?
The commentary states:

The generation of the mind and the initiation of practice are distinct. If one discusses the generation of the mind, it must first be for the sake of others, because compassion is the foundation of all practices.
Regarding the arousal of practice, one must first cultivate it for oneself before benefiting others.
The former refers to the arousal of the mind, while this refers to the arousal of practice; therefore, they are distinct and not the same.

Within the first section, Vimalakīrti was the first to request [instruction]; thus, the narrator (the *sūtrakāra*) sequences the events as follows: having "received permission and been further exhorted" by the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s previous words, "Ask whatever you wish," constitute the granting of permission; the subsequent words, "Therefore, you should receive this with a focused mind," constitute the exhortation.
He then said, "How does one hear what has not been heard? This is precisely the request. The Buddha’s response consists of four parts:

first, praising his excellent question and clarifying that he is already capable of answering; second, commanding him to listen and granting permission to speak; third, instructing on the meaning of listening; and fourth, providing the correct explanation in accordance with the question.
At the beginning, "Excellent" (*sādhu*) is a term of praise; "you now wish," etc., clarifies that he is already capable of answering.
Within this, there are six phrases:
the first four clarify that he already possesses the capacity for such discourse; the next one indicates his intention; and the last one indicates the Dharma.
Regarding the first four [points]: "You wish to exhaust the ocean" cites what he seeks; from "It happens to coincide with... onwards, it clarifies that [the Buddha] is already able to explain it.
"You have the barb of doubt" cites his affliction; "I am the physician," etc., clarifies that [the Buddha] is already able to treat it.
"You [are confused] regarding the Buddha," etc., cites his delusion; "I possess wisdom," etc., clarifies that [the Buddha] is already able to show him the way.
"‘You wish to cross,’ and so forth, cites what [the other] has set out to do; ‘I am able to do it,’ and so forth, clarifies that one is already capable of transporting them.
To clarify the state of mind, ‘You [are dear] to me,’ and so forth, cites their affection; ‘I [am compassionate] toward you,’ and so forth, reveals one’s own loving-kindness."

Within the section clarifying the existence of the Dharma: "You covet the treasure of the Dharma" identifies what is required; "It has already been obtained by me," etc., clarifies that he is already able to bestow it.
In the second exhortation: first there is the exhortation, then the granting of permission, and finally the instruction to listen attentively, which serves to solemnly rouse his mind.
In the third teaching, there is first a detailed exposition and subsequently a summary.
Within the detailed exposition, there are twenty-one phrases, which, when grouped according to their characteristics, form three sections:

first, eight phrases that teach the departure from the ordinary mind; second, seven that teach the relinquishing of the mind of the two vehicles; and last, six that teach the cultivation of the bodhisattva mind.

Regarding the instruction to depart from the mundane, the first—“hearing the Dharma with reverent faith”—instructs one to depart from doubt and slander; the second—“listening and receiving it with a sincere mind”—instructs one to depart from laxity and indolence; the third—“revering and honoring it”—instructs one to depart from treating it as trivial or inferior; the fourth—from “toward the True Dharma” downward—instructs one to depart from hatred and aversion; the fifth—from “do not harbor thoughts of greed” downward—instructs one to depart from a defiled mind; the sixth—from “do not look upon [it with disdain]” downward—instructs one to depart from a mind of resentment; the seventh—from “having heard the Dharma” downward—instructs one to depart from a mind of pride; the eighth—from “do not act for oneself” downward—instructs one to depart from a mind of deluded thoughts and seeking after other things.
Next, regarding the seven teachings that depart from the mind of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), the first four teachings depart from the narrow-mindedness of the Two Vehicles:

"Furthermore, do not give rise to the thought: 'Having heard the Dharma, I shall first deliver myself and only thereafter deliver others. This refers to the narrowness within [the realm of] suffering.
The preceding teachings departed from the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) while simultaneously exhorting the abandonment of the Small Vehicle; therefore, it says, "Furthermore, do not."
"To first liberate oneself and then liberate others" is narrowness within concentration;
"to first settle oneself and then settle others" is narrowness within the Path;
"to first attain nirvana for oneself and then cause others to do so" is narrowness within cessation.
The latter three teachings depart from the narrow-mindedness of the two vehicles:
by teaching that "one should conceive of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha with equanimity," they instruct one to abandon the mind of partiality;

by teaching that "one should conceive of birth and death as great suffering," they instruct one to abandon the mind of attachment—recognizing that even the birth and death of the transformation realm is truly great suffering, and not regarding it as pleasure to become attached to it therein.
The teaching that "one should conceive of Great Nirvana as permanent" and so forth is intended to eliminate perverted thoughts.

Within the subsequent six teachings for cultivating the bodhisattva mind, the first is the teaching to cultivate a broad mind for the sake of others, which is also called the teaching to cultivate the mind that keeps sentient beings in mind;

the [second] is the teaching that "you should aim for the Mahāyāna and not the Two Vehicles," which is the teaching to cultivate a great mind, also called the teaching to cultivate the mind seeking the Buddha's wisdom.
The final four lines teach the cultivation of the profound mind, which is also called teaching the cultivation of a mind detached from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Within these, the first two teach detachment from views: "one should not dwell on any phenomena" means not dwelling in non-existence;
"nor should one exclusively cling to the characteristics of any phenomena" means not clinging to existence.
"Do not covet dharmas" teaches the abandonment of the mind of attachment; "always give rise to the mind that knows and sees the Dharma" teaches the abandonment of the mind of delusion.
"If one can thus [regard] fame as neither heard nor unheard" summarizes and manifests the benefits.

From here below is the fourth section, the correct explanation in response to the questions. First, the meaning of "hearing" and "not hearing" is explained; subsequently, it is clarified by categorizing them through their arising.
Within the first part, there are four propositions; what is their distinction?
According to the method explained below, there are two kinds of dharmas:
first, the dharma of birth and death that can be heard; second, the dharma of nirvana that transcends hearing.
There are likewise two kinds of persons:
There are two types: the ordinary person and the noble one.
Taking the ordinary person and the noble one in relation to that *nirvāṇa*, the first two phrases are as follows:

the noble one is able to hear and receive the Dharma not previously heard regarding *nirvāṇa*, which is termed "hearing what was not heard"; the ordinary person is unable to hear and receive the Dharma not previously heard regarding *nirvāṇa*, which is termed "not hearing what was not heard."
The ordinary person and the sage are contrasted with respect to birth and death to form the latter two phrases:

the sage, regarding the teachings that can be heard within birth and death, no longer consumes or receives them—this is called "not hearing what is heard"; the ordinary person, regarding the teachings that can be heard within birth and death, consumes and receives them without ceasing—hence it is called "hearing what is heard."

Among these four [statements], the first sentence directly answers the preceding question; the second is included to illustrate the noble by means of the ordinary; and the third and fourth are included to illustrate the pure by means of the defiled.
Within the latter category, there are four sets of propositions each regarding that which is born first and that which arrives later; these will be explained in the text below.

Second, from this point on, Vaidūrya himself asks about birth and non-birth from the perspective of the former, requesting the Buddha to provide an explanation so that the newly arrived bodhisattvas may understand.
Regarding the phrase "whether they arrive or not," the following answers King Devarāja.
Among the initial questions, the Buddha himself provided an extensive explanation, which will not be discussed here.
This section contains four parts:
There are four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the objection;
and fourth, the resolution. "World-Honored One!

How is it that there is no arising of what has not yet arisen?"—this is the initial question. Although, according to the preceding four propositions, all should have been questioned together, [the text] mentions only the beginning for the sake of brevity.
In the second response, first the internal [perspective] is addressed, followed by the external.
Sentient beings constitute the internal, while insentient things constitute the external.
Within the internal, there is first an explanation and subsequently a summary.

In the commentary, the initial statement, "Abiding in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), at the time of first emerging from the womb, it is called 'the birth of the unborn'," explains the first phrase [of the verse].

One is said to "abide in the world" because one undergoes birth only within the conventional truth; furthermore, because one receives a body that does not perish within the conventional truth, this is also termed "abiding in the world."
At the moment of first emerging from the womb, one correctly understands the meaning of "arising. Here, "first" excludes what follows, and "emerging from the womb" differs from what preceded it.

The phrase "This is called" below serves as a conclusion: when originally not yet born, it is termed "non-arising"; at the time of emergence, it is termed "arising"; when these preceding and succeeding states are spoken of together, it is termed "the non-arising of arising."

Regarding the question "What is non-arising non-arising? which refers to the second phrase: "This Great Nirvana has the characteristic of no-birth" means that the essence of nirvana is quiescent, which is the first non-arising; furthermore, that it is not produced by the characteristics of arising is the second non-arising.
The section beginning with "This is called" serves as a conclusion; herein, it is not intended to clarify the dharma of nirvāṇa.

Rather, by means of the dharma of nirvāṇa, it clarifies that the body of saṃsāra is neither-arising-nor-non-arising; one must attain nirvāṇa before one can truly be said to be neither-arising-nor-non-arising, and thus this is discussed in relation to that.

"How is it that birth is non-birth? asks the third phrase. "At the time of death according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)" explains and clarifies its characteristic. This refers to the present retribution as conventional truth; conventional truth is birth, while death is termed non-birth. The section beginning with "This is called" concludes [the explanation].
"What is 'birth of birth'? This asks about the fourth phrase. Below, there are four parts to the explanation:

first, a general indication regarding persons: "All ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are called 'birth of birth'. This refers specifically to ordinary worldlings because the births of noble ones (*ārya*) do not continue in succession.

Second, the section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation, first posing a question and then resolving it. The phrase "the arising of arising is uninterrupted" explains the meaning of "arising of arising" in terms of the impermanence of the segmented [birth-and-death]. The phrase "all contaminated phenomena arise moment by moment" explains the meaning of "arising of arising" in terms of the impermanence of moments. The section beginning with "This is called" concludes the explanation.

Third, from "the Bodhisattva of the Fourth Abode" downwards, the noble is contrasted with the ordinary. Because the Bodhisattva of the Fourth Abode is called "arising yet non-arising," the ordinary is called "arising and arising. The Bodhisattva of the *Yan* stage is termed the "Fourth Abode. Within the mutual entry of the stages (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa-praveśa*), those from the third stage downwards are called "worldly," while those from the fourth stage upwards are called "transcendent. The Bodhisattva of the Fourth Abode abandons that worldliness and realizes entry into transcendence; this wisdom of non-arising practice is called "arising yet non-arising."

4. From "Why" onwards, the meaning of the arising and non-arising of those four dwellings is explained; first there is a question, followed by the explanation. Because one has attained mastery over the elimination and severance of arising, that which was originally born does not arise again now. From "This is called" onwards is the conclusion: this is called the internal dharma.

Subsequently, regarding the external dharmas, he first asks about their origination: "How is it that external dharmas have not yet arisen? asks about the first phrase; "non-arising and non-arising" asks about the second phrase; "arising and non-arising" asks about the third phrase; and saying "arising and arising" asks about the fourth phrase.

The subsequent section explains their characteristics: within the resolution of the first question, the phrase "like a seed not yet produced" explains the meaning of "not yet produced," while "attaining the four great elements" and so forth explain the meaning of its "production"; the section beginning with "this is called" concludes the explanation.

In explaining the second [category], first the question is posed and then it is explained: "For example, like a rotten seed" explains the former type of non-arising; "and not having encountered conditions" explains the latter type of non-arising; "such as these" cites this to include other similar cases; and "is called 'non-arisen'" concludes the section.

Regarding the third [section], first the question is posed and then it is explained: "Just as a sprout grows" explains the meaning of initial arising; "does not increase" explains the subsequent state of non-arising; the phrase "this is called" concludes [the section].

Regarding the fourth phrase, first a question is posed and then it is explained: "Just as a sprout grows" correctly explains the arising of arising (*jātijāti*); "If there were no arising, there would be no growth" cites non-arising to clarify the aforementioned arising of arising; the meaning is similar to what precedes. "In this way, all such [cases]" extends this category to other instances; "this is called" and below concludes the section.
Question: For what reason are these four meanings explained by means of internal and external phenomena?
It is to demonstrate that the meaning of all dharmas is not fixed or partial; because they are neither fixed nor partial, all things can be empty.

"Under 'Lapis Lazuli White,' the third section presents a critique consisting of six statements. The first two statements challenge the claim that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena arise moment by moment.
What was previously hidden that necessitates this challenge?"
The commentary states:

It was previously explained that the essence of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) arises moment by moment; however, the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) external to the phenomenon itself had not yet been distinguished. Therefore, this objection is raised to prompt the Buddha to provide an explanation.
The latter four objections concern the meaning of the four propositions regarding "arising from non-arising" and so forth mentioned above.
Why were they not fully addressed previously, such that they must be raised again as objections?

The previous section explained by means of coarse phenomena concerning internal and external matters, but did not yet analyze them in relation to the dharma of "arising. Therefore, these objections are raised again to compel the Buddha to provide an analysis.

Regarding the initial statement in the first section, "If there are conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that arise," this refers back to the previously mentioned *sāsrava* phenomena to cite the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). This citation of the characteristic of arising external to those phenomena—rather than the arising of the essence of the phenomena themselves—is intended to formulate a challenge; it is cited so as to definitively examine [the position] through the dialectic of whether [these phenomena] are permanent (*nitya*) or impermanent (*anitya*).
Below, the objection is set forth and analyzed in five points: first, the determination of the nature of dharmas;

second, the definition of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) based on those dharmas. Regarding the four characteristics, there are two types: 1. Determining the nature of dharmas: Form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and that which is neither form nor mind (*arūpacittaviprayukta*) constitute contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas.
2. Distinguishing the meaning of the four characteristics with respect to the aforementioned dharmas. There are two [types of] four characteristics:

First, the four characteristics of the essence of a single dharma: within every moment of dharmas such as form and mind, there are each four characteristics—initial arising, subsequent abiding, final alteration, and ultimate cessation.
Second, the four external characteristics of dharmas: simultaneously and separately from the dharmas such as form, there are the four characteristics of arising and so forth.

In general, there are four characteristics, which when subdivided, become eight; namely, the four primary characteristics and the four secondary characteristics, also called the "minor characteristics. At the limit of the arising of each primary characteristic, there is one minor arising, and likewise, at the limit of its cessation, there is one minor cessation.

Because the four preceding characteristics are broad and extensive, they are termed "great"; because the latter four characteristics are narrow and limited in their function, they are termed "small. These eight characteristics are spoken of as four, and these four characteristics are named according to their functional capacity.

Regarding what is called "arising" (*jāti*): it is so named because it can cause others to arise; it is not an arising that begins only after the stage of abiding (*sthiti*). Likewise, regarding the characteristic of "cessation" (*nirodha*): it is so named because it can cause others to cease; it is not a cessation that occurs as total destruction following the stage of change (*anyathātva*). When analyzed according to their essential nature (*svabhāva*), all eight [conditioned characteristics] are present.

There is arising first, followed by abiding, then change at the end, and finally cessation; such are the four characteristics. Now, this discussion specifically addresses the meaning of arising with respect to the four characteristics external to the dharma itself.

Third, regarding the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), one clarifies permanence and impermanence: it should be understood that this arising is both permanent and impermanent, as explained in the following passage.
Within the delimitation of phenomena, this arising is eternally present at the limits of dharmas such as form (*rūpa*); therefore, it is called "permanent."
Regarding the demarcation of phenomena (*dharmapradeśa*), this characteristic of arising (*utpādalakṣaṇa*) arises and perishes moment by moment; once something has passed away, it does not reappear.

Therefore, it is called "impermanent" (*anitya*). Fourth, the purpose of the objection: Vimalakīrti now asks the Tathāgata to explain the meanings of permanence and impermanence, as well as existence and non-existence, based on the principle of arising, so that the newly arrived bodhisattvas may understand them; thus, he raises a counter-objection.

Fifth, the word-by-word commentary first challenges the meaning of permanence: "If birth were permanent" cites what was previously established; "then dharmas with outflows would have no birth" refutes this by means of the dharma itself. Since dharmas with outflows are impermanent, how could there be a permanently abiding birth within the realm of impermanent dharmas?
Since that which exists within the limits of the outflows (*sāsrava*) is clearly known to be impermanent, the following objection challenges this impermanence:

"If arising were impermanent"—this restates what was previously established. Because once something has arisen and passed away, it never returns, it is called impermanent. The statement "then the outflows would be permanent" is a refutation by means of a logical dilemma regarding the nature of phenomena.

If birth were impermanent, once it had arisen and passed away, it would never return; thus, at the limit of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), there would be no further birth. That which is without birth and does not undergo transformation would be permanent; yet, the nature of contaminated phenomena is impermanent, as they are constantly accompanied by the characteristic of birth and undergo transformation. Therefore, it is clear that the characteristic of birth is itself not impermanent.

Among the latter four objections, the first objection concerns the meaning of "the arising of arising"; the second objection concerns the meaning of "the non-arising of arising"; the third objection concerns the meaning of "the arising of non-arising"; and the fourth objection concerns the meaning of "the non-arising of non-arising."
This raises an objection regarding the relative nature of the factors about to arise: for what reason does it not follow the previous order?

It is because the first two pairs concern the relative relationship between self and other, while the latter two concern the relative relationship between existence and non-existence during childhood; thus, following this convenience, it does not follow the previous order.

Regarding the first two [positions], the first sentence raises an objection specifically concerning the capacity to produce, while the latter sentence raises an objection in relation to that which is produced.
What is the first objection?

If that characteristic of production (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) could produce itself, it might be called "the production of production" (*utpādasyotpāda*); however, since production does not produce itself, how can it be designated as "the production of production"?
The meaning of the objection is as follows:

However, that characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is only able to produce dharmas such as matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), but it cannot produce itself; therefore, [the opponent] now raises this counter-argument.
[The author] refutes it with reasoning: "If arising were to arise by itself, then arising would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which it could arise, then it could be said to arise;
but since arising has no intrinsic nature, how could it arise of itself?
Question:

Previously, it was stated that apart from the limits of dharmas such as form (*rūpa*), there exists a distinct characteristic of arising that is neither form nor mind. How, then, can it now be said that arising lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
The explanation is as follows:
this characteristic is defined as the "ariser. Apart from this ariser, there is no further intrinsic nature of a dharma that is "arisen"; therefore, it is said to be non-existent.
What is the second [point]?
If that characteristic of arising were able to produce other non-arising phenomena, the Tathāgata could say it is "arising yet non-arising.
Since it cannot produce other non-arising phenomena, how can it be called "arising yet non-arising"?
The meaning of the objection is as follows:

however, that characteristic of arising can only produce those dharmas that arise simultaneously with it and are capable of being produced; it cannot produce other dharmas that are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), untainted (*anāsrava*), or incapable of being produced. Therefore, this [objection] is now raised by way of counter-argument.
"If it can produce another, by what cause and condition does it not produce the untainted (*anāsrava*)?"—this is a refutation by means of reasoning.
"If it can produce another, by what cause and condition does it not produce unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted phenomena?"
Because it cannot arise, it is neither arising nor non-arising.

Regarding the latter two [of the four alternatives], the first phrase refutes the existence of arising by focusing on the time prior to its arising, while the subsequent phrase refutes the non-existence of arising by focusing on the time prior to its arising.
What is the meaning of the first statement?
If that which has not yet arisen already possessed its arising, then the Tathāgata could speak of "the non-arising of arising.
Since that which has not yet arisen cannot possess arising, how could the Tathāgata speak of "the non-arising of arising"?

The meaning of the objection is as follows: When dharmas such as form arise, they are called "birth"; when they have not yet arisen, they cannot be called "birth. Therefore, [the opponent] now raises a counter-objection:

"If there is birth even when [a dharma] has not yet arisen, why is it only at this present moment of arising that it is called 'birth'? This is refuted by reasoning: if birth already existed previously when [the dharma] had not yet arisen, why would it only be designated as "birth" at this present time of manifestation?
What is the meaning of the latter phrase?
If, prior to arising, there were absolutely no nature of arising, then the Tathāgata could say "non-arising and non-arising.
But if the nature of arising already existed at the time before arising, why does the Buddha say "non-arising and non-arising"?
The intent of the objection is as follows:

although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) do not yet possess the actual event of arising when they have not yet arisen, they nonetheless already possess the nature of arising (*utpattidharmatā*). Therefore, the opponent now raises a counter-objection based on logic:
"If that which has not yet arisen lacks arising, why is space (*ākāśa*) not also said to arise? Thus, he refutes [the position] through reasoning.

If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) were originally devoid of the nature of arising yet subsequently attained birth, then since space (*ākāśa*) is likewise originally devoid of the nature of arising, why does it not arise?
That space does not arise may be because it was originally without the nature of arising;
however, that conditioned phenomena can arise clearly demonstrates that they originally possessed the nature of arising.

Because they have arisen from their own source, they are not "non-arising" in the sense of being unarisen. From this point downward is the fourth section, in which the Tathāgata provides an explanatory clarification. He begins by praising the question with "Excellent," followed by the formal exposition, which consists of four distinct parts:

first, reiterating the previous six difficulties to clarify that what is ineffable serves to dispel people's fixed attachments; second, from "There are causes and conditions" onward, clarifying that what was previously said to be expressible is intended to lead people toward understanding; third, from "How is it that non-arising arises? onward, explaining the meaning of the first point regarding ineffability; and fourth, from "How can there be causes and yet it be expressible? onward, explaining the meaning of the second point regarding expressibility.
Within the first section, the statement "the non-arising of arising is ineffable" reiterates the fifth objection raised by Vairocana, clarifying its ineffability;
the statement "the arising of arising is ineffable" reiterates the third objection raised by Vairocana, clarifying its ineffability;
and the statement "the arising of non-arising is ineffable" reiterates the fourth objection raised by Vairocana, clarifying its ineffability.
"Non-arising is unspeakable" reiterates the sixth objection raised by Vairocana above, clarifying that it is unspeakable;
"arising is unspeakable" clarifies the first objection raised by Vairocana previously, that constant arising cannot be definitively described;

and the statement "non-arising is unspeakable" clarifies the second objection raised by Vairocana previously, that after the characteristic of arising has ceased, there is an absolute absence of arising within the realm of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), and thus it cannot be definitively described.
All of these cannot be definitively explained; thus they are called "inexplicable," yet this does not mean they are entirely unspoken. Question:
For what reason are these six propositions clarified as all being inexplicable?
To reveal that the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*) is not fixed or partial, and because it is not fixed or partial, the six meanings are fully present.
What is this meaning?
Because "non-arising arising" cannot be fixed, there is the meaning of "arising arising."
What is the meaning of this?

The latter refutes the former by means of subsequent arising, clarifying that conditioned phenomena possess the nature of being able to arise before they have arisen; thus, it cannot be definitively stated that they are non-arising.

Because it is not the case that [the primary arising] does not arise, when that characteristic of arising brings about such producible phenomena as these, it is then designated as "arising of the producible"; therefore, the principle of the "arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) is established.
Because that which arises and arises cannot be definitively established, there is the sense of "arising" and "non-arising.
What is the meaning of this?

Below, by refuting subsequent arising through the lens of initial arising, it is clarified that conditioned phenomena are designated as "arising" because they are produced by the characteristics of being produced by others; their essential nature, however, is not arising.

Because its essence is not produced, when that characteristic of production brings forth this dharma, it is termed "producing the unproduced"; thus, the meaning of producing the unproduced is established.
Because arising and non-arising cannot be definitively asserted, there are the principles of "arising from arising" and "non-arising from non-arising.
What is the meaning of this?

Below, the initial arising refutes the subsequent non-arising, clarifying that conditioned phenomena are produced by the characteristics of being produced by another; therefore, their essence is not non-arising.

It is not because [the primary arising] does not arise; rather, when that characteristic of arising gives rise to this dharma, it is termed "arising-of-arising. Therefore, the principle of the arising-of-arising is established.

In the subsequent passage, the latter phrase "non-arising" refutes the initial arising, clarifying that while the characteristic of initial arising is called "arising" because it can produce form and other non-arisen dharmas, its essential nature is not itself arising.

The nature of that which gives rise and that which is given rise to are both non-arising; thus it is termed "non-arising and non-non-arising. Therefore, the meaning of "non-arising and non-non-arising" is established.
Because "non-arising and non-non-arising" cannot be expressed in words, there is the meaning of "arising from non-arising."
What is the meaning of this?
It is because it will be explained below that even the dharma of non-arising, which is nirvāṇa, possesses arising; thus, the dharma of non-arising can have the sense of arising.
Since this is the case for nirvāṇa, it is the same for other dharmas; therefore, there exists the principle of "non-arising arising."
Furthermore, because the meaning of arising is not fixed or exclusive, there is the meaning of non-arising; and because non-arising is not fixed, there is the meaning of arising.
Question: For what reason are these six meanings established?
This is to clarify that the meaning of all phenomena is not fixed or partial; because they are not fixed, all things can be empty.
In the second section, the phrase "because there are causes and conditions, they may also be spoken of" clarifies that all six [categories] may be spoken of by virtue of causes and conditions.
What is the meaning of this?

The characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), which exists apart from the dharmas themselves, is able to give rise to the dharmas that are subject to arising, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; therefore, the principle of "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*) is established. Thus, while those [dharmas] such as form possess the essence of being produced, they are not themselves called the "characteristic of arising," and are therefore termed "non-arising."

When characteristics arise outside of phenomena, they give rise to this form and so forth; these are not phenomena that arise, and are thus called "arising of non-arising. Since the nature of arising already exists even before they have arisen, it is therefore possible for there to be the principle of "the arising of non-arising."
Before they have arisen, there is no event of arising; therefore, there is the sense of "non-arising of non-arising.

Within the limits of phenomena (*vastu*), the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is constantly present at the periphery of dharmas such as form (*rūpa*); therefore, there is the sense of "arising.

Within the limits of the dharma-nature (*dharma-tattva*), each moment arises and ceases; once something has passed away, there is no principle by which it could return. Therefore, the sense of "non-arising" is established.
In the third section, the preceding six phrases are explained in their respective order.

Regarding the question, "Why is 'non-arising arising' unspeakable?", this restates the first phrase; the subsequent portion explains its characteristics by specifically using subsequent arising to refute initial non-arising, thereby establishing that it is unspeakable.
The term "non-arising" refers back to the initial non-arising, while "called arising" refers to subsequent arising.
Since there is the sense of being capable of arising at the time of non-arising, how can it be definitively stated?
The term "non-arising" is reiterated below for emphasis; "for what reason? is the question.
As for "because of arising," since there is that which can arise, one cannot categorically state that it does not arise.

Regarding the phrase "Why is the arising of arising unspeakable?": this restates the second question; what follows explains its characteristics, showing that because the prior characteristic of arising subverts the subsequent formation of dharmas, it is unspeakable.

"Because arising arises, there is arising" clarifies that the former gives rise to the latter. The first instance of the word "arising" (生) cites the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); the subsequent statement "that which arises" clarifies that the aforementioned characteristic of arising is capable of producing all phenomena; and the phrase "therefore it arises" demonstrates that those phenomena only come into existence because they are produced by that [characteristic].

"Because arising arises, there is no arising" means that the former negates the latter; since conditioned phenomena arise only through the arising of those [conditions], they lack a fixed nature of arising, and thus it is said they do not arise.
Regarding "ineffable": because it is unarisen, its arising cannot be spoken of.
Furthermore, both the prior and subsequent arisings are refuted; since there is the arising of arising, this arising refutes the prior arising.

The preceding moment arises and gives rise to all phenomena; therefore, it is called "arising," yet its own essence is not arising. Because it is not arising, it does not arise, thereby refuting subsequent arising.
The succeeding phenomenon arises as an arising for the sake of another; therefore, it is called "arising," yet its own essence is not arising.
Regarding "that which is inexpressible," both the preceding and succeeding births are inexpressible.
The phrase "Why is it that birth and non-birth are inexpressible? restates the third question.
The statement "arising is precisely what is called arising" refutes the latter by means of the former;
for since that which arises is precisely what is called arising, it is not definitively non-arising.
The statement "arising does not arise from itself" refutes the former by means of the latter.
The preceding characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) is called "arising" only because it can produce another; its own substance (*svabhāva*) is not itself arising.
Because its substance is not arising, it is termed "non-arising.
Since it is non-arising, it cannot be definitively stated that it constitutes arising.
Regarding "inexpressible": because both arising and non-arising are entirely indeterminate, they are inexpressible.

As for the question, "Why is the non-arising of non-arising inexpressible?", this restates the fourth inquiry. It states that "non-arising" is termed "nirvāṇa," and because it explains that the aforementioned non-arising nirvāṇa is eternally quiescent, it is called "non-arising."
"Because *nirvāṇa* is non-arising, it cannot be described" explains that subsequent non-arising cannot be described.
Since *nirvāṇa* exists through conditions and is capable of arising, it cannot be definitively stated to be non-arising.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: it is spoken of as "arising" in the sense of being attained through cultivation and realization; it does not mean that there is an arising of something previously non-existent. Here, one does not intend to clarify an arising of *nirvāṇa*, but rather cites that *nirvāṇa*—which is a phenomenon of non-arising—possesses the principle of arisability, thereby analogically revealing that worldly phenomena which are non-arising likewise possess the principle of arising.

"Arising is ineffable" addresses the fifth question. Regarding "because arising does not exist": the characteristic of arising is impermanent; because that which has once perished does not return again, it is said that arising does not exist. Therefore, it cannot be definitively described as arising.

Regarding the phrase "Why is non-arising unspeakable?": this restates the sixth question. Since there are those who attain [realization], and because the characteristic of arising is constantly perceivable in accordance with phenomena, it cannot be definitively stated that there is no arising.

In the fourth section, the phrase "How can that which has conditions also be said [to exist]? restates the question from the preceding section; what follows provides the explanation. "The ten factors of dependent origination act as causes for arising; for this reason, it can also be so described" is the general explanation.
Among the twelve links of dependent origination, the first ten causal conditions can be said to "give rise" [to birth] because they act as causes for the eleventh link, birth (*jāti*).

Furthermore, one may also designate the ten causes explained in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* (or *Śīlaparivarta*) as these ten, for they are able to universally serve as causes for all phenomena; thus, they can be said to "give rise."

The following provides a detailed explanation. First, the procedure for listening to the teaching is given: "Do not enter the emptiness-samādhi, for the assembly is dull-witted. Below this is the actual exposition; among the first six difficult questions, only the first two are explained and the fourth is interpreted, while the remainder are omitted without discussion.
In the explanation of the first two [characteristics], having already discussed the nature of arising (*jāti*) in connection with the treatise, the remaining three are now distinguished.
Within this section, the text first presents them individually and subsequently clarifies them collectively.

Regarding the individual treatment, it first provides a general analysis of the meaning of the four characteristics as being either permanent or impermanent, and then proceeds to explain the actual text.
In terms of their functional scope (*vastu-viṣaya*), the four characteristics are called "permanent," because they always coexist with phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest;
in terms of their ontological scope (*dharma-viṣaya*), all four are impermanent, because the four characteristics themselves succeed one another without any moment of abiding.
What is the meaning of this?
As analyzed above, the four characteristics, when subdivided, have eight distinct aspects; these eight exist simultaneously and exert a mutual pressure upon one another.
By the power of the great "arising" (jāti), with the exception of its own self-substance, it causes the remaining seven characteristics and the phenomena they accompany to arise all at once.
By the power of the minor abiding, the major abiding is produced.
By the power of the major abiding, with the exception of its own self-nature, it causes the remaining seven characteristics and their concomitant dharmas to abide simultaneously;
by the power of the minor abiding, it causes the major abiding itself to abide.
Up to the fourth stage, by the power of great cessation, with the exception of its own substance, it causes the remaining seven characteristics and their concomitant dharmas to cease simultaneously;
by the power of minor cessation, it causes the great cessation itself to cease.

Therefore, all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as well as the essence of those phenomena possess the meanings of initial arising, subsequent abiding, final alteration, and ultimate cessation; thus, they are impermanent.
Next, I shall explain the text, beginning with the analysis of the characteristic of arising.
Regarding the statement, "The arising of conditioned phenomena is also constant," it means that the limit of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*) is eternally present.
Regarding the statement, "Because abiding is impermanent, arising is impermanent," although abiding is eternally present, its activity is merely temporary; thus, it is called "impermanent abiding."
Because one transmigrates and is born from this, birth is impermanent.

The impermanence of birth is fully accounted for by the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); because the function of "abiding" (*sthiti*) is proximate to that of birth, it is mentioned specifically [here].
As for the statement "abiding is also permanent," it exists eternally at the periphery of phenomena (*dharma*).
Regarding the statement, "Arising is impermanent, and abiding is impermanent": although arising is ever-present, its activity is likewise momentary; this is called the impermanence of arising.
Because it shifts through this [arising] into abiding, it is therefore the impermanence of abiding.

The impermanence of abiding (*sthiti*) is also due to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); however, because its function of arising is closely associated with abiding, it is explained specifically [as such].
The meanings of change (*anyathātva*) and decay (*bhaṅga*) can be understood by analogy.
What has preceded is an individual explanation; what follows is a general interpretation.

As for the statement, "Because of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), arising, abiding, change, and destruction are all eternal," it means that according to the specific limits of each phenomenon, they each maintain their own nature and exist eternally; this is what is meant by "eternal."

Regarding the statement, "Because it perishes moment by moment, it is not said to be permanent": within the limits of phenomena (*dharmāvadhi*), because they shift and perish with every movement, they are impermanent.

In reality, each moment also possesses arising, abiding, and change; it is according to their final state that they are said to "perish. As for the statement, "This Great Nirvāṇa can sever and extinguish [them], therefore it is called impermanent," this is the antidote to the impermanence of cessation.

The section on "impure phenomena" (*sāsrava-dharma*) explains the fourth objection raised in the preceding text. Previously, the objection stated: "If [arising] can produce another, by what cause and condition does it not produce the untainted (*anāsrava*)? Therefore, this now provides the explanation: "Impure phenomena possess the nature of arising even before they have arisen;
therefore, arising can produce them. Unconditioned untainted phenomena fundamentally lack the nature of arising; for this reason, the characteristic of arising cannot produce them."
In this passage, the primary principle is presented first, followed by three analogies used to illustrate it.
A question is asked:
"For what reason are the remaining difficulties not explained?"

Having resolved this objection, one immediately understands that the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) does not arise from itself within the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); therefore, the third objection need not be further explained.

Furthermore, since this text states that the nature of arising already exists when the tainted phenomena have not yet arisen, the fifth and sixth objections—which concern whether there is arising or non-arising at the time they are unarisen—have already been refuted and thus are not discussed again.
The preceding fifth section consists of questions and answers to clarify the Dharma; from here below is the sixth section, Vimalakīrti’s realization.
First, he leaps into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees, and upon descending, he formally expresses his realization.
"I have received your instruction; through the Great Nirvana, I have attained understanding regarding what was heard and what was not heard. This refers to one's own realization.

"Having received the Buddha’s prior teaching" means having received the Tathāgata’s earnest instruction on the ritual of listening. "Having realized the Buddha’s prior explanation of what was heard and what was not heard" means attaining understanding through the Great Nirvana regarding what was heard and what was not heard.
"Furthermore, he causes eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to understand birth and non-birth. This indicates that he speaks on behalf of the assembly to provide their understanding.

Based on this, it is certain that the questions regarding "hearing" and "not hearing" are asked for his own sake, whereas the questions regarding "birth" and "non-birth" are asked for the sake of others.
These two points are the two types of meanings within the previously mentioned "Knowledge of the Secret Treasury.
From here on, the third section—the meaning of attaining birth in the Pure Land through fearless inquiry—is elucidated by the Tathāgata.
The textual analysis consists of four parts:

first, the Bodhisattva Vaidūrya summarizes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one to initiate the discourse. "I have now understood" summarizes what preceded; "I wish to inquire without fear; may you deign to grant me your hearing and permission" introduces what follows.
Second, the Tathāgata grants permission.
Third, the fearless and correct inquiry: first arising [the intention], one then asks the question.
There are four phrases to this inquiry:
First, the question "What karma did they create to be born in the Immovable Realm? asks about the causes of merit cultivated by those of lower capacity;

second, the passage beginning with "How do the bodhisattvas of that land attain wisdom and achieve [enlightenment]? asks about the causes of wisdom cultivated by those of inferior grade—those who have been reborn there are precisely what are called the bodhisattvas of that land;

third, from "Among humans" onwards, it asks about the causes of merit cultivated by those of superior grade. This text is somewhat abbreviated; if it were complete, it should state: "What karma did these people create to be born there as elephant-kings among men, possessing great majestic power and fully cultivating all practices?"

4. Regarding "sharp wisdom" (*tīkṣṇa-prajñā*) and below, the question concerns the causes of wisdom cultivated by those superior persons. This text is also concise; were it complete, it should state what karma they performed to be born in that land. [The Buddha possesses] sharp and swift wisdom, such that upon hearing [the answer], he is able to understand it immediately.
The third section above concerns the "Fearless Correct Questioning.
The Tathāgata provides an exposition in four parts, containing twenty-one verses within the text:
the first twelve verses answer the initial question, clarifying the causes of merit cultivated by those of inferior capacity.
Next, there are two verses that answer the second question above, clarifying the causal conditions for wisdom cultivated by those of inferior capacity;
next, there are five verses that answer the third question above, clarifying the causal conditions for merit cultivated by those of superior capacity;
