"The person" represents this meditative concentration; dwelling securely in the True Dharma is called "sitting at a crossroads. "Seeing [people] coming and going" represents seeing the arising and ceasing of all phenomena. The application of the analogy in the following text is clear.
The third section further explains the ability to see distant phenomena, first through a simile and then through its application;
the fourth section further explains the ability to see distant lands, first through a simile and then through its application; the texts for both are readily understandable.

Within the seven subsequent instances of non-conceptuality, the first three instances involve non-conceptuality within one's own practice, while the latter four instances involve non-conceptuality within the practice of transforming others.

In the preceding section on self-practice, the first sequence clarifies the self-extinguishing of obstacles. The analogy "like Mount Gandhamādana" establishes the metaphor to reveal the Dharma; the application [of this analogy] below can be understood accordingly.

The two subsequent "furthermore" (punar-aparam) sections clarify that within the preceding practice for eliminating obstacles, the mind is free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*). In the former "furthermore" section, a vajra serves as the metaphor; in the latter "furthermore" section, six things—namely a pond, water, fire, and so forth—serve as metaphors. These may be understood by combining them.

Regarding the latter four successive instances of non-conceptuality within the practice of benefiting others: the first two pertain to bodily action (*kāyakarman*), the next one to vocal action (*vākkarman*), and the final one applies to both bodily and vocal actions; in these three types of action, the mind is without conceptual discrimination.
Among the former karmic deeds, in the first instance, "he manifests his body as a Buddha filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet his mind is without discrimination";
in the final instance, "in a single thought-moment he can reach worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," yet his mind is without discrimination;

and next, within a single mouth, "in a single thought-moment he preaches the Dharma, able to sever the afflictions of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions," yet his mind is without discrimination.

In the following section clarifying bodily and vocal karma, it first elucidates the two types of transformative manifestations of body and speech: "preaching with a single voice" refers to vocal karma, while "manifesting a single form" refers to bodily karma. Furthermore, "abiding in a single place" again clarifies bodily karma, and "expounding a single dharma" again clarifies vocal karma.

The following clarifies that the bodhisattva’s mind is free from discrimination: although they perceive birth and so forth, they do not grasp at the mark of a person; although they perceive form and so forth, they do not grasp at the mark of phenomena.
Within this, the first section provides the analysis, while the section beginning with "Why" offers the explanation.

Regarding the analysis within the middle [truth], it is first stated that although one perceives form and so forth, one does not grasp at the characteristic of suffering; although one perceives afflictions and so forth, one does not grasp at the characteristic of origination; although one perceives the Eightfold Noble Path and so forth, one does not grasp at the characteristic of the path; and although one perceives nirvana and so forth, one does not grasp at the characteristic of cessation.

In the commentary, the initial question asks why all [phenomena] are non-existent; the subsequent section provides the explanation. "The Dharma is fundamentally without marks" correctly explains the aforementioned non-existence, while the passage beginning with "by means of samādhi" clarifies the basis for such vision.
The preceding section has defined the characteristics; the following section explains the meaning of the name.
The question, "For what reason is it called the Vajrasamādhi? serves to introduce the topic, which is then explained through three meanings beginning with "Like a vajra":
first, the meaning of indeterminacy. Just as a worldly vajra changes its color when placed in the sunlight, this samādhi likewise manifests various bodies within the great assembly.
Second is the sense of supreme excellence: just as the substance of worldly vajra is so preeminent that it cannot be weighed, this samādhi is likewise such that it cannot be measured.

Third is the sense of power: just as worldly vajra has great power to eliminate poverty and remove poison, this samādhi is likewise such that whoever attains it will be freed from the suffering of afflictions and the various poisons of Māras and heterodoxies.
"This is called" serves as a summary.
The six virtues mentioned above constitute the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāva*), while the four below represent progressive advancement (*viśeṣa*).

Within the section on progressive advancement, the first clarifies the merit of cultivating remedies (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*); this is presented by first posing a question and subsequently providing an exposition.
In the "Exposition" (*vibhaṅga*), first there is a general clarification that four factors constitute the causes for *nirvāṇa*: first reflection (*cintā*) and subsequently knowledge (*jñāna*).
Within the section on knowledge, there is first the concordant, second the contrary, and finally the explanation.

"Knowing that these four dharmas are the causes of nirvāṇa" constitutes the positive [argument], while "if one says 'diligence'" and so forth constitute the negative [argument]; the section beginning with "the reason why" provides the explanation.
Next, four names are listed; they are first questioned and then enumerated.
Below, they are explained in detail. Within the explanation, five sections follow the text: the first three provide a general explanation, while the latter two offer specific interpretations.

To explain this according to its practice: the first section clarifies the meaning of abandoning faults; the second section clarifies the meaning of embracing wholesome qualities; the third section again clarifies the abandonment of faults; and the final two sections once more clarify the embracing of wholesome qualities.
Within the first section, there is first the illustration and then the application. In the illustration:

"a person with an illness goes to a physician" illustrates drawing near to a virtuous friend; "the physician prescribes medicine" illustrates hearing the true Dharma; "receiving it well with a sincere heart" illustrates focused mindfulness and reflection; and "acting in accordance with the instructions" and so forth illustrate practicing as taught.
The lower section provides the application [of the analogy]. In the second section, the analogy is presented first, followed by the application. Within the analogy: "As when a king...

consults his ministers as to what the law is" illustrates relying on a virtuous friend. Here, the "king" represents the practitioner; wishing to cultivate and refine the mind through the True Dharma is called "governing according to the law. Desiring that one's practice emerge from obstacles and attain peace is called "bringing the people security and happiness. Inquiring about the meaning of the practice is called "consulting the wise ministers as to what the law is. The passage beginning with "The ministers then... illustrates hearing the True Dharma; proclaiming the practices of past Buddhas and transmitting them is called "expounding the ancient laws of former kings. The passage beginning with "Once the king has heard... illustrates focused mindfulness and reflection. The passage beginning with "Governing according to the law... illustrates practicing as taught.
The lower [sections] may be understood accordingly.
In the third section, the avoidance of faults is explained again.
How does this differ from the first?

The preceding section relied on the Bodhisattva to clarify the avoidance of minor evils; this section addresses ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) to manifest the avoidance of grave transgressions, likewise beginning with a metaphor.

The initial metaphor concerns approaching a friend: "As if a person encounters illness" explains the reason for approaching a friend; "having a good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) represents that virtuous companion (though the specific act of approaching is omitted); "and he speaks" and following represent hearing the true Dharma; "that person arrives" and following represent focused mindfulness and reflection; "he immediately goes there" and following represent practicing according to the teaching.

In the subsequent section on the application [of the analogy], the comparison regarding associating with virtuous friends and hearing the Dharma is omitted for brevity. The passage beginning with "faith with a sincere mind" applies the analogy to clarify reflection (*cintā*). The Bodhisattva’s deliberation consists of abandoning faults and seeking liberation for the benefit of sentient beings; therefore, the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) are taught as "mindfulness through focused reflection."
From the passage beginning with "The young" onwards, the practice of cultivation is explained in its proper order; the text is clear enough to be understood.
Below this, two further sections again clarify the inclusion of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgraha*); how do these differ from what preceded?
The preceding second section generally elucidates the inclusion of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgraha*), while the following section explains it specifically.
Within this, the first part discusses both the superior and inferior aspects in general, whereas the latter part distinguishes the superior from the inferior.
Within the first section, the practice of associating with spiritual friends is first elucidated; this passage is divided into two parts:

first, the actual explanation of associating with spiritual friends; second, from the words "If there is one who is intimate... onwards, the benefits of associating with spiritual friends are explained.
The preceding section has six parts:
first, knowing the mind, meaning that those who possess intelligence constantly teach without weariness;
second, knowing persons, also termed "substance" (*tǐ*), referring to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
Third is the meaning of the knowledge: the question "For what reason is it so named? initiates the inquiry, while the subsequent section provides the explanation through which it may be understood.
Fourth is the ritual of the knowledge: to speak in accordance with the Dharma and to act in accordance with what has been spoken is its ritual; this is first presented and subsequently explained.
The analysis of the three stages:
the first stage concerns the abandonment of unwholesome discrimination; the latter two concern the cultivation of wholesome discrimination, proceeding first from the fruit and then to the cause.
The five types of knowledge regarding phenomena are for the purpose of seeking happiness through cultivation; to perceive faults yet fail to speak of them is contrary to that dharma.
Within this, the first part presents the heading; from "What is" onwards, it provides the exposition.
"Not seeking one's own pleasure, but always for the sake of sentient beings" explains the Dharma in terms of the mind.
"Seeing faults but not speaking of them" clarifies the Dharma in terms of speech.
The section beginning with "By this" concludes [the preceding].
The six benefits of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are explained through the analogy of the moon in the sky; the application [of the analogy] below can be understood accordingly.

Thus far, the friend has been clarified; below, the immediate benefit is clarified. The passage beginning with "If one is near a spiritual friend who has not yet attained precepts" and so forth, clarifies the benefit of initiating practice.

"Causing what has not yet arisen to arise, causing what has already arisen to expand, and further attaining mastery of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures]" and so forth—these describe the benefit of generating understanding.
Next, the listening to the Dharma is explained, which consists of three parts:
first, a general reference to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, meaning that being able to listen to and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures is called "listening to the Dharma."
Second, to distinguish the small for the sake of taking up the great—listening to the Vaipulya sutras is called listening to the Dharma;
third, within the Mahāyāna, to distinguish the inferior for the sake of taking up the superior—listening to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is called listening to the Dharma.
Among these, the initial statement, "One who truly hears the Dharma listens to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*," serves as a general heading.
The subsequent section, beginning with "Hearing of the Buddha-nature within the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*," specifically elucidates what is heard.
What is heard consists of six statements in three pairs:
first, hearing the cause for the concealment of Buddha-nature; second, hearing the fruit of its manifestation as the Tathāgata’s ultimate non-extinction—these two form one pair.
Third, hearing the practice of the Eightfold Path that can realize [the truth]; fourth, hearing the principle realized through the eleven kinds of emptiness—these two form another pair.
Fifth, through hearing and generating the mind of awakening, one attains great bodhi; sixth, through hearing and generating the mind, one attains great nirvāṇa—these two form a pair.
Next, the section on contemplation is divided into two parts:

first, explaining the cultivation of mindfulness by means of the twelve links of dependent origination as a remedial method; second, explaining the cultivation of mindfulness by means of the three samādhis as remedial practices.

In the preceding section, the analogy first illustrates that "hearing a physician’s instructions and the names of medicines cannot cure an illness," which distinguishes this from the previous case of mere hearing; the analogy that "one recovers by taking [the medicine]" illustrates the necessity of subsequent reflection.
Next is the conclusion of the preceding section.
Within this latter section, first the question is posed: "By what further meaning is it called 'mindfulness and reflection'? Next comes the exposition, followed by the conclusion.
In the exposition, first the phrase "namely, the three samādhis" briefly introduces the subject; next follows the enumeration, and finally the detailed explanation.
The following clarifies the practice. "How so? is the interrogative inquiry, to which the subsequent section provides the response and explanation.

Within this explanation, the first part clarifies practicing in accordance with the Dharma; the passage beginning with "The Dharma is precisely permanence, bliss, self, and purity" clarifies the Dharma that is to be practiced.
In the first part of the preceding section, the statement "the practice of giving up to wisdom" clarifies the cultivation of correct conduct;
"knowing the aggregates and sense bases," etc., clarifies the cultivation of correct understanding.
In the subsequent section clarifying the Dharma, the initial statement, "The Dharma is itself permanence and bliss," etc., elucidates the essential nature and characteristics of the Dharma.
The passage beginning with "Understanding the profound meaning of the Great Nirvāṇa" explains the Dharma by way of its realization.

The preceding section provided a general discussion of both superior and inferior aspects; from here on, the following section distinguishes the superior from the inferior by first clarifying the cultivation of spiritual friendship (*kalyāṇamitra*). This passage is divided into two parts:
first, identifying Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as virtuous friends; second, from the phrase "by reason of such spiritual friends," clarifying the benefits derived from cultivating such friendship.

In the preceding explanation of "friends," there are eight successive stages: the first stage is able to harmonize the minds of beings; the middle six stages skillfully provide beneficial aid; and the final stage consists of inner equanimity.
At the beginning, the statement "The foremost spiritual friend is the Buddha and Bodhisattvas" distinguishes the superior from the inferior, setting aside the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation; first, there is an interrogative inquiry, followed by a brief response to that inquiry stating, "Because they are always well-disciplined by means of the three kinds [of training].
Below this, it is explained in detail: first the question is posed, then the items are enumerated, and finally, the section beginning with "By this" provides the conclusion.

Regarding the six subsequent [sections] within the "Skillfully Benefiting Others": the first two subsequent sections are able to transform others so they may leave behind faults; the next two subsequent sections are able to instruct them to give rise to goodness; the following one subsequent section again transforms them to leave behind faults; and the final one subsequent section again instructs them to give rise to goodness.

Regarding the first two successive instances of transforming others to lead them away from faults: the former transformation causes people to abandon evil causes, while the latter transformation causes them to cross over [the suffering of] results.

Within the section on abandoning evil causes, the statement "The Buddha and Bodhisattvas are great physicians, and thus they are called spiritual friends" serves as a brief thematic introduction; the section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation.
In the explanation, first is the Dharma, next is the simile, and finally is the application; the section beginning with "By this" serves as the conclusion.
Regarding the phrase "causing [beings] to cross over suffering," the simile of "the great shipmaster" is established to manifest the Dharma, followed by the application and the conclusion.

Regarding the two subsequent sections on teaching the generation of wholesome states (*kuśala*), the first section teaches the causes for generating wholesome states; it consists of the initial presentation of the principle (*dharma*), followed by a simile, then an application (*upanaya*), and finally a conclusion.

The latter "subsequent section" teaches the attainment of the fruit of happiness; first, it establishes a simile: "superior medicine" represents the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; "seeing" represents beholding their physical forms; "those who touch" represent those who draw near to hear the Dharma; and "mindfulness" represents practicing in accordance with it. The subsequent application of the analogy and the final conclusion follow the text as they are clearly understandable.

Next, regarding the second section on "Transforming Away Faults," the passage beginning with "As at Lake Anavatapta in Mount Gandhamādana" cites the false to reveal the true. Worldly people falsely claim that bathing in Lake Anavatapta can extinguish sins; therefore, it is cited here.

"Beyond this, what is real? The following section distinguishes the true from the false: first the question is posed, then the distinction is made; "The reason why" provides the explanation, and "Because of this" concludes it.
In the next section, which further teaches the generation of wholesome qualities, there is first a simile followed by an application (*yōjya*), and the conclusion begins with "By this.

These six successive sections skillfully provide beneficial aid; the eighth section, beginning with "For example, like a skilled physician proficient in the eight arts," clarifies the inner equality of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, consisting of a simile, its application, and the conclusion beginning with "By this."

The preceding section clarifies the "good friend"; the subsequent section, beginning with "by being close to this," clarifies the benefit of proximity; next, it clarifies listening to the Dharma, first through questions and subsequently through exposition.

Within the exposition, the initial portion correctly clarifies that hearing the Dharma leads to proximity with Nirvana; the section beginning with "I have everywhere" cites scriptural teachings to manifest its benefits.
In the preceding section of the sūtra text, there are five successive repetitions: the first is an exposition in terms of the Dharma, and the latter four are illustrative analogies.

Within the Dharma exposition, the initial statement—“Because of hearing the Dharma, one possesses the faculty of faith, up to the fruit of Buddhahood”—clarifies that hearing [the Dharma] is beneficial; the section beginning with “Therefore” concludes this. Herein, it is correctly clarified that one attains Buddhahood by means of hearing, while the passage beginning with “The Srotāpanna” and so forth uses a vehicle analogy to elaborate upon this.

Among the four subsequent metaphors, the first metaphor of the elder clarifies the ability to admonish from afar; the second metaphor of the mirror clarifies the ability to demonstrate what is near; the third metaphor of the merchant clarifies the ability to guide from afar; and the fourth metaphor of the elephant clarifies the ability to restrain what is near.

At the beginning of this section, first there is an analogy. Within the analogy, the passage up to "nor associate with them" illustrates the Dharma heard; "the elder" represents the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); "the son" represents the practitioner; "sending him to another country" illustrates being taught to turn toward the Buddha; practicing the causes to trade for the fruit is called "purchasing what is needed"; explaining the characteristics of obstacles and their remedies throughout the various stages (*bhūmi*) is called "showing the places where the road is passable or blocked"; teaching how to guard against all transgressions is called "further admonishing him"; "prostitutes" represent the spheres of the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); and urging him to abandon them is called "having no affection."

Frequenting and indulging in the five desires can destroy the Dharma-body, sever the life-force of wisdom, and cause one to lose the wealth of merit; therefore, it is said: "If one is intimate with them, one loses one's body, perishes in life, and forfeits one's treasures."

The "wicked person" is a metaphor for an evil spiritual friend (*pāpamitra*); teaching one to abandon and distance oneself from such a person is expressed as "do not associate with them. The passage beginning with "his son paid respect" serves as a metaphor for the benefits gained by a practitioner who hears the Dharma.

Next, the text combines [the analogy] to reveal the Dharma: "The Bodhisattva likewise expounds the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings" corresponds to the elder previously sending his son to another country to trade for necessities; "showing all sentient beings the openings and blockages of the various paths" corresponds to indicating the places where the roads are passable or obstructed; "yet he further admonishes them... not to associate [with such people]" is omitted and not combined [here]; "these [beings], having heard the Dharma" corresponds to revering their father’s instructions; "staying far away from all evils" corresponds to their physical safety and well-being; "being fully endowed with wholesome dharmas" corresponds to obtaining precious goods; and the section beginning with "by this" concludes the passage.
In each of the final three sections, a simile is first established, followed by an application (*yoga*), and finally a conclusion;

the text is clear and easily understood. Above, it has been extensively explained that hearing the Dharma is beneficial. Below, citations of scriptural teachings are introduced to further establish this benefit, which is divided into four parts:

first, explaining how listening to the Dharma enables one to abandon the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); second, enabling one to abandon fear; third, enabling one to abandon delusion; and fourth, extinguishing suffering and affliction.

Within the first section, the phrase "I have taught in various places that one should listen to and abandon the five hindrances" clarifies that which is to be abandoned; "cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment" clarifies that which is to be aroused; and the passage beginning with "by cultivating the seven" clarifies that which is to be accomplished.

In the second section, the phrase "By means of listening to the Dharma, Srotāpannas are freed from fear" precisely clarifies that which is abandoned; the subsequent passage beginning with "What is it? illustrates this through concrete instances, first posing a question and then providing an explanation.
Regarding the "four virtues," as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*, they are: associating with spiritual friends, hearing the Dharma, reflecting on its meaning, and practicing accordingly. These are the four.

Regarding the "Ten Consolations," as stated in the *Śāriputra-saṃyukta-vyādhi-pariṣkāra-sūtra* of the *Madhyama Āgama*: there was a householder named Sudatta who suffered from a grave illness; his son at that time dispatched a messenger to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health and to request that Śāriputra deign to visit him, whereupon Śāriputra went.

When Sudatta saw him approaching, he immediately wished to descend from his bed, but Śāriputra stopped him; instead, he sat on a separate bed and consoled the elder, saying, "Do not fear, do not fear."
Why is this? All ordinary worldlings, being possessed of lack of faith, fall into evil paths and are born in the hells upon the dissolution of the body after death;

whereas you, Elder, now possess supreme faith, and by virtue of this faith, you are able to extinguish suffering and pain and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, or attain the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, or the stage of Anāgāmin.
The elder had previously attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and for this reason he did not speak [of it].

This was the first consolation; the second was good precepts, the third much learning, the fourth generosity, the fifth wise discernment, the sixth right view, the seventh right intention, the eighth right resolve, the ninth right liberation, and the tenth right knowledge. Within each of these, the words of consolation were identical to the first.
Among these ten, the first five are mundane virtues and the latter five are supramundane.
Within the supramundane, right view and right intention constitute the path of non-obstruction: wisdom is termed right view, and right reflection is termed right intention.
Right liberation and right deliverance constitute the path of liberation: wisdom is termed right liberation, while the remaining mental states and mental factors are termed right deliverance.

The "equal vision" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is called "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*); the repeated contemplation by those in training of the principle of the Four Truths is called the "equal vision" of one in training.
The section beginning with "By this" concludes [the preceding], while the section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation.
This is the second [point] on how listening to the Dharma removes fear.
From here below, the third [point] clarifies how listening to the Dharma enables one to leave behind ignorance by being able to know the three distinct types of worldly people.

First, three individuals are cited; next, they are listed; then, the analysis follows; subsequently, it is clarified that one who listens to the Dharma can fully comprehend it; the section beginning with "For this reason" concludes [the preceding].

Below this, the fourth section clarifies how listening to the Dharma can extinguish suffering and affliction; first, the past story of Śāriputra is cited to illustrate this, and the section beginning with "For this reason" concludes it.

Next, the contemplation is explained, first by posing questions and then by providing analysis; there are five successive stages. The first three eliminate faults, the next one generates goodness, and the final one comprehensively clarifies both the elimination of faults and the generation of goodness.
Regarding the first three [sections], the initial one concerns detachment from the five desires, the next detachment from the four inversions, and the final detachment from the four characteristics;
these texts are all intelligible. Below, the practice of cultivation is clarified in three sections:

the first provides a general explanation of abandoning faults and cultivating goodness as the essence of practice. This is understood through its initial inquiry, subsequent exposition, and concluding summary.

The second section specifically clarifies that observing the dharma while remaining free from faults constitutes spiritual practice; this is understood through an initial inquiry, followed by an exposition, and finally a conclusion.

The third section specifically clarifies that understanding the dharma to achieve goodness constitutes spiritual practice; it begins with an inquiry and proceeds to an exposition, which contains two enumerations, listing the names "the real" and "the unreal."
The following explains its characteristics: first, the unreal is explained; subsequently, the real is explained. This is done by first posing questions and then providing explanations.
Within the explanation, there are first seven headings listed, followed by a detailed analysis and exposition.

In the aforementioned opening of the gates, "Nirvana" is the fruit and "Buddha-nature" is the cause; "Tathāgata, Dharma, and Saṃgha" are themselves bodhi; "true reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is the conventional truth, and "emptiness" (ākāśa) is the ultimate truth. To know these seven dharmas is called true practice.
Some people claim that emptiness is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Based on this, the seven gates clarify that emptiness is not an intrinsic nature.
This explanation has two parts:
first, a general discussion of all phenomena to demonstrate the seven specific distinctions; [the second part follows].

II. "The non-arising of afflictions in all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is called nirvāṇa. The following section discusses the seven [aspects] from the perspective of the Buddha, clarifying that these seven are without distinction.
Regarding the first part, the meaning of nirvāṇa is initially explained: first the question, next the explanation, and finally the summary.

In the explanation, first it clarifies that the eightfold meaning of *nirvāṇa* shows the Great Vehicle is vastly different from the Small; this is understood through a sequence of question, analysis, and conclusion.
Subsequently, the eight [aspects] and the six [aspects] show the Small Vehicle is different from the Great; herein there are four parts:
first, citing the eight matters of *nirvāṇa* pertaining to ordinary persons.
1. The second section lists the six matters of *nirvāṇa* according to the Hīnayāna; it should properly contain eight, but impermanence (*anitya*) and non-self (*anātman*) are omitted for brevity.
2. From "There are ordinary beings" (*yǒu fán*) downward, the *nirvāṇa* of ordinary beings is explained: first they are introduced, then explained, and finally concluded, as can be seen.
3. From "How is it? (*yúnhé*) downward, the *nirvāṇa* of the Small Vehicle is explained: first there is the question, followed by the explanation.
The preceding section concealed the impermanence [of the Buddha-nature]; this section explains its presence within the intermediate state.
From the words "If it were thus" onwards, the conclusion contrasts the former with the latter, naming it "knowing that nirvāṇa is not the Buddha-nature," and so forth.

Next, the Buddha-nature is explained; first there is a question, followed by an exposition. The first six and the subsequent seven are all spoken in terms of the cause, distinguished according to their respective characteristics. As for the meaning of "I am a Buddha," it resides in the cause and is not discussed here.

"Bliss" (sukha) is the meaning of nirvāṇa; since this principle applies universally, there is also nirvāṇa within the causal stage, and bliss follows accordingly within that causal stage as well. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The nirvāṇa of a bodhisattva possesses both bliss and purity."

In another sense, nirvana exists only at the stage of Buddhahood; since bliss accompanies nirvana, it is not mentioned in relation to the causal stages. Therefore, the text below states: "Because the Buddhas and Tathāgatas do not give rise to afflictions, they possess nirvana; although Bodhisattvas have severed them, they are not yet non-arising, and thus they lack nirvana. Because they lack nirvana, bliss is not mentioned for them.
According to a comprehensive discussion based on reality, the essential nature within the causes also possesses self and bliss.
The section beginning with “This is called” concludes [the preceding]. Next, the Tathāgata is explained;

first a question is posed and then analyzed, consisting of eleven characteristics. Regarding “this is the characteristic of awakening”: the Tathāgata is the person, and awakening is the realization of the Dharma. “Wholesome” and so forth can be understood accordingly. The section beginning with “This is called” concludes [this part].
Next is the explanation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). First, the questions are posed; second, they are analyzed.
Phenomena encompass both the defiled and the pure; therefore, they include the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth, as well as eleven pairs of categories.
The section beginning with "This is called" concludes [the preceding discussion].
Next is the explanation of knowing the Sangha, which first poses questions and then provides an analysis.
Within the analysis there are nine points: "Eternal, blissful, self, and pure" refers to the Mahāyāna Sangha; from "the characteristics of disciples" downward refers to the Hīnayāna Sangha.

Presently receiving the holy teachings is termed the "characteristic of a disciple. Because this is coarse and easily perceived by people, it is said to be "visible. Conduct that accords with the Dharma is termed "good. As for "true" and "unreal," these will be explained in the subsequent text.
First, the "explanation of the good meaning" (*śubhārtha*): it is called "good" because it interrogates with "for what reason" all *śrāvakas* shall attain the Buddha-way.
Below, the "explanation of the true" (*tattvārtha*): it is called "true" because it interrogates with "for what reason" one realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in the present.
The section beginning with "This is called" serves as the conclusion.
Next, the *shixiang* (reality-mark) is explained, first by posing a question and then by providing an analysis.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *zhendi* (ultimate truth) alone is designated as the *shixiang*; this sūtra’s later sections likewise explains that the *zhendi* constitutes the *shixiang*.

What is now being discussed belongs to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because it is conventional truth, all phenomena—birth and death, nirvana, defilement and purity—are included therein. Therefore, such categories as "permanent" or "impermanent" are called the true nature (*dharmatā*), and there are thirteen such pairs.
The phrase "This is called" below serves as a conclusion; "This is called the true mark, not nirvana," and so forth, concludes that this is distinct from others.
"This is called the Bodhisattva practicing the Great Nirvana, knowing the distinct characteristics of nirvana and so forth" concludes that what precedes is distinct from what follows.

It concludes that the preceding six gates are distinct from the subsequent term "space" as a distinct characteristic; furthermore, knowing that each of the preceding six is individually different is also termed "distinct."
Next, the emptiness of space (*ākāśa*) is explained. First, there is the direct exposition; subsequently, *nirvāṇa* is cited as an analogy to clarify space.
Within the former, the bodhisattva’s knowledge of emptiness is first elucidated, followed by a discernment of the characteristics of emptiness.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the middle [truth]:

the first statement, “The Bodhisattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa does not perceive space,” briefly clarifies that the Bodhisattva is free from marks and does not perceive. At the time of realizing emptiness, one does not perceive a mind existing separately outside of emptiness; because there is no such mind, one does not perceive a space existing separately outside of the mind. Since there is no mind outside of space, there is no perceiving subject; since there is no space outside of the mind, there is nothing perceived. Therefore, one does not perceive space.
Second, from "Why" onwards, the text explains and establishes the point of "not seeing. First, it poses a preliminary inquiry:
If a bodhisattva practicing the sutra should see emptiness, for what reason is it now said that they do not see it?

Regarding the statement, "Although the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the five eyes, they do not see [it]," this is a response to a question that provides an analytical explanation. The names and meanings of the five eyes have been fully explained above.

Among the five eyes, it is wisdom (*prajñā*) that truly perceives emptiness (*śūnyatā*). However, when perceiving emptiness, one does not see an eye existing outside of emptiness that is capable of seeing; because such an eye does not exist, there is likewise no emptiness existing outside the eye that could be seen. Therefore, it is said that they do not see it.

3. Regarding the passage "Only wisdom" and below: what was previously described as "not seeing" is here briefly explained as "seeing. This wisdom is the same as the "eye of wisdom" among the five eyes mentioned above. When this wisdom realizes emptiness and there is nothing to be seen, it is truly called "seeing emptiness"; therefore, it is said that only wisdom is able to see.

4. Regarding the passage "What is seen by the wisdom-eye is that there is nothing to be seen," this explains the meaning of "not seeing" as being "seeing. This is because having [ordinary] vision contradicts the aforementioned "not seeing"; therefore, it is now explained.
Regarding what is here called "seeing," there is no dharma that can be seen; therefore, it is named "seeing.
Above, the capacity for knowing was clarified; next, we shall distinguish the essential nature and characteristics of this space. Coarsely divided, there are two types; finely divided, there are six.

Regarding the two coarse divisions: from the beginning up to "sentient beings and the nature of space are both without reality," the characteristics of emptiness are briefly expounded; from "as a person says" onwards, the characteristics of emptiness are extensively revealed.
Regarding the sixfold subdivision, there are briefly three parts:
first, the explanation of emptiness through the teaching of the Dharma;

second, the explanation of emptiness through analogy from the passage "Emptiness is called non-existence" onwards, which uses the mundane great void as a metaphor to manifest the emptiness of principle.

Third: From "the nature of sentient beings" (*sattvadhātu*) onwards, the shallow is raised to illustrate the profound, using the emptiness of sentient beings to illustrate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
In the subsequent extensive text, these three are further elaborated; thus, there are six sections.

Regarding the preceding brief explanation, I shall first interpret the initial section. The phrase "If it is a non-entity, it is called space" restates what was previously seen by the wisdom-eye—that the absence of phenomena is spoken of as emptiness—and explains that this refers to the original absence of intrinsic nature as being space, rather than the removal of an existing entity to constitute emptiness. The phrase "Such space is called real" distinguishes the true from the false; because it differs from the deluded perception that negates phenomena to create emptiness, it is termed "real."

Regarding the phrase "Because it is real, it is called eternally non-existent": this clarifies that emptiness is not something that begins; it is primordially and eternally quiescent. It differs from a remedial emptiness that destroys existence; therefore, it is called "eternally non-existent."
Furthermore, this principle of emptiness is not like the permanent and constant fruit-virtues of the Buddhas;

therefore, it is said to be "permanently non-existent. Because it is permanently non-existent, it lacks pleasure, self, and purity. This demonstrates how emptiness differs from existence: it is called "non-existent" because it does not correspond to existent dharmas that possess a self, pleasure, or purity; nor is it called "non-existent" because it is like the self, pleasure, and purity grasped by deluded sentiments—it is not that the principle of emptiness itself lacks purity.

In the second analogy, the statement “emptiness is called the absence of phenomena, and the absence of phenomena is called emptiness” restates the preceding doctrinal explanation. The phrase “for example, in the world, the absence of things is called emptiness” introduces a simile to clarify the point; since the great void of the world is by its very nature devoid of things, it is cited as a parallel because it resembles the emptiness of the principle of *dharmatā*. The passage beginning with “the nature of empty space is also like this” explains how the phenomenon corresponds to the simile.

Within the third section, "Citing the Shallow to Classify the Deep," it says: "The nature of sentient beings and the nature of empty space are both without reality. Here, the nature of sentient beings refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while empty space refers to the previously explained emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Although they differ in their relative depth, both are inherently devoid of intrinsic nature from the very beginning; therefore, they are termed "empty."
The preceding three sections briefly expound the meaning of emptiness; the following section expands upon this, and its text likewise consists of three parts:

first, a detailed exposition of the aforementioned phenomena; second, from "Just as in the world" onwards, a detailed exposition of the aforementioned analogies; and third, from "Just as in the world" onwards, an expansion of the third previous point by using the shallow to illustrate the profound.
Within the first section, there are two interrogations and two explanations.

First, the phrase "Why is this so? interrogates the preceding discourse on phenomena (*dharma*) to introduce what follows. Since the preceding discourse on phenomena stated that the absence of things is called "space" (*ākāśa*) and further stated that this space is called "eternally non-existent," it now interrogates:
if the absence of things is called space, why is it said to be eternal?

The following explains this in response: "As when a person says that space is created by removing objects" cites a divergent view held by others; "but this space is in reality uncreatable" refutes it to reveal the true principle; because it is uncreatable, it is called "non-existent."
The phrase "For what reason? (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) serves as a repeated inquiry based on the preceding statement:
if the Bodhisattva’s contemplative understanding resolves all marks into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), why then is it said that emptiness cannot be produced?

The following section provides the explanation, first correctly elucidating the meaning of non-production (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and then, with the words "If it were producible," refuting the notion of production to establish non-production.
In the first part of the middle section, the phrase "because there is nothing" correctly explains non-action: since emptiness is a non-existent phenomenon (*dharma*), how could it be acted upon?

The statement "Because it does not exist, one should know that the emptiness which is the nature of space is non-existent" reiterates this to conclude the point: because that space has nothing whatsoever, one should know that the emptiness which is a non-existent entity in its own right is the nature of space; for this reason, it cannot be acted upon.

In the refutation of the "act of creation," the phrase "if it were something that could be created" cites what the opponent has established; "then it would be called impermanent" uses an inquiry to reveal the fault; and "if it were impermanent, it would not be called space" uses a reprimand to demonstrate its incorrectness.
The preceding section extensively elaborated upon the previous explanation of the Dharma; from here on, the second part extensively clarifies the previous parable.
Why is it necessary to clarify this?

Previously, the great void was cited as an analogy for the emptiness of principle (*tattva-śūnyatā*); yet, most people in the world claim that the great void possesses a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If it possessed a distinct nature, it could not be called "empty," which would contradict what has been stated.
Now, because it is necessary to refute existence (*bhāva*) in order to establish the meaning of non-existence (*abhāva*), this must be further elucidated.

In the text, the initial statement—“As worldly people say that space is colorless, unobstructed, and immutable, and for this reason the world designates the dharma of space as the fifth great element”—cites what others have established. The subsequent phrase—“Yet this space actually has no intrinsic nature” (*svabhāva*)—refutes it to reveal its non-existence. Finally, “Because of luminosity, it is called space; in reality, there is no space” explains existence to reveal non-existence.
Because it is light, it is called "space"; this explains its existence.
Yet, in reality, there is no such thing as space; this reveals its non-existence.

When worldly people perceive no other objects within that solar radiance, they give rise to the notion of space and say, "there is space. However, this space actually has no substantiality at all; thus, it is said that what is truly non-existent is designated as "space."

This is the third section from below, which expands upon the preceding summary by citing the shallow to illustrate the profound. Previously, the nature of arising was cited to illustrate emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature; now, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is cited as an aid to manifest this: "Just as that conventional truth has no real intrinsic nature, it is spoken of as existing for the sake of arising."
Space is thus: it has no inherent nature at all, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it is said that space exists.
Having correctly analyzed emptiness above, the following section cites *nirvāṇa* as an analogy to clarify this point; herein there are five parts:
first, the formal citation of *nirvāṇa* as an analogy for the preceding emptiness.
2. From "Nirvāṇa is" below, [the text] distinguishes it from a void that possesses difference;

3. From "Although nirvāṇa" below, [the text] explains through reasoning that nirvāṇa is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, and further clarifies that the tranquility and bliss of nirvāṇa are not [ordinary] sensation;

4. From "The Buddhas" below, [the text] explains through reasoning the bliss of the quiescence of nirvāṇa, and further clarifies the distinctions between the characteristics of the bliss of the Buddhas and others.

5. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Virtuous King said," those points within the preceding meaning that were difficult to understand are further clarified through a series of questions and answers.
At the outset, the phrase "Nirvana is also like this" provides a general comparison to emptiness; because the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*) is identical, it is described as "like this."
"There is no place of abiding; it is simply the place where all Buddhas sever afflictions, and is therefore named Nirvana"—this explains the emptiness of continuity.
In the second phrase, "Nirvana is itself permanence, bliss, self, and purity," this distinguishes it from a different kind of emptiness.
Why must this be distinguished?

Previously it was stated that space is without self (*anātman*), bliss (*sukha*), or purity (*śubha*); now it is stated that *nirvāṇa* is likewise like space. Fearing that worldly people might take that *nirvāṇa* to be entirely identical to space—being without self, bliss, or purity—it is therefore necessary to distinguish between them.
How is this to be understood?
Emptiness is devoid of principle; it lacks self, bliss, and purity.
Because the essence of the fruit-virtue of nirvāṇa exists, it is fully endowed with these four meanings; therefore, it is said that nirvāṇa is precisely permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

In the third statement, regarding the phrase "Although nirvana is blissful, it is not the experience of pleasure; it is the bliss of tranquility," the preceding discussion described it as bliss, yet fearing this might be equated with worldly sensation, he further clarifies it.

Within this, it first clarifies that although there is pleasure, it is not [ordinary] sensation (*vedanā*); subsequently, it clarifies that it is exclusively the bliss of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). Such is the distinction between their characteristics.

However, according to the characteristic of inclusion, the Buddha’s wisdom is subsumed within the *prajñā* of Great Nirvana; thus, Nirvana also possesses the knowledge of bliss. Therefore, the preceding text proclaims that Nirvana is fully endowed with four kinds of bliss: the cessation of sensation, quiescent extinction, and indestructible cognitive awareness.
Now, when non-feeling is taught, one should first sever feeling;
now, when quiescent extinction is taught, one should first experience quiescent bliss.
Since this is realized as the Buddha, it is not discussed here.
That which is indestructible is eternal, and for this reason it is not [further] analyzed.

From here below, the fourth section explains the preceding teaching on the quiescent bliss of *nirvāṇa*, and proceeds to clarify the distinctions between the characteristics of bliss, such as those of the Buddha and others.
The Buddha has two kinds of bliss:
there is "bliss of tranquility" because he has extinguished and departed from all sufferings; there is "bliss of knowledge" because he has realized the Dharma that accords with the spirit.

Since the meaning of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) regarding the true nature (dharmatā) permeates both the defiled and the pure, there are thus three kinds of bliss:

When the true nature is proclaimed with respect to the phenomena of birth and death, there is the bliss of sensation; when the true nature is proclaimed with respect to the virtues of the Buddha-fruit, there is the bliss of tranquility and the bliss of awakening.

The essence of Buddha-nature is quiescent, being solely quiescent bliss; because it has not yet manifested, there is no bliss of conscious awareness, but because it shall be seen, at the time one attains Bodhi, there is also the bliss of the conscious awareness of Bodhi.
The fifth section from here on provides a re-explanation of points that were hidden within the preceding meaning.
Why is this necessary?

Previously, the Tathāgata taught that the exhaustion of body and wisdom constitutes *nirvāṇa*; now, he teaches that the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*) in all Buddhas constitutes their *nirvāṇa*. Since these two statements appear contradictory, a re-explanation is required.
Furthermore, the Buddha previously stated that the cessation of afflictions within the body is *nirvāṇa*, yet now he proclaims that *nirvāṇa* is like space, its essence being non-existent.
Since these two statements appear contradictory, they must be analyzed and explained.
King Śubhavyūha asks first; within his inquiry, there is first a specific analysis and finally a summary reproach.

Within the specific analysis, there are five points, which may be grouped into three: (1) the address to Māra regarding the Nairañjanā River; (2) the statement that the Bodhisattva has already severed [the fetters]; (3) the address concerning the names given at birth; (4) the address to Māra regarding Vaiśālī; and (5) the teaching to the Mallas concerning the Parinirvāṇa in the final watch of the night.

Regarding the threefold sequence: the first two lines hold that the place where both body and wisdom are utterly extinguished is *nirvāṇa*, and they refute the view that the place where afflictions are severed is such.
The third line holds that the place where delusions are severed is itself the body and wisdom as *nirvāṇa*, and it refutes the preceding view that *nirvāṇa* is like space, having no place of abiding.
The final two lines again hold that the extinction of body and wisdom is *nirvāṇa*, and they refute the view that the place where afflictions are severed is such.

In the critique of the first proposition, the phrase "If the cessation of afflictions were nirvana, this meaning would not be so" sets forth a general negation; the section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation, first posing a self-reflexive challenge. The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata in the past... cites the Buddha’s former words to challenge and reveal the error, while the statement "The Tathāgata in the past, having already severed the afflictions, said he had not yet entered [nirvana]" clarifies that cessation is not [itself] nirvana.
In the second statement, there are two parts:

"If that which is severed were [nirvana], then since bodhisattvas and others have already severed their afflictions over immeasurable kalpas, why are they not called 'nirvana'? This is the first part, which, following the previous pattern, uses the superior to challenge the inferior.
The Buddha has severed and attained this, and the Bodhisattva has likewise severed it; for what reason is it not called *nirvāṇa*?
This also follows the principle of using what comes below to question what comes above.
Since the place where the Bodhisattva severs is not called *nirvāṇa*, it clarifies that the place where the Buddha severs is likewise not *nirvāṇa*.

"Since both are points of abandonment, for what reason is it said that only the Buddhas possess them while Bodhisattvas do not? This is the second sentence, which raises a commonality to challenge a specific distinction.
Since the locus of cessation is no different, why does it exist for the Buddha while it is specifically absent for the bodhisattva?
This is also a case of inferring the above from the below: since the bodhisattva has cessation but lacks nirvāṇa, it is clear that the Buddha’s nirvāṇa is not a locus of cessation.
Regarding these two phrases, the Buddha provides a specific answer below; they should be carefully noted and understood.

In the third question, concerning the point at which the grasping delusions are severed, both body and wisdom constitute *nirvāṇa*. This refutes the previous notion that *nirvāṇa* is like space, having no place of abiding.

Regarding the phrase "if one were to sever what is not [the self]," this is a counter-argument intended to anticipate the Buddha's intention; fearing that the Buddha might be challenged on this point, [the opponent] asserts that the state where delusions are severed is not the body as nirvana, and thus raises this objection.

"Why did the Tathāgata formerly declare that the one born as 'I' is this very body of mine which is nirvāṇa? He raised this statement to pose a challenge: "If it was previously said that the body is [nirvāṇa], how can you now say that nirvāṇa is like space, having no place of abiding?"
In the fourth sentence, first the invitation of Māra is presented, followed by the Buddha’s response.

Below, an objection is raised; therein, first the exhaustion of the body is challenged as being incorrect, and from the words "If [it] were severed" onwards, the point at which afflictions are exhausted is challenged as being correct.

In the fifth sentence, "If at that time it were nirvāṇa," [the text] re-examines the Tathāgata; with "how" and what follows, it interrogates [the premise] to reveal its falsity. Since he was already in nirvāṇa at the moment of severing the afflictions, why did he tell the Mallas of Kuśinagara that he would enter parinirvāṇa during the last watch of the night?
The preceding section constitutes a specific refutation; the phrase "The Tathāgata is truthful, how could he utter such false words?

serves as a general summary of this censure. Below, the Buddha provides an explanation to resolve the matter: first, he absolves himself of fault in response to the aforementioned general censure; then, from the words "As you have said," he provides a detailed answer based on the previous specific questions.

In the preceding section, the statement, "If one says he has attained a broad and long tongue, one should know that the Tathāgata has already abandoned false speech for immeasurable kalpas," serves primarily to exempt himself from fault and to demonstrate that his own words are not false. The subsequent passage beginning with "All Buddhas" cites others by way of analogy, thereby establishing that his own words are indeed not false.
In the subsequent section resolving the objections, the responses are both incomplete and out of order.
Among the first five objections, only three points are answered; the third and fifth are omitted and left unanswered, which is why it is said they are "incomplete."
It is not exhaustive; therefore, it shall be explained separately later.
Within the answers provided, the fourth is answered first, followed by the first, and finally the second; hence, it is said that they are "not in order."
Regarding the meaning of the answer to the fourth [question]:

it clarifies that the state where one has previously severed the afflictions is in fact nirvana; since nirvana is eternal and unchanging, it is proclaimed that one shall enter parinirvāṇa in accordance with the transformation of sentient beings.

Within this response, the passage beginning with "At that time, my śrāvakas... first explains the reasons why Māra previously requested the extinction [of the Dharma], while the section starting from "At that time, my śrāvakas" clarifies the reasons why he had already granted permission for its extinction in the past.
Regarding the opening section, "You say, 'Pāpīyān has invited me,'" this restates the previous question; what follows provides the response and explanation.

Within this, it first clarifies that Māra does not know the truth, and thus requested my extinction. This may be understood through the initial teaching, followed by the analogy, and finally the application.
The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata does not speak of Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha" clarifies that the essence [of the Three Jewels] is eternal, such that Māra remains unaware of it.
The text consists of three sections:

first, it clarifies that the Three Jewels are eternal and without distinction. Because the characteristics of the Three Jewels are distinct, the Buddha does not speak [of them as identical]; yet because the Buddha and the others are without difference—being equal in the sense of being eternal and pure—it is said that they are without distinction.
Because they are eternally without difference, the Buddha-body is eternal.
Māra does not understand this, and therefore he requests my parinirvāṇa.

Second, regarding the Buddha, the Buddha-nature, and nirvāṇa, these three meanings are distinct; therefore, the Buddha does not say that they are without difference, because their causes and effects, as well as their persons and dharmas, are distinct.
It is eternally constant and unchanging, equal for both self and others; therefore, it is said to be without distinction.
Because it is eternally without distinction, the essence of the Buddha is permanently abiding. The Māras do not understand this, and thus they entreat me to enter extinction.

Third, regarding the two dharmas of *nirvāṇa* and *tathatā*, they are explained as being eternally without difference; yet because these two meanings are distinct, the Buddha did not say that these two are without difference.
This point has been argued above.
Because it is eternal, constant, and unchanging, and because it is equal for both self and others, it is said that there is no aging.
Māra did not understand this, and therefore he requested my extinction.

Within the section where Śākyamuni granted permission for his extinction, the initial part explains granting Māra permission for extinction on behalf of evil persons; from the passage "seeing from afar" (*xuánjiàn*) onwards, it clarifies granting Māra permission for extinction on behalf of virtuous persons.
In the first part of the preceding section, the Buddha proclaimed his parinirvāṇa because he was confronted by wicked people who were quarreling and opposing him;

thus, "Because it is so" and the following passages clarify, based on that proclamation of nirvāṇa, the distinctions between the ignorant and the wise, as well as their respective grasping and relinquishing, and their gains and losses.
"Therefore, regarding my [declaration] at Vaiśālī," the following clarifies the reasons for my proclamation of extinction in the past.
The first section is self-evident.
Within the second section, there are six distinct textual divisions:

First, it clarifies that when evil bhikṣus proclaimed that the Tathāgata would enter extinction, his śrāvaka disciples neither saw nor heard this, and thus they believed the Buddha had truly passed away.
Second, from the words "Only the bodhisattvas" onwards, it clarifies that the various bodhisattvas always see and always hear [the Buddha], and therefore do not say the Buddha has entered extinction.

Third, from the words "Although the śrāvaka disciples further say" onwards, it clarifies that what the aforementioned śrāvakas perceived was unreal; although they say the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, the Buddha has in truth not entered extinction. These three points constitute the foundation.

4. From "If those who are my śrāvakas... onwards, based on the first [point] above, it clarifies the loss resulting from false grasping: they are not my disciples, but are the faction of Māra. 5. From "If one says that the Tathāgata does not enter...

onwards, based on the second [point] above, it clarifies the attainment of the correct realization: they are true disciples of the Buddha and not the faction of Māra; this follows the sequence of first conforming and then reversing. 6. From "Like the elder...

onwards, based on the third [point] above, it extensively clarifies that what the śrāvakas perceive is unreal. There are five successive repetitions, each of which first establishes a metaphor, followed by an application to the subject, as can be understood.

Regarding the third conclusion, the phrase "Therefore, I have declared to the Vaiśyas that I shall enter parinirvāṇa" serves as the conclusion based on the first of the preceding two sections; it means that for the sake of those wicked bhikṣus, I have declared my entry into nirvāṇa.
The preceding section clarifies the proclamation of extinction for the sake of evil persons; from here on, it clarifies the proclamation of extinction for the sake of virtuous persons.

Within this, it clarifies that the proclamation of imminent extinction is made for seven types of virtuous persons. The passage beginning with "Kāśyapa... down to Sunakṣatra, having completed the summer retreat, came to my presence" indicates that after the summer *vassa*, the Tathāgata entered *parinirvāṇa* during the autumn.

The *Āgama* sūtras state that the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the eighth month, which corresponds to this [text]; however, throughout this scripture, it frequently states that he entered parinirvāṇa in the second month. This must be due to differences in what was seen or heard by various people.
This concludes the explanation of the fourth objection regarding the King of Virtue.
Next, the first objection is explained; what is the intended meaning of the response?

It clarifies that although he had already previously severed the afflictions and was thus in *nirvāṇa*, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and because his traces of transformation had not yet ceased, he told Māra in the past that he had not entered *nirvāṇa*.

In the text, the initial statement, "For what reason did I formerly at the Nairañjanā River reject Māra? poses a question to initiate the discourse, which is subsequently explained by the author himself. This clarifies that he refused to enter parinirvāṇa because he intended to proclaim the essential Dharma for the seven types of virtuous persons; his activities are immeasurable, and this instance is merely cited as an example.
The passage beginning with "It has a name" answers the second objection, which consists of two points:
"The Bodhisattva has already severed [the defilements]; why then cannot he be called 'nirvāṇa'? is the first point;
"Both are places where [defilements] are severed; why does the Buddha possess this while the Bodhisattva does not? is the second point.
Now, regarding this separate response: first, the initial phrase is answered; then, from "Nirvāṇa means 'no'" (*ne yan bu*) downward, the second phrase is answered.
Within the first phrase, how is the intended meaning answered?

It is explained that the state where bodhisattvas sever afflictions is termed "nirvāṇa"; however, because they do not see the nature [of reality] while severing afflictions, it cannot be termed "Great.
Regarding the latter phrase, what is the intended meaning of the answer?

It clarifies that "nirvana" merely signifies the absence of meaning [in the conventional sense], not the sense of annihilation. Although a bodhisattva does sever all afflictions, they cannot fail to arise; thus, it cannot be called "nirvana in the sense of non-meaning. For this reason, the Buddha possesses it, whereas the bodhisattva does not.
The meaning of the answer is as follows.

Within the preceding passage, it first clarifies that the point at which a bodhisattva attains cessation is not "great," and subsequently clarifies that the point at which a Tathāgata attains cessation is "great.

Regarding the clarification concerning bodhisattvas, the phrase "There is a named nirvāṇa, but it is not the Great Nirvāṇa" briefly sets forth the topic; the section beginning with "How so? provides the explanation, first posing the question and then resolving it.
These two meanings are explained as follows:
first, because one severs afflictions without seeing the Buddha-nature, the severance is not ultimate; therefore, it is not called "Great.
Second, because one does not see the nature, the nirvana attained possesses only bliss and purity, but lacks self and permanence; since these four attributes are incomplete, it is not called "Great."

In the section below explaining the Buddha, the phrase "if one sees the Buddha-nature and severs afflictions, it is called 'Great'" reverses the first clause, while "because one sees the nature, it is called 'Eternal and Blissful,'" etc., reverses the subsequent clauses.

In the answer to the latter part of the verse, first the definition and meaning of *nirvāṇa* are established as being neither [existence] nor non-existence; from the phrase "one who has severed the afflictions is not so named" onwards, the teaching is revealed according to its name.

In the preceding Chinese text, there are eleven successive sections: the first seven and the final four. In the eighth section, the Tathāgata himself provides an explanation, taking what others have said to demonstrate its lack of meaning.
However, in this text, *nir* is definitely not named as "non-existence," as it is explained in the first sentence and not further discussed elsewhere;
*vāṇa*, moreover, contains many meanings that differ in every instance.
In the subsequent exposition of the Dharma, it is clarified that the severing of afflictions is not the meaning of "non-existence"; therefore, the severing of afflictions is not called *nirvāṇa*.
"Not giving rise to afflictions" is its underlying meaning; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
One who merely eliminates afflictions is not said to possess *nirvāṇa*, as this was explained in resolving the aforementioned objection regarding the Bodhisattva’s lack thereof;
"not giving rise to afflictions" explains that which belongs exclusively to the Buddha in resolving the aforementioned objection.

Question: For what reason is the bodhisattva’s severance of fetters not called "non-arising," whereas the Buddhas’ locus of severance is specifically termed "non-arising"? There are three explanations: 1. The fetters severed by the bodhisattva are still subject to arising; therefore, they are not called "non-arising. The fetters severed by the Buddhas are never again subject to arising; therefore, it is specifically called "non-arising. 2. The bodhisattva has severed the fetters of the desire realm but has not yet severed those of the form and formless realms; therefore, it is not called "non-arising. The Buddhas have completely severed the fetters of all three realms; therefore, it is specifically called "non-arising. 3. The bodhisattva has severed the fetters of the present life but has not yet severed those of future lives; therefore, it is not called "non-arising. The Buddhas have eternally severed the fetters of all past, present, and future lives; therefore, it is specifically called "non-arising."

First, distinguishing them according to their delusions: although a Bodhisattva severs the fetters according to his capacity, he does not sever them completely; because they arise again within his mind, it is said that they are not non-arising.
The Buddha, however, has severed them exhaustively so that they never arise again; therefore, it is called non-arising.

Second, regarding the distinction based on the mind: although a bodhisattva has severed coarse afflictions, the seven consciousnesses still remain; because the nature of the mind undergoes arising and ceasing, it is not "unborn.
The Buddha possesses only the true mind, and the true mind is eternally abiding; therefore, it is said to be "unborn."
Third, distinguishing according to principle: the Bodhisattva perceives that there are afflictions to be severed; because they were not originally non-arising, they are not "unborn.
The Buddha realizes the suchness of dharmas (*dharmatā*); he knows that all afflictions have never arisen from the beginning and likewise do not cease now; therefore, they are called "unborn."
Question: The King of Virtue previously raised five objections; you have answered three of them above. Why have you not explained the third and the fifth? Answer:
When answering the second and fourth objections above, the remaining two became intelligible by implication; therefore, they were not answered separately.
How can this be understood?

In the response to the fourth objection, the Tathāgata stated that he spoke to the Mallas to inform them that [the Buddha] would pass away; in the fifth [objection], he stated that he spoke to the Mallas to tell them that he would pass away during the last watch of the night. Since these statements are similar, why trouble yourself to answer again?

Furthermore, in the response to the second objection raised previously, it was clarified that the severance of afflictions is termed "nirvāṇa" or described as "great nirvāṇa. Since the refutation of the third point—which argued that the locus of the severance of afflictions is untenable—has already been made manifest, why labor further to explain it?
Therefore, there is no separate answer.

Above, the first section generally addressed all phenomena to demonstrate the seven distinctions; from here on, the second section discusses the seven in relation to the Buddha to clarify that these seven are non-distinct.
Within this section concerning the Buddha, only five meanings are elucidated; the two sections on the Dharma and the Sangha are omitted and not analyzed.
Regarding the statement, "The Buddha’s non-arising of affliction is called *nirvāṇa*," this clarifies the meaning of *nirvāṇa* with respect to the Buddha.
"Unimpeded wisdom is called the Tathāgata" explains the meaning of "Tathāgata" from the perspective of the Buddha.
"That which is not ordinary beings and so forth is called Buddha-nature" explains the meaning of "Buddha-nature" from the perspective of the Buddha.
“Filling immeasurable lands with wisdom of body and mind is called ‘space’” explains the meaning of space according to the Buddha.
“Permanently abiding and unchanging is called ‘true reality’ (dharmatā)” explains the meaning of true reality according to the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "For this reason, the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa," it is because the Buddha is eternally abiding and immutable; thus, in reality, he never ultimately enters final nirvāṇa. "This is called the seventh" serves as a general conclusion.
Regarding the eighth virtue, there is first the initial inquiry, followed by the exposition, and finally the conclusion.
Within the exposition, the eight dharmas are declared to constitute its essence; they are first enumerated here, and will be explained in detail below.
Among these eight, the first seven encompass the skillful means of practice, while the last one constitutes accomplishment.

Within the first seven, the first two are practices for detachment from the conditioned; the next three are practices for seeking enlightenment; and the final two are practices for gathering in sentient beings.
Regarding the former two [categories], "eliminating five things" means severing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and thereby departing from the fruit of birth and death.
"Being free from five things" means distancing oneself from the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) and extinguishing the cause of birth and death.
Furthermore, by abandoning five things, one leaves behind the dharmas of birth and death; by distancing oneself from five things, one removes the dharmas that obstruct the Path.
Moreover, by abandoning five things, one leaves behind the sources of outflows (*āsrava*); by distancing oneself from five things, one correctly eliminates the substance of the outflows themselves.

Next, among these three types, "accomplishing six and cultivating five" refers to the practice for proceeding toward enlightenment; that is, accomplishing the six recollections, cultivating the five concentrations, guarding one matter, and encompassing the vow for enlightenment.
Within the latter two types, "approaching through the four matters" refers to the mind that transforms sentient beings, namely the four immeasurables;
"faithfully conforming to the single reality" refers to the method for delivering sentient beings, namely the path of the One Vehicle.

These seven expedient means, culminating in the perfection of virtue, sever the afflictions of the five abodes and their inherent fetters; when the true mind emerges from these obstructions, it is called "liberation of the mind."
Being free from attachment to phenomena and possessing mastery over worldly knowledge is called "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*).
This will be explained extensively below.
Within the first section of this explanation, there is first a question followed by the exposition.
The commentary consists of five parts:
first, a general introduction;
second, a listing of the five names.

Third, a general explanation of the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*): first the question is posed, then the answer is given, explained through six points. They cause sentient beings to continue in the cycle of birth and death, never being separated from their heavy burden.
These two meanings are explained in terms of their faults:
because one relies on them to create causes, they "cause sentient beings’ birth and death to continue in succession";
because one relies on them to receive retribution, they cause sentient beings "not to be free from the heavy burden."

Regarding the two phrases "dispersion" and "aggregation," their meanings should be correctly understood as follows: the *skandhas* (aggregates) carry the sense of "multitude" and also the sense of "collection.
"Dispersion" refers to the multitude;
"aggregation" refers to the collection.
They are called "dispersed" because they are subdivided into the immeasurable; they are called "aggregated" because they are collectively described as five.
This explains the nature and characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas) by showing that when sought within the three periods of time, their essential meaning cannot be found.
The characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) are impermanent; therefore, they are subsumed within the three periods of time.
The nature of the aggregates is false and provisional; when traced to its source, it lacks reality; therefore, they cannot be apprehended.
The section beginning with "By this" concludes [the argument].
Fourth, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) is presented by way of wisdom.

First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is clarified; within the discussion of form, it is first shown that it is not existent, and from the words "for the sake of the world" onwards, it is demonstrated that it is not non-existent.
To clarify that [the aggregates] do not exist within existence: "Although one sees the aggregate of form, one does not see its characteristics" briefly clarifies their non-existence.
Since the discussion of existence necessarily implies non-existence, the word "although" (*sui*) is used.

The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: because one cannot find a self-nature when seeking it within the ten forms, one does not perceive their characteristics; these ten forms consist of the five sense organs and the five sense objects.

This sutra frequently discusses ten types of matter throughout its sections, yet it does not mention non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa). This is because the characteristics of non-informative matter are subtle and hidden; they constitute the body but do not manifest externally, and for this reason, it is not mentioned here.
The preceding section clarified that [the aggregates] are not existent; by stating "they are called aggregates for the sake of the world," it clarifies that they are not non-existent.
Next, regarding the aggregate of sensation, the statement "there are one hundred and eight sensations" clarifies that sensation is not non-existent.
