"There is no agent" clarifies, with reference to the first phrase, the mindlessness of inhalation.
"There is no destroyer" clarifies, with reference to the subsequent phrase, the mindlessness of non-inhalation.
Regarding the statement that "one dharma arises from another dharma," there are three distinct types of dharmas:
First, stone; second, iron; third, when a person is required, the stone approaches the iron.

Within this context, when the two things—stone and iron—are compared with one another, it can be said that there is difference and distinct arising; the two distinct entities, stone and iron, are both termed "distinct phenomena" (*dharmāntara*).
This is because the iron exists as a distinct phenomenon (*dharmāntara*), and the magnet produces the function of attraction as a distinct phenomenon.

When these three phenomena are compared with one another, they can likewise be described as being distinct existents and distinct productions; both the person and the stone are different from each other and are thus termed "distinct phenomena."
This is because that person exists as a distinct phenomenon (*dharmāntara*); just as a magnet arises as a distinct phenomenon with the property of attraction.
Since a distinct phenomenon does not exist, that distinct phenomenon is destroyed; this may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
There are six analogies [in this section].
First, the phrase "like fire" is an analogy for the aforementioned magnet;
"unable to burn wood" is an analogy for its inability to attract iron.
Furthermore, it is because of the absence of mind that it is said not to burn.
The metaphor "fire arises and the fuel is destroyed" illustrates that the preceding distinct phenomena exist and thus give rise [to the fire].
In the second metaphor, "the mugwort and the heliotrope follow the sun," this again illustrates the magnet.
"Nor is there respect, etc. is a metaphor for not attracting iron.
"Different from the nature of phenomena," etc., is a metaphor for the prior difference wherein different phenomena arise.
The remaining metaphors and their applications are all understandable from the text.
The nature [of these] is the same as the preceding analogy; therefore, it is said, "Thus.
Apart from conditions, one cannot draw forth and attain bodhi.
To clarify this through further analogies: "Ignorance cannot draw forth the formative forces" means that apart from conditions they do not arise, and the same applies to the others.
It may also be called "conditioned by ignorance, formations arise," meaning that conditions are capable of producing [results]; the same applies to the others.
Since this principle is eternally constant, it is said: "Whether a Buddha appears or not, [this nature] abides forever."
The preceding first section refutes the latter attachment to clarify that the path must be cultivated.
From here on, the second section refutes the former attachment to clarify that there is no fixed nature abiding within sentient beings.

Within this, first the essential nature and characteristics of the Buddha-nature are clarified; the section beginning with "If all sentient beings understand the Buddha-nature" exhorts them to practice and enter it.
The former part contains four sections:
first, refuting the notion that the Buddha-nature merely dwells within sentient beings.
2. From "Just as the four great elements" onwards, [the text] refutes the notion that Buddha-nature definitely exists within sentient beings;
3. From "As the King declared" onwards, it extensively clarifies—relative to the first point—that Buddha-nature is neither identical to nor separate from [sentient beings];
4. From "The Tathāgata’s eternal abiding is called the Self" onwards, it extensively clarifies—relative to the second point—that sentient beings are neither existent nor non-existent.
At the beginning of the text, the phrase "if one says that nature abides within arising" cites what was previously grasped.
It refers to the prior statement that all sentient beings possess a nature, which is termed "abiding within arising."
Below the phrase "permanently non-abiding," the text proceeds to refute [the opponent's view].
First, it provides an exposition by means of principle (*dharma*), followed by an analogy, and finally an application.

Within the exposition of principle, the initial statement "a permanent phenomenon has no abiding" establishes the correct reasoning, while "if it were to abide, it would be impermanent" refutes the false and reveals the correct.
There are six analogies [in this section].
First, the twelve links of dependent origination are cited as an analogy.
"Just as the twelve links have no fixed place of abiding" clarifies the aforementioned lack of abiding.
The passage beginning with "If there were abiding" clarifies that prior abiding is itself impermanent.
A question is raised:
Since causes and conditions constitute the essence of sentient beings, how can the absence of abiding be called permanent?
The commentary states:
If one discusses matters from the perspective of a person, then because the conditions truly possess abiding, one cannot say they are permanent.

However, if one sets aside the person and discusses the general principle of the mutual arising of the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no fixed attribution; therefore, there is no place of abiding.
The characteristics and their arising are fixed and have never been absent even for a moment; therefore, they are called "constant.
Second, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is cited as an analogy.
Third, the Dharma-realm is cited.
Fourth, the enumeration of the bases (āyatana).
Fifth, the enumeration of the aggregates (skandha); this also refers generally to the designations of the aggregates, elements, and bases, such as the "dharma-element" (dharmadhātu) and so forth.
Sixth, the enumeration of space (ākāśa).
The section on "Buddha-nature" concludes here.

From this point onward is the second part, which refutes the notion that Buddha-nature definitely exists within sentient beings; it clarifies that all sentient beings are said to "possess" it because they will attain it in the future, not because the essence of the fruit already exists within their bodies.
The passage contains two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Buddha-nature manifests when the time arrives;
second, from the phrase "all beings possess the nature of non-retrogression" onwards, it clarifies that all sentient beings certainly deserve to be called "possessing [the Buddha-nature]."
In the preceding section, the analogy was first presented; in the following section, the Dharma is clarified through that analogy.
How do the Dharma and the analogy correspond?

Just as those four great elements—solidity, moisture, warmth, and so forth—are distinct in their mental characteristics yet each has a separate essence, such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). It is simply so by its own nature.
This analogy clarifies that the Buddha-nature has no intention to emerge; yet when the time arrives, it manifests, for such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Within the analogy, the "four great elements" are cited as the illustrative entities.
Next, the characteristics of the analogy are analyzed.
The merit of their creation is equal, and thus they are said to have "equal power.
Although their power is equal, their essential natures differ; therefore, there is a distinction between solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
Because that which is produced varies, there are distinctions such as red, white, yellow, and black.
The following provides a general explanation:
"Furthermore, these four great elements also have no karma" means that they lack the mental karma that would differentiate them through desire.

Regarding the phrase "because they belong to different dharma-realms, they are not similar": the four great elements (mahābhūta) are called "different dharma-realms" because they are distinct; thus, solidity and the other qualities are each dissimilar.
"Buddha-nature is also like this" combines [the analogy] with the preceding four great elements.

Regarding the phrase "Because it belongs to a different dharma-realm, it manifests when the time arrives": this means that the distinct dharma-realm is inherently dissimilar [to other non-existent things].
Buddha-nature is different from the non-existence of a rabbit's horns; therefore, when sentient beings cultivate the path and the time arrives, it immediately manifests.

Furthermore, false dharmas are extinguished when cultivation reaches its culmination, whereas the Buddha-nature, being distinct from them, manifests when cultivation reaches its culmination; thus it is called the "distinct Dharma-realm.
From here on, the second section explains that sentient beings possess [the Buddha-nature] by means of five meanings.
First, it is called "existent" because there is no principle by which sentient beings could lose or extinguish their Buddha-nature;
this phrase is spoken with reference to the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
Second, it is called "existent" because [the Bodhisattvas] are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*).
"Avaivartika" is here termed "non-retrogression. Since at the time of its realization there is never again any falling back, one knows that it definitely exists.
This phrase is spoken with reference to the middle period [of existence].
The latter three are explained in relation to the future limit (*aparānta*).
Among them, regarding the initial statement that "it is called 'existence' (*bhava*) because it will come to be," there are two meanings of "existence":

first, the fruit of the means (*upāya-phala*) which is about to arise is called existence; second, the fruit of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-phala*) which is about to manifest is called existence.
Because sentient beings currently possess the certainty of attaining the fruit, it is said that they "have" it.
This phrase is the general statement;

the following two are the specific details. Regarding "because of the certainty of attainment," this refers to the fruit of the means: since the cause is presently present, the fruit will certainly be attained.
Regarding the phrase "to see with certainty," this means that in view of the fruit of intrinsic purity, one should see it as certain because its present causes exist.
The section beginning with "Therefore" concludes [the argument].
From here on is the third section, which extensively clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither identical to nor separate from [phenomena]; first the analogy, followed by the application.
Regarding the phrase "there are difficulties below," the following provides a detailed analysis.
Within the analogies, there are six parts:
first, the analogy of the Tathāgata preaching the sūtras to reveal the nature and instruct people.
The "king" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata; the "minister" is a metaphor for this sutra; the "elephant" is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature; and the "blind man" is a metaphor for sentient beings.
The Buddha’s manifestation and exposition of the Dharma through vocal sound is called "addressing a minister."
Explaining the sutra to reveal the nature (dharmatā) in order to instruct sentient beings is called "leading an elephant before a group of blind men.
Second, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the minister," the sūtra provides a metaphor for revealing the nature through the Dharma.
The Sūtra being spoken for the sake of the noble ones is called "Receiving the King’s Edict.
Causing people to read it together is called "Gathering the Blind.
Revealing the nature so that they may know it is called "Showing the Elephant."
3. From "At that time, that blind man" onwards is the analogy for sentient beings knowing their own nature.
The act of the mind and thought grasping at objects is described as "touching with the hand.
4. From "The minister returned to himself" onwards is the analogy for the transformative Dharma being received by others, which conversely reveals the sacred mind.
The manifestation of the Sage’s mind is termed "White King.
Having completed the revelation of the nature, it is termed "Demonstration Concluded.
From the fifth section, "At that time the King," onwards, there is the parable of the Tathāgata interrogating sentient beings and receiving their various answers.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the question as to whether [he] has seen;
second, the answer that he has already seen.
Third, the questions regarding what was seen;
fourth, the answers concerning what was seen, each interpreted according to their own inclinations, resulting in various different responses.
Sixth, from the passage "Just as those blind men did not describe the elephant" onwards, there is the analogy of neither being identical with nor separate from [the object].

"He does not say 'elephant'" clarifies that it is neither identical [to the elephant] nor is it the case that he does not speak of it; "apart from this there is no elephant" demonstrates that it is not separate [from it].
Next, the following lines combine these two.
The passage beginning with "The king is like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha," etc., corresponds to the first [section] mentioned previously.
The section beginning with "When these sentient beings have heard this teaching" skips ahead to correspond with the fifth.

In the analogy, there are eight distinct objects of contact; in the synthesis, there are six: the five aggregates constitute five, and the integration of these five aggregates to form a "self" or "person" constitutes the sixth.
Within these six [sections], each first establishes the essential nature (*dharmatā*), while the portion beginning with "Why... provides the explanation.
Within the explanations, there is first the teaching (*dharma*), next the analogy (*upamā*), and finally the application (*anusandhi*).

From "Just as those blind men each spoke... onwards, it applies the preceding sixth point—that [the parts] are neither identical nor separate. This first cites the previous analogy, then applies it to reveal the teaching, and finally concludes with "Therefore."
What is the meaning of this?
It is as follows: just as the nature of the barley does not exist apart from the sprout, the stalk, and so forth up to the fruit, it is called "not separate.
Yet, while the sprout, stalk, branches, and leaves undergo successive changes, the nature of the barley remains eternally constant; thus, it is said to be "not identical."
The nature of these six dharmas is similar to this description.
However, since it was previously stated that my [teaching] might be confused with the "self" (ātman) propounded by non-Buddhists, the following section distinguishes between them.

By stating, "The self spoken of by non-Buddhists is truly no-self," one sets the heterodox aside from the orthodox; and by stating, "The self of sentient beings is precisely the five aggregates," one clarifies the orthodox as distinct from the heterodox.
Among these, the first teaching is illustrated by a metaphor.
There are six distinct metaphors:
the first metaphor presents the illustration and the application separately, while the subsequent five metaphors distinguish the illustration and then provide a collective application.
From here below is the fourth section, which extensively clarifies that sentient beings are neither existent nor non-existent.

First, it clarifies that they are not non-existent: "Because [the fruit] will be attained. Then, from "If I were to say that form is the Buddha-nature" onwards, it demonstrates that they are not existent, because the aggregates (skandhas) are not the nature itself.

In the preceding section, the first part provides a detailed exposition and the latter part offers a summary. Within the detailed exposition, there are eight sections: first, explaining the self (*ātman*) as the nature;

second, explaining the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) as the Buddha-nature; third, explaining faith (*śraddhā*) as the nature; fourth, explaining the supreme love for an only child as the nature; fifth, explaining the fourth faculty and power (*indriya-bala*) as the nature; sixth, explaining the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as the nature.
"Buddha-nature is called the twelve links of dependent origination" is a brief statement of the heading; the meaning is as explained above.

From "Why? onwards is the explanation: "Because of dependent origination, the Tathāgata is eternal" means that because the Tathāgata has thoroughly realized the essence of the twelve links of dependent origination, he attains eternity; because he realizes and achieves the eternity of the Buddha, it is called Buddha-nature.
The passage "All sentient beings" [and below] clarifies that all sentient beings definitely possess such causal conditions and a real nature, which is termed "having Buddha-nature.

This explanation of causal conditions might be confused with the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) pertaining to birth and death; therefore, the distinction between them is clarified below.
These twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Buddha-nature; this nature is the Tathāgata.
In the seventh [chapter], the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom are proclaimed as the Buddha-nature.
In the eighth, the gateway of the *mūrdhan-samādhi* is proclaimed as the Buddha-nature.

The preceding section was a detailed discussion; from the passage "As I have previously explained various dharmas" onwards, it concludes them collectively to clarify that the aforementioned dharmas should properly be designated as "existent."
The twelve links of dependent origination constitute the very substance of sentient beings; why, then, do you say they "shall be obtained" as existence (*bhava*)?
It is called "to be obtained" because its realization occurs in the future, not because its substance exists in the future.
The preceding section clarified that [the self] is not non-existent; the following section reveals that it is not existent.
First, it was stated that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); subsequently, this is applied by analogy to the remaining aggregates.

Thus far, the first part—combining the individual and collective aspects—has elucidated the characteristics of the essential substance. Hereafter, there is the exhortation to practice and realize [this truth].
"If one has already produced the nature [of awakening], there is no need for cultivation"—this is an exhortation to practice and realization by way of counter-argument.
"The cultivation of the ten abodes" and below is an exhortation to practice and realization in accordance with the principle.
Within this, there are four parts:
First, it clarifies that although those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) practice, they see only a small portion;

second, from "how much more so for those who do not practice" onwards, it uses the noble ones as a contrast to the ordinary, clarifying that ordinary beings do not see [the truth] and must therefore cultivate the Path;
third, from "like Mañjuśrī" onwards, it demonstrates that Mañjuśrī saw [the truth] only after long cultivation.
4. From "How so? onwards, the Great is used to illustrate the Small, clarifying that the Small cannot be seen [without effort] and that one must necessarily cultivate the Path.

From the beginning of this chapter up to this point constitutes the first section of questions and answers, which distinguishes the Dharma; from here on follows the second section, which praises the sutra and exhorts study.
First, there is the exhortation to study; from "The Buddha-nature is inconceivable" onwards, the text praises its own excellence.
Within the former section, there are three parts:
first, the exhortation to cultivate the aspiration to see the Buddha-nature by personally upholding this sutra.
2. From "Those who see existence" below, there is an exhortation to make offerings to and uphold those who possess [this teaching];
3. From "If there be" below, the rarity of hearing this sutra is cited to inspire people to revere and study it.
Below, the praise for the sutra is divided into three parts:
First, lamenting that people do not reflect, thereby using this to categorize the sutra;
second, from "The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is also like this" onwards, distinguishing the sutra as being identical to humanity;
third, from "Like the great ocean" onwards, providing a formal eulogy of the Dharma.
Regarding the praise of those among humanity, there are three distinct categories:
first, praising the inconceivable faith that arises from the sutras based on the ten levels of faith;
second, the words of the Lion:

From "How is it that a bodhisattva does not regress? onwards, there is praise for the inconceivability of initiating practice based on the sūtras from the perspective of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

Third, from "The bodhisattva clearly knows and sees that there is no... onwards, there is praise for the inconceivability of accomplishing virtues based on the sūtras from the perspective of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The beginning and middle [of this section] have three parts:
first, a formal praise of the reliance on the sūtra that gives rise to inconceivable faith;
second, from the words "The Lion said" onwards, citing many instances of lack of faith to establish the inconceivability of faith; [and third, the conclusion].
3. From "Good son" onwards, it clarifies the manifold benefits of this sutra, showing that those who hear it now will certainly be able to believe it.
The first part consists of five phrases:
the first four clarify the inconceivability of what is believed, and the last one manifests the inconceivability of the capacity to believe; these mutually illuminate one another.

Regarding the first four [points], the first clarifies that the Buddha-nature is inconceivable; the second clarifies that the Three Jewels are inconceivable; the third, based on the first, clarifies that all sentient beings possess a nature that is inconceivable; and the fourth, based on the second, clarifies that the essential attributes of the Buddha Jewel are inconceivable.
Because this sūtra reveals faith through the very dharmas in which one has faith, it can be understood that the capacity for faith is thereby made known.
In the second section, the Lion first states, "As the Buddha has taught, one can believe in the inconceivable," thus recounting the Buddha’s previous words;
then, from the phrase "This great assembly" onwards, he cites the many who lack faith in order to establish the inconceivability of faith.
The third point is as previously understood.
From here on, the second section clarifies the inconceivability of initiating practice based upon the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
This text is divided into two parts:

First, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s undertaking of practice is non-regressive; second, from "Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is inconceivable" onwards, it praises his conduct as being inconceivable.
Within the former [section], the Lion first asks about the initiation [of practice]: "How does a Bodhisattva know for himself that he is not regressing?"
The Buddha explains this for them, first distinguishing the points and subsequently concluding them.

Within the section on distinctions: first, he tests his mind amidst harmful suffering; from the phrase "for the sake of destroying suffering" onwards, he fortifies his mind amidst beneficial suffering.
There are four aspects within "increasing":
first, maintaining firm resolve without regressing during the practice of bestowing happiness;
second, from the phrase "for the sake of the Dharma" onwards, maintaining firm resolve without regressing during the practice of seeking the Dharma.
3. From "In order to destroy the suffering of all sentient beings" onwards, [the text describes] the firm resolve that does not retreat within the practice of rescuing from suffering;
4. From "Cultivating deliverance" onwards, [it describes] the firm resolve that does not retreat within the six practices of gathering virtuous conduct.
The first section is clear.
In the second section, the initial part describes how the Bodhisattva burns his own body to seek the Dharma with a firm mind that does not regress;
from the passage "Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses afflictions" onwards, it describes how he seeks the Dharma through other forms of suffering with a firm mind that does not regress.
In the third section, the first part rescues from the suffering of hunger, and the latter rescues from the suffering of illness.
Within the former, he first rescues from hunger at other times;
the passage beginning with "in times of famine" describes how he can rescue beings from hunger during the kalpa of scarcity.
In the preceding section on other times, there is first a general exposition followed by a specific one.

Within the general exposition, the initial portion clarifies receiving a physical body to save sentient beings; the subsequent section, beginning with "Although he receives the body of a beast, he ultimately does not commit [evil]," definitively establishes its cause.
Within this, the first part clarifies not creating new karma;
from "If in the future" onwards, it clarifies the application of past karma, first through the Dharma and then through a simile.
Past evil karma is like a ghost within the body; by the power of compassionate vows, one undergoes all of it, just as the forms of ghosts manifest entirely through the power of a mantra.
The lower [categories] may be understood accordingly. Question:
Among the two types of birth—*paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformation)—into which type are these received bodies subsumed?
The commentary states:
"Segmented" [existence] is so called because it is the fruit of tainted, unwholesome karma. Question:

If this were merely the death of the segmented [body], why does the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* state that above the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) there is the "death of transformation" (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*)?
The explanation is as follows:
from the stage of the spiritual lineage upward, Bodhisattvas possess five kinds of bodies.
First is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* as the excellence of the six sense bases that is beginningless and naturally so;
second is the Body of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*), which refers to what is obtained from having cultivated goodness since time immemorial;
third is the Responsive Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which arises through the application of function based on the former two.
The fourth is the body of transformation, which refers to the fruit of untainted karma conditioned by [wisdom] illumination;
the fifth is the body of fragmented birth, which refers to the fruit of tainted karma within the three realms.
Among these five, the first two are its true body, while the third is its response-body.
Within the aforementioned *ābhisaṃskārika* [death], there is the confusion of transformation; within the aforementioned *prātibhāsika* [death], there is the confusion of segmentation.
That which is called "transformative death" (*pariṇāmikī-maraṇa*) in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* refers to the fourth category;
what is now called "segmented" corresponds to the fifth category, and thus they do not contradict one another.
The preceding section concludes the general overview.
From "Receiving the Bear" (*pārṣad*) onwards is the specific analysis.

Within the section on "relieving the suffering of illness," the first part clarifies how Bodhisattvas can relieve the suffering of illness during the *roga-kalpa* (age of pestilence); from "If there are sentient beings afflicted by ghostly illnesses" onwards, it clarifies how they can relieve the suffering of illness at other times.
In the fourth section, the non-retrogression in the cultivation of goodness is clear from the text and thus easily understood.
The preceding portion concludes the individual explanations.
The passage beginning with "When making this vow, it is called non-retrogression" serves as a general conclusion.
The preceding section, the first, clarifies that one who possesses the spiritual lineage (gotra) gives rise to practice and does not regress.
From here on, the second section praises its inconceivability.
"Furthermore, it is inconceivable" serves as the general heading; "Why? and what follows provides the explanation.
The commentary consists of eight sections, the text of which is clear and easily understood.
Below, the inconceivable perfection of virtues achieved through world-transcendence is elucidated.
The initial passage, “The Bodhisattva clearly knows and sees that there are no sentient beings,” etc., refers to the internal realization of equality, which is termed "inconceivable."
Below the section "The Final Stage of Rebirth," the skillful mastery of the eight aspects is termed "inconceivable.
Regarding the first [aspect], birth in Tuṣita, there are four distinct textual sections:
first, a general explanation that the Bodhisattva’s birth in Tuṣita Heaven is inconceivable.

Second, from "Why" onwards, the reason why Bodhisattvas are born predominantly [in the desire realm] is explained; first there is the question, followed by the explanation. Because it is superior, they are born predominantly [there].
"Superior within the desire realm" is stated as a general heading.

The following provides a specific explanation: "The lower heavens are characterized by negligence, while the higher heavens are characterized by dullness. This indicates the superiority of this retribution by contrasting it with other heavens.

Regarding the statement, "By practicing precepts and generosity, one attains a body in the upper or lower [heavens]; by practicing generosity, precepts, and meditative concentration, one attains Tuṣita," this indicates its superiority by contrasting it with other heavens.
How can there be meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within the distracted stages of the desire realm?
This is not the eight dhyānas.

Because the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) arises within the stages of the desire realm and leads to birth in that heaven, it is said that by practicing concentration one obtains a body in Tuṣita.
3. From "Censuring" onwards, it reveals the distinction between the noble and the ordinary.
The passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva censures existence and never performs the karma for Tuṣita" explicitly clarifies this distinction from the ordinary.
The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation.
What is the intent of this explanation?

It clarifies that a Bodhisattva attains the capacity to teach and transform sentient beings wherever they are born, not solely in Tuṣita; therefore, one does not exclusively crave birth there by creating karma for that purpose.
4. From "There are three excellences in being born in Tuṣita" onwards, the superiority [of this state] over inferior states is distinguished.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, clarifying that the Bodhisattva’s three matters of retribution are superior.
The section beginning with "The three profound joys" clarifies the excellence of its cause.
Question: Previously it was stated that one is born without creating karma; how can it now be said that there is an excellence of cause?
The commentary states:
Although one does not create contaminated karma that leads to rebirth, because there is the power of great compassion and vows as the cause, it is said that "the cause is superior.

Third, from the passage "Although these three matters are superior" onwards, it clarifies the superiority of purity regarding the aforementioned three matters: not envying others' views and not being conceited in one's own mind.
4. From "Not creating [karmic] destiny" onwards, the superior characteristics are revealed by means of the preceding three matters.
Second, it clarifies the descent from Tuṣita and entry into the womb.

Within this, first it clarifies that at the time of descending from Tuṣita, the great earth trembles; below, the reason for this trembling is explained through two meanings, the text of which is clear and easily understood.
The entry into the womb, the dwelling in the womb, and the emergence from the womb are easy to understand; the rest is omitted for brevity.
Thus far has been the praise of the person [who taught].
Regarding the statement, "The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is likewise thus inconceivable," this is the second section, which demonstrates that the sūtra is identical to the person.

The section beginning with "Like the ocean" constitutes the third segment, which is the formal praise of the Dharma itself; it first provides a simile and then applies it to the subject, and for those points that are difficult to understand, there follows a further detailed analysis.
In the analogy, first the subject is introduced, followed by the enumeration of the eight names, and finally their characteristics are distinguished.
Within each instance, there are three factors:

first, the power of the sentient beings' merit causes the ocean to gradually deepen, making it easier to enter; second, as the wind blows favorably, one moves further from the shore, which is also termed "gradually deepening"; third, as the river waters flow into it, the water level subsequently rises, which is also termed "gradually deepening."
Regarding the other two matters within the intermediate section, the text is abbreviated and does not analyze them.
Within the "Synthesis" (*he*) section, the initial statement, "Nirvana thus has eight inconceivables," synthesizes the first general summary.
Next, they are combined individually.
The first section may be understood as it stands.
Within the second section, first the profundity is revealed by way of the person, and subsequently the profundity of the treatise is explained.
Among human beings, first [the text] refers to the Tathāgata’s profound clarity; next, it refers to ordinary persons; and finally, it refers to those of the two vehicles.
That "those of the two vehicles can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" is one inconceivable matter.
"The minds of those of the Two Vehicles are free from afflictions and their bodies have no fixed abode, yet they are not called 'eternal'"; these are the two inconceivables.
Below, within the discussion of the Middle Way, the manifold dharmas are distinguished, though they cannot be fully expounded here.
The remainder of the text is intelligible.
"Therefore, this sutra is like the ocean" serves as the conclusion.
First was the analogy, followed by the application [to the teaching], and now it is further elucidated.
The Lion first asks:
"If it is said that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished, and this is called 'profound,'" this cites the Buddha’s previous statement which employed a metaphorical analogy.
From the words "There are four modes of birth" (*catur-yoni*) onwards, he poses a question based upon that [analogy].
What is the intent of this question?

It was previously stated that since the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished, he is free from the bondage of birth; being thus free from the bondage of birth, he possesses mastery over birth. For what reason, then, among the four modes of birth, does he not undergo transformation-birth (*upapāduka*) but instead undergo womb-birth (*jarāyuja*)?
Within this, first there is a general enumeration of the four modes of birth;
next, their names are listed, the meaning of which is as explained in the separate chapter;
finally, they are analyzed with respect to human beings.
Below, a challenge is posed: "The Buddha has attained mastery; for what cause and condition does he not undergo transformation-birth (*upapāduka*)?
Below, the Buddha answers this:
"All sentient beings are born by way of the four modes of birth" (*catur-yoni*), distinguishing ordinary beings from the Sage.

"Having attained the noble dharmas, one does not obtain birth from an egg or moisture as before"—this distinguishes the noble from the ordinary and explains that the Tathāgata does not undergo the two lower modes of birth.
From "At the beginning of the kalpa" onwards, there are eight successive explanations clarifying why he is not born by transformation (*upapāduka*):
first, it clarifies that because the Tathāgata did not appear at the beginning of the kalpa, he is not born by transformation.
Why does he not appear?
At the beginning of a kalpa, sentient beings have not yet given rise to afflictions and lack the vessel for the Path.
Second, it is clarified that because the Tathāgata relies on the supreme penetration of the Dharma, he does not undergo transformation-birth.
Their place of birth is noble and preeminent because all who hear their teachings believe them.
Third, they do not undergo transformation-birth (upapāduka) because they teach people the practice of filial piety and support for parents.
What is the meaning of this?
For those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), there is neither father nor mother; how, then, can one know how to teach them to show respect and provide for their parents?

Regarding this, the initial statement—"the father performs the karma of the son, and the son performs the karma of the father"—is a general reference to worldly affairs: the father must necessarily perform the duty of nurturing his child, and the son must necessarily perform the duty of respecting his father.

The passage beginning with "If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, were to accept transformation" clarifies that [the Buddha] must necessarily conform [to the conditions], arguing by way of reductio ad absurdum; the textual structure is clear.

Because he provisionally protects the Dharma through kinship, he does not undergo birth by transformation (*upapāduka*). First, two numbers are raised; next, two names are listed; below, they are analyzed; and finally, the conclusion is reached.
In this analysis, the positive case comes first, and the negative case can be understood by contrast.
As for why those in the five [pure abodes] do not undergo transformation-birth (*upapāduka*) because they have already stilled pride:
what is the meaning of this?
The Buddha was born into a royal lineage to shatter the arrogance and pride that sentient beings rely upon.
Regarding the statement that he did not undergo miraculous birth because of the slander concerning the six types of conception and respiration—
what is the meaning of this?
Even when the Buddha was personally and fully perfected, the world still spoke of him as an illusion; how much more so when he was entirely absent?
Seventh, he did not undergo transformation-birth (upapāduka) because he left behind his remaining physical body to benefit the world.
What is the meaning of this?
As for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), their bodies must vanish upon transformation without leaving behind any physical remains; how, then, could they benefit the world?
Therefore, he is not born by transformation.
Eighth, he is not born by transformation because he is to be equal to all Buddhas.
What is the meaning of this?
The Dharma by which the Buddhas of the three periods transform beings in the womb is always birth from a womb; therefore, the Buddha conforms to this.
For what reason do all Buddhas undergo birth from a womb?
The meaning is as in the preceding seven [cases].
Furthermore, in order to increase the power of those born together, he undergoes birth from a womb.
This concludes the third section: the Lion’s Grateful Understanding and Praise.
The *Kāśyapa Bodhisattva Chapter* (9–10). Regarding the *Kāśyapa Chapter*, there are three modes of training and practice:
first, cultivation according to conditions, which refers to the preceding five practices and ten merits;
second, relinquishing marks to enter realization, which is the *Siṃha Chapter*.
The third is the fruit of the realization of truth, also called the arising of function, which is discussed in this chapter.
Since this meaning was proclaimed upon the request of Kāśyapa, the title of the chapter is designated by the name of the requester as the "Kāśyapa Chapter."
The thematic intent within this chapter is twofold:
first, to cite the conversion of icchantikas to manifest the Buddha’s virtuous conduct;
second, to cite the Buddha’s virtuous conduct to clarify the meaning of his ability to transform and benefit icchantikas.
Therefore, in the subsequent text, this sutra is praised as the "Staff for Icchantikas," by means of which icchantikas are enabled to attain awakening.
This section consists of two parts:
first, an explanation of how the Tathāgata’s wondrous activity and virtuous conduct can benefit icchantikas; second, at the end of the chapter, Kāśyapa’s realization and praise.

"The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of all beings; therefore, he is able to know all births. This passage answers the previous question regarding the "wondrous medicine of the two-footed," clarifying that the Buddha's speech is the leaves.
3. "Kāśyapa said:

'To sever the causes of the three periods of time is called severing the roots of goodness. The passage below this answers the previous question regarding his current desire to ask about the aggregates (*skandhas*) while admitting he lacks wisdom; it clarifies that such profound matters are solely the domain of the Buddha, thereby elucidating the Buddha’s mental activity (*manas-karman*).
Furthermore, in answering the first question, he clarifies that the Tathāgata is the refuge for all beings, in order to inspire faith in the Buddha within those of icchantika nature.

In answering the second question, he clarifies that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is a sublime medicine, in order to cause those of icchantika nature to abandon their slander and develop faith in the Buddha’s teachings.

Answering the third question, it clarifies that the Buddha’s wisdom is supreme and its objects of knowledge are uniquely peerless, intended to cause icchantikas to look up to and infer the meaning of the Buddha’s teachings, thereby establishing faith.
At the beginning, Kāśyapa first poses the inquiry to initiate the discourse.
The previous question has already been concluded; why trouble yourself to ask again?
Since the place to which you wish to go is far distant, it is necessary to ask once more; this is common in many cases regarding higher and lower [realms].
What difference is there between this question and the previous one?
Previously, Kāśyapa’s question was solely for the purpose of praise, extolling the Tathāgata as the refuge for all beings.
Now, at this point, he poses two questions:
first, one of praise; second, one of challenge.
From the beginning up to “acting as a great king of physicians” constitutes the praise-question;
from “Sunakṣatra is a son of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas” onwards constitutes the challenging question.
Kāśyapa, why did you not raise this objection earlier, but only do so now?

If you had raised the case of Sunakṣatra as an objection previously, your words would have been superficial and expansive, failing to establish the meaning of the verse; therefore, you did not object before.
Since the former was not difficult, this must now be performed.
Why, in this context, do you not expect a direct objection, but instead first offer praise?
To take away by first giving is the natural way of raising an objection; therefore, one first offers praise.
Within the section on praise, the initial statement, "The Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings," praises the Buddha’s possession of loving-kindness as his altruistic intention.
The passage beginning with "those who are undisciplined" praises his possession of skillful means as his wisdom for benefiting others.
Among these, there are seven phrases: the first four concern the capacity for transformation.

"To tame the untamed" refers to uprooting the beginning of evil; "to purify the impure" refers to uprooting the end of evil. "To provide a refuge for those without refuge" refers to rescuing from suffering at its beginning; "to liberate those not yet liberated" refers to rescuing from suffering at its end.
The latter three virtues of transformation are: the virtue of saving from suffering by "possessing the eight masteries";
and the virtue of uprooting evil by acting as a "great physician" and a "great king of medicines," knowing the illness like a doctor and curing it like medicine.
The Tathāgata first gave [it] to him, yet later rightfully confiscated it.
This was done to manifest the Tathāgata’s compassionate conduct and transformative teachings; therefore, he raised the case of the evil person Sunakṣatra as a challenge.
Within this passage, there are two intended points of the challenge:
First, the objection that the Buddha lacks compassion, which reverses the first [point] above;
second, the objection that he lacks skillful means, which reverses the second point above.
The text must contain three essential elements:
First, by citing the Buddha’s prediction that the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra would remain in hell for an eon as an icchantika, [the text] reveals that the Buddha lacks compassion;
second, from "incurable" onwards, by citing the Buddha’s declaration that Sunakṣatra cannot be cured, it clarifies that he lacks skillful means;
third, from "if he cannot save Sunakṣatra" onwards, both preceding points are concluded together.
There are seven distinct phrases:
"Sunakṣatra was the son of the Buddha when he was a Bodhisattva" is the first phrase, clarifying that their physical forms were similar.
He must have been a member of the Buddha’s own clan or a son born of a concubine; therefore, he is referred to as a "son."

"The second phrase, 'After leaving the household life, one recites and upholds the twelve divisions of the scriptures, destroys the fetters of the desire realm, and attains the four dhyānas,' reveals the intimacy of his practice."
"How can it be said that this icchantika will dwell in hell for an eon? is the third phrase; it rebukes the Buddha’s prediction that he has attained Buddhahood yet lacks compassion.

"An incurable person" is the fourth phrase; it rebukes the Tathāgata for failing to exercise his transformative guidance, stating that he is "incurable" because he cannot be brought to spiritual transformation.
"Why did you not first preach the Dharma for him? is the fifth phrase, reproaching the Buddha-Tathāgata for failing to provide effective instruction.
"If you cannot save [him], how can you be called one who possesses great compassion? is the sixth phrase, concluding that the Buddha lacks compassion.
"How can one be said to possess great skillful means? This is the seventh phrase, which concludes the section on the absence of skillful means.
Below, the Buddha provides specific answers; these should be carefully noted and understood.
Within the Buddha’s response, the answers do not exhaust all the questions and are presented out of order.
Among the first seven statements, he only answers the latter six; therefore, it is said that they are not exhaustive.
Within those responses, he first answers the fifth, then the fourth, then the second, then the sixth, then the third, and finally the seventh; hence, it is said that they are not in sequence.
First, the response to the fifth [objection]: "Why did you not first preach the Dharma to Sunakṣatra?
This section contains two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Tathāgata acts according to what is appropriate for conversion, and thus could not have preached the Dharma to Sunakṣatra first.
Second, from "Like a lion" onwards, it clarifies that although [the Buddha] does not speak first, his mind is without increase or decrease.

Within the preceding section, there are six rounds; in each, he first establishes a metaphor and poses a counter-question to Kāśyapa, next Kāśyapa provides an answer, and finally the Buddha uses this to reveal what he has taught.
The subsequent section provides the middle [explanation] preceded by a simile; the subsequent application [of the teaching] can be understood accordingly.
From the passage beginning "At one time I was staying in Rājagṛha" onwards, he answers the fourth point, clarifying the reason why it is impossible to cure Xuanneng (Sunakṣatra).
There are five further points:
first, it clarifies that Sunakṣatra was instead seized and held captive, and thus terrified the Tathāgata;
second, he effaced the Buddha’s footprints.
Third, seeing a Nirgrantha eating fermented rice-scum and claiming he is an Arhat, which contradicts the Buddha’s words.
Fourth, seeing one who attains [the state] through suffering and claiming he is an Arhat, and thus contradicting the Buddha’s words.
The five Buddhas preached the Dharma for him, yet he had no mind to believe or accept it.
The first two [types of misconduct] were evil deeds of body; the next two were evil deeds of speech; and the last was an evil deed of mind.
From the passage beginning "Although Shanxing recited and chanted" onwards, the text returns to answer the second point, clarifying that despite his meditation and recitation, he could not be saved.
First, his faults are exposed, followed by Kāśyapa’s personal journey to investigate and test him. Within the preceding section, there are four points:

first, it clarifies that although Sunakṣatra recited the scriptures, he did not understand their meaning in his heart; second, it clarifies that Sunakṣatra attained meditative concentration but subsequently lost it; third, it describes how he gave rise to evil and heterodox views, slandering [the Buddha] by claiming there is no Buddha; fourth, from the words "At that time, I... onwards, it shows that although the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he had no intention to believe or accept it.
This can be known through personal experience.
From the passage "Although Shanxing has entered the Buddha-dharma" onwards, the sixth question is answered by skipping ahead, clarifying that [the Buddha] already possesses compassion.
This section contains three parts:
First, it clarifies that compassion already exists;
second, from "If originally greedy" onwards, it demonstrates the depth of that existing compassion;
third, from "My disciples" onwards, it cites others who share this pity to reveal the reality of one's own compassion.
The first part further consists of three sections:
first, explaining how Shanxing has lost the wholesome dharmas, with the Dharma teaching followed by a simile;
second, from "Furthermore, it is like... onwards, explaining the destruction of the Dharmakāya, with the simile presented first and the application to the Dharma second.
In the analogy, "killing oneself" refers to one's own mind destroying goodness, while "being killed by a rākṣasa" refers to evil friends destroying goodness;
the application of these terms can be understood accordingly.
Third, it clarifies the Buddha’s compassion: "Next, out of pity, he spoke with much lamentation, constantly saying that Shanxing was excessively negligent."
In the second section, which clarifies the depth of one’s own compassion, the metaphor comes first, followed by the application to the teaching, and finally the conclusion, as can be understood.
In the third section, which reveals the reality of one’s own compassion, the principle is presented first, followed by the metaphor.
The passage beginning with "For many years I have constantly [tried to]... answers the third question, clarifying why it is said that Sunakṣatra is an icchantika who dwells in hell.

This section contains four parts: first, showing that he could not be converted despite many years of effort; second, explaining that because he could not be converted, he is described as an icchantika dwelling in hell for kalpas; third, clarifying the purpose for making this statement; and fourth, demonstrating that the statement is not false.
Regarding the beginning, "serving him for many years": because the Buddha had accepted him as his attendant for twenty years, it is said that he served for "many years.
Within the second section, there is first an exposition by way of Dharma (dharmadeśanā), followed by a simile, and finally the application (upanaya).

Within this teaching, the initial section clarifies that there is no mention of "good" because it is not taught; the subsequent section, beginning with "Because he proclaims," explains that there is no "good" therein, and the same applies to both the analogy and its application.
Regarding the third section, Kāśyapa first asks, "For what reason is it predicted?"
The Buddha’s answer can be understood.
Within the fourth section, the initial part clarifies that what the Tathāgata has taught is non-dual; the passage beginning with "śrāvaka" illustrates the superior by means of the inferior.
"Śunakṣatra constantly undergoes immeasurable births," and so forth, answers the seventh question, clarifying that there are skillful means (*upāya*).
This is explained through two points:
first, the distinction between transformation and benefit.
There are two kinds of benefit:

first, by taking in Sunakṣatra and allowing him to dwell with them for many years, they prevent him from remaining outside their community and teaching others to commit evil; this is called possessing skillful means.
Second, by taking in Sunakṣatra and causing him to leave the household life, they prevent him from remaining a layperson and generating many transgressions; this is called possessing skillful means.
Second, the differentiation of the transformative merit (*nirmāṇa-guṇa*). There are two aspects to this transformative merit:

first, clarifying that there are skillful means (*upāya*) from the perspective of the Buddha’s power of understanding; second, clarifying that there are skillful means from the perspective of the Buddha’s power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*).

Within the power of understanding (*jñānabala*), the first section clarifies that Sunakṣatra constantly preached to sentient beings that there is neither good nor evil. From the words "I have known for a long time" onwards, the Buddha fears that this man’s heterodox influence will cause much harm, so he gathers him in and allows him to dwell together with the community. From the words "If I were far away" onwards, it clarifies the intent behind allowing him to dwell together. The phrase "This is called the power of understanding" serves as the general conclusion.
Within the section on the Powers of the Faculties (*indriyabala*), there are three distinct parts:

first, knowing the severing of the roots of goodness; second, from "The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties" onwards, knowing the production of the roots of goodness; and third, from "The Buddha observes sentient beings possessing wholesome dharmas" onwards, knowing both the production and the severing [of the roots].
In the initial section on "Knowing and Severing," five questions and answers arise in succession.
Kāśyapa first asks for what reason icchantikas lack wholesome dharmas; the Buddha replies that it is because icchantikas have severed their wholesome roots.
"The icchantikas sever the roots of goodness" is the general answer;
"all sentient beings possess the five faculties, such as faith, yet the icchantikas have severed them forever" is the specific answer.
"By this principle," and so forth, the following section clarifies non-existence by means of the example of killing.
Second, Kāśyapa follows up by asking whether those with *icchantika* tendencies lack wholesome dharmas;
the Buddha answers that it is so.
The third Kāśyapa, seizing upon the words to challenge the Buddha, asked: "If among the virtues of the three periods of time the future is not severed, how can you say it does not exist?
His initial statement that "sentient beings possess three kinds of virtue" was a general and inclusive enumeration.
The passage lists three names: "past, future, and present.

It then raises an objection regarding the statement that *icchantikas* have severed [the roots of goodness], asking: "Since an *icchantika* cannot sever future goodness, how can it be said that they have severed them? This constitutes the formal objection.
The Buddha answers this below.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, it clarifies that there is cessation.
2. From "Just as a person" onwards, it clarifies that among those who have severed their roots of goodness, there is the sense of those who can be saved and those who cannot;
3. From "Just as rotten and decayed" onwards, it clarifies that regarding the roots of goodness that have been severed, there is the sense of those that can be regenerated and those that cannot.
At the beginning of this section, one should first clarify the meaning of the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and subsequently explain the text.
There are ten topical gates (*daśamukha*) for this meaning:
first, clarifying the characteristics of severance.
There are three paths of abandonment:
first, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), which views the existence of cause and effect as erroneous and views the non-existence of cause and effect as correct.
Second, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), which perceives existence as erroneous.
The three paths of liberation consist in seeing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Each of the unhindered liberations (*anāvaraṇa-vimukti*) has nine grades, ranging from the lowest-lowest (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) to the highest-highest (*adhimātra-adhimātra*), which correspond respectively to the nine grades of that equalized knowledge (*samatājñāna*) in severing the fetters.
The second [section] distinguishes the differences in abandonment with reference to two kinds of wholesome dharmas.

Regarding these two kinds of wholesome dharmas: first is the wholesome arising from application (*prayoga-kuśala*), which refers to those currently produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
second is the wholesome acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), which was formed in the past and has become manifest in the present.

Within the first three paths, the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) abandons the wholesome states acquired through effort (*prāyogika-kuśala*); the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) abandon the wholesome states acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*).
These three [paths] clarify the abandonment of the two types of wholesome states in terms of cause and fruit.
If one discusses their abandonment in terms of wholesome causes, the abandonment of causes pertaining to the three periods of time is called "cutting off the roots of goodness.
What is the meaning of this?

When a wrong mind manifests, one abandons past wholesome [roots]; this is termed "abandoning past causes" in the sense that what has arisen is now severed. Because the present [wholesome] does not arise, it is termed "abandoning present causes" in the sense that it will not be produced in the future. Because future goodness will not be produced and cannot be initiated thereafter, it is termed "abandoning future [causes]."
Therefore, the text below states: "To sever the causes of the three periods of time is called 'severing the roots of goodness'.

Among these, that which has arisen in the past can be severed as it manifests in the present; however, the principle of that which has arisen in the future can never be severed, and thus it subsequently comes into existence.

If one discusses its abandonment in terms of wholesome fruits, it abandons only the present and obstructs the future, but does not abandon the past; for that which has already arisen and passed away cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, it is said: "The present roots of goodness are extinguished, and the obstruction of those in the future is called 'severing the roots of goodness'.
Fourth, regarding the classification by realm of rebirth (*gati*):
this occurs only among human beings and does not extend to other realms, because only humans are capable of reflecting and seeking out the arising of heterodox views.
Fifth, regarding the distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties among human beings:
as stated in the following passage, "It must be one of sharp faculties who is capable of investigation, not one who is foolish and dull," the same applies to the schism of the Saṃgha.
Sixth, the classification according to time:

it is through the accumulation of practice over many lifetimes that one is able to sever the roots of goodness, rather than in a single lifetime; therefore, the preceding section describes this as an obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Seventh, the classification according to place.
This occurs only in Jambudvīpa and not in other regions, because the mental faculties of the beings in Jambudvīpa are sharp.
Regarding the eighth cause of ignorance:
due to hearing Mahāyāna sūtras that accord with emptiness, one clings to non-existence and slanders existence, thereby severing the roots of goodness.

Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "When such a person hears a sutra on emptiness that is difficult to understand, they fail to comprehend the teaching as it truly is; instead, they engage in improper reflection and declare that 'everything is non-existent.'"
Ninth, it clarifies the gravity [of this offense]:
among all evils, this transgression is the most serious, with none surpassing it, because it severs all roots of goodness.
Tenth, it clarifies the principle of the severance and subsequent regeneration of the roots of goodness.
When does it arise? As stated in the subsequent passage:
"At the time of entering hell and at the time of exiting hell—the former for those with light [karma] and the latter for those with heavy [karma]—one's roots of goodness are restored."
Question: Among the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—at which state of mind does it arise when emerging?
It certainly does not arise from a wholesome state of mind, because there was no prior wholesome state.
It mostly arises within a state of unwholesome doubt. Question:
Since the wholesome and the unwholesome are diametrically opposed, how can wholesome roots arise from within that unwholesome mind?
The commentary states:
The two minds of good and evil are diametrically opposed and cannot arise simultaneously.

Since the nature of the attainment of goodness is not of the same substance as form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), it does not obstruct the mind; therefore, it can arise alongside that which is unwholesome.
Just as when descending from a higher stage to a lower stage, one acquires wholesome roots of the lower stage at the edge of a defiled mind, this case is likewise.
Next, the text is explained:
"There are two kinds of abandonment" serves as a general heading; next, their names are listed; and the phrase "possessing these two" below cites them to conclude the section.
Regarding the second section on those who can be saved and those who cannot be saved: first, concerning those who perform virtuous deeds, they cannot be saved in the present;
later, concerning those with an inherently virtuous nature, they can be saved in the future.
Within the discussion of conduct, the analogy is presented first.
"The person submerged in a latrine" is a metaphor for the icchantika, who has severed their roots of goodness and is headed toward hell.
"A single hair emerging from the water" is a metaphor for the sense that past goodness gives rise to future meaning; thus, the icchantika has not severed [their roots].
The phrase "though a single [strand] has not yet perished, it cannot support the body" is a metaphor for how those roots of goodness do not prevent one from falling into hell.
Next, regarding the manifestation of the Dharma, the statement "an icchantika is like this" corresponds to a person falling into a latrine.
"Although there shall be roots of goodness in future lives"—this corresponds to having only a single hair remaining that has not yet sunk.
"Yet one cannot save oneself from the suffering of hell"—this corresponds to being unable to sustain the body.
The passage beginning with "Although they may be saved in future ages" serves as a summary to conclude the section.

Within the subsequent explanation of how salvation is possible based on the inherent goodness of nature, the statement "If the causes and conditions for Buddha-nature are present, then one can be saved" clarifies that salvation is certain. This is because nature is neither past, future, nor present, and thus there is no point at which it could be severed. This demonstrates that salvation is definitively possible.
Because their nature is uninterrupted and they are necessarily visible.
Regarding the third case—those that can arise and those that cannot—it clarifies that the severed roots of goodness do not arise.
The sequence of the metaphor followed by its application to the subject is clear and can be understood from the text.
The fourth Kāśyapa raised a further objection, saying:
"The Tathāgata has just stated that the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted; how then can it be called the severance of all wholesome roots?
The Buddha then answered him, clarifying that while the nature itself is not manifest, there is nevertheless such a thing as severance.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, a general explanation that sentient beings currently lack Buddha-nature, whereby they sever their roots of goodness and become icchantikas.
To argue by way of inversion, the principle is stated first, followed by the analogy.
"If one who has been born is currently existing, they are not called an icchantika"—this is the teaching in terms of phenomena (*dharmadeśanā*).
There are two meanings to its interpretation:
first, because the essence of nature (*prakṛti*) is eternally abiding and is not subsumed within the three periods of time, it does not exist as a present phenomenon; [the second meaning follows].
Because the second type of sentient being has not yet seen it, it is called "non-existent in the present.

To illustrate this with an analogy, the text says, "like the 'self' and 'dharmas' of sentient beings in the world. Within the delusions of the present, from the perspective of their emotional faculties, there is absolutely no Buddha-nature; thus, it is taken as an analogy, just as there is ultimately no self among sentient beings.

Second, from "The Buddha-nature is eternal" onwards, the initial meaning is clarified: it demonstrates that the essence of the nature is eternal and is not subsumed within the three periods of time; therefore, it is not something currently existing.
This is presented first in the affirmative and subsequently in the negative.
"Buddha-nature is eternal and is not subsumed within the three periods of time" is an affirmative clarification.
"If it were subsumed within the three periods of time, it would be called impermanent" is a negative clarification.
Third, the passage beginning with "The Buddha-nature will be seen in the future" clarifies the meaning for subsequent times.
It is called "to be seen" because it exists as a potentiality rather than being presently manifest; therefore, it is said to be non-existent in the present.
"Because the Buddha-nature will be seen in the future, it is said that sentient beings possess it. This precisely establishes its present non-existence by means of its future visibility.
The section beginning with "By this meaning" indicates the locus of that future visibility.
Because one should see that names possess meaning, it is only when the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are fully adorned that one can perceive them even slightly.
The fifth [section], Kāśyapa’s "Mounting" (*abhirūḍha*), presents a further objection.
This objection consists of two points:
The first objection concerns the Buddha-nature mentioned previously: "If its nature is like empty space, why does the Tathāgata say it is 'future'?

The second objection concerns the meaning of the icchantika’s lack of goodness: "If you say that because icchantikas have severed [their roots] they possess no goodness, yet these icchantikas also give rise to feelings of affection toward their fellow students; is this not goodness?"
The Buddha first offers a preliminary praise and subsequently provides the formal response.

First, he answers regarding the Buddha-nature; within this initial formal explanation, there are points that are difficult to understand, which are further clarified through a series of questions and answers.
Within the formal explanation itself, the passage beginning with "The nature is like empty space and is not of the past" sets forth the established thesis.
The section beginning with "All sentient beings have three bodies" explains the preceding difficulty; first, there is the direct explanation, followed by an analogical demonstration.
Within the direct explanation, the statement "All sentient beings have three kinds of bodies" is a general enumeration.
"Past, future, and present"—these three names are listed.
"Because the future body is pure and attains its nature, I speak of the future"—this correctly explains the question asked.
This clarifies that what is obtained is the body of the future, while its nature is not itself future.
Within the manifestation of its category, it first cites that which belongs to its class.
"I teach causes as effects and effects as causes" is stated briefly as a general heading.
"Therefore, it is said in the Sūtra that 'life is food' and 'the perception of forms is contact'; this briefly explains their characteristics.
To speak of the cause as the effect is like the common worldly expression of 'food is life.'"
The four great elements and name-and-form are not mentioned here in detail.
To speak of the effect as the cause is like the common people speaking of "life" as "food.
Seeing form is called contact; this shall now be discussed specifically.
Visible form (*rūpa*) consists of derived matter, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which act as the primary causes.
Although visible form is not actually tangibility, because the effect is designated by the name of its cause, one speaks of "touching" when seeing visible form.
The claim that seeing forms is called "contact" (sparśa) is entirely incorrect.

Because the future body is pure, it is called Buddha-nature; this is a way of manifesting the Dharma by means of analogy. The purity of the future body is like the aforementioned life-force and like food.
If one explains the Buddha-nature by means of the preceding categories, the cause of food is not life; yet because the cause is spoken of as the effect, it is termed "life.
What is thus revealed is that the causal nature is not the future body-effect; however, because the cause is spoken of as the effect, the Buddha-nature is designated as the future.

If one elucidates the Buddha-nature by means of the subsequent category of statements, life is not the cause of nutriment; yet, because the effect is spoken of as the cause, it is termed "nutriment. This applies likewise to form and touch; such is what is revealed.
The fruit of the future is not itself the Buddha-nature; however, because the fruit is spoken of as the cause, it is said that the purity of the future body constitutes its nature.
The preceding section should have been understood as the correct interpretation, yet for those who find it difficult to comprehend, it is further elucidated below.

Kāśyapa first asked: "If, as the Buddha has taught, the future body is pure and can be said to possess the nature [of Buddhahood], yet sentient beings do not currently possess a pure body, for what reason does the Tathāgata say that all living beings possess Buddha-nature?"
The Buddha’s answer is threefold:
first, he clarifies that although the Buddha-nature lacks manifest function, its essence is not non-existent; therefore, it can be said to exist.

"Although its nature is currently absent" means there is no manifest function; "it cannot be said to be non-existent" means its essence is not absent; "like space" serves as the metaphor to illustrate this.
"Emptiness has no manifestation" corresponds to the first phrase; "it cannot be said that it is non-existent" corresponds to the latter phrase.
Second, because the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and indestructible, it can be said to exist.

"Sentient beings are impermanent" distinguishes the difference between characteristics and nature; "yet their nature is eternally abiding" distinguishes the difference between nature and characteristics.
Thus, it is known that although Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, it can be said to exist.
Within this, first is the principle (*dharma*), next is the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and finally is the application (*upanaya*).
This answers the first question; what follows answers the subsequent question.
"What you say is not so" restates the question and provides a general negation; "for what reason" and below explain [the negation].
In the explanation, first is the principle (*dharma*), next is the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and finally is the application (*upanaya*).
Within the principle, first the act to be performed is presented:
"If an icchantika possesses any karma of body, speech, or mind," which is stated by way of its full possession.

“Karma of grasping (upādāna-karman) and karma of seeking (paryeṣaṇā-karman)” are raised by way of the afflictions: karma created by the mind of views is called karma of grasping, while karma created by the mind of craving is called karma of seeking.

“Karma of giving (dāna-karman) and karma of understanding (parijñā-karman)” are raised by way of their essential characteristics: even icchantikas have the relinquishing of wealth, which is called giving, and they also have the recitation and discernment [of teachings], which is called understanding.
"Thus all are false" concludes the clarification that there is no goodness.
The section "For what reason" below provides the explanation.
The analogy and its application may be understood accordingly.
The preceding section concerned the knowledge of abandonment.
From here on is the second [section], the knowledge of the arising of wholesome roots.
This contains three parts:
First, it is known that the faculties of sentient beings shift and are not fixed.

"The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing all faculties" serves as the general heading; "therefore he can distinguish superior, middling, and inferior faculties" briefly reveals the characteristics of his knowledge; "he can know their shifts" and so forth extensively reveal the characteristics of his knowledge; and the section beginning with "for this reason" provides the conclusion.
Second, knowing that the arising and severing of the faculties is indeterminate.

Because it is indeterminate, "sometimes they are severed and then arise again. This clarifies the indeterminacy in accordance with the principle. The phrase "if the faculties were determinate" below serves as a counter-illustration of this indeterminacy. The section beginning with "for this reason" concludes the argument.
Third is the response by way of explaining the underlying conduct.

Kāśyapa first asked: "The Buddha possesses the faculties and powers; he must have known with certainty that Sunakṣatra would sever his roots of goodness. For what reason did you permit him to go forth?"
The Buddha’s answer is threefold:
first, he permits ordination to prevent the manifestation of their current offenses, for if they remain in secular life as kings, they would surely destroy the Dharma.
Second, he permits ordination to generate future goodness, so that they may cultivate the wholesome roots of world-transcending liberation in the distant future.

The passage beginning with "If one does not leave the household life, one will also sever the roots of goodness" cites harm to highlight benefit; the passage beginning with "Now, by leaving the household life" demonstrates that benefit as distinct from harm.
Third, the section below "Therefore" provides a conclusion, first following the positive case and subsequently the negative.
From here below is the third section, the dual knowledge of arising and abandonment.
Within this, there are three parts;
the first is the knowledge of the abandonment of the roots of goodness.
“The Buddha observes that sentient beings possess both the wholesome and the unwholesome,” thus he knows what has been previously accomplished.
“Although this person possesses them, they will not long be able to sever them,” thus he knows what is to be severed in the future.
The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation: because one is unable to associate with spiritual friends, listen to the Dharma, reflect upon it, and practice according to the teachings.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides the conclusion.
Second is knowing the arising of goodness.
"The Tathāgata further knows that this person manifests... and so forth; this clarifies the knowledge of the Dharma-exposition.
Next, it is illustrated by means of a metaphor: "spring" symbolizes bodhi, and "village" symbolizes saṃsāra. Since bodhi is not separate from the transcendence of saṃsāra, it is said to be "not far."
The fruit of virtue, being pure and sublime, is termed "sweet"; the complete perfection of all practices is called "possessing the eight virtues.

Those who produce wholesome roots and loathe worldly existence are termed "hot"; their seeking of liberation is called "thirst"; and their generating the resolve to advance toward it is termed "desiring to go."
"The wise one" is a metaphor for the Buddha; because he knows for certain that [the person] will go, it is said to be "without doubt.
The section beginning with "Why? provides the explanation.
The application [of the analogy] below can be understood accordingly.
Third is the meaning of the extent of the arising and abandonment [of afflictions].

Within this, the Tathāgata first takes up soil from the ground and questions Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa subsequently answers, and the Buddha then uses this as a basis to reveal the meaning of the extent of the arising and abandonment.
There are four distinct points:

first, knowing that those who will proceed toward goodness in the future are few; second, knowing that those who will head toward evil in the future are many; third, from "protecting and upholding" downward, knowing that those who cultivate goodness in the present are few; and fourth, from "violating the precepts" downward, knowing that those who commit evil in the present are many.
From here below begins the second section, answering the two questions regarding the "wondrous medicine for those with two feet" mentioned above.
Within this, Kāśyapa first poses the introductory inquiry. One might ask:
since the previous question has already been answered, why is it necessary to ask again?
Because it is asked in reference to what is distant.
How does this question differ from the previous one?
The former was a direct praise of the question, praising the Dharma taught by the Buddha as a wondrous medicine.
Now, at this point, two sections are presented in full:

first, praise, and second, objection. From the beginning up to "He also knows the faculties of future beings" constitutes the question of praise; from "When such sentient beings [live] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" onwards constitutes the question of objection.
